en: Oṃ Oṃ Tat Sat. Salutation to Brahman.
Herein lies the *Siddhayoga*, composed by Vṛnda and also known by the name *Vṛndamādhava*, together with its commentary titled *Kusumāvalī* written by Śrīkaṇṭhadatta.
Having meditated upon Śiva, who is to be known through the investigation of the supreme reality; upon Caṇḍī, the bestower of desired fruits, along with Gaṇeśa and his attendants;
and having mentally prostrated before Dhanvantari, the eminent sage Ātreya, Suśruta and other sages, and those of fierce austerity—1.
Here, this *Siddhiyoga*, accompanied by introductory verses and containing various well-known methods whose efficacy has been observed,
is compiled in the sequence of the *Gadanigraha* by the dull-witted Vṛnda, who seeks his own welfare.
First one should examine the disease, and immediately thereafter the medicine.
Therefore, a physician should subsequently perform his actions preceded by knowledge.
But that physician who begins treatments without having understood the disease—
even if he is an expert in the application of medicines— achieves success only by chance.
But for one who knows the specific characteristics of diseases, is skilled in all medicinal remedies,
and understands the distinctions of place and time, success is certain.
At the beginning and at the end, the physician should strive for the knowledge of diseases.
Therefore, one who understands the distinction between curable and incurable [diseases] should administer medical treatment.
Since there is no disease that exists without the humors (doṣas), a wise physician should treat a disease even if it has not been specifically mentioned, by means of the symptoms of the humors.
One who is unskilled in the names of the bodily humors (vikāra) should not feel ashamed in any way,
for there is no permanent stability in the names of all these humors.
That very same humor, when provoked, becomes [a different disorder] due to the specific nature of its arousal.
Even when it has moved to another location, it produces many transformations.
The knowledge of disease is considered to be threefold: through sight, touch, and questioning.
Longevity and so forth are known by sight; coldness and so forth by touch; and the remainder by questioning.
Treatment is said to be of two kinds: difficult and easy.
It should be understood that there are two kinds of incurable cases: those that are palliable and those for which no remedy exists.
Some diseases are palliable by their very nature, while others become palliable through neglect even when they are curable.

By their very nature, some diseases are incurable, while others are manageable if neglected. Curable diseases may turn into manageable ones, and manageable ones likewise into incurable ones; however, incurable diseases destroy the life-force of men who fail to take action.
A disease must be treated as soon as it arises; it should not be neglected because of its smallness.
Even in its slightest form, it is like fire, an enemy, or poison—it causes great harm.
Furthermore, even when a disease has subsided, it may recur due to even a minor cause.
When the disorder has been diminished and brought onto the path [of treatment], the remnant is like a subtle fire.
Therefore, one should pursue it with an uninterrupted application until it returns to its natural state in terms of both the disorder and the vital breaths.
Thorough knowledge of the nature of the disease and the suppression of its symptoms—this constitutes the physician's true medical skill; the physician is not the master of one's lifespan.
Some diseases are born of past karma, while others arise from the bodily humors (doṣas).
Others arise from defects in past actions; among these, those born of karma are considered causeless [in the present life].
A disease that does not subside when properly diagnosed according to the scriptures and treated according to its nature is to be known by the wise as being born of karma.
That which is a minor fault yet grave should be known as arising from the defect of karma.
A fault born of karma caused by karma is pacified by its own specific medicines;
that which arises from the defect of karma goes to destruction through the destruction of the defect of karma.
Just as poison, a weapon, fire, or a thunderbolt [is harmful], so too is medicine when unknown; yet when known, it is like nectar.
By those specific actions through which the bodily constituents (dhātus) are produced in equilibrium, [health is maintained].
That is the treatment for disorders; that is considered the duty of physicians.
For indeed, such a condition arises with respect to place, time, and strength, in which what is to be done becomes not to be done, and an action that was to be performed must be avoided.

When there is obstruction of sweat, a burning sensation, and a seizing of all the limbs simultaneously in a disease, that is designated as fever (jvara). Residing in the stomach (āmāśaya), it destroys the digestive fire and obstructs the channels while accompanied by undigested matter (sāma).
The *doṣa* produces fever; therefore, one should practice fasting (*laṅghana*).
No verses from the *Siddhayoga* appear on this page.
The *Kusumāvalī* commentary has not been digitized.
When the dosha has been reduced by fasting and the digestive fire has been kindled,
freedom from fever, lightness of body, and hunger arise for him. This is especially true when fever occurs immediately after eating, particularly when it is associated with ama.
Vāgbhaṭa states that emesis is recommended for one who is fit for emesis.
(27) If one should, out of delusion, induce emesis when the humors have not been provoked, he may suffer from body aches and other ailments, as well as heart disease and irregular fever. (28)
Fasting for one whose digestive fire is unstable pacifies the humors,

destroys fever, stimulates the appetite, and produces a desire for food, relish, and lightness. A wise physician should administer fasting to one who has been made to vomit, but he should not induce vomiting in one who has already fasted.

One who is emaciated by fasting should be treated with emesis due to the abundance of morbid humors (doṣas). After considering the state of the humors and the vital breath (prāṇa), depleting therapy (apatarpaṇa) should be administered;
for that [therapy] is indicated for one afflicted by wind (māruta), hunger, thirst, dryness of the mouth, and vertigo.
This treatment should not be administered to a child, an elderly person, a pregnant woman, or one who is weak;
nor likewise to one suffering from fatigue from travel, anger, grief, desire, emaciation, or fever. One should treat such a patient with fasting that does not impair their strength.
Health is the empowerment of strength, for the sake of which this sequence of actions is undertaken:
when there is the discharge of flatus, urine, and feces; lightness of the limbs; purity of the heart, eructations, throat, and mouth; and when drowsiness and fatigue have passed. (33–34)

When perspiration has arisen, or when there is a relish for food, or when hunger and thirst manifest together, and the inner self is free from distress, the fasting (laṅghana) is declared to have been successfully performed.
[Otherwise, there may be] splitting of the joints, aching of the limbs, cough, and dryness of the mouth.
The destruction of hunger, loss of appetite, thirst, weakness of the ears and eyes,
constant agitation of the mind, upward movement of wind (ūrdhvavāta), darkness in the heart, and the loss of bodily heat and strength occur when fasting (laṅghana) is performed in excess. || 36-37 ||
Even without medicines, disease is cured simply by wholesome diet;
however, for one who lacks a wholesome diet, it is not cured even by hundreds of medicines.
(38) Red rice (*rakta-śāli*) and other grains, when old, are recommended along with *ṣaṣṭika* rice.
Barley gruel, boiled rice, and parched grain flour alleviate fever in those suffering from it.
Light, appetizing, and digestive, this thin gruel (peyā), prepared with appropriate digestive agents, is beneficial for those afflicted by fever at the time of eating. || 39-40 ||
To one afflicted by burning sensations and vomiting, who is emaciated, has abstained from food, and is overcome by thirst,

one should administer a satiating drink of parched grain (lāja-tarpaṇa) mixed with sugar and honey. For fever arising from exhaustion, fasting, or wind (vāyu), meat broth with rice is always beneficial.
Mudga-bean soup with rice should also be given when [fever] arises from kapha;
that same preparation, combined with sugar and served cold, is beneficial for pitta-type fever.
Mudga-bean and āmalaka soup, however, is beneficial for fever characterized by both vāta and pitta.
Soup made from short radish (hrasvamūlaka) is beneficial for a condition characterized by kapha and vāta.
Soup made from nimba and kūlaka is beneficial for a condition characterized by pitta and kapha.
For a condition characterized by vāta, pitta, and kapha, soup prepared with digestive (pācana) agents appropriate to each respective humor is indicated.

The physician should administer, in their proper sequence, foods prepared with the small *pañcamūla* together with long pepper (*pippalī*) and coriander (*dhānyaka*), and with the large *pañcamūla* together with *vyāghrī*, *duḥsparśā*, and *gokṣura*. || 46 ||
In cases of vāta-pitta, śleṣma-pitta, kapha-vāta, or disorders arising from all three doṣas (tridoṣaja), one should crush one añjali of the decoction ingredients and boil them in one āḍhaka of water;
then, with that liquid reduced by half, one should prepare gruel (yavāgū) and other such preparations. || 47-48 ||
Senior physicians prescribe one *pala* of the medicinal substance in one *āḍhaka* of water;
however, due to the excessive abundance of the medicine, there may sometimes be a lack of palatability.
Therefore, the *ṣaḍaṅga* and other preparations are administered when the water has been boiled and then cooled.
From that, one should prepare a quantity of one karṣa of the substance in one prastha of water; when half-boiled, it should be used for drinking or in the preparation of gruels and similar foods.
Alternatively, half a karṣa of long pepper (kaṇā) and ginger (śuṇṭhī), or one pala of the paste-substance, may be used.
Having strained it, one should cook it with logic using one *prastha* of water; by this same method, one should prepare other soups and meat broths.
In cases of fever caused by *kapha* and *vāta*, hot water should be given to the thirsty patient.
In cases arising from bile, alcohol, or poison, [one should give] water boiled with bitter herbs and then cooled.
To alleviate thirst and fever, one should give water that has been boiled and then cooled with mustā, parpaṭaka, uśīra, candana, udīcya, and nāgara.
A decoction that has been boiled with sixteen parts of water should be reduced to one-fourth;
therefore, preparations such as the "six-part" (ṣaḍaṅga) are not prohibited even in cases of acute fever (navajvara).
For loss of appetite, the filaments of the citron (mātuluṅga) mixed with ghee and rock salt [should be used].
Or one should hold in the mouth a paste of *dhātrī*, grapes, and sugar.
A person suffering from fever should eat what is beneficial even if he has no appetite; for by not eating at mealtime, he wastes away or even dies.
A person suffering from fever should by no means eat heavy, obstructive, or unwholesome food at any time;
for such unwholesome food leads neither to longevity nor to comfort.
One should feed the feverish patient, or one recently recovered from fever, light food at the end of the day.

Then, the digestive fire (analas) becomes powerful, with its heat increased by the depletion of phlegm (śleṣman). Because of its constant nature and its sweet quality, wholesome food (pathya) comes to be loathed; one should, however, restore its palatability through various methods of preparation.

One suffering from acute fever should avoid affusions, plasters, oleation therapies, and purification procedures; as well as sleeping during the day, sexual intercourse, physical exercise, cold water, anger, exposure to wind, and unwholesome food. (61)
By the use of affusions (pariṣeka) and similar treatments, one incurs these complications: emaciation, vomiting, intoxication, fainting, giddiness, thirst, and anorexia.
The wise say that fever is considered "acute" (taruṇa) for up to seven nights.
The middle stage lasts for fourteen days, and beyond that is the chronic (purāṇa) stage.
One should recognize the doshas as ripened when the fever is mild, the body is light, and the impurities are mobile; at that time, the medicine should be administered.
According to some, the characteristic of maturation [of the fever] depends on the specific nature and transformation of the humors (doṣas):
a fever caused by Vāta reaches maturation in seven nights, one caused by Pitta in ten nights, and one caused by Kapha in twelve days. (65–66)
For a matured humor (doṣa) that remains in the body without being eliminated may cause a severe complication, an irregular fever, or even the loss of strength.
Some authorities maintain that the medicine should be administered after seven nights have passed.
Some have determined that after ten nights, [the medicine] should be administered.
(68) No verses of the *Siddhayoga* appear on this page.
The commentary *Kusumāvalī* was not digitized.
They do not recommend astringent decoctions for men suffering from a fresh fever;
for when the humors are agitated by a decoction, they become exceedingly difficult to conquer.
However, this does not mean that the use of decoctions is prohibited as a general therapeutic principle.
Any decoction (kaṣāya) that is astringent (kaṣāya) should be avoided in acute fever (taruṇajvara).
Because of its astringency, the humors (doṣas) become bound; in acute fever, they are suppressed and do not undergo digestion, thereby causing irregular fever (viṣamajvara).
He who, out of delusion, administers a purgative to one suffering from undigested fever (āmajvara),
is like one who touches with the tip of his hand a black cobra that is fast asleep.
One who has drunk water, one who has undergone fasting, one who is emaciated, one with indigestion, one who has just eaten, and one who is thirsty [should not be given a purgative].

A person should not drink medicine for purification, whether it be of that specific kind or otherwise. However, when a disease is curable by purification, the physician, having observed that the patient is weak due to the morbid humors (doṣa), should perform a mild evacuation of those humors.
When the doshas have moved, the digestive fire (kostha) is mild, one need not consider the strength of men in this case;
for even in a weak person, purification (shodhana) will then result in no harm.
[This is done] with forty-two mashas and eighteen nibaddhakas.
A *pala* consists of twelve [units] bound together with six *guñjās*.
For the best quality [substance], the measure is one *pala*; for the middling, three *akṣas*; and for the lowest, half a *pala*, in the case of oils, decoctions, and medicinal herbs.
For one pala of medicinal substance to be boiled, water sixteen times the weight is prescribed;
when reduced to one-fourth, four palas of liquid are to be drunk.
Those with a blazing digestive fire and large bodies may drink a handful (añjali) of water.
However, other physicians, desiring to avoid discarding half [of the liquid],
discard instead one *prasṛti*; yet the elder physicians, following traditional instruction, maintain that two *palas* should remain when eight parts have been boiled down.

On the seventh day, one should administer a digestive (pācana) enema to the patient in its natural state, or otherwise treat him with a pacifying (śamana) enema once he is observed to be free of undigested matter (nirāma). [The ingredients are:
ginger (nāgara), devadāru, coriander (dhānyaka), and the two types of bṛhatī.

One should first administer a digestive (pācanaka) medicine, for it is a digestive agent in all fevers. Medicine that is potent becomes even more effective when not diminished by food; it then undoubtedly and swiftly destroys the disease.
However, children, the elderly, women, and those of delicate constitution, having drunk such [potent] medicine, suffer extreme exhaustion and a loss of strength.

The downward movement of wind, restoration of health, hunger, thirst, cheerfulness of mind, lightness of body, purity of the sense organs and eructations—these are the signs that the medicine has been digested.
Fatigue, burning sensation, weakness of the limbs, giddiness, fainting, and headache [are signs of improper digestion]. || 84 ||
There is a loss of appetite and a decline in strength; this is the characteristic of medicine that has been left over.

Indeed, when medicine is consumed while there is still food remaining, or when medicine remains while food is present, it does not bring about the alleviation of disease, but rather provokes other ailments. (85–86)
Medicine taken before a meal undergoes digestion quickly; its potency is not impaired when covered by food, nor does it repeatedly escape from the mouth.
This very same medicine should be administered to the elderly, children, the timid, and women.
Water boiled with the five roots beginning with Bilva (bilvādi-pañcamūla) is a digestive aid in fever caused by Vāta.
That which does not purify the humors, nor excites them when they are balanced,
but rather pacifies those that are provoked— that is called "pacification" (saṃśamana).
[This is achieved] with *kirātatiktaka*, *musta*, *amṛtā*, *udīcya*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, and *gokṣura*.
A decoction made with *sasthira*, *akalashī*, and *viśva* removes fever caused by Vāta.
(89) A medicinal extract prepared from *pippalī*, *sārivā*, *drākṣā*, *śatapuṣpā*, and *hareṇu*, taken with treacle, destroys fever born of Śvasana (Vāyu). (90)
This decoction of guḍūcī, sārivā, drākṣā, śatapuṣpā, and punarnavā, taken with jaggery (guḍa), is a destroyer of vāta-fever. [91] Drākṣā, guḍūcī, kāśmarya, trāyamāṇā, along with sārivā—
One should drink the decoction boiled with jaggery to alleviate vāta-fever.
For pitta-fever, a digestive (pācana) decoction made from *tikta*, *aragvadha*, and *indrayava* should be taken with honey.
[A cooling drink] made from *lodhra*, *utpala*, *amṛtā*, *padma*, and *sārivā*, mixed with sugar, [is also recommended].
A decoction [of these] would destroy fever caused by pitta, or likewise one derived from *parpaṭa*.

One afflicted by thirst, internal hemorrhaging, fever, and burning sensations should drink water saturated with sugar, prepared from *durālabhā*, *parpaṭaka*, *priyaṅgu*, *bhūnimba*, *vāsā*, and *kaṭurohiṇī*.

A decoction of *paṭola* and barley, sweetened with honey, subdues acute bilious fever upon drinking; it destroys thirst and burning sensations. *Parpaṭaka* alone is the best for eliminating bilious fever.
How much more so, however, if it is prepared with sandalwood, uśīra, and nāgara?
One should administer very cold water prepared with viśva, ambu, parpaṭa, uśīra, ghana, and sandalwood; it cures thirst, vomiting, fever, and burning sensations.
A decoction of parpaṭa, amṛta, and dhātrī conquers pitta-fever;
likewise, one may use a decoction of drākṣā and āragvadha, or of kāśmarya.
Alternatively, one should administer a decoction of drākṣā, abhayā, parpaṭaka, musta, and tiktā, along with the fruit of śamyāka. (99)
In a fever born of Pitta accompanied by delirium, fainting, vertigo, burning sensations,
emaciation, and thirst, rice-water that has stood overnight, drunk in the morning with sugar, instantly pacifies even a greatly increased internal burning sensation in men. (100–101)
One should apply a plaster made from the well-cooled, sour-ground leaves of the *palāśa* tree,
or with the foam produced from *badarī* sprouts and *ariṣṭaka*.
[Likewise, one may use] *vidārī*, pomegranate, *lodhra*, *dadhittha*, and *bījapūraka*.
With these [medicinal substances], one should plaster the head of the embodied being suffering from thirst and burning sensations.
Having placed a deep, copper-colored vessel made of bell-metal or similar material upon the navel of the person lying on their back,
a thick stream of very cold water falling there quickly destroys the burning heat.
Ponds with blooming lotuses, auspicious houses equipped with mechanical fans, and women whose limbs are anointed with sandalwood paste are considered removers of burning heat and dejection.
[One should dwell] in a palace resembling a white cloud, cool as the rays of the moon.

Or a man suffering from a fever caused by bile (pitta) should sleep after being sprinkled with water infused with *malaya* sandalwood. In cases of dryness of the tongue, palate, throat, and *kloma*, one should apply the filaments (*kesara*) of the *mātuluṅga* fruit mixed with honey and rock salt to the head.
A decoction of the pippalyādi group is digestive and is used for fever born of kapha;
likewise, one should drink a preparation of kuṣṭha, indrayava, mūrvā, and paṭola, combined with black pepper and honey, in cases of fever caused by phlegm. 108

Triphalā, paṭola, vāsā, chinnaruhā, tiktarohiṇī, and ṣaḍgranthā, taken with honey, [are used] when [the disease] arises from phlegm; or else, a decoction of daśamūla and vāsaka [is used]. (109) The proportions of honey, ghee, and so forth in decoctions and medicated fats are the same as those for powders. (110)

This group consisting of *āmalakī*, *abhayā*, *kṛṣṇā*, and *citraka* breaks up all fevers and afflictions caused by *kapha*, and acts as a digestive stimulant and a carminative. (111) *Kaṭphala*, *pauṣkara*, *śṛṅgī*, and *kṛṣṇā*, together with honey—
This excellent linctus removes dyspnea, cough, and fever, and brings an end to phlegm.
The combination of honey and long pepper (upakulyā) cures cough, dyspnea, and fever;
it destroys splenic enlargement and hiccup, and is highly recommended for children. (112–113)

One *karṣa* of powder, paste, or pills should always be licked with two handfuls (*śukti*) of liquid, or drunk with four handfuls of liquid. There is no fixed rule for the dosage, as it depends on the humors (*doṣa*), the digestive fire (*agni*), strength, and age.

Having examined the disease, the substance [of the patient], and the state of the digestive tract (koṣṭha), one should administer the proper dose. For those with combined doṣas, a combined digestive treatment (pācana) is beneficial, such as that prepared from triphalā, śālmalī, rāsnā, rājavṛkṣa, and āṭarūṣaka.
Boiled water quickly removes fever arising from Vāta and Pitta.
A decoction prepared with Viśvā, Amṛtā, Abda, Bhūnimba, and the two Pañcamūlis, swiftly destroys fever arising from Vāta and Pitta. (116–117)

Having decocted kirātatikta, amṛtā, drākṣā, āmalakī, and śaṭhī, one should drink that decoction with jaggery (guḍa) for a fever born of pitta and vāta. [One may also use] a combination of nidigdhikā, balā, rāsnā, trāyamāṇā, and amṛtā.
A decoction made from *masūravidala* beans conquers fever caused by *vāta* and *pitta*. 119.
*Guḍūcī*, *parpaṭa*, *musta*, *kirāta*, and *viśvabheṣaja*—this auspicious "Five-Blessed" (*pañcabhadra*) formulation should be administered in cases of fever caused by *vāta* and *pitta*. 120.
One should drink kirāta, nāgara, musta, and guḍūcī when kapha is predominant;
and with pāṭhā, uśīra, and mṛṇāla, one should drink it when pitta is predominant.
[One should also take] kaṇṭakārī, amṛtā, bhārṅgī, nāgara, and indrayava.
One should administer a decoction of bhūnimba, candana, musta, paṭola, and kaṭurohiṇī;
this removes fever caused by pitta and śleṣman, and cures burning sensations, thirst, fever, vomiting, cough, and pain in the heart and flanks. || 122–123 ||
Guḍūcī, nimba, dhānyaka, candana, and padmaka— this group,
beginning with guḍūcī, destroys all fevers,
stimulates the digestive fire, and cures nausea, anorexia, vomiting, thirst, and burning sensations.

The group of drugs consisting of paṭola, candana, mūrvā, pāṭhā, tiktā, and amṛtā removes fever caused by pitta and śleṣman, as well as vomiting, burning sensations, itching, and poison. (126) The juice of vāsā, including its leaves and flowers, combined with honey and sugar [is likewise effective].
It destroys fever born of phlegm and bile, as well as blood-bile and jaundice.
By drinking one *akṣa* measure of *kaṭukā* with sugar and warm water, a person may conquer fever arising from phlegm and bile. (127–128)
This decoction prepared from paṭola, picumanda, triphalā, madhuka, and balā should be used for fever arising from pitta and śleṣman;
it stimulates the digestive fire, breaks up kapha, and facilitates the downward movement of pitta and vāta.

A decoction of coriander and bitter melon is fever-destroying, digestive, and purgative. Indeed, *vālukāsveda* (sand-sudation), performed by heating a vessel over a fire, placing it on a cloth, sprinkling it with *kāñjika* (fermented gruel),
and applying it, pacifies diseases of wind and phlegm, as well as headaches, body aches, and other such ailments.
By softening the channels, drawing [the fever] into the digestive tract,

and destroying the stiffness caused by Vāta and Kapha, sudation dispels the fever. A filament from the fruit of the mātuluṅga, held in the mouth together with rock salt and black pepper, [achieves this].
It destroys diseases of wind (vāta) and phlegm (kapha), as well as dryness of the mouth, sudden numbness, and loss of appetite.

(133) The group consisting of long pepper (pippalī), long pepper root (pippalīmūla), chaba pepper (cavya), leadwort (citraka), and dry ginger (nāgara) is known as the digestive stimulant (dīpanīya); it removes diseases caused by phlegm and wind. (134)

A decoction prepared with *āragvadha*, *granthika*, *musta*, *tiktā*, and *harītakī* is beneficial in fever associated with *āma*, colic, and *kapha-vāta*; it is both digestive-stimulant (*dīpana*) and carminative (*pācana*).
Water boiled with *pippalī* is non-obstructive (*anabhiṣyandi*) and digestive-stimulant.
[This decoction] destroys disorders of vāta and śleṣman, cures splenic enlargement, and alleviates fever.
Mustā, parpaṭa, duspārśa, guḍūcī, and viśvabheṣaja remove kapha, vāta, anorexia, vomiting, burning sensations, emaciation, and fever.

A decoction prepared with *kṣudrāmṛtā*, *nāgara*, and *puṣkarāhvaya* is recommended even for a fever born of the three doṣas, provided it is characterized by a predominance of *kapha* and *vāta*, and is accompanied by dyspnea, cough, loss of appetite, and pain in the flanks.
The juice of the ten roots (*daśamūlī*) mixed with *kaṇā* (long pepper) should be drunk in cases of *kapha-vāta*.
In cases of lack of digestion (avipāka), excessive sleep, pain in the sides, dyspnea, and cough,
one should first suppress the phlegm (śleṣman) even when the disease is caused by all three doṣas;
for once the phlegm has been removed and his channels have been opened, [the other doṣas can be treated].
Lightness arises immediately, and drowsiness is indeed pacified.
Just as a wise man would quickly seize a vessel sinking in deep water before it reaches the bottom, so too should one [seize] that which is afflicted by *abhinyāsa*.
One should recognize that a patient who has lost sleep, suffers from mental exhaustion, and has diminished vitality is one whose *ojas* has been destroyed.

In cases arising from the three *doṣas*, fasting, sand-sweating (*vālukāsveda*), nasal medication (*nasya*), gargling (*niṣṭhīvana*), electuaries (*avaleha*), and collyrium (*añjana*) should be employed first.
In cases of *saṃnipāta* (combined humors), one should perform fasting for three nights, five nights, or even ten nights, until health is observed.
That very capacity to endure is the power of the *doṣas* themselves regarding fasting.
However, when the doshas have been exhausted, no one can tolerate fasting and similar therapies.
While the liquid elements, kapha and pitta, can tolerate severe fasting,
once the āma is depleted, even vāyu cannot tolerate it for even a moment.
One should hold rock salt (*saindhava*) and the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*) mixed with the fresh juice of ginger in the mouth up to the throat, and spit it out again and again.
By this, the phlegm located in the heart, the neck, the sides, the head, and the throat [is expelled].
Even if it is stuck, it is drawn out when dry, and lightness arises in it.
Joint-pain, fever, fainting, sleepiness, cough, throat ailments, heaviness of the mouth and eyes, numbness, and nausea subside. (148–149)
One should administer it once, twice, three times, or four times, having observed the relative strength and weakness of the doshas;

for this is said to be the supreme remedy for those afflicted by the combination of all three doshas (saṃnipāta). [One should take] the juice of mātuluṅga and fresh ginger, slightly warmed and mixed with the three salts.
Or one should administer another sharp nasal medication (nasya) prescribed for success;
by that, the phlegm is broken up, and once broken up, it is discharged, while pain in the head, heart, throat, mouth, and sides is pacified. || 151–152 ||

Equal parts of *madhūka* pith, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), *vaca*, black pepper (*uṣaṇa*), and long pepper (*kaṇā*) should be finely ground with water and used as a nasal drop (*nasya*) to restore consciousness.
[Likewise, one may use] *śirīṣa* seeds, cow’s urine, long pepper, black pepper, and rock salt.
An ointment for awakening [the senses] should be prepared with *sarala*, *srotoñjana*, and *manaḥśilā*.
One should also lick a fine powder made of *kaṭphala*, *pauṣkara*, *śṛṅgī*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *yāsa*, and *kāravī*, mixed with honey. (154–155)

This electuary destroys even the most dreadful *saṃnipāta* fever, and it subdues hiccups, dyspnea, cough, and constriction of the throat; this powder should be administered with the juices of fresh ginger when there is an excess of *kapha*. (156)
In all combined conditions (saṃnipāta), one should not administer honey;
for honey is a cooling treatment, and cold is contraindicated here.
When treatments are of a similar nature, a blending of treatments (kriyāsāṃkarya) is desired.
However, because they are of different natures, they do not cause that defect.
It is recommended to first take a mouthful of food that is easy to swallow; parched grain flour mixed with *kapātha* and sprinkled with rock salt (*saindhava*) would be wholesome. (158–159)

Because they are beneficial for bleeding disorders (raktapitta) and alleviate burning fever (dāhajvara), parched grain flour (saktu) is cold in potency; however, that which is prepared with parched rice (lāja) is not beneficial. The scum of parched rice (lājamaṇḍa) is digestive (pācana), appetizing (dīpana), and is therefore desired to be warm.
Therefore, this [mixture] prepared with the ten roots (daśamūla) and other ingredients is approved by physicians;
if it is digested without obstruction, the patient suffering from fever will certainly survive.
[This may be taken] with a soup made from five handfuls of grains or one prepared from Trikaṇṭaka.
One should prepare wholesome food until the disorders are pacified using *trikaṇṭaka* alone.
Having taken one handful each of barley, jujube, horse-gram, mung bean, radish, and ginger, one should boil them in eight times the amount of water.

This group known as *pañcamuṣṭika* is praised for overcoming wind, bile, and phlegm, and is recommended for abdominal tumors (*gulma*), colic (*śūla*), dyspnea (*śvāsa*), cough (*kāsa*), wasting (*kṣaya*), and fever (*jvara*).
The *pañcamūlī* and *kirātādi* groups should be employed in cases arising from all three *doṣas*.
In cases where pitta is predominant, it should be taken with honey; in cases where kapha is predominant, with kaṇā.
Bilva, syonāka, gambhārī, pāṭalī, and gaṇakārikā constitute this "great five roots" (mahat-pañcamūla), which is digestive and destroys kapha and vāta. || 166–167 ||
Śāliparṇī, pṛthakparṇī, the two types of bṛhatī, and gokṣura constitute the minor pañcamūla; it alleviates vāta and pitta, acts as an aphrodisiac, and is the lesser [of the two] pañcamūlas.
Both together form the daśamūla, which removes fever caused by the combination of all three doṣas (saṃnipāta).
Combined with powdered long pepper (pippalī), it is recommended for cough, dyspnea, drowsiness, and pain in the flanks; it destroys afflictions of the throat and heart.
In chronic fever, whether dominated by vāta and kapha or arising from all three doṣas, it should be mixed with daśamūla.
The kirātatiktādi group of drugs should be employed for one seeking purification, or mixed with trivṛt.
Daśamūlī, śaṭhī, śṛṅgī, pauṣkara, durālabhā, bhārgī, kuṭaja seeds, paṭola, and kaṭurohiṇī [are also used]. || 170–171 ||

This eighteen-ingredient [decoction] removes fevers caused by the combination of all three humors (saṃnipāta), and it cures cough, cardiac oppression, pain in the flanks, dyspnea, hiccups, and vomiting. [It consists of:
Bhūnimba, Dāru, Daśamūla, Mahauṣadha, and Abda...

A decoction of *tikta*, *indrabīja*, *dhanika*, *ibhakaṇā*, and *kaṣāya* quickly destroys all fevers accompanied by drowsiness, delirium, coughing, loss of appetite, burning sensations, fainting, dyspnea, and other such symptoms. (173)
Grapes, amṛtā, śaṭhī, śṛṅgī, mustaka, and red sandalwood;
ginger, kaṭuka, pāṭhā, bhūnimba along with durālabhā;
uśīra, padmaka, coriander, vālaka, and kaṇṭakārikā. || 174–175 ||
This auspicious eighteen-ingredient formulation consists of *puṣkara*, *picumanda*, and so forth;
it destroys chronic fever, anorexia, dyspnea, cough, and edema.
[The ingredients are: *kaṭphala*, *pauṣkara*, *śṛṅgī*, *mustaka*, *kaṭuka*, and *śaṭhī*.
One should have these made into smooth powders, either in equal parts or individually.
One should lick [this preparation] with the fresh juice of ginger and honey; it destroys kapha and removes colic, wind-disorders, anorexia, vomiting, cough, dyspnea, and consumption.
Mustā, parpaṭaka, uśīra, devadāru, mahauṣadha, triphalā, dhanvayāsa, nīlī, kampillaka, trivṛt,
kirātatiktaka, pāṭhā, balā, and kaṭukarohiṇī. (179)

Madhuka, pippalīmūla, and the group beginning with mustā are said to constitute the eighteen-ingredient formulation (aṣṭādaśāṅga). This is declared by the wise to be beneficial for the alleviation of sannipāta, particularly when pitta is predominant.
In cases of stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha), oppression of the chest (uroghāta), and pain in the chest, sides, and head (uraḥ-pārśva-śiro-graha),
one should use the two types of *bṛhatī*, *pauṣkara*, *bhārgī*, *śaṭhī*, *śṛṅgī*, *durālabhā*, the seeds of *vatsaka*, *paṭola*, and *kaṭurohiṇī*.
The group beginning with *bṛhatī* is declared to remove *saṃnipāta* fevers; it is beneficial for all types of coughs and other ailments, as well as for their complications.
[The drugs are: *śaṭhī*, *puṣkaramūla*, *vyāghrī*, *śṛṅgī*, and *durālabhā*.
Guḍūcī, nāgara, pāṭhā, kirāta, and kaṭurohiṇī—
this group beginning with śaṭī removes fever caused by the derangement of all three humors (saṃnipāta) and is recommended for cough, cardiac oppression, pain in the flanks, dyspnea, and drowsiness.
They say that when perspiration breaks out, the application of roasted horse-gram (kulattha) powder is recommended.

Furthermore, for a person afflicted by cold, death may occur because of the excessive sliminess of that sweat; as it flows all over the body from the forehead, the sweat of a man suffering from cold becomes like a mass of ice and is exceedingly slippery.
That mortal whose [medicine] does not pass from the throat into the chest surely goes to the house of Yama.
A decoction prepared from trivṛt, viśālā, kaṭukā, triphalā, and āragvadha, mixed with alkali, should be drunk; it is a purgative that destroys all fevers.

Due to the increase of pitta, kapha, and vāta, the fever born of the three doṣas destroys or releases the person after ten days, twelve days, or seven days, through the digestion of the bodily tissues and wastes (dhātumalapāka).

Those which are the seventh, the double [fourteenth], the ninth, and likewise the eleventh [days]— (Note: This verse fragment refers to specific days of fever duration associated with the destruction or release of the patient.)
This is the boundary of the three humors, leading both to liberation and to death.
How can that man who feeds a person—trembling and lamenting during a derangement of the humors—with meat, deserve the title of a physician? 190–191.
If one should feed or even cause to drink ghee to someone who is trembling and lamenting during a *saṃnipāta* [fever], how could those two possibly become auspicious?
Likewise, if one should sprinkle cold water upon one suffering from the burning heat of *saṃnipāta* fevers...
How could that patient live, or how could that physician exist?
Who has not performed merit by rescuing a human being submerged in the ocean of *saṃnipāta*? What kind of worship does he not deserve? 193–194.

One who treats a *saṃnipāta* fever must fight with death itself; whoever emerges victorious therein is the victor over the confluence of diseases. [This applies even] in the case of the great and terrible swelling of the ear that brings an end to *saṃnipāta*. (195–196)

One should first conquer that [condition] with bloodletting and the drinking of ghee, followed by external applications (pradeha) that subdue kapha and pitta, as well as emetics and gargles (kavalagraha).
[The drugs used include] the roots of bījapūraka and likewise agnimantha. 197.
Devadāru with ginger, along with rāsnā and citraka, ground together—
this is an excellent external application for destroying swelling of the throat.
Likewise, kulaṭṭha, kaṭphala, śuṇṭhī, and kāravī in equal parts [are used similarly].
A lukewarm medicinal paste should be applied repeatedly at the base of the ear.
One should conquer fevers arising from malevolent spells or curses through fire-offerings (homa) and other rites;
those born of portents or planetary afflictions should be overcome by acts of charity, auspicious ceremonies, and hospitality toward guests.
The wise physician should overcome poison arising from herbs and poison arising from scent with decoctions that subdue poisonous bile and are prepared with all types of fragrant substances.
[201] For poison born of anger, the desirable objects are those that conquer bile, as well as virtuous speech. [202]
The fevers of desire, grief, and fear are pacified by consolation, by the attainment of what is desired, by the calming of the bodily humors (vāyu), and by exhilarating means; likewise,
[they are pacified] by the binding, exorcising, and worshiping prescribed in the science of spirits (bhūtavidyā).
One should conquer mental affliction arising from the possession by spirits through the pacification of the mind.
One should drink a decoction of *nidigdhikā*, *nāgaraka*, and *amṛtā* mixed with *pippalī* in cases of chronic fever, anorexia, cough, colic, dyspnea, weak digestion, facial paralysis, and catarrh.

This [Gudapippali] generally destroys diseases arising in the upper part of the body; it is administered in the evening and cures cough, indigestion, anorexia, dyspnea, heart disease, anemia, and worm infestations.
It is highly recommended for chronic fever and weak digestion. 206.
A decoction made from *guḍūcī* combined with powdered *pippalī*,
or one prepared with the five roots (*pañcamūlī*), destroys chronic fever and phlegm;
it removes heaviness and pain in the head and awakens the sensory faculties.
In chronic fever, one should administer head-purgatives that stimulate the appetite.
For a fever— whether continuous or intermittent— that has arisen long ago in a weakened patient, one should treat it with wholesome, fever-alleviating foods.

For the sake of vegetables, the wise man should appropriately provide *taṇḍulīyaka*, *vāstūka*, young radish, *parpaṭa*, *paṭola*, the leaves of *amṛtā*, and the leaves of *dārvī*. For the sake of meat, he should provide the meat of the *eṇa* deer, the *lāva* bird, and others. || 210–211 ||
For one emaciated by fever, emesis or purgation is not beneficial;
however, one may remove the impurities at will by means of milk or decoction enemas (nirūha).
[This applies] in cases of anorexia, lassitude of the limbs, discoloration, and the presence of bodily filth.

Even a person whose fever has subsided should be purified [with emetics or purgatives] out of fear of residual complications (anubandha). In chronic fever (jīrṇajvara), when the phlegm (kapha) has been depleted, milk is like nectar; yet that very same milk, if drunk during the acute stage (taruṇa), kills a man like poison.
One suffering from fever is freed from cough, dyspnea, headache, pain in the flanks, and catarrh by drinking milk boiled with the five roots (pañcamūlī). [Likewise,
one is cured by] that which is prepared with trikaṇṭaka, vacā, vyāghrī, jaggery, and ginger.

Milk cures the obstruction of feces and urine and removes wasting diseases and fever. When preparing milk-decoctions, the rule is that the liquid should consist of eight parts of water for every one part of the medicinal substance, and it should be boiled until only the milk remains.
Milk boiled with the five roots (pañcamūlī) along with four parts of water, or milk boiled with chips of *śiṃśapā* wood, or even warm fresh milk, removes fever.
[This applies] to those who are emaciated, those freed from fever, and those who indulge in improper diet and lifestyle.

Even a very small defect, once increased and driven by the wind (vāyu), indeed produces in embodied beings fevers known as *sātata*, *anyedyuṣka*, *tṛtīyaka*, and *caturthaka*, along with *pralepaka*,
according to the respective locations of phlegm (*kapha*). || 219–220 ||
Moving from station to station day and night, the *doṣa* then reaches the stomach (*āmāśaya*) and produces fever in men.
This occurs in a person whose wind (*vāta*) and phlegm (*kapha*) are equal, while their bile (*pitta*) is deficient.
Generally, his fever occurs at night, as he has diminished kapha during the day.
Pralepaka fever, however, is non-remittent and generally causes suffering for those who are emaciated.
[The decoction consists of] Kaliṅgaka, the leaf of Paṭola, and Kaṭurohiṇī.
Paṭola, sārivā, musta, pāṭhā, kaṭukarohiṇī,
nimba, paṭola, triphalā, mṛdvīkā, musta, vatsaka, kirātatikta, amṛtā, candana, and viśvabheṣaja. || 224 ||
These five decoctions— guḍūcī, āmalaka, and musta— concluded in half-verses, quickly pacify the five types of fever.
These five decoctions for [fevers] such as *saṃtata* were taught by Caraka and others.
Excluding *pralepaka* and likewise *vātabalāsaka*.
(226) Prose—Decoctions (*kaṣāyas*) are prepared either in their regular order or by transposition.
(227) Cumin seeds combined with jaggery destroy irregular fevers (*viṣamajvara*).
One should properly conquer sluggish digestion and destroy diseases of Vāta; or one afflicted by irregular fever (viṣamajvara) should drink Triphalā mixed with plenty of jaggery,
or a decoction of Guḍūcī, Nimba, and Dhātrī combined with honey.
A decoction of mustā, āmalaka, guḍūcī, viśvauṣadha, and kaṇṭakārikā, drunk with powdered kaṇā and honey, destroys irregular fever (viṣamajvara).
Alternatively, one should consume garlic with ghee every morning.
Or one may drink *pippalīvardhamāna* while subsisting on milk and meat broth. After resting for one day, the *tṛtīyaka* (tertian) fever returns;
after resting for two days, the *caturthaka* (quartan) fever returns. || 231–232 ||

One should avoid common karma; therefore, the third and fourth [types of fever] must be treated with specific medicinal remedies, such as mahauṣadha, amṛtā, musta, candana, uśīra, and dhānyaka. || 233 ||
A decoction combined with sugar and honey destroys tertian fever (234).
A root of *apāmārga* tied around the waist with seven red threads on a Sunday quickly destroys tertian fever (235).
If a childless ascetic has died on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā, one should offer him water with sesame seeds; thus he releases the fever that lasts for a single day.
[This remedy] is prepared with vāsā, dhātrī, sthirā, dāru, pathyā, nāgara, and sā (salt).
A decoction combined with sugar and honey wards off quartan fever (cāturthika).
An errhine (nasya) made from the fresh juice of Agasti leaves destroys even the most violent form of quartan fever,
as does [the application of] the morbid humor (doṣa) situated in the seats of phlegm (kapha), whether in two, three, or four locations.
It produces contrary results and brings about uneven, difficult-to-accomplish outcomes.
(238) He who, afflicted by irregular fever, daily consumes a paste of garlic mixed with sesame oil, is soon liberated from that fever as well as from most terrible wind-related diseases. (239)
Having ground together red aśvamāra flowers, dhātrī, dhānya, and vacā, a lukewarm paste should be applied during fever; it removes pain in the head. [Also:
palankaṣā, nimba leaves, vacā, kuṣṭha, and harītakī.
Mustard seeds, barley, and clarified butter used as incense destroy fever.
Or, for one who is trembling, cat dung should be employed as incense.
[One should worship] the Lord Soma, together with his attendants, the divine assembly of Mothers, and the Sovereign.
By worshipping with self-restraint, one is swiftly liberated from irregular fever (viṣamajvara).
By praising the omnipresent Viṣṇu— the thousand-headed Lord of the moving and unmoving— with the Thousand Names, one dispels all fevers.
The root of bhūmijayantī, or likewise that produced from sahadevā, or the root of taṇḍulīyaka, when bound upon the head, removes fever.
In cases of intermittent fevers (viṣamajvara), purification by means of emetics and purgatives should be performed both upwards and downwards.
Alternatively, *trivṛt* mixed with honey brings peace even to chronic fever.
Or, *abhayā* licked with honey quickly destroys intermittent fever.
However, he who suffers from fever while contemplating the intensity of the fever and the time [of its onset] is indeed afflicted by it.
One should destroy his memory by means of desired objects or even wonderful ones.
Ghee should be administered after twelve nights in a fever where the phlegm has been diminished. [The following are used:
long pepper, sandalwood, nut-grass, ushira, and katurohini.
Kaliṅgaka, tāmalakī, sārivā, ativiṣā, and sthirā;
|| 249 || drākṣā, āmalaka, bilva, trāyamāṇā, and nidigdhikā—clarified butter prepared with these quickly dispels chronic fever. || 250 ||

It subdues consumption, cough, headache, pain in the flanks, loss of appetite, burning in the shoulders, and irregular digestion. Four times the amount of paste is the oil (or fat), and four times the amount of oil is the decoction.
Water four times the quantity of the substance to be boiled is used; the decoction is considered to be equal in volume to the substance itself.
Ghee prepared with the juices of the ten roots (daśamūlī), along with alkalis, the five spices (pañcakolaka), and milk, when duly processed, cures fever, cough, and weak digestion.

Ghee prepared with one *prastha* of milk and one *pala* each of the five spices (*pañcakola*) and rock salt (*saindhava*) cures diseases of wind, bile, and phlegm, as well as splenic enlargement, jaundice,
and abdominal tumors (*gulma*). (253–254)
Viśālā, triphalā, kauntī, devadāru, elabāluka, sthirā, nata, the two types of haridrā, the two types of sārivā,
priyaṅgu, nīlotpala, elā, mañjiṣṭhā, dantī, dāḍima, and kesara. || 255–256 ||
Viḍaṅga, pṛśniparṇī, kuṣṭha, candana, padmaka,
tālīsapatra, bṛhatī, and fresh mālatī flowers— using these twenty-eight ingredients as a paste, each weighing one akṣa. || 257 ||
Having added four times as much water, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee.
It is used for epilepsy, fever, cough, consumption, weak digestion, wasting, vātarakta, catarrh, and tertian or quartan fevers. (258–259)

In cases of vomiting, hemorrhoids, dysuria, complications of erysipelas, itching, anemia, insanity, urinary disorders, and poisoning; and for those whose minds are afflicted by spirits, those with stammering speech, and those lacking semen—[this [remedy] is indicated]. (260)

This ghee is recommended for women, especially those who are barren; it bestows longevity, complexion, and strength. It destroys misfortune, sin, and demons, wards off all malevolent planets, and is auspicious and excellent for use in rites for procreation.

Oil prepared with *suvarcikā*, *nāgara*, *kuṣṭha*, *mūrvā*, *lākṣā*, *niśā*, *lohita*, and *yaṣṭikā*, boiled with six times the amount of buttermilk (*takra*), removes coldness and burning sensations when used as an ointment during fever.
In this case, the buttermilk should be desired as sour and containing whey (*sāra*).
One should prepare ghee, oil, jaggery, and so forth on the very same day; for if they are prepared after having been kept overnight, they produce particularly superior qualities.
When the medicinal paste, rolled with the finger, takes on the form of a wick, [the preparation is complete].
If no sound is heard when [the substance] has been cast into the fire, then one should indicate success.
When the sound has ceased, and likewise when the froth has subsided,
and when there is excellence of fragrance, color, taste, and so forth, one should declare success.
A skilled physician should recognize that when ghee has been cooked in this manner, there is an excessive amount of froth; he should prescribe the remainder as being like oil. 267.
O Mukunda, Govinda, Hare, Murāri, Vaikuṇṭha, Śauri, have compassion for me!
O Physician, beginning with Brahmā, you who are skilled in providing protection for the three worlds, forgive this fault.
Sandalwood and other beneficial oils prescribed for consumption disorders, as well as Nārāyaṇa oil, are supreme removers of chronic fever.

One should cook one *prastha* of oil with one *āḍhaka* of fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*) and the following ingredients: *mūrvā*, lac, the two types of turmeric, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *indravāruṇī*, *bṛhatī*, rock salt, *kuṣṭha*, *rāsnā*, *māṃsī*, and *śatāvarī*. (270)
Oil known as *Aṅgāraka* liberates one from all fevers.
Clarified butter (*ghṛta*) that has been cooked for more than a year becomes weak in potency;
however, one should know that the opposite is true for oil, whether it has been cooked or remains uncooked.

The body becomes light, free from exhaustion, delusion, and feverish heat; there is a burning sensation in the mouth, excellence of the sense organs, absence of pain, perspiration, sneezing, a natural desire for food, and itching on the head—these are the signs of the departure of fever.
One should avoid physical exercise, sexual intercourse, bathing, and walking about.
One who has been freed from fever should not indulge [in usual activities] until he has regained his strength.
(274) Adhikāra 2:
Determination of Fever and Diarrhea according to their distinct etiological factors.
In this case, the physician should follow the prescribed procedure in its proper sequence;
for the medicines that have been taught separately for fever and diarrhea should not be administered together, since they would aggravate one another.
Therefore, one should treat those two with specific prescribed medicines;

lightening therapy (laṅghana) is said to be indicated for both, especially when they are combined, followed by the entire range of preparations such as parched rice gruel (lājāmaṇḍa) prepared with the *utpala-ṣaṣṭhaka* decoction.
A person suffering from fever and diarrhea should drink a gruel (peyā) prepared with *pṛśniparṇī*, *balā*, *bilva*, ginger, blue lotus (*utpala*), and coriander, along with sour agents;
or one prepared with ginger, *ativiṣā*, *mustā*, *bhūnimba*, *amṛtā*, and *vatsaka*.
This decoction removes all fevers and destroys all types of diarrhea.
Pāṭhā, indrayava, bhūnimba, mustā, parpaṭaka, amṛtā,
and mahauṣadha, when combined, conquer both diarrhea and fever that has not yet been digested.

One should drink *hrīvera*, *ativiṣā*, *mustā*, *bilva*, *nāgara*, and *dhānyaka*; this destroys the obstruction of slimy mucus (*picchā*), cures colic and undigested morbid matter (*doṣa-āmāpācana*),
and overcomes diarrhea accompanied by blood, whether with fever or without fever.

A cold decoction made from *guḍūcī*, *ativiṣā*, coriander, ginger, *bilva*, *musta*, vetiver, *pāṭhā*, *bhūnimba*, *kuṭaja*, sandalwood, *uśīra*, and *padmaka* should be drunk for the pacification of fever and diarrhea.
It destroys nausea, anorexia, vomiting, thirst, and burning sensations. Kaliṅga, ativiṣā, śuṇṭhī, kirātatiktaka, and yavāsaka unerringly destroy fever, diarrhea, and high fever.
Vatsaka fruit, dāru, rohiṇī, gajapippalī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, pippalī, dhānyaka, bilva, pāṭhā, and yavānikā—
both of these proven formulations (siddhayoga) have been described by half a verse each.
These two [decoctions] pacify fever and diarrhea, and especially destroy burning sensations.
Water boiled with the five roots (pañcamūlī), balā, bilva, guḍūcī, musta, nāgara, pāṭhā, bhūnimba, hrīvera, and one pala each of kuṭaja bark [is used].
It destroys all types of diarrhea, as well as fever, disorders, vomiting, and asthma accompanied by the complication of pain; it also overcomes cough that is very difficult to cure.
Regarding the *pañcamūlī*, the general one should be used for pitta, while the smaller one (*kanīyasī*) should be employed.
The great five roots (mahatī pañcamūlī) are beneficial when vāta and śleṣman predominate.
One should drink blue lotus (utpala), pomegranate bark, and lotus filaments with rice-water to destroy fever and diarrhea.

Uśīra, bālaka, musta, dhānyaka, and bilva, along with samaṅgā, dhātakī, rodhra, and viśva, are digestive stimulants and appetizers; they destroy anorexia, slimy stools, constipation, and excessive pain. (18)
One should drink one akṣa of viśva with a decoction of daśamūla in cases of bloody diarrhea, whether accompanied by fever or free from it,
as well as in fever, diarrhea, edema, and disorders of the grahaṇī. (19–20)
Viḍaṅga, ativiṣā, musta, devadāru, pāṭhā, kaliṅgaka,
combined with marica, destroys swelling and diarrhea.
[21] With guḍūcī, citraka, bilva, abda, raktacandana, and vālaka—
Combined with *kaliṅga* alone, it cures fever, diarrhea, and swelling (22).
[A compound] of *kirāta*, *abda*, *amṛtā*, *nimba*, *candana*, *udīcya*, and *vatsaka* pacifies consumption and diarrhea, and especially destroys fever (23).
White *añjana*, *kaṇā*, *lāja*, *madhuka*, and blue water-lily (*nīlotpala*),
when licked with honey, destroy fever caused by *pitta* and diarrhea.
(24) Chapter 3.
Except for fasting (laṅghana), there is no other medicine here that pacifies and even digests the aggravated accumulation of the humors (doṣas) in a strong person.
Water boiled with coriander and uśīra should be given to one suffering from thirst, burning sensations, and diarrhea.
To one who is excessively thirsty, water boiled with *hrīvera* and *śṛṅgavera*, or with *mustā* and *parpaṭaka*, or water boiled with *mustā* and *udīcya*,
should be given; or water boiled with *nāgara*, *ativiṣā*, and *mustā*, or with *dhānya* and *nāgara*.
It cures thirst, colic, and diarrhea; it is highly appetizing and a supreme digestive stimulant.
One should consume food prepared with either hrivera and śṛṅgavera, or with musta and parpaṭaka, or with these two along with pāṭhā.
A diet of barley-meal (lāja-saktu) along with lentil soup prepared with *śāliparṇī* and other herbs, together with rock salt (*saindhava*), is wholesome.
A bolus (*piṇḍī*) that is heavy and excessively coarse is unwholesome, whereas the same bolus becomes light by the opposite qualities.

A linctus made of roasted barley flour (saktu) is digested quickly because of its softness. A *hastamaṇḍikā* is prepared with those same preparations using parched grain (*lāja*) and gruel-soup (*maṇḍa*). Alternatively, it may consist of gruel strained through a cloth or thin, diluted rice-mash.
Suniṣaṇṇaka, vārtāka, and kañcaṭa are said to be beneficial.
Śāliparṇī, pṛśniparṇī, bṛhatī, kaṇṭakārikā, balā, aśvadaṃṣṭrā, bilva fruits, pāṭhā, nāgara, and dhānyaka [are likewise beneficial].
This is beneficial for all those suffering from diarrhea when combined with food.
Gruels prepared with vegetables, meat, or fruits, as well as sour ones, are difficult to digest.
[However, a gruel] prepared with śāliparṇī, balā, bilva, and pṛthakparṇī [is beneficial].
A gruel (peyā) soured with pomegranate is beneficial for those suffering from diarrhea caused by pitta and kapha.

Alternatively, food prepared with the five grains (dhānyapañcaka), or even with coriander and ginger (dhānya-viśva), should be administered by the physician to those suffering from diarrhea caused by vāta and kapha.

The minor pentad of roots (laghu-pañcamūla) is recommended for disorders of wind and bile; however, since there is no treatment that bypasses the sequence of treating the undigested (āma) and the digested (pakva), all cases of diarrhea should be understood by their signs of being either undigested or digested. (13)
Undigested feces sink due to their heaviness, whereas digested feces float in water, provided there is no excessive liquidity, massing, coldness, or vitiation of phlegm (śleṣman).
Feces that are foul-smelling, accompanied by flatulence (āṭopa), distension (viṣṭambha), pain, and salivation— [are signs of disease]. 14.14–15ab.
Conversely, that which is free from āma and ripened by kapha sinks [in water].
One should never administer astringent (saṃgrahaṇa) therapy in the case of diarrhea characterized by āma; for if it is checked prematurely, it produces many complications.

[It cures] swelling, anemia, splenic disorders, skin diseases, abdominal tumors, abdominal enlargements, fever, as well as colic, intestinal torpor, flatulence, malabsorption syndrome, and hemorrhoids; likewise,
for one whose tissues and strength are diminished, it [remedies] excessive morbidity and excessive depletion.
Even undigested matter (āma) should be suppressed; otherwise, through its ripening, it may lead to death.
One who suffers from diarrhea that is scanty, frequent, obstructed, or accompanied by colic should be purged with lukewarm pastes of Abhayā and Pippalī.
In cases of undigested food (āmadoṣa), the wise physician should administer either the *haridrādi* group or the *vacādi* group;
he should also add the *pippalyādi* group to soups of goat meat (*khaḍayūṣa*) and gruels (*yavāgū*). Furthermore, [one may use] coriander, dry ginger, musta, vālaka, and bilva.
It destroys colic and constipation caused by undigested matter (āma), acts as a digestive, and stimulates the digestive fire.

Indeed, they say that in cases of Pitta-type disorders, the "four grains" (dhānyacatuṣka) are used with the exclusion of ginger (śuṇṭhī). When there is frequent diarrhea due to the chronicity of the disorder or the weakness of the digestive tract (grahaṇī)...
When it occurs, then the "attracting" (sāṃgrāhika) treatment should be performed quickly.
One should drink lodhra, dhātakī, bilva, mustā, the stone of the mango, and kaliṅgaka with buffalo buttermilk; this destroys matured diarrhea (pakvātīsāra). 23–24ab.

The five roots (*pañcamūlī*), *balā*, *viśva* (ginger), *dhānyaka* (coriander), blue lotus (*utpala*), and *bilva* should be given with buttermilk (*takra*) or any one of the other [fermented liquids] to one suffering from diarrhea caused by Vāta.
[One should also give] *kañcaṭa*, rose-apple (*jambū*), pomegranate (*dāḍima*), water-chestnut (*śṛṅgāṭaka*), leaves, *bilva*, and *hrīvera*.
One might even stop the swift-flowing Gaṅgā together with its clouds and serpents.
One should drink Kirātatiktaka, Musta, Vatsaka, and Sārasāñjana with honey; this destroys bilious diarrhea and relieves pain.
One who subsists on a liquid diet and drinks water boiled with one *pala* of *vatsaka* seeds will quickly conquer bile-born abdominal disease (*paitta-jaṭharāmaya*).
[The following is the formula: *kuṭaja*, *ativiṣā*, *musta*, *haridrā*, and the two types of *parṇinī*.
[This preparation] with honey and sugar is recommended for those suffering from diarrhea caused by pitta and kapha.
Having boiled the bark and fruit of *kuṭaja*, *musta*, and water, one should drink it combined with sugar and honey; this quickly conquers diarrhea.
A decoction of the seeds of *bilva* and *cūta*, taken with honey and sugar,
destroys vomiting and diarrhea just as fire consumes an oblation. One should administer a powder of *priyaṅgu*, *añjana*, and *mustā* according to the patient's strength.
[This] with honey and rice-water destroys thirst, diarrhea, and vomiting.
A very cold decoction of *paṭola*, barley, and *dhānyaka*, mixed with sugar and honey, should be drunk; it is a destroyer of vomiting and diarrhea.
A preparation consisting of *pṛśniparṇī*, *balā*, *bilva*, ginger, blue lotus, coriander, *viḍaṅga*, *ativiṣā*, *musta*, *dāruharidrā*, *pāṭhā*, *kaliṅgaka*, and black pepper,
when combined together, destroys swelling and diarrhea.
In cases of diarrhea caused by phlegm (śleṣmātisāra), fasting and digestive treatments (laṅghana-pācana) should be performed first;
then, the previously mentioned group of appetizers (dīpana-gaṇa) that cures diarrhea with undigested mucus (āmātisāra) should be employed.
[This group consists of: the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), ativiṣā, asafoetida (hiṅgu), vacha, sauvarcala salt, and abhayā.
Having drunk it with warm water, one should abandon severe diarrhea caused by undigested matter (āmātīsāra).
The fresh juice extracted from the leaves of *vijjala*, drunk with honey,
or a decoction of *kuṭaja* bark, conquers diarrhea caused by undigested matter.
A beautiful decoction made from the bark of *kuṭaja*, thickened and mixed with *ativiṣā*,
when taken as a linctus, destroys all types of diarrhea.
In a linctus where no specific proportion for the liquid or the paste has been specified, [the standard rule applies].
Generally, a wise person should prepare a paste (kalka) consisting of one-fourth part [of the drug] from the liquid;
however, in this case, they desire the powder of ativiṣā to be one-eighth part of the decoction. Similarly, the fresh juice of kārpāsa and parkaṭī is considered to be mixed with honey.
A decoction of the barks of *dāḍima* and *vatsaka*, drunk with honey,
immediately conquers even difficult-to-cure diarrhea caused by blood (*raktātīsāra*). One should eat *bilva* with jaggery (*guḍa*) to destroy bloody diarrhea.
It destroys colic caused by undigested food (āma), constipation, and cures diseases of the abdomen.
The barks of śallakī, badarī, jambu, priyāla, āmra, and arjuna,
when drunk separately with milk and enriched with honey, prevent the discharge of blood.
By drinking a paste of *śatāvarī* with milk and then consuming only milk,
or by drinking ghee prepared with it, a person shall conquer bloody diarrhea (*raktātisāra*). A decoction made from *vatsaka*, *ativiṣā*, *bilva*, *udīcya*, and *musta* [is also effective].
In cases of diarrhea characterized by mucus, pain, and blood, even when it has persisted for a long time, this [treatment] is beneficial;
likewise, in cases arising from fear or grief, the treatment provides relief for both.
In the case of that caused by all three [humors], a *puṭapāka* procedure is considered appropriate due to the presence of many colors.
One should treat diarrhea that is painless, well-cooked, accompanied by a blazing digestive fire, long-standing, and characterized by various colors with *puṭapāka* (herbal poultices).
Having taken the ungnawed bark of *kuṭaja*, which is unctuous and thick, and having crushed it thoroughly at that very moment—
Rice grains soaked in water within a pouch made of *jambū* and *palāśa* leaves, tied with *kuśa* grass and smeared on the outside with thick mud, should be well-steamed.
Having pressed this to extract the juice, one should administer it mixed with honey to a patient suffering from diarrhea.
This formulation, honored by Kṛṣṇātreya and his followers, is the king among all remedies for curing diarrhea.
One pala of the juice from the *puṭapāka* preparation should be drunk because of its medicinal properties.
A ball of bark from the *dīrghavṛnta* tree, wrapped in *kāśmarī* leaves, well-prepared and coated with clay, should be roasted over charcoal embers.
Having extracted the steamed plant and squeezed it to diligently obtain the juice, one should cool it, mix it with honey, and administer it for abdominal disease.
This is the method of cooking by *puṭapāka*; its completion is indicated by a reddish color on the exterior.
Because it serves as a medicine, a measure of one pala is accepted for it, just as with fresh juices and the like.
One should boil one hundred palas of crushed *kuṭaja* root in one *āḍhaka* of water;
when this decoction is reduced to one-fourth, it should be strained and then boiled again into a linctus (*leha*).
Having added two palas of the powder of sauvarcala, yavakṣāra, viḍa, saindhava, pippalī, dhātakī, indrayava, and ajājī,
one should lick a quantity the size of a jujube fruit, cooled and saturated with honey.
It conquers diarrhea with both cooked and uncooked stools, various colors, and pain; it overcomes the difficult-to-cure disease of the *grahaṇī* as well as dysentery (*pravāhikā*).
(54) Then, having crushed one *tulā* of fresh *girimallikā* and boiled it, one should take the decoction.
In that well-purified [liquid], having ground one pala each of the following into a fine paste—
pāṭhā, samaṅgā, ativiṣā, musta, bilva, and the flowers of dhātakī—
and having added them, one should boil it again until the decoction reaches the consistency of a *darvīpralepa* (a coating that adheres to the back of a ladle).
This yellow [turmeric], when taken with water, parched rice gruel (maṇḍa), or even goat's milk by one who knows the proper time,
destroys all severe diarrhea— whether black, white, red, or yellow—
as well as various disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī), blood, bile, and hemorrhoids.
This *kuṭajāṣṭaka* (the eight-fold preparation of *kuṭaja*) certainly destroys even that form of menorrhagia which is otherwise incurable.
(58) One *tulā* of medicinal substance [is measured] against one *droṇa* of water; one *tulā* of substance is considered to be [the standard] for one *droṇa* of water.
One *pala* of *kuṭaja* should be taken and boiled in water reduced to one-eighth. (59)
In the same manner, one should cook ghee combined with pomegranate juice until it has the appearance of lymph (lasikā); once boiled,
one should prepare it so that a patient suffering from bloody diarrhea drinks half a karṣa of it with buttermilk.

Even one who is destined to die does not fall within the reach of death [if this is taken]; here, the juice of the pomegranate is considered equal to a decoction of *kuṭaja*. Furthermore, the seeds of *vatsaka* and the excellent bark of *dārvī* [are likewise used].
Ghee prepared with these six ingredients— pippalī, śṛṅgavera, lākṣā, and kaṭukarohiṇī— and consumed with peyā or maṇḍa,
quickly conquers even severe diarrhea caused by all three doṣas.
Just as nectar is, so is milk esteemed in cases of diarrhea; it should be drunk when the condition is long-standing, boiled with three parts of water.
When blood and feces have been discharged and the stool is devoid of mucus due to the wind (vāyu), [milk is indicated].
That which is known as *pravāhikā* is characterized by the discharge of matter resembling foam.
When the *vāta* is obstructed, accompanied by pain and *pravāhikā*, one should lick a paste of young *bilva* fruit, jaggery, oil, long pepper (*pippalī*), and ginger (*viśvabheṣaja*).
A paste of *pippalī* or that derived from *marica*, when drunk with milk,
destroys chronic diarrhea (*nirvāhikā*) that has arisen over a long period, even after three days.
[Likewise,] a paste of *bilva*, jaggery, *rodhra*, and oil combined with *marica* [is effective].
Having licked [this], one destroys dysentery and quickly attains comfort.
One afflicted by diarrhea should eat with whey mixed with curd and honey,
or else with well-heated boiled copper water, or even with cold milk profusely mixed with honey.
In cases of burning or suppuration of the anus, physicians recommend sprinkling with the decoction of *paṭola* and *madhuka*, or alternatively, with goat’s milk (60).
Or one may apply fomentation using the flesh of mice, as well as anointing with cow’s fat (61).
For the evacuation of the rectum, the excellent *cāṅgerī-ghṛta* (ghee prepared with sorrel) is recommended;
furthermore, one should treat swelling and other complications with their respective specific therapies.
[It cures] swelling, colic, fever, thirst, dyspnea, cough, and loss of appetite.
One should abandon a patient suffering from diarrhea upon observing vomiting, fainting, and hiccup.
A patient with diarrhea should avoid bathing, oil massage, immersion baths, heavy and unctuous foods, physical exercise, and exposure to fire.
Chapter 4:
One should treat the disorder localized in the *grahaṇī* as one would indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), and one should digest its undigested matter (*āma*) according to the procedure prescribed for diarrhea.
A gruel prepared with wood-apple (kapittha), bilva, cāṅgerī, sour gruel (takra),
and pomegranate (dāḍima) digests undigested matter (āma) and also transforms it into feces.
[This is further enhanced] by the small five-roots (laghu-pañcamūla), the five-spices (pañcakola), and pāṭhā.
The wise man should prepare foods with bilva, sour fruits, and pomegranates.

For those suffering from disorders of the *grahaṇī*, buttermilk is beneficial because it stimulates digestion, is constipating due to its lightness, is wholesome owing to its sweet post-digestive effect, and does not provoke *pitta*.
Because it is astringent, hot, and drying, it is beneficial for kapha;
because it is sweet, sour, and thick, it is immediately effective and non-burning for vāta.
One should drink equal parts of śuṇṭhī, mustā, viṣā, and guḍūcī boiled with water.
In cases of weak digestion, chronic indigestion, persistent indigestion,
and disorders of the *grahaṇī*, one should administer coriander, ativiṣā, uśīra, yavānī, musta, ginger, balā, dviparṇī, and bilva as a digestive stimulant and carminative.
One should grind together citraka, the root of pippalī, the two types of alkali (kṣāra), the salts, vyoṣa, hiṅgu, ajamodā, and cavya;
these may then be made into pills with the juice of mātuluṅga or pomegranate.

The paste of the tender fruit of the *śrīphala* (bilva), mixed with the powder of *nāgara* (ginger) and combined with jaggery, digests undigested matter (*āma*), quickly kindles the digestive fire, and when consumed by one who eats only buttermilk,
conquers even the most violent disease of the *grahaṇī*. (9–10)
Jackfruit, pomegranate, water chestnut, *pāṭhā*, and the tender leaves of *kañcaṭa*,
cooked with immature *bilva* fruit, jaggery, and ginger, and then allowed to stand overnight, cures all types of diarrhea and even the most difficult-to-overcome chronic dysentery (*grahaṇī*).
A decoction of *nāgara*, *ativiṣā*, and *mustā* serves as a digestive for undigested matter (*āma*).
Alternatively, one may use the powder known as *hiṅgv-aṣṭaka*, or, in cases involving *vāta*, the *aṣṭapala-ghṛta*.
[The ingredients are: *nāgara*, *ativiṣā*, *mustā*, *dhātakī*, and *rasāñjana*.
One should drink an equal portion of the powder of vatsaka-bark, madana-fruit, bilva, pāṭhā, and kaṭurohiṇī, mixed with honey and rice-water,
in cases of pitta-type grahaṇī disorder and when blood is passed in the stool. || 13–14 ||
This powder, beginning with ginger (nāgara), honored by Kṛṣṇātreya, conquers hemorrhoids, pain in the rectum, and dysentery.
One pala of husked rice should be given along with eight times its amount of water.
Having prepared this, it should then be administered during the ritual of rice-water (taṇḍulodaka).
One should powder equal parts of bhūnimba, kaṭukā, vyoṣa, mustaka, and indrayava, along with two parts each of citraka and vatsaka-bark, totaling sixteen parts. || 16–17 ||

When drunk with cooled jaggery-water, it cures disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī-doṣa) and abdominal tumors (gulma), and overcomes jaundice, fever, anemia, urinary disorders, loss of appetite, and diarrhea.
[This applies] when the digestive tract is vitiated by phlegm (kapha) in one who has been properly vomited according to the prescribed method.
One should increase the digestive fire with pungent, sour, salty, alkaline, and bitter substances. In cases of *grahaṇī* caused by all [three] doshas, however, a general treatment is prescribed.
One should cook ghee with a paste of *bilva* in a decoction of *masūra*.
It destroys all diseases of the abdomen, as well as *grahaṇī*, anemia (*pāṇḍu*), and jaundice (*kāmalā*).
They know that a decoction of rice and animal parts that has been left overnight increases the *doṣas*.
One should cook ghee with a *tula* of *masūra* decoction and *bilva* as the internal ingredient.
In cases of intestinal perforation (bhinnaviṭka), they praise excellent masūra-ghṛta.

Having cooked eight palas of ghee with one pala of jaggery and a paste of the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa) and the three myrobalans (triphalā) in the quantity of a bilva fruit, a person with weak digestion should drink it in appropriate doses.

Ghee prepared with a decoction and paste of bilva, agni, cavya, ārdra, and śṛṅgavera, along with goat’s milk, is a superior remedy for disorders arising from the *grahaṇī* and the rectum, as it removes swelling, weak digestion, and loss of appetite.
(24) [The paste consists of] moca, sindhu, utpala, vyōṣa, lajjā, bilva, ambu, and dhātakī. (25)
Clarified butter prepared with goat’s milk and the juice of *cāṅgerī* (sorrel), when administered to a child who eats both wholesome and unwholesome food, quickly destroys *grahaṇī* and diarrhea.
According to another reading, *kapittha* (wood-apple) is also added here to the clarified butter.

Clarified butter cooked with the expressed juice of *cāṅgerī* and a paste of these— namely, *nāgara*, *pippalīmūla*, *citraka*, *hastipippalī*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *pippalī*, *dhānya*, *bilva*, *pāṭhā*, and *yavānikā*— [is beneficial].

This ghee, prepared with four times as much curd, alleviates phlegm and wind; it removes hemorrhoids, disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī), dysuria, dysentery, pain from prolapse of the rectum, and flatulence. (29)
Marica, the root of pippalī, nāgara, and likewise pippalī;
bhallātaka, yavānī, viḍaṅga, hastipippalī, hiṅgu, sauvarcala, as well as biḍa, saindhava, and cavya. || 30–31 ||
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with half-*pala* portions each of sea salt, alkali from barley (*yavakṣāra*), *citraka*, and *vacā*,
along with the decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūlī*) and twice as much milk.

Ghee is the best for those with weak digestion; it destroys disorders of the *grahaṇī*. It removes constipation, weakness from undigested matter (*āma*), and splenic enlargement, as well as cough, dyspnea, consumption, hemorrhoids, and fistula-in-ano.
It destroys diseases born of phlegm (kapha), those born of wind (vāta), and those arising from worms;
it quickly annihilates all of them, just as fire consumes dry wood.
It is prepared by boiling [the drug] with the essence of Viśvauṣadha in water decocted with Daśamūla.
Ghee cures swelling, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), and disorders of undigested matter (āmātisāra).
Ghee prepared with a paste of ginger promotes the downward movement of flatus and wind,
destroys malabsorption syndrome and anemia, and removes splenic enlargement, cough, and fever.
Having added three *prasthas* of pure *āmalakī* juice and half a *tulā* of jaggery, [one should prepare this with] one *pala* each of the powdered *granthika*, *jīra*, *cavya*, *vyoṣa*, *ibha-kṛṣṇā*,
*hapuṣā*, *ajamoda*, *viḍaṅga*, *sindhu*, *triphalā*, *yavānī*, *pāṭhā*, *agni*, and *dhānya*.

Having added eight *pala*s of *trivṛt* powder and eight *pala*s of oil, one should cook it according to the prescribed method. One should consume it in the measure of an *akṣa*-fruit, combined with the three aromatics (*trisugandhi*), acting as one pleases.
By this, all disorders of the *grahaṇī*, along with asthma, cough, hoarseness of voice, and swelling, [are cured].
This well-known jaggery known as *Kalyāṇaka* pacifies hemorrhaging, increases the internal fire, promotes virility, and quickly destroys sterility and diseases in women.
(41) Having slightly fried one *pala* each of *trivṛt* and the three aromatics (*trisugandhi*) in oil, [one should add...]

When it is established, the remedy should be applied right here with jaggery (guḍa) preceded by auspicious rites. That disorder of the digestive tract (grahaṇī-vikāra) which is incurable by signs—the disease of dysentery (atisāra)—would not be cured; indeed, in an elderly person, the disorder of the digestive tract, having destroyed the body, does not desist.
Chapter 5:
Three disorders which are generally the causes of one another—
hemorrhoids, diarrhea, and the disorder of the digestive tract (grahaṇī-doṣa).
When their digestive fire (*agni*) is diminished, there is decline; when it is increased, there is growth. Strength in men is rooted in the digestive fire, for life itself is rooted in strength.
Therefore, one should always protect the digestive fire, especially among these three [stages].

The means for the treatment of diseases known as *durnāman* (cutaneous leprosy) are proclaimed to be fourfold; among them, the first is said to be that which is curable by medicine, alkaline therapy, surgery, and fire.
Furthermore, [these methods are employed] for the sake of restoring the downward movement of *vāyu* and for increasing the strength of *agni* (the digestive fire).

All food, drink, and medicine should be constantly consumed by those suffering from hemorrhoids (arśas). One should treat hemorrhoids characterized by loose stools caused by Vāta according to the methods for Vāta-type diarrhea.
And those with hard stools should be treated repeatedly according to the protocol for Udāvarta.
For those with excessive discharge, [medicines] that destroy bile and blood are beneficial;
in cases of constipation, buttermilk combined with *yavānī* and *biḍa* salt is wholesome.
Struck by buttermilk, hemorrhoids do not grow again.
When the channels have been purified by buttermilk, the nutrient essence (rasa) enters them properly;
through that, nourishment, strength, complexion, and great vitality arise,
and a hundred disorders of wind and phlegm are eliminated.
One should consume Abhayā (chebulic myrobalan) mixed with jaggery and Pippalī, or fried in ghee and combined with Trivṛt and Dantī, which promotes the downward movement of the bowels;
or one may consume a mixture of sesame seeds and Aruṣkara, which increases the digestive fire.
This is excellent for removing skin diseases (kuṣṭha) and is supreme for destroying hemorrhoids (arśas).
Sesame, bhallātaka, harītakī, and jaggery, taken in equal parts,
destroy piles, asthma, and cough, and remove splenic disorders, anemia, and fever.
Having cooked a *sauraṇa* tuber coated with clay in the fire using the *puṭapāka* method, one should eat it with oil and salt for the eradication of hemorrhoids (*durnāman*).
First, one should consume a *prakuñca* measure of black sesame seeds followed by cold water.
For one who eats it, hemorrhoids are pacified; it bestows firmness to the teeth and nourishment to the body.
(13) Whoever eats a steamed eggplant fruit fried in ghee and mixed with jaggery, along with the alkaline water of *ghoṣā*, to their heart's content, [attains these benefits]. (14)
If he drinks buttermilk, his hemorrhoids—whether congenital or long-standing—will surely perish within seven nights;
it pacifies pitta and kapha and removes itching, scratching, and pain. || 15 ||
