Abhayā taken with jaggery, when administered, quickly destroys hemorrhoids (gudaja).
Alternatively, one should give Citraka, Hapuṣā, and Hiṅgu combined with buttermilk;
or one should cause him to drink buttermilk mixed with Pañcakolaka.
Having ground the bark of the *citraka* root, one should smear a jar with it;
the buttermilk or curd produced therein should be drunk to remove hemorrhoids.
[18] One *pala* each of *triphalā*, *daśamūla*, *agni* (*citraka*), and *nikumbha*... [19]
One *droṇa* of water boiled down to one-quarter remains and mixed with one *tulā* of jaggery;
kept in a vessel of clarified butter for a month, this *dantyariṣṭa*, when consumed,
cures hemorrhoids, worms, upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī*), and anemia.
The preparation of ariṣṭa and other such preparations should be done in a vessel smeared with dhātakī.
Take half a prastha of harītakī, one prastha of āmalaka, ten palas of kapittha, and half of that amount of indravāruṇī.
One should boil two-pala portions each of viḍaṅga, pippalī, lodhra, marica, and elavāluka in four droṇas of water;
when the decoction is reduced to one droṇa, it should be strained, cooled, and then [the following] should be added.

Two hundred palas of jaggery should remain for half a month in a vessel of clarified butter. After a fortnight, it becomes thus; then, by the practice of this *ariṣṭa* in accordance with one's strength, hemorrhoids go to their destruction.

This perfected Abhayāriṣṭa cures malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), anemia (pāṇḍu), heart disease, splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, and abdominal enlargements; it removes the eight types of swelling and loss of appetite, and increases strength, complexion, and digestive fire. It also destroys jaundice and vitiligo.
It cures worms, glandular swellings, tumors, moles, consumption, and fever.

Regarding the drinking of fermented liquors (ariṣṭa) and the like, some authorities say that drinking them as a decoction is equal [in efficacy]; others maintain that because it is a medicinal substance, the first dose should be one pala, which is characterized by its mildness.
Take equal parts of bhallātaka, triphalā, dantī, and citraka; the rock salt (saindhava) should be double the amount of all these combined.
This should be cooked in a closed crucible (kapālasaṃdhi) over a gentle fire of cow dung.
This excellent "Salt of Virtue" (kalyāṇalavaṇa) is the best for those suffering from hemorrhoids (arśas).
[Take] three palas of ginger (śṛṅgavera), a fourth part (one pala) of black pepper (marica), half a kuḍava of long pepper (pippalī), and one pala of chaba pepper (cavyā). 30–31.
One *pala* of *tālīśapatra*, half a *pala* of *kesara*,
two *palas* of *pippalīmūla*, half a *karṣa* of *patra*,
one *karṣa* of *sūkṣmailā*, and one *karṣa* each of cinnamon (*tvak*) and lotus stalk (*mṛṇāla*).
One should prepare a powder from thirty palas of jaggery and combine it all together.
Pills the size of an akṣa fruit are renowned as "life-givers" (prāṇadā);
they should be consumed first, before the meal, according to one's strength.
One should drink wine, meat broth, soup, milk, or water after [the application];
this destroys all types of hemorrhoids—those congenital, those born of blood, and those arising from vāta, pitta, kapha, or their combination (saṃnipāta). || 35 ||
In cases of excessive thirst, difficulty in urination, diseases of the wind (vāta), and throat-obstruction;
likewise in irregular fever, weak digestion, and jaundice; and for those suffering from worms, heart disease, abdominal tumors (gulma), and the pain of colic—36–37.

For those afflicted by dyspnea and cough, these [medicines] are like nectar; however, in cases of obstruction by feces (viḍ-graha) or pitta-type diarrhea, abhayā should be substituted for śuṇṭhī. This life-giving formulation should be administered with sugar added four times the weight of the powder.
It should be employed in cases of sour bile (amlapitta), weak digestion (agnimāndya), and diseases of the anus (gudaja).

As for the after-drink (anupāna) to be administered: one pala should be used for a disease arising from phlegm (śleṣma), two palas for a wind-born (vātaja) disease, and three palas for a bile-born (pittaja) disease.

Five *palas* of *pathyā* (harītakī), one *pala* each of *ajājī* (cumin) and black pepper, and [one *pala* each of] long pepper, long pepper root, *cavya*, *citraka*, and ginger; then [the remaining ingredients] increase by one *pala* in sequence, ending with two *palas* of barley alkali (*yavakṣāra*).
Eight palas of bhallātaka and twice that amount of kanda are prescribed.
Having made balls (vaṭakas) of these with twice the quantity of jaggery, each weighing one akṣa, one should eat one every morning and drink buttermilk or water afterwards. || 42-43 ||
This stimulates a weak digestive fire and cures malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī) and anemia (pāṇḍuroga).
This supreme remedy for those suffering from hemorrhoids was proclaimed by Kāṅkāyana to his disciples as a medical conquest achieved without the use of surgery, caustics, or thermal cautery. 44.
Drink for seven days salt, *uttama-vahni*, *kaliṅga*, barley, *cirabilva*, and great *picumanda* mixed with churned curd (*mathita*), if you wish to destroy the growths upon your body.
Take ginger, long pepper, black pepper, *nāgadalatvak*, and cardamom, powdered and increased in sequence, starting from the last ingredient.
One should consume this equal measure [of the powder] in cases of hemorrhoids, sluggish digestion, abdominal tumors, loss of appetite, asthma, and diseases of the throat and heart.

(46) He who makes a magnificent bolus (*modaka*) with jaggery from *nāgara*, *aruṣkara*, and *vṛddhadāraka* acts as a destroyer of the disease of all types of hemorrhoids; he makes even an old man suddenly become young again. (47)
The powder of trikaṭu, citraka, āruṣkara, viḍaṅga, sesame, and abhayā, taken daily together with jaggery,
cures hemorrhoids, edema, poisons, skin diseases, and constipation.
Fire overcomes weakness and the pale-yellow discoloration caused by worms.
(48) In a powder, the quantity of jaggery should be known to be equal [to the other ingredients]; in a bolus (modaka), it should be double.
(49) There are sixteen parts of *sūraṇa* reduced to powder, and half of that amount of *citraka*.
Two parts of *mahauṣadha* and one part of black pepper, made into a bolus with jaggery, lead to the conquest of hemorrhoids.

(50) One part each of black pepper, *mahauṣadha*, *citraka*, and *sūraṇa*, increasing twofold respectively, with a portion of jaggery equal to the total weight of all these ingredients—this celebrated medicinal bolus (*modaka*) should be consumed for its well-known results. (51)
It kindles the digestive fire, uproots diseases such as colic and abdominal tumors, eliminates swelling, and quickly destroys elephantiasis and hemorrhoids.
[The formulation consists of] sixteen parts of surana, eight parts of fire (citraka), and also eight parts of the great medicine (mahauṣadha). || 52 ||
Then, add half a part of black pepper, and half of that again [of the same].

Next, take equal parts of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), long pepper (*kaṇā*), its root, *tālīsa*, *aruṣkara*, and *kṛmighna*; these are equal to the portion of great medicine (*mahauṣadha*), while *tālamūlī* is one-sixteenth part.
A portion equal to that of the Sūraṇa should be given of Vṛddhadāraka as well;
with Bhṛṅgarāja and a part of Marica, one should have all these made into a powder.
This modaka, combined with double the amount of jaggery, should be consumed by those possessing abundant wealth.
It causes affliction in others who are devoid of gurus, vṛṣyas, and wholesome foods.
By this [medicine], Bhasmaka was previously produced in Agastya by Yogarāja, and even in Bhīma Māruti, by which those two became great eaters. || 56–57 ||

In this case, the strength of the digestive fire (*agnibala*) is the primary cause; it is not merely the great potency of *sūraṇa* that effects this, for it overcomes hemorrhoids even without the use of surgical instruments, caustics, or fire.
It also removes swelling, elephantiasis, and indigestion (*grahaṇī*) caused by *kapha* and *vāyu*.
It destroys wrinkles and graying hair, bestows intelligence, and virility;
this elixir (rasāyana) quickly destroys hiccup, asthma, cough, consumption with its various symptoms, urinary disorders, and even severe enlargement of the spleen in men.
Having ground cavya, the three pungents (trikaṭu), pāṭhā, alkali, kustumburu, yavānī, pippalīmūla, both viḍa and saindhava salts,
citraka, bilva, and abhayā, one should cook ghee with them.
When this ghee is prepared with four times the amount of curd, it promotes the downward movement of wind and stool;
it cures dysentery, prolapse of the rectum, difficulty in urination, discharge from the anus,
and pain in the rectum and groin.

Having ground together long pepper (pippalī), licorice (madhuka), wood-apple (bilva), dill (śatāhvā), madana fruit, sweet flag (vacā), the plant known as puṣkaramūla, śaṭhī, costus (kuṣṭha), leadwort (citraka), and deodar (devadāru),
one should cook oil mixed with twice the amount of milk.
This is the best unctuous enema (anuvāsana) for those with hemorrhoids and obstructed flatus;
it cures prolapse of the rectum, colic, dysuria, tenesmus,
weakness of the waist, thighs, and back, and distension localized in the groins.

One should conquer the discharge of mucus from the rectum, swelling, and the suppression of flatus and feces, as well as frequent straining, by means of an oil enema (anuvāsana). Trivṛt, tejovatī, dantī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, citraka, and śaṭhī [are used for this purpose].
One pala each of gavākṣī, viśvamustaka, viḍaṅga, and harītakī; eight palas of aruṣkara;
six palas of vṛddhadāru; and sixteen palas of sūraṇa. || 68–69 ||
One should boil [the ingredients] in two droṇas of water until reduced to one-fourth; that strained decoction should then have three times its weight of jaggery added,
and one should cook it as a linctus until it reaches the consistency for coating a ladle.
Having removed [the patient] from there, one should subsequently cause these powders to be administered:
three palas each of *trivṛt*, the root of *tejovatī*, and *citraka*;
and six palas each of cardamom, cinnamon, black pepper, and *nāgāhvā*.
Having added thirty-two palas of powder, one should set it aside; then one should administer the dose, and once it has been digested, the patient should subsist on milk and meat broth.
[This cures] the five types of gulma, urinary disorders (prameha), anemia (pāṇḍuroga), and chlorosis (halīmaka).
It conquers all types of jaundice as well as all abdominal enlargements;
it kindles a sluggish digestive fire and even consumes consumption (yakṣman), as well as chronic catarrh, acute rhinitis, and obesity-related wind disorders.

This is the most excellent and auspicious electuary for all diseases; it is a swift destroyer of hemorrhoids, having been witnessed [to be effective] thousands of times. Those who employ this live free from illness for a hundred years.
This "Glorious Bahuśāla" jaggery is proclaimed as a producer of longevity, a destroyer of wrinkles and grey hair,
the best among elixirs (rasāyana), a supreme generator of intelligence,
and an enemy of chronic diseases.
When a piece of jaggery thrown into a vessel filled with water does not float, but remains motionless when cast in, and does not dissolve once fallen;
when it can be smeared with a ladle or becomes stringy—[then it is ready]. (79)
This is the description of the ripening of all substances such as jaggery (guḍa) and the like.
When jaggery has reached its proper ripening, it is easy to knead, pleasant to the touch, and endowed with excellent fragrance, color, and taste; when pressed, it maintains its seal.
One should boil two thousand *bhallātaka* fruits in one *droṇa* of water until the liquid is reduced to one-fourth; then the physician should cook one *tulā* of jaggery in that decoction.
He should also add five hundred *bhallātaka* fruits, having split them, into that very same preparation.
When this [preparation] is prepared, one should add one *karṣa* each of the powdered triphalā, vyoṣa, yavānī, musta, and saindhava, along with tvak, elā, patra, and kesara;
a person, considering their digestive fire and strength, should consume it after rising in the morning. || 83–84 ||

This jaggery preparation of *bhallātaka* indeed destroys leprosy, hemorrhoids, jaundice, urinary disorders, malabsorption syndrome, abdominal tumors, anemia, splenic enlargement, cough, worms, and fistula-in-ano; it is the best remedy for those suffering from hemorrhoidal diseases. (85)

A wise person should boil one thousand *bhallātaka* fruits along with one *pala* each of the ten roots (*daśamūlī*), *amṛtā*, *bhārgī*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *citraka*, and *śaṭhī*. Once it has thickened into a consistency suitable for licking, one should add one *tulā* of jaggery (*guḍa*) and remove it from the heat.

One should administer honey, long pepper, castor oil, and *aurubūka* oil, each by one *kuḍava*, along with cinnamon, cardamom, and black pepper, likewise by one *kuḍava*. This cures hemorrhoids, cough, upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), jaundice, and swelling.
Jaggery and *bhallātaka* are known to destroy the exhaustion caused by fire (fever).
*Citraka*, *triphalā*, *musta*, *granthika*, *cavikā*, *amṛtā*, *hastipippalī*, *apāmārga*, *daṇḍotpala*, and *kuṭheraka* [are likewise used]. (89–90)
One should boil four-pala portions of these [drugs] in one droṇa of water;
having cut two thousand bhallātaka fruits, one should add them right there.
When reduced to one-fourth by that [decoction], the physician should cook it in an iron vessel.
One should take half a *tulā* of sharp iron (*tīkṣṇaloha*) and two *kuḍavas* of clarified butter;

one should also prepare one *pala* each of the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *vahni*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *biḍa* salt, *audbhida* salt, black salt (*sauvarcala*), and *viḍaṅga*. || 92–93 ||
One *kuḍava* each of *vṛddhadāru* and *tālamūlī*,
and eight *palas* of *sūraṇa*, should be made into a powder and added [to the preparation]. When it has been cooked and cooled, two *kuḍavas* of honey should be administered.
Or, at the time of breakfast in the morning, one should eat it according to one's strength.
It quickly dispels hemorrhoids, disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī), anemia, loss of appetite, worms, abdominal tumors, urinary stones, urinary disorders, and colic. (95–96)
It promotes the increase of semen, destroys wrinkles and graying hair,
and is the most excellent elixir (rasāyana), supreme in curing all diseases. Regarding hemorrhoids with blood, the physician should first ignore the bleeding blood.
When a malignant hemorrhage has been suppressed, however, colic, abdominal distension, and blood diseases may arise.

A decoction of *kuṭaja* bark with *nāgara* (ginger) is unctuous and astringent for blood; likewise, the bark of the pomegranate with *nāgara*, or sandalwood juice with *nāgara*, serves the same purpose.
Candana, kirātatiktaka, dhanvayavāsa, and nāgara, when decocted, pacify hemorrhoids with blood; so too do dārvītvak, uśīra, and nimba.
Through the habitual use of fresh butter and sesame, or through the habitual use of saffron, fresh butter, and sugar [hemorrhoids are likewise cured].
By the habitual consumption of the cream of curd churned [with water], hemorrhoids that involve the flow of blood are pacified.
Goat’s milk mixed with *samaṅgā*, blue lotus, *mocāhvā*, *tirīṭa*, sesame, and sandalwood should be administered to remove the blood in hemorrhoids. 101–102.
A physician should administer ghee prepared with the paste of *kuṭaja* fruit, bark, and filaments, *nīlotpala*, *lodhra*, and *dhātakī* for hemorrhoids with blood and pain.
One hundred palas of *kuṭaja* bark should be boiled in one droṇa of water.
One should remove the decoction when one-eighth remains. Having strained it again through a cloth, one should cook the decoction until it reaches the consistency of a linctus (leha),
adding bhallātaka, viḍaṅga, trikaṭu, and likewise triphalā.
One pala each of rasāñjana, citraka, the fruits of kuṭaja, vacā, ativiṣā, and bilva—
having powdered these and thirty palas of jaggery— one should store [the mixture].
One should give one *kuḍava* of honey and likewise one *kuḍava* of clarified butter.
This linctus pacifies hemorrhoids arising from blood,
as well as those caused by *vāta*, *pitta*, *kapha*, and their combination (*sāṃnipātika*).
It destroys all those diseases known by difficult names,
including acid dyspepsia (amlapitta), diarrhea, anemia (pāṇḍuroga), anorexia,
weakness of the digestive tract (grahaṇī), emaciation, edema, and jaundice (kāmalā).
One should administer ghee as a post-drink, or honey, buttermilk, water, or milk;
this linctus made from *kuṭaja* is prescribed for the destruction of the multitude of diseases.
One should boil one *āḍhaka* of the ashes of black *muṣkaka* in six times that amount of water.
In a firm vessel made of iron, the wise one should slowly stir with a ladle;
having burnt many pieces of conch-shell navel in the fire, he should cast them into the remaining purified liquid.
If this excellent alkali produced from castor stalks burns [the skin], it is superior to a hundred verbal rebukes. || 111 ||
For drinking and for medicinal processing, four times as much filtered water should be added.
Even in the case of an *āḍhaka* measure, there is no doubling [of the liquid], because this refers merely to the proportion of the ingredients.
When the mixture becomes clear, slimy, and red, alkaline water is desired to be used.
Alkali is praised as being of two types: *pānīya* (for drinking) and *pratisāraṇīya* (for external application).
Of these, the former is for pacifying abdominal tumors, swellings, and the like, while the latter is for treating hemorrhoids and similar ailments.
It should be prepared by mixing [the ingredients] with one-fourth, one-eighth, or one-sixteenth part of the fourth [ingredient].
The *kṣārodaka* (alkaline water) and the *śaṅkhaka* (conch-shell instrument) are prescribed in sequence as medium and superior [treatments].
A thread that has been repeatedly saturated with the powder of *rajanī* (turmeric) and *snuhī* milk,
when tied very tightly, cuts away hemorrhoids and fistula-in-ano.
First the southern [hemorrhoid], then the left, the posterior, and finally the anterior, in sequence;
having moistened them with a five-fold alkaline solution (pañcatikta), one should cauterize hemorrhoids born of Vāta and Kapha with alkali, and those born of blood and Pitta with fire.
Having scraped away the hemorrhoids with the leaves of *gojī* and *śephālikā*,
one should apply an alkaline solution (*kṣāra*) and remain for a hundred recitations of the Veda while closing the opening of the instrument.
Then, having removed it, one should examine [the site] until it resembles a ripe *jambu* fruit.
If that occurs, it is auspicious; if not, one should smear it again.
Having soaked it in cold water, one should apply a paste of liquorice mixed with clarified butter.
It should not be depressed, resembling the ear of a palm tree, nor should blood remain when it has been cauterized with fire.
Having extinguished the pain produced by the fire with honey and ghee,
once it is properly cauterized, the physician should apply an ointment consisting of tugākṣīrī, plakṣa, candana, and gairika, combined with amṛta and ghee.
Having seated him for a short time, one should apply an alkaline substance with warm water to a vessel filled with water in cases of obstruction of urine and feces.
For burning sensations arising from the bladder and other regions, an ointment made with ghee washed a hundred times should be applied.
Fresh grain, black gram, buttermilk, and similar items should be consumed in moderation for the sake of digestion.
For the purpose of purifying the ulcer, one should drink a decoction of *varā* with *guggulu*.
Once the meal is digested, old *śāli* rice, green gram, and other such foods, along with bitter substances, clarified butter, and rock salt, constitute wholesome diet.

Once all the wounds have healed, the physician, having applied caustic (kṣāra), should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) with oil prepared from the pippalyādi group; the patient should consume digestive stimulants (dīpana-bhaiṣajya).
Having thus excised large and deep-seated [tumors], one should cauterize them in a strong person.
Likewise, having cut out the *carmakīla* (fistula-in-ano), one should cauterize it with either [alkali or fire].
A color resembling that of a ripe jambū fruit is praised in the case of a cauterization with alkali.
One should avoid suppressing natural urges, riding on the back of a woman, and sitting in a squatting posture (*utkaṭaka*).
One should avoid foods that aggravate the specific doshas associated with hemorrhoids (arśas).
Chapter 6:
Preservation of equilibrium should be maintained when it exists; when it is disturbed, the wind (vāta) must be subdued.
When [the digestive fire] is sharp, there is treatment for pitta; when it is dull, there is purification of kapha.
Trikaṭuka, ajamodā, rock salt (saindhava), and the two types of cumin (jīraka)—of these, each part being equal, the eighth portion is asafoetida (hiṅgu).
This powder, consumed with ghee as the first morsel of food, kindles the gastric fire and destroys diseases of wind (vāta).
First, one should drink warm scum (maṇḍa) mixed with asafoetida (hiṅgu) and sauvarcala salt; by this, even a disturbed fire becomes regular, and a sluggish fire is kindled.
It awakens hunger, cleanses the bladder, bestows vitality, and increases the blood.
Maṇḍa indeed possesses eight qualities: it removes fever, destroys phlegm and bile, and conquers wind.
(4) Two handfuls of well-husked rice, half that amount of green gram, ginger, sour gruel, cumin, rock salt, asafoetida, and oil—by combining all these, maṇḍa is prepared. (5)
The great fire known as *bhasmaka* becomes increasingly sharp;
therefore, the physician should conquer it with buffalo ghee, curd, and milk.
Whatever medicine is heavy, nourishing, and increases *śleṣman* (phlegm) [should be avoided].
All that is consumed when hidden beneath the fire, as well as sleeping during the day [destroys the digestive fire].
Harītakī, when eaten continuously with ginger, jaggery, or combined with rock salt, is an inflamer of the digestive fire.
The consumption of salt and fresh ginger at the beginning of a meal is always wholesome, cleansing the tongue and throat, stimulating the digestive fire, and pleasing to the heart. Indeed,

he whose digestive fire has been extinguished who drinks powdered rock salt (*sindhūttha*), *pathyā* (yellow myrobalan), and *magadhodbhava* (long pepper) along with the powder of *vahni* (cinnamon) with warm water [regains his strength].
If one eats even fresh food mixed with meat and ghee, it is reduced to ashes in an instant as soon as it is swallowed.

For the suppression of phlegm and for a sluggish digestive fire, one should drink a decoction of viśvā, abhayā, and guḍūcī, along with the six pungents (ṣaḍūṣaṇa), rendered fragrant with cinnamon-bark and leaves.
One should prepare pills with equal parts of rock salt, asafoetida, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *yavānī*, and the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), along with portions of jaggery (*guḍa*).
One who consumes them will attain satiety; even one with weak digestion can eat a great quantity.
Alternatively, one may take ginger with jaggery, or long pepper (*upakulyā*) with three parts of chebulic myrobalan (*pathyā*), or pomegranate.
One should always consume [this] in cases of undigested raw matter (āma), indigestion, anal diseases, and constipation.

Those men with weak digestive fires who lick a mixture of viḍaṅga, bhallātaka, citraka, and amṛtā along with equal parts of jaggery and ghee, become possessed of a fire equal to that of the submarine Vāḍava fire.

Harītakī prepared with grain-washings (dhānyāmla), combined with long pepper (pippalī), rock salt (saindhava), and asafoetida (hiṅgu), immediately overcomes even severe indigestion accompanied by eructations and belching, and instantly kindles the digestive fire. It [also cures] lassitude, heaviness, flatulence, vertigo, and the obstruction of the vital winds (māruta-mūḍhatā).
Obstruction or excessive discharge are the general symptoms of indigestion (ajīrṇa).
For the most part, indigestion arises in humans from an imbalance in diet;
it is the root of the multitude of diseases, and it perishes through its own destruction.
Emesis with water mixed with vacā and salt is recommended for one suffering from indigestion (āmavāta).

For when a man's food is partially digested (vidagdha), it indeed reaches full digestion quickly through cold water; for its coldness subdues the pitta, and due to its moist nature, it causes the [undigested matter] to fall downward.
In the case of *viṣṭabdha* (obstruction), sudation should be administered and salt water should be drunk;

when there is residual digestive fluid (*rasaśeṣa*), one should avoid daytime sleep, fasting, and exposure to wind. [One should also avoid administering this] to those exhausted by physical exercise, sexual indulgence, travel, riding vehicles, or labor, nor to those suffering from diarrhea.

One should allow those suffering from colic and dyspnea, those overcome by thirst, those afflicted by hiccups and wind, the emaciated, those with depleted phlegm, children, those intoxicated, the elderly, those with indigestion of meat-juice, those who have stayed awake at night, and those who have fasted, to sleep freely during the day. || 20 ||
A wise person should administer water prepared with *dhānyanāgara* (coriander and ginger),
which pacifies undigested food (*āmājīrṇa*), destroys colic (*śūla*), and cleanses the bladder.
One should drink a powder of *sauvarcala* salt combined with *pathyā* (harītakī) and *pippalī* (long pepper).
Having ascertained the movement of the humors even with warm water mixed with mastu,
the physician quickly subdues the four types of indigestion, weak digestion, loss of appetite, flatulence, vātagulma, and colic.

If a person who is unctuous and strong should have a doubt regarding indigestion at the time of eating, that consumer of wholesome food should, being free from doubt, first eat a beneficial dose of *abhayā* with *śuṇṭhī*. However,
for one whose food immediately causes a burning sensation after eating, or for whom there is a burning in the heart, stomach, and throat—
Having licked an *abhayā* (chebulic myrobalan) combined with grapes, sugar, and honey, he shall indeed obtain well-being.
If the morning meal is not digested, the evening meal does no harm; however, if the evening meal is not digested, the morning meal is indeed harmful.
Let there be one part of asafoetida and two parts of *vacā*;
three parts of long pepper should be given, and ginger four parts;
five parts of *yavānikā* and six parts of *harītakī*. (27–28)
Citraka should be sevenfold and Kuṣṭha eightfold; this powder, which removes Vāta, should be drunk immediately after preparation with clear wine (prasannā),
or with curd, whey, liquor, or lukewarm water.
It cures chronic constipation, indigestion, as well as splenic enlargement and abdominal diseases; it is beneficial for one whose limbs are wasting away or who has consumed poison.
It destroys hemorrhoids, stimulates the digestive fire, alleviates colic, and destroys abdominal tumors.
This powder named Agnimukha quickly destroys cough and dyspnea, as well as consumption; it is never rendered ineffective by anything.
[It consists of] two types of alkali, citraka, pāṭhā, karañja, and the salts.
Sūkṣmailā, patra, bhārṅgī, kṛmighna, hiṅgu, and puṣkara; śaṭhī, dārvī, trivṛt, musta, vacā, and likewise indrayava;
dhātrī, jīraka, vṛkṣāmla, śreyasī, and upakuñcikā. || 33–34 ||
Amlavetasa, amlīkā, pomegranate, the three pungents (kaṭutrika),
bhallātaka, ajamoda, yavānī, devadāru, abhayā, ativiṣā, śyāmā, hapuṣā, and āragvadha— these should be taken in equal parts. || 35 ||
One should prepare fine powders of equal parts of sesame, muṣkaka, śigru, kokilākṣa, and palāśa;
[these], along with iron rust heated and sprinkled with cow's urine, should all be made into a fine powder. || 36-37 ||
One should saturate it for three days with the juice of citron,
and for three days with sour gruel and the fresh juice of ginger.
This powder produces an extremely powerful digestive fire and possesses a brilliance equal to a blazing flame.
When used according to the prescribed method, it quickly destroys diseases:
indigestion, abdominal tumors, splenic enlargement, hemorrhoids, abdominal dropsy, hernia, stones, and gout. (39–40)
It drives away formidable diseases and rekindles a diminished digestive fire; having given food accompanied by all kinds of seasonings for his meal,
one should cause him to take a dose of this powder the size of a cat's paw.
From the mere milking of the cow, all that becomes liquid and warm.
Pippalī, pippalīmūla, citraka, hastipippalī, hiṅgu, cavya, ajamodā, and the five salts. (42–43)
One should add two *pala*s each of the two alkalis and *hapuṣā*, measuring half a *pala* each;
and curd, sour gruel, and vinegar, equal in measure to the quantity of ghee.
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee in one *prastha* of ginger juice.
This is known as Agnighṛta; it is highly recommended for those with weak digestive fire.

It is the best destroyer of hemorrhoids (arśas), and likewise removes abdominal tumors (gulma) and enlargement of the abdomen (udara), as well as nodules (granthi), tumors (arbuda), scrofula (apacī), cough, kapha, fat, and wind disorders.

It destroys disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī-doṣa), swelling, and fistula-in-ano; it quickly eradicates all diseases located in the bladder as well as those residing in the abdomen, just as the risen sun dispels the darkness. || 47 ||
In two hundred palas of the decoction of agni and the five roots (pañcamūla),

when one āḍhaka of the juice of amṛtā has been added and this mixture strained, one should cook one āḍhaka of abhayā with a tula of jaggery until the signs of completion of the cooking process appear.
On another day, one should add two kuḍavas of honey,

two palas each of the three aromatics (trisaugandhya), and two palas each of the three pungents (trikaṭu); in that elixir (rasāyana), there should be one pala each of yavakṣāra and so forth, along with fermented gruel (śukta).
This supreme [formula] was taught by the Aśvins for the increase of the digestive fire in men.
It digests even pieces of wood and destroys cough, dyspnea, consumption, and worms;
it also cures abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, hemorrhoids, colic, and hernias.
One conquers chronic catarrhs (pīnasa), which remain undefeated even by hundreds of yogas, within three days; in another version of this text, one hundred palas of dhātrī juice are added here.
One prastha of rice-water and three prasthas of sour gruel from husk-water [are also included].

Having placed half a *prastha* of curd, eight *palas* of radish, two *mānikās* of jaggery, two pieces of cleaned ginger, two *palas* each of rock salt and cumin, black pepper and long pepper, and a pair of *palas* of turmeric into a sturdy vessel; || 54 ||
One should let it sit for three days placed upon a heap of moist grains such as barley;
in summer, at the end of the rainy season, for four days;
in the rains, for six; and in the cold season, for eight days. After that, having drained this, one should grind it into a powder.

This fermented vinegar (śukta) and sour gruel (cukra), prepared with one pala each of the four spices (cāturjātaka), destroys various diseases born from the defects of wind (vāta), phlegm (kapha), and undigested matter (āmadoṣa);
having cured hemorrhoids (durnāma), wind-disorders, colic (śūla), abdominal tumors (gulma), and stomach ailments (jaṭhara), it kindles the digestive fire. || 55 ||

Sugar-cane juice and other such substances, together with jaggery, honey, and sour gruel, placed in a clean vessel and kept for three nights in a heap of grain, become *śukta*; that is called *cukra*.
Jaggery, honey, and sour gruel, when combined, are progressively superior [in quality].
They recommend double portions for the sake of properly preparing the sour gruel (cukra).
A lukewarm massage with a paste of kuṣṭha and saindhava salt, combined with sour gruel and oil, cures cholera (viṣūcī) and relieves the pain of sciatica (khallī-śūla).
A decoction made from *karañja*, *nimba*, *śikharī*, *guḍūcī*, *arjaka*,

and *vatsaka*, when drunk, cures severe *viṣūcikā* (cholera) through emesis. [59] Having added *vyoṣa*, the fruit of *karañja*, *haridrā*, and the root of *mātuluṅgī*, [one should prepare the remedy].
Pills made from these [drugs] dried in the shade, when used as an ointment for the eyes, destroy *viṣūcī*.

An unguent made from *tvak*, *patra*, *rāsnā*, *aguru*, *śigru*, *kuṣṭha*, *vacā*, and *śatāhvā*, ground with sour liquids, destroys *khalivisūcikā*; likewise, oil cooked with these same ingredients performs the same purpose.

In the absence of nausea during thirst, water with cloves is recommended, or cold water infused with nutmeg, or boiled water with *bhadraghana*. When dysentery has become excessively aggravated, the application of heat to the heels is praised.
One should apply a plaster made of sour flour (amlapiṣṭa) to the abdomen that is painful and distended;
this plaster consists of *dāru*, *haimavatī*, *kuṣṭha*, *śatāhvā*, *hiṅgu*, and *saindhava*.
Warm barley powder mixed with buttermilk (*takra*) and alkali (*kṣāra*) destroys pain in the abdomen.
One may apply sudation using jars filled with much steam and heat, or likewise by other means such as the warmth of the palms.

Even if suffering from intense pain, one who has indigestion (ajīrṇa) should not drink medicine for colic; for the digestive fire (anala), when covered by the humors (doṣa), is incapable of digesting either the humors or the medicinal food.

Having recognized that a person has been properly emeticated, purged, or treated with fasting, one should attend to them when they are properly afflicted by hunger, using drinks and other substances that stimulate digestion and promote maturation.
(7) Chapter 7.
Pārasīya-yavānī taken in the morning with water that has been left standing overnight,
preceded by jaggery, quickly expels a mass of worms located within the abdomen.
One should drink the juice extracted from the leaves of the pāribhadraka tree mixed with honey.
One should cause [the patient] to drink either the juice of *kambuka* or the juice of *pattūra*,
along with a digestive soup made from rice-scum (*anna-maṇḍa*) combined with *viḍaṅga* and the three pungents (*vyoṣa*).
This destroys worms and greatly stimulates the digestive fire.
One should lick either the powder of horse dung or *viḍaṅga* mixed with honey.
A gruel prepared with buttermilk and *viḍaṅga*, long pepper root, drumstick, black pepper, and *suvarcikā* salt is a destroyer of worms.
A decoction of *mustā*, *ākhuparṇī* fruit, and *dāruśigru*, combined with a paste of *kṛṣṇā* and *kṛmiśatru*,
destroys even long-standing worms through both passages [anus and urethra], as well as diseases born of worms. (5) A *pūlikā* should be prepared from ground *ākhuparṇī* leaves and flour.
After eating sauvīraka, one should drink [it] as a supreme destroyer of worms;
or one should drink the fresh juice of palāśa seeds mixed with honey,
or drink the paste of those seeds with buttermilk to destroy worms.
Or one may employ the group of drugs beginning with *surasā* in every way.
Ghee prepared with *triphalā*, *trivṛtā*, *dantī*, *vacā*, and *kampillaka* in cow's urine is a destroyer of worms.
One should take three *prasthas* of *triphalā* and one *prastha* of *viḍaṅga*, and as many as may be available, the *daśamūla* that stimulates digestion;
having boiled these in one *droṇa* of water until a quarter remains, one should cook ghee in that decoction.
That [mixture] measured by one *prastha* and combined with *sindhuyuta* (rock salt) should be drunk; it destroys worms.
This *viḍaṅga-ghṛta* should be licked together with sugar;
it drives away all worms, just as the thunderbolt [destroys] the Asuras.
Mercury combined with the juice of *dhattūra* leaves or *tāmbūla* leaves,
when applied as an ointment, destroys lice.
[One should avoid] milks, meats, clarified butters, curds, and leafy vegetables.
In brief, one desiring to destroy worms should avoid sour, sweet, and cold substances.
Chapter 8:
Having examined a patient suffering from anemia (pāṇḍvāmaya) who is fit for treatment, one should first administer oleation with ghee and then purify them through both emesis and purgation.
One should prepare [the treatment] with formulations enriched with honey and ghee and combined with the powder of *harītakī*.
Alternatively, one should drink ghee cooked with turmeric (*rajanī*), or ghee prepared with the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), or even ghee from the *tailvaka* tree;
or one may drink ghee processed with purgative substances, or take purgative medicinal formulations with ghee.
The procedure for Vata-originated [fever] is unctuous; for Pitta-originated, bitter and cold;
for Kapha-originated, pungent, dry, and hot; and for mixed types, it should be applied according to the combination.
In the case of Pitta, one should drink half a pala of Trivṛt powder mixed with two parts sugar.

One should drink the decoction of the two groups of five roots (dvipañcamūlī) along with viśva in cases of kapha-type anemia, fever, diarrhea, edema, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), dyspnea, anorexia, and diseases of the throat and heart. Alternatively, [one may take] a preparation made from triphalā, amṛtā, vāsā, tiktā, bhūnimba, and nimba.
The decoction mixed with honey destroys anemia (pāṇḍuroga) along with jaundice (kāmalā).
Iron filings, sesame, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), and jujube (kola)—each taken in equal parts—with an amount of honey-ore (mākṣikadhātu) equal to all of them combined:
a bolus (modaka) made from these and taken with honey and buttermilk is recommended even for advanced cases of anemia.
Iron rust, heated and repeatedly sprinkled with cow’s urine,
should be combined with honey and ghee as a powder and administered with food; it stimulates the appetite, generates digestive fire, and cures edema and anemia.
Take equal parts of the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), the three myrobalans (triphalā), musta, viḍaṅga, and citraka; add nine parts of iron powder. One should consume this powder with honey and ghee;
it cures anemia (pāṇḍu), heart disease, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), hemorrhoids (arśas), and jaundice (kāmalā).
For one afflicted by jaundice who has first been treated with oleation, the physician who knows [his condition] should first administer a purgative, and thereafter perform the pacifying treatment.
The juice of triphalā, or of guḍūcī, or of dārvī, or of nimba [is to be used].
When consumed in the morning combined with honey, it removes jaundice (kāmalā). For those afflicted by jaundice, the juice of *droṇapuṣpī* is an auspicious collyrium (*añjana*);
alternatively, one may prepare a powder of *niśā*, *gairika*, and *dhātrī*.
Karkoṭa root should be used as a nasal drop (nasya), or the fruit of Jālinī should be inhaled.
One should lick a powder of iron filings, Vyōṣa, and Viḍaṅga; or Haridrā combined with Triphalā and sugar is beneficial for those suffering from jaundice (kāmalā).
Likewise, Tribhaṇḍī, Gavākṣī with jaggery, and Śuṇṭhī are also wholesome.

A linctus composed of *dhātrī*, iron filings, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *niśā*, honey, clarified butter, and sugar quickly wards off even severe jaundice. Iron dross, burnt with *akṣa* wood and quenched eight times in cow’s urine, [is likewise effective].

When powdered and licked with honey, it quickly destroys the disease known as Kumbha-pāṇḍu. One should employ all the treatments for pāṇḍuroga (anemia) in cases of halīmaka; furthermore, those treatments which have been prescribed for kāmalā by the best of physicians should also be administered.
Buffalo ghee prepared with turmeric, triphalā, nimba, balā, and madhuka, along with milk, is an excellent remedy for jaundice (kāmalā).
[Likewise, ghee prepared] with mūrvā, tiktā, niśā, yāsa, kṛṣṇā, candana, and parpaṭa...
One *prastha* of ghee, prepared with four times as much milk and one *akṣa* each of *trāyantī*, *vatsaka*, *bhūnimba*, *paṭola*, *ambuda*,
and *dāru*, conquers anemia, fever, eruptive boils, swelling, hemorrhoids, and *raktapitta*. || 19–20 ||

Ghee boiled with these— vyoṣa, bilva, the two types of rañjanī, triphalā, the two types of punarnavā, musta, iron filings, pāṭhā, viḍaṅga, devadāru, vṛścikālī, and bhārṅgī— along with milk, [is used for healing].
This [preparation] pacifies all disorders caused by [contaminated] clay.
Tryūṣaṇa, triphalā, musta, viḍaṅga, cavya, citraka, the bark of dārvī, the mineral mākṣika, granthika, and devadāru [are the ingredients]. (22–23)

Having separately ground two-pala portions of each of these into powder, one should cook them in eight times the amount of urine; then, one should add to that [mixture] purified maṇḍūra, which is twice the amount of the powder and resembles collyrium.

One should make these Vaṭakas (pills) the size of Udumbara fruits and consume them with buttermilk according to one's digestive fire; once they are digested, one should eat food that is wholesome to the patient. Indeed, these Maṇḍūra-Vaṭakas are life-givers for those suffering from jaundice (Pāṇḍu-roga).
It destroys skin diseases, chronic fever, edema, stiffness of the thighs, disorders of kapha, hemorrhoids, jaundice, urinary disorders, and enlargement of the spleen.
Punarnavā, trivṛt, dry ginger, long pepper, and black pepper [are used for this].
Viḍaṅga, devadāru, citraka, and puṣkaramūla;
the two types of haridrā, triphalā, dantī, and likewise cavikā;
the fruit of kuṭaja, tikta, pippalīmūla, and mustaka. || 28–29 ||

These [drugs] should be taken in equal parts, with iron rust (maṇḍūra) added in double that amount; having cooked them in eight times the quantity of urine, one should store the preparation in a greased vessel.
It cures anemia, edema, abdominal enlargement, flatulence, colic, hemorrhoids, worms, and abdominal tumors.
Five parts each of *pañcakola*, black pepper, *devadāru*, and the three fruits (*phalatrika*), along with *viḍaṅga* and *musta*, in portions measuring three *palas* each;
of these powders, there should be twice as much *maṇḍūra*. || 31–32 ||

Having cooked [the ingredients] in eight times the amount of urine until it becomes thick, one should extract that [preparation]. Then, one should eat pills (vaṭakas) the size of an akṣa with buttermilk while eating only at night. This conquers anemia (pāṇḍuroga), weak digestion, and loss of appetite.
This preparation, named Maṇḍūra-vajra, destroys hemorrhoids, disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī), stiffness of the thighs,
chlorosis, worms, splenic enlargement, abdominal diseases, and throat ailments; it is the destroyer of the entire host of diseases.

For those two [the patient and the physician], a meal consisting of barley, wheat, or rice, along with wholesome juices from wild animals and dishes made of mung beans, āḍhakī, masūra, and so forth, is prescribed. (36) Section 9.
That which is excessively heavy should not be administered at the beginning to one who is strong;
for it causes heart disease, anemia, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, splenic enlargement, abdominal tumors, fever, and so forth.
[This applies] to one whose humors have already been provoked upward, and first of all, to one suffering from *raktapitta*.
For one whose strength, flesh, and digestive fire have not diminished, fasting (apatarpaṇa) should be prescribed.
As wholesome food, parched grain flour mixed with sugar and served with the soup of *satīna* beans is recommended.
In cases where the disorder moves upward, purgation should be administered first; in cases where it moves downward, emesis is beneficial.
A bolus (modaka) made from trivṛt, triphalā, śyāmā, pippalī, sugar, and honey cures fever arising from the derangement of the three humors (saṃnipāta), as well as raktapitta and fever.
[Verse 2] Milk mixed with musta, indrayava, yaṣṭimadhu, and madana, along with honey...

A cooling emetic should be administered, which is excellent for removing blood-pitta (raktapitta). When the blood has moved downwards, a gruel (peyā) prepared with the *śāliparṇī* group of herbs should be given;
furthermore, the entire therapeutic regimen for curing dysentery with blood (raktātīsāra) should be applied in its entirety.

One should treat with stabilizing (stambhana) therapies a child, an elderly person, one whose flesh and strength are wasted, or one afflicted by consumption (śoṣa), provided they are unfit for emesis or purgation.
[One may administer] the juice of vṛṣa leaves, squeezed out and mixed with honey and sugar.
By drinking this, even the most severe *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disease) is pacified.
Having dissolved *priyaṅgu*, clay, and *añjana* in a decoction of *āṭarūṣaka*, one should drink it along with *lodhra* and honey to alleviate *raktapitta*.

Having drunk the decoction of *vāsā*, blue lotus, clay, *priyaṅgu*, *lodhra*, collyrium, and the filaments of the white lotus, combined with sugar and honey, one will quickly subdue the violent onset of *pitta* and blood.
As long as the *vāsā* plant exists, there remains hope for one's life.
Why should one suffering from *raktapitta*, consumption, or cough despair?
The fresh juice of *vāsaka* mixed with the powder of *tālīsa* and honey should be drunk;
it removes phlegm and bile, cough, *tamaka* asthma, dyspnea, hoarseness of voice, and *raktapitta*.

A decoction of *āṭarūṣaka*, *mṛdvīkā*, and *pathyā*, mixed with sugar and enriched with honey, destroys cough, dyspnea, and *raktapitta*. Alternatively, the juice extracted from the fruit of *phalgu*, drunk with honey, quickly stops hemorrhaging.
Sandalwood, indrayava, pāṭhā, kaṭukā, durālabhā,
guḍūcī, vāsaka, lodhra, and pippalī, combined with honey,
overcome blood associated with kapha and alleviate skin diseases, cough, and fever. || 15 ||

When the fire has been kindled by various applications of astringents and the kapha has been conquered, if the rakta-pitta is not pacified, then milk should be used for that condition where vāta is predominant;
goat's milk is supreme for this application, or cow's milk boiled with five parts of water may be used.
Or milk boiled with the Vidārigandhādi group of drugs, combined with sugar and honey;
or milk prepared with grapes, the Parṇinīs, Balā, Madhuka, Śvadaṃṣṭrā, or Śatāvarī, which overcomes hemorrhaging. || 17–18 ||
Ripe udumbara, kāśmarya, pathyā, kharjūra, and gostana, when licked individually with honey, destroy raktapitta.
By licking flower powder with honey, one attains health.

Likewise, one should lick the powder of *vāstuka* seeds combined with honey; or the powder known as *taṇḍulajākhyā*; or the powder of parched grain (*lāja*) and collyrium (*añjana*) alone; or similarly, *tugākhyā* combined with sugar and honey. (20–21)
Pathyā (Terminalia chebula) soaked seven times in the juice of vāsaka, or kṛṣṇā (Piper nigrum) licked with honey, quickly conquers raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorders).
[The quantity of liquid] should be such that the powder becomes a single mass and attains moisture.
Such is the measure prescribed by physicians for the method of medicinal saturation (bhāvanā).
Abhayā combined with honey is considered digestive, appetizing,
and it destroys phlegm (śleṣman) and hemorrhagic fever (raktapitta), while removing colic and diarrhea.
If one's breath and eructations smell of iron, one should eat pṛthvīkā smelling of smoke, measuring a śāṇa, along with double the amount of sugar.
Likewise, take half an akṣa each of cardamom, cinnamon leaves, and cinnamon bark, and half a pala of long pepper.
Having ground one pala each of sugar, licorice, dates, and raisins,
one should prepare pills mixed with honey;
then, one should consume one pill, the size of an *akṣa*, day after day.
Cough, dyspnea, fever, hiccup, vomiting, fainting, intoxication, vertigo, spitting of blood, thirst, pain in the flanks,
loss of appetite, wasting, splenic disorders, abdominal dropsy, voice changes, and consumption [are cured]. || 28 ||
This pill is nourishing, aphrodisiac, and destroys *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic diseases).
Finely ground *āmalaka* fried in ghee, when applied as a plaster to the head, stops bleeding from the nose just as a dam restrains the force of water.

If the discharge occurs through the nose, water mixed with sugar should be given immediately; or milk through the nostrils, or grape juice, or one should drink milk and ghee, or sugared sugarcane juice, or cold water. As a nasal medication (nasya), the juice extracted from pomegranate flowers or from dūrvā grass should be used.

A decoction derived from mango stones or from onions cures bleeding from the nose; however, when there is excessive discharge from the penis, an urethral enema (uttara-basti) is indicated. Juice made from pomegranate flowers, along with goat's milk and sugar, is also beneficial.
One should drink boiled milk prepared with the *pañcamūla* known as *tṛṇāhvaya*,
along with *dūrvā*, the filaments of the blue lotus, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *elavāluka*,
white and black *uśīra*, *musta*, *candana*, and *padmaka*.
One should cook this king of ghees with these grains over a mild fire.
Having added four times as much rice-water and goat's milk,
its drinking is for one vomiting blood, and its administration as nasal drops is for when it has reached the nose.
If blood flows from the ears, one should fill the ears with it;
if blood flows from the eyes, one should fill those eyes with it. If it flows from the penis or the anus, it is beneficial for the administration of enemas (vasti-karma).
And when that ointment has been applied to the pores of the skin, one should employ it.

Having prepared a decoction of vāsā along with its branches, leaves, and roots, and adding its flowers as a paste, one should cook ghee with honey; this quickly destroys [excessive] blood. || 38–39 ||
Because of the richness of the pastes from śaṇa, kovidāra, vṛṣa, and kakubha, they praise four palas of flower-paste [to be added].
[The ingredients are] śatāvarī, dāḍima, tittiḍīka, kākolī, medā, madhuka, and vidārī.
Having ground the root of the citron (*phalapūraka*), one should cook ghee with four times as much milk;
this ghee destroys cough, fever, abdominal distension, constipation, colic, and hemorrhagic disorders (*raktapitta*). (41) Two *prasthas* of juice from the roots of *śatāvarī* are prescribed. (42)
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with an equal amount of milk,
along with *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, *medā*, *mahāmedā*,
as well as *kākolī*, *kṣīrakākolī*, *mṛdvīkā*, and *madhuka*.
The physician should administer Mudgaparṇī, Māṣaparṇī, Vidārī, and red sandalwood,
prepared with sugar and honey, for the purpose of inducing purgation in cases of blood-bile disorders and diseases of Vātarakta. || 44-45 ||
When the semen is depleted, the highest form of aphrodisiac therapy (vājīkaraṇa) should be administered.
[It cures] burning sensations in the shoulders, burning sensations in the head, fever arising from pitta,
pain in the vagina, burning sensations, and pitta-type dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra).
This destroys these diseases quickly, just as the wind disperses hidden clouds.
This ghee made from śatāvarī increases strength, complexion, and digestive fire;
in this śatāvarī-ghṛta, sugar and honey should be added in one-quarter part each.
One part of honey should be added, as is traditionally prescribed for ghee used with the leaves;
then one hundred palas of well-steamed *kuṣmāṇḍaka* (pumpkin) with the seeds removed should be cooked slowly in a prastha of ghee in a sturdy copper vessel.
When the cooking has reached a honey-like consistency, one should add a hundred pieces of sugar-candy (khaṇḍa). Then,

two palas each of long pepper (pippalī) and ginger (śṛṅgavera), half a pala of cumin (jīraka), and half a pala each of cinnamon (tvak), cardamom (elā), cinnamon leaf (patra), black pepper (marica), and coriander (dhānyaka) should be added.
One should place the powder there and then stir it with a ladle; when it has become a paste and is well-cooled, one should add honey and half as much ghee.
A patient suffering from raktapitta or from chest-wound and consumption should eat this according to the strength of their digestive fire.
It alleviates cough, dyspnea, darkness of vision, vomiting, thirst, and fever;
it is aphrodisiac, rejuvenating, clarifies strength and complexion,
heals the chest, is nourishing, and restores the voice.
This excellent *kūṣmāṇḍaka* elixir was prepared by the Aśvins according to the method of the *khaṇḍakāmalakī*, as described using two *prasthas* of juice.
In the case of *khaṇḍakūṣmāṇḍaka*, the vessel [is filled] with the liquid from the steamed *kūṣmāṇḍaka*.

Except for the *khaṇḍakūṣmāṇḍa* preparation, all other juices are considered acceptable; however, the cooking of *kūṣmāṇḍa* with clarified butter should be done with its characteristic fragrance as the seal.
Fifty palas of cooked *kūṣmāṇḍa* and one prastha of clarified butter [are required]. (56–57)
One hundred palas of processed sugar candy should be cooked in one āḍhaka of vāsā decoction, along with one karṣa each of śuṇṭhī, dhātrī, musta, bhārṅgī, and the three aromatics (trisaugandhya),
and one pala each of aileya, viśva, dhānyaka, and marica.
One should administer one kuḍava of pippalī along with honey.
This cures cough, dyspnea, consumption, hiccup, hemoptysis, halīmaka, heart disease, amlapitta, and chronic rhinitis.
Taking one *tulā* of *vāsā*, the physician should boil it in eight times as much water; when reduced to one-fourth,
he should then cook one *āḍhaka* of powdered *abhayā* along with one hundred palas of purified sugar.
Two palas of powdered pippalī, one kuḍava (four palas) of honey once it has cooled after being prepared,
and one pala of well-powdered cāturjāta should be added; having stirred this together, the patient suffering from raktapitta should consume it according to their strength.
One afflicted by cough and dyspnea, and oppressed by consumption (yakṣman),
[should take] śatāvarī, chinnaruhā, vṛṣa, muṇḍitikā, balā, tālamūlī, gāyatrī, and likewise the bark of triphalā.
Five *palas* each of *bhārṅgī* and *puṣkaramūla* should be boiled in one *droṇa* of water until reduced to one-eighth.
This [mixture] may be used for [the purification of] mercury killed by divine herbs or killed by honey.
Twelve palas of powdered gold and copper should be given,
along with sixteen palas of ghee equal in measure to the sugar-candy;
the wise should cook this in a copper vessel until it reaches the consistency of molasses.
Half a *prastha* of honey should be added, along with auspicious *aśmajatuka*,
*tvac*, *śṛṅgī*, *viḍaṅga*, *kṛṣṇā*, ginger, and *ajājī*, each weighing one *pala*;
likewise, *triphalā*, *dhānyaka*, and *patra* [each] two *akṣas*, and *marica* and *kesara*.
Having added the powder and stirred it well, one should store it in a greased vessel;
then, at the appropriate time, one should administer a dose the size of a cat's paw (biḍālapadaka). Cow’s milk should be used as a post-drink, and meat broth or milk may also be consumed.
Guru (heavy), vṛṣya (aphrodisiac), and nourishing foods and drinks, as well as unctuous meat and other strengthening substances [are indicated].
They [cure] raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorders), consumption (kṣaya), cough, and especially colic of the digestive tract (paktiśūla),
as well as vātarakta (gout/rheumatism), prameha (urinary disorders), śītapitta, vomiting, and exhaustion.

It destroys swelling, anemia, skin diseases, as well as splenic enlargement, constipation, urinary discharge, and acid dyspepsia. It is beneficial for the eyes, nourishing, aphrodisiac, auspicious, and increases joy.

The celebrated sweetmeat known as *khaṇḍakhādya* is declared to be the best for bestowing health and sons, increasing the digestive fire and physical strength, bringing prosperity, and producing lightness of body.
The meat of goats, pigeons, partridges, *krakaras*, and hares [is likewise beneficial]. (75–76)
One should employ the meat of kuliṅga birds and black antelopes (kṛṣṇasāra), along with coconut milk, suniṣaṇṇaka, vāstuka,
dried radish, jīvā, paṭola, and the fruit of bṛhatī. (77)
Fruits such as the eggplant, ripe mango, date, and sweet pomegranate;
and whatever meat begins with the letter "ka" (kha) and originates from marshy lands—these must be especially avoided by one preparing sugar-candied sweets. || 78-79 ||

Whatever medicine has been prescribed for internal and external use in pitta-type fever is beneficial in raktapitta, as is that which is beneficial for those suffering from chest wounds and emaciation.
[One should consume] śāli rice, ṣaṣṭika rice, wheat, chickpeas, mung beans, and masūra lentils.
Śyāmāka and priyaṅgu are the food for those suffering from rakta-pitta.
Patola, nimba, vetrāgra, taṇḍulīya, and others are beneficial; likewise, pigeons, doves, and the like, as well as rabbits, eṇa-deer, and hariṇa-deer [are recommended]. 81–82.
Having prepared the fresh juice of the vṛṣa plant, one should employ it with these substances;
one should powder together priyaṅgu, mṛttikā, lodhra, and añjana.
This powder should be administered with the juices of those [plants], combined with honey.
This proven king of formulations destroys bleeding from the nose, mouth, anus, and penis when it flows with force;
it also stops blood that gushes forth from a wound caused by a weapon.
Even that [disease] remains completely covered by this powder. Indeed,

among the formulations prescribed in general, one should employ a remedy for blood-bile (raktapitta) and similar conditions after carefully considering the potency of the substances, whereas a different formulation should be used for diseases born of wind (vāta).
Chapter 10: Rice, sixty-day rice, wheat, barley, mung beans, and so forth are wholesome;
likewise, liquors and the meat of wild birds and animals are recommended for one who is emaciated. 1.

One should drink the unctuous meat broth of a goat, prepared with long pepper, barley, horse gram, ginger, pomegranate, and emblic myrobalan; by this, six disorders, such as chronic rhinitis (pīnasa) and others, are eliminated.
Meat should be double the quantity [of the liquid], water eightfold in all cases; when prepared with a quarter part of clarified butter, it is called a six-ingredient broth (ṣaḍaṅga-yūṣa).
One should drink water boiled with coriander, long pepper, ginger, and the ten roots (daśamūlī).
For the cessation of pain in the flanks, fever, dyspnea, catarrh, and other such ailments,
aśvagandhā, amṛtā, bhīru, daśamūlī, balā, vṛṣa, puṣkara, and ativiṣā destroy consumption for those who subsist on milk and meat broth. || 4-5 ||

A decoction prepared with the ten roots (daśamūlī), balā, rāsnā, puṣkara, devadāru, and nāgara should be drunk for the pacification of wasting cough and other ailments. [7] Powdered bark of kakubha, nāgabalā, and seeds of vānari should be taken with milk. [8]
Ripe [pippalī] combined with honey, ghee, and sugar cures consumption (yakṣma) and cough.
7 Honey, tāpya, viḍaṅga, ashman-tu, iron, ghee, and āmalaka, when consumed by one who eats wholesome food, destroy even the most violent consumption. 8
A linctus made from black grapes, black jujube, and sugar, combined with honey and oil, or one derived from *aśvagandhā*, black pepper, and sugar, combined with honey and ghee, cures consumption.
A patient suffering from consumption should lick fresh butter mixed with sugar and honey.
One who subsists on milk attains nourishment; or [one may take] ghee and honey in equal parts.
[One should take] sugar, *tugākṣīrī*, long pepper, and cinnamon bark, with each subsequent substance being double the amount of the preceding one; this should be licked with honey and ghee.
One should also administer this powder to those afflicted by dyspnea, cough, and phlegm; to those with pain in the flanks, weak digestive fire, numbness of the tongue, and loss of appetite;
and to those suffering from burning sensations in the hands, feet, and shoulders, as well as in fever, blood disorders, and upward-moving hemorrhage.
The fresh ghee that rises from milk boiled with the ten roots (daśamūlī), when combined with long pepper (kaṇā) and honey, purifies the voice;
it destroys pain in the head, shoulders, and sides, and removes dyspnea, cough, and fever.
This proven remedy, renowned throughout the world, is the supreme medicine for those suffering from consumption (śoṣa).
Having ground together śatapuṣpā, nata, kuṣṭha, madhuka, and devadāru, this paste mixed with ghee should be applied to alleviate pain in the back, the sides, and the shoulders.
The powder of *kākubha*, processed many times with the juice of *vāsaka* and licked with ghee,
honey, and sugar, removes consumption, cough, and hemorrhagic fever (rakta-pitta). [One should take] cardamom,
*ajamodā*, *āmalaka*, *abhayā*, *akṣa*, *gāyatrī*, neem, *āsana*, and *śālasāra*.
Having boiled viḍaṅga, bhallātaka, citraka, the three pungents (kaṭutrika), ambhoda, and surāṣṭrajā in water,
one should cook ghee with that decoction; when it has been well-cooked and removed from the heat,
one should add thirty palas of white sugar and six palas of tugākṣīrī.
One should add twice as much honey to a *prastha* of ghee, then churn it with a churning-stick;
one should lick it, one *pala* at a time, every morning, and thereafter drink milk without weariness.
For this is supremely beneficial for the intellect, purifying, good for the eyes, and likewise most conducive to longevity.

It truly and swiftly destroys consumption, as well as anemia, fistula-in-ano, dyspnea, hoarseness of voice, cough, and diseases of the heart, spleen, abdominal tumors, and malabsorption syndrome; moreover,
while this rejuvenative therapy (rasāyana) is being practiced, there is nothing whatsoever that must be avoided.

Balā, vidārī, the small pañcamūla, punarnavā, and the fruits of the five milky trees (kṣīrivṛkṣa), each in the measure of a handful—these, along with two parts of milk and one part of the juice of vidārī and aged jaggery, [should be boiled]. In their decoction... [23]
One should cook one āḍhaka of ghee with one akṣa each of the pastes of the vitalizing (jīvanīya) drugs.
When it has been strained and cooled, one should add thirty-two palas of sugar and the powder of wheat, long pepper, vāṃśī, and śṛṅgāṭaka.

One *kuḍava* measure of all these ingredients, including honey, should be thoroughly stirred with a churning stick until thickened; having formed them into balls of ghee-jaggery (*sarpirguḍa*), one should wrap them in birch bark.
Having eaten those *pālika* measures, one should subsequently drink milk or wine in cases of phlegm (*kapha*).

They are beneficial in cases of emaciation, cough, wasting due to chest injury, exhaustion from physical labor, sexual indulgence, or carrying heavy loads; as well as in the spitting of blood, fever, chronic catarrh, injuries to the chest,
pain in the sides or head, and disorders of the voice or complexion.
In this water-sugar decoction (vāriguḍa) containing one droṇa, sixteen *prasthas* of water should be added.
[The ingredients are: *bilva*, *agnimantha*, *śyonāka*, *kāśmarya*, *pāṭalī*, *balā*, the four *parṇīs*, *pippalī*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, and the two types of *bṛhatī*.
Śṛṅgī, tāmalakī, drākṣā, jīvantī, puṣkara, aguru, abhayā,
amṛtā, ṛddhi, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, śaṭhī, mustā, punarnavā, medā, sūkṣmailā, utpala, and candana. || 30–31 ||
One pala each of vidārī, vṛṣamūla, kākolī, and kākanāsikā,
along with five hundred āmalaka fruits— one should place these together and boil them in one droṇa of water.
Having ascertained that the substance has lost its juice, one should take the strained essence.
Then, having extracted that āmalaka fruit and removed the seeds, the physician should fry it in twelve palas of oil and ghee, and add half a tulā [of sugar].
One should properly prepare one *ṣaṭpala* (six palas) of purified sugar-candy as if making a linctus; once it has been cooked and cooled, one should add six palas of honey,
four palas of *tugākṣīrī*, and likewise two palas of *pippalī*.
And one should add one pala each of cinnamon-bark, cardamom, cinnamon-leaves, and saffron.
This is called Cyavanaprāśa, which is declared to be a supreme elixir (rasāyana);
it specifically teaches the remedy for cough and dyspnea.
It promotes the growth of the limbs of those who are emaciated, wounded, aged, or young;
it removes loss of voice, diseases of the chest, heart disease, and gout (vātaśoṇita),
as well as thirst and disorders of the urine and semen.
One should administer its dose such that it does not obstruct one’s meal;
by its use, Cyavana, though very old, became young again.
It bestows intelligence, memory, luster, freedom from disease, longevity, and strength of the senses.

By the use of this elixir, even an old man, through confinement in a chamber, shall obtain supreme delight with women, a blazing of the highest fire, clarity of complexion, and favorability of the bodily winds;
casting off his former appearance produced by old age, he bears the form of fresh youth. (40–41)
Some desire white sugar in place of granulated sugar;
the cooking of roasted *dhātrī* is praised when it reaches the consistency of a soft paste.
[The following ingredients are used: *daśamūlī*, *svayaṃguptā*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *śaṭhī*, and *balā*. (42–43)
One should boil two palas each of *hastipippalī*, *apāmārga*, *pippalīmūla*, *citraka*, and *bhārgī*, along with *puṣkaramūla* and one *āḍhaka* of barley,
as well as one hundred *harītakī* fruits, in five *āḍhakas* of water.
One should boil that strained decoction made from steamed barley with one hundred *abhayā* fruits;
then, adding one *tulā* of jaggery, one *kuḍava* each of ghee and oil, and the powder of long pepper, once it is prepared and cooled, one should add honey.
One should take one *kuḍava* of well-powdered *cāturjāta*, weighing one *pala*, and daily consume two *abhayā* fruits; from this elixir (*rasāyana*), one should eat.
It destroys wrinkles and graying hair, and increases complexion, longevity, and strength. (47)

It destroys the five types of cough, dyspnea, hiccup, and irregular fever; it cures abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, malabsorption syndrome, hemorrhoids, heart disease, anorexia, and chronic rhinitis.
This auspicious and excellent elixir was proclaimed by Agastya.
If the bile (pitta) acts according to the qualities previously described,

then this very jaggery (guḍa) should be administered in the evening in a small dose. When the decoction has been reduced to one-quarter and the myrobalans (harītakī) have been steamed, [they should be added].
Having fried [these] in ghee and oil, one should cook them until they turn reddish. [The ingredients are:
jīvantī, kuṭaja, grapes, the fruits of kuṭaja, śaṭhī, puṣkara root, vyāghrī, gokṣuraka, and balā. || 51–52 ||
Having ground together blue lotus, *tāmalakī*, *trāyamāṇā*, *durālabhā*, and long pepper in equal parts, the physician should cook ghee;
this [remedy] is for the multitude of diseases arising from the Lord of Disease.
Ghee prepared with eleven kinds of spices and *pippalī* and jaggery,
combined with goat’s milk, removes even severe consumption; this ghee is for the purpose of increasing the digestive fire in those suffering from wasting and cough.

Ghee prepared with long pepper (pippalī), long pepper root (pippalīmūla), chaba pepper (cavya), leadwort (citraka), dry ginger (nāgara), and barley-alkali (yāvaśūka), along with milk, cleanses the channels;
[in this case, the paste should be one-fourth part and the milk four times the quantity]. || 56 ||

One should boil one *tulā* each of *yaṣṭīmadhu*, *balā*, *guḍūcī*, and the minor *pañcamūla* in a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) until eight parts remain of the water. Into that, one should cook one *pātra* of ghee for the purpose of healing eye diseases,
along with three *pātras* each of the juices of *dhātrī*, *vidārī*, and sugarcane, and [three] *pātras* of milk.
This Pārāśara ghee, when consumed regularly with well-ground vitalizing (jīvanīya) herbs, uproots even king’s consumption (rājayakṣman) along with its army.
Taking one tulā of goat meat, one should cook it in non-saline water.
With that same remainder of the decoction,
one should cook one *prastha* of ghee with the pastes (*kalka*) of *ṛddhi*, *vṛddhi*, the two types of *medā*, *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, *kākolī*, and *kṣīrakākolī*, each weighing one *pala*.
Once it is known to be properly prepared and has cooled, one should cause it to be given; one should add eight *palas* of sugar and one *kuḍava* of honey.
One should drink it every morning, *pala* by *pala*, and it destroys even difficult-to-overcome consumption (*yakṣman*).
It cures wasting due to chest wounds, the five types of cough, pain in the flanks, loss of appetite,
hoarseness of voice, diseases of the chest, and even most severe dyspnea.
It is strengthening, flesh-building, aphrodisiac, and an excellent stimulator of the digestive fire.
Having boiled one hundred palas of goat meat in two droṇas of water until reduced to one-eighth,
one should cook one prastha of ghee in that well-prepared liquid with a *kuḍava* of the paste of the *jīvanīya* drugs; this is *māṃsasarpiḥ*.
When combined with meat broth and drunk, it destroys pitta and vāta, as well as the diseases born from them;
it pacifies severe cough and dyspnea, consumption, and the terrible pain of the sides and heart, as well as emaciation from travel and sexual excess—there is nothing superior to this. (66–67)

One should boil two *prasthas* of the decoction of the "two groups of five roots" (*dvipañcamūla*) with one *prastha* of meat broth, having properly added a paste (*kalka*) of *balā* as an internal ingredient; this ghee, when prepared and combined with one *prastha* of milk, is prescribed for curing all injuries from trauma, consumption, colic, chest wounds, wasting, and cough. || 68 ||
Having prepared a decoction of balā, śvadaṃṣṭrā, bṛhatī, kalaśī, dhāvanī, sthirā, nimba, parpaṭaka, musta, trāyamāṇā, and durālabhā,
one should add tāmalakī and śaṭhī as a paste.
Grapes, puṣkaramūla, medā, and āmalaka—
clarified butter prepared from these with milk is a supreme remedy for fever;
it pacifies wasting cough and relieves pain in the head and the sides of the chest.
One should also plant sandalwood water, nakha, yaṣṭī, śaileya, padmaka,
mañjiṣṭhā, sarala, dāru, śaṭhī, elā, pūtika, kesara, patra, ela, murā, māṃsī, kaṅkola, vanitā, and ambuda. || 72–73 ||
With haridrā, sārivā, tiktā, lavaṅga, aguru, kuṅkuma, tvak, reṇu, and nalikā, oil mixed with four times as much mastu (whey) and an equal amount of lac-resin, when prepared,
destroys the influence of malevolent spirits and increases strength.
It destroys epilepsy, fever, insanity, sin, and ill fortune; it promotes longevity and nourishment, and is an excellent means of subjugation.
In cases of fever, burning sensations, and weakness, one should employ lac-resin oil (lākṣātaila).
As stated in the section on diseases of children, according to traditional oral instruction:
Balā, aśvagandhā, śrīparṇī, bahupatrī, and punarnavā,
when practiced daily with milk, pacify chest wounds and wasting (kṣatakṣaya).
A patient suffering from consumption (kṣaya) should drink ghee combined with milk and honey, along with *ikṣvālikā*, *viśvagandhā*, *padmakesara*, and *candana*, for the purpose of healing.
One should also drink ghee prepared with the decoction of *balā*, *nāgabalā*, and *arjuna*, together with a paste (*kalka*) consisting of one-quarter part of *yaṣṭīmadhu*.
It pacifies heart disease, colic, wounds, hemorrhaging, wasting, and aggravated wind-blood disorders.
In this regard, the preparation known as *khaṇḍakūṣmāṇḍa* is especially beneficial.
For the strength of men depends on semen, and indeed, life depends on the impurities [of the body].

Therefore, one should carefully guard the waste and semen of a patient suffering from consumption (yakṣman). A patient who constantly honors his own body and is devoted to medicine, deities, and teachers, living on goat meat and milk, shall live for a long time with fortitude.
One should overcome complications such as disorders of the voice by carefully consulting the relevant scriptures;
one should abandon grief, women, anger, and malice,
and instead cultivate noble objects of experience.
One should worship the gurus, the twice-born, and the gods,
and listen to sacred stories from the twice-born.
[One who suffers] from cough, dysentery, pain in the flanks, hoarseness of voice, loss of appetite, and fever—
Or it may be afflicted by three symptoms: dyspnea, cough, and blood disorders. Aversion to food, fever, dyspnea, cough, hemoptysis, and hoarseness of voice arise in the sixfold form of *rājayakṣman*.
If a young man afflicted by consumption is treated by skilled physicians, he may live for at most a thousand days.
(86) Chapter 11.
A decoction prepared from the five roots (pañcamūlī), combined with the powder of long pepper (pippalī), when taken daily with meat broth or rice, dispels cough caused by Vāta.
[2] A preparation made from Bhārgī, grapes (drākṣā), Śaṭhī, Śṛṅgī, long pepper, and Viśvabheṣaja...
A linctus combined with jaggery and oil is beneficial for those suffering from coughs caused by Vāta.
(2) Viśva, Duḥsparśā, Śṛṅgī, Drākṣā, Śaṭhī, and sugar, when powdered and licked with oil, conquer even a difficult-to-cure cough arising from Vāta. (3)
Water boiled with *balā*, *vibhītaka*,

and *rākṣā* should be drunk, combined with sugar and honey, to cure cough caused by *pitta*. Likewise, [water boiled with] the five roots beginning with *śara*, as well as *pippalī* and *rākṣā*, [should be used].
One should drink milk boiled with a decoction [of the aforementioned herbs], mixed with honey and sugar.
Indeed, this—combined with grapes, madhuka, dates, long pepper, and black pepper—removes pitta-type cough; one should lick it with honey and ghee.

Equal parts of dates, long pepper, grapes, sugar, and parched rice, taken as a linctus combined with honey and ghee, is an excellent remedy for curing pitta-type cough. [7] [Likewise, preparations may be made] from mung beans and *āmalaka*, or from barley and pomegranate, or from *karkandhu* and radish with ginger.
A soup made from ginger, long pepper, and horse gram is the "nine-ingredient" (navāṅga) preparation that destroys cough caused by phlegm.
One should drink a decoction prepared with lotus stalk, katphala, bhārṅgī, long pepper,
and dry ginger in cases of excessive phlegm, cough, dyspnea, and cardiac oppression.
One should cause [the patient] to drink the fresh juice of ginger combined with honey;
it destroys dyspnea and cough, and removes catarrh and phlegm, [as well as] pain in the flanks, fever, asthma, and cough arising from kapha. (10)
One should drink water boiled with *daśamūlī* combined with the powder of *pippalī*.
[Alternatively,] *kaṭphala*, *kattṛṇa*, *bhārṅgī*, *musta*, *dhānya*, *vacā*, *abhayā*, *śuṇṭhī*, *parpaṭaka*, *śṛṅgī*, and *surāhva* boiled in water [should be drunk].

It should be drunk with honey and asafoetida in cases of cough caused by vāta and kapha, as well as in major diseases of the throat, asthma, hiccups, and fever. Tālīśapatra, marica, nāgara, and auspicious pippalī [should be used].
With each subsequent ingredient increasing by one part, half a part each of cinnamon (tvak) and cardamom (ela) should be added;
here, white sugar should be given in eight parts of long pepper (pippalī).
This [mixture] cures dyspnea, cough, anorexia, vomiting, splenic disorders, and pain in the heart and flanks.
One should prepare pills and powder by cooking white sugar, which destroys jaundice, fever, and diarrhea, and facilitates the downward movement of obstructed wind (mūḍhavāta).
Indeed, pills are considered lighter than powder due to their contact with fire.
In cough caused by vāta and kapha, one should employ the tālīsādyacūrṇa;
when associated with pitta, it is best when combined with vaṃśalocana.
The fresh juice of vāsaka should be drunk mixed with honey by one who follows a wholesome diet.
In cough caused by pitta and kapha, and especially in raktapitta (hemoptysis),
as well as in cough due to chest injury, treatment should consist of strengthening, nourishing, and vitalizing measures,
along with the pacifying remedies prescribed for pitta-type cough and other sweet medicinal drugs.
Madhuka, pippalī, drākṣā, lākṣā, śṛṅgī, and śatāvarī—each of these [in equal parts]—with twice as much tugākṣīrī and four times as much sugar;
one should lick this with honey and ghee for the cessation of cough due to chest injury (kṣatakāsa). || 20–21 ||
A linctus made from long pepper (pippalī), lotus stalk (padmaka), lac (lākṣā), and the fruit of bṛhatī,
cooked together and mixed with ghee and honey, destroys cough caused by chest injury (kṣatakāsa).
Abhayā, dry ginger (śuṇṭhī), kaṇā, or vibhītaka, when held in the mouth, [achieve the same].
Alternatively, a single *vibhītaka* fruit dispels both cough and dyspnea.
One should hold a pill made of *pathyā*, ginger, *ghana*, and jaggery in the mouth for all types of dyspnea and cough; or simply a single *vibhītaka* fruit alone.
One should inhale smoke made from realgar, orpiment, black pepper, māṃsī, musta, and iṅguda; thereafter, one should drink pleasantly warm milk with jaggery.
This [remedy] cures coughs arising from individual doṣas, from combinations of two, or from all the doṣas together.

One may quickly cure even those conditions that are incurable by hundreds of other applications. A leaf smeared with realgar (manaḥśilā), dried in the sun after being placed on a *badarī* tree, when used as an inhalation with milk, is a remedy for severe cough. (26–27)
One *karṣa* is a *pala* consisting of four parts; two *palas* shall be half a *karṣa* each of black pepper, long pepper, pomegranate, jaggery, and *yavaśūka*.
Those coughs which are incurable by all other medicines and abandoned by all physicians— [these are cured by this]. (28)
Even for those vomiting pus, this is the supreme medicine.
Then, the knower of yoga should drink the powder of equal parts of *arka* bark and *śilājatu*, with half as much of the three pungents (*kaṭutrika*), cast into fire, and inhale its smoke. (29–30)
Then one should consume betel leaf, or drink milk or water;
the five types of coughs will quickly reach pacification, of this there is no doubt.
A decoction made from Kaṇṭakārī with Kṛṣṇā (Pippalī) destroys all coughs. (31)
Having prepared one akṣa each of the parts of cloves, nutmeg, and long pepper, one should add half a pala of black pepper and four palas of ginger;
this powder, equal in weight to sugar, swiftly and forcibly destroys these diseases by its strength.

One should cook ghee with the paste of bhārṅgī and a decoction of daśamūla; when prepared in the broth of a cock or a common partridge, it is supreme for conquering cough caused by vāta, as well as fever, anorexia, urinary disorders, abdominal tumors, dyspnea, weak digestion, and disorders of the grahaṇī. || 33–34 ||

One *prastha* of ghee should be cooked in one *āḍhaka* of the decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*) with the following ingredients in the measure of one *akṣa* each: *puṣkaramūla*, *śaṭhī*, *bilva*, *surasā*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), and asafoetida (*hiṅgu*).
