This should be drunk with milk as an after-drink in cases of cough caused by *vāta* and *kapha*.
In all diseases of the breath (śvāsa), as well as those characterized by phlegm and wind (kaphavātātman),
one should take an āḍhaka of the juice from Kaṇṭakārī, including its roots, leaves, and branches,
along with a prastha of ghee and [the paste of] balā, vyoṣa, viḍaṅga, śaṭī, and citraka. || 36–37 ||
With sauvarcala salt, yavakṣāra, bilva, āmalaka, and puṣkara;
with vṛścīva, bṛhatī, pathyā, yavānī, dāḍima, and ṛddhi;
and with drākṣā, punarnavā, cavya, durālabhā, and amlavetasa. || 38–39 ||
One should cook [this] with the pastes of śṛṅgī, tāmalakī, bhārṅgī, rāsnā, and gokṣuraka;
this Kaṇṭakārī-ghṛta is recommended for all types of cough and for hiccup and dyspnea, as it destroys all diseases caused by kapha. (40)
One *prastha* of ghee prepared with thirty *palas* each of the decoctions of *kaṇṭakārī* and *guḍūcī* cures vāta-type cough and stimulates the digestive fire.
One should boil *rāsnā*, *daśamūlī*, and *śatāvarī* in one *droṇa* of water. [41–42]
Three *palas*, one *māṇika*, and three *aṃśas* of *kulattha*, *badara*, and *yava*;
half a *tulā* of goat meat; with that [decoction] reduced to one-fourth, along with one *āḍhaka* of ghee, an equal amount of milk, and one *pala* each of the *jīvanīya* drugs.
That [preparation] is perfected with ten types of pastes for use as nasal drops, internal potions, and oil enemas.
One should employ it according to the specific condition in all diseases of Vāta, including the five types of cough, tremors of the head, and pain in the vagina and groin.
It conquers diseases of all the limbs or of a single limb, as well as splenic disorders and upward-moving wind (ūrdhvānila),
and likewise asthma, consumption, pain in the flanks, and loss of appetite. [The drugs used are] Jīvaka, Ṛṣabhaka, the two Medās, the two Kākolīs, Madhuka, and the two Saha varieties.
This group of drugs beginning with Jīvantī is vitalizing, sweet, and life-sustaining.
Ghee prepared with a paste of Rāsnā, Balā, Vyōṣa, and Śvadaṃṣṭrā,
boiled in the decoction of Kaṇṭakārī, destroys the five types of cough when consumed.

Four *prasthas* of the decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūlī*) should be boiled with one *prastha* of clarified butter, along with the paste (*kalka*) of the five pungent spices (*pañcakola*) and the alkalis (*kṣāra*). When properly prepared, this cures cough and pain in the heart and flanks, and it eradicates hiccup and dyspnea. (49)
A pill should be prepared from equal parts of tālīśa, vahnidīpyaka, cavikā, amlavetasa, and vyoṣa, combined with the three aromatics (trisugandhi) and jaggery.
It is used for cough, dyspnea, anorexia, chronic rhinitis, and disorders of the heart, throat, and speech.
And for disorders arising from *grahaṇī* and the rectum, there is the pill named Vyoṣāntikā. (Adhikāra 12) [The ingredients are:
the marrow of a jujube fruit (*kola*), collyrium (*añjana*), parched grain (*lāja*), *tiktā*, and golden ochre (*kāñcanagairika*).
Black *dhātrī*, white sugar, ginger, *kāsīsa*, and *dadhināman* (copperasol);
the fruit and flower of *pāṭalī*, black [sugar], date-palm, and *mustaka*— these six linctuses, mixed with honey and prepared with one-fourth part [of the other ingredients], destroy hiccup.
Madhuka mixed with honey, Pippalī combined with sugar, and Nāgara mixed with jaggery— these three nasal drops (nāvana) destroy hiccup.
Alternatively, the excrement of flies mixed with breast milk, or lac dissolved in water, may be used as a nasal drop.
Or milk mixed with sandalwood should be administered to one overcome by hiccups.
One afflicted by hiccups should drink the juice of *mātuluṅga* combined with honey and *sauvarcala* salt;
or one suffering from hiccups should lick a mixture of dry ginger, *dhātrī*, and *kaṇā* with honey.
The powder of black pepper, āmalaka, and ginger, combined with honey and sugar,
should be administered repeatedly to ward off hiccup and dyspnea.
[6] By means of restraining the breath, threatening, startling, and the sprinkling of cold water...
One should pacify hiccup through various narrative applications and by striking the mind.

For one afflicted by hiccup and dyspnea, sudation with oil is desired first; once the patient is capable, purification (śodhana) from above and below is prescribed, while for the weak, palliative treatment (śamana) is considered appropriate.
One suffering from hiccup and dyspnea should drink bhārṅgī with viśvā along with warm water; or ginger combined with sugar, bhārṅgī, and sauvarcala salt.
Alternatively, one may take a paste of abhayā and nāgara, or a paste of puṣkara, yavaśūka, and marica.
One suffering from hiccup or asthma should drink it with warm water for their pacification.
Or, one afflicted by hiccup and asthma who is thirsty should drink a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*) or of *devadāru*, or wine, in the appropriate manner.

One should drink the powder of śṛṅgī, the two types of kaṭutrika, triphalā, kaṇṭakārī, bhārṅgī, and the root of puṣkara, along with the five salts, with non-cold water for hiccups, dyspnea, upward-moving wind (ūrdhvavāta), cough, loss of appetite, and chronic catarrh (pīnasa).
[12] Śaṭhī, coraka, jīvantī, tvak, musta, and that which is called puṣkara—
Having made an equal powder of *surasā*, *tāmalakī*, cardamom, long pepper, *aguru*, ginger, and *vālaka*, one should add eight times as much sugar;
this should be employed at all times in cases of *tamaka* asthma, dyspnea, and hiccups.

Soup made from the leaves of *kāsamarda* and *saubhāñjana*, as well as soup of dried radish, prevents hiccup and labored breathing (asthma). Whatever [substance] destroys phlegm and wind, is hot, and facilitates the downward movement of wind [is beneficial]. || 15 ||
Medicine, whether as a drink or food, is beneficial in cases of hiccup and dyspnea.
A decoction prepared from *amṛtā*, *nāgara*, *phañjī*, *vyāghrī*, and *parṇāsa*, when drunk with the powder of *kaṇā*, quickly conquers cough and dyspnea.
A decoction of the ten roots (daśamūlī), equal in measure to ginger, black pepper, and abhayā, when sprinkled with puṣkara powder, removes cough and dyspnea;
it pacifies cough and dyspnea and destroys pain in the flanks and the heart.

Water boiled with *kulattha*, *nāgara*, *vyāghrī*, and *vāsā*, when drunk together with *puṣkara*, prevents asthma and cough. One should lick an equal amount of jaggery mixed with pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*).
By practicing this for three weeks, one shall conquer asthma from its very root.
By licking a mixture of grapes, harītakī, kṛṣṇā, karkaṭa, and durālabhā with honey and clarified butter, one destroys even the most severe forms of asthma.

One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with twice as much milk and four times as much water, along with *hiṃsrā*, *viḍaṅga*, *pūtīka*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), the three pungents (*tryoṣa*), and *citraka*, each in the measure of a *kola*. This indeed cures asthma and cough.
It cures hemorrhoids, loss of appetite, abdominal tumors, diarrhea, and wasting;
in this case, one *karṣa* should be used in place of the *kola*, according to the reason observed by others.
Having taken one hundred [palas] of *bhārṅgī* and likewise of *daśamūlī*.
One should cook one hundred *harītakī* fruits in four times as much water; when that liquid has been reduced to one-fourth and strained through a cloth,
one should then dissolve a purified *tulā* of jaggery and an *abhayā* fruit into it.
One should cook it again over a gentle fire until it reaches the consistency of a linctus (leha), and once cooled, one should add six palas of honey.
Then, one pala each of the three pungents (trikaṭu) and the three aromatics (trisugandha) should be added separately. || 27 ||
Then, having powdered two karṣas of barley-alkali (yavakṣāra), one should add it [to the mixture]. One should consume one abhayā fruit and lick half a pala of the linctus;
this destroys even most dreadful asthma as well as the five types of cough.
This electuary bestows a beautiful voice and complexion and kindles the digestive fire.
For this, one hundred *harītakī* fruits require one *prastha* of water in addition [to the other ingredients].
Likewise, there should be *kulattha*, *daśamūla*, and *dvija-yaṣṭikā*.
One should take one hundred [palas] each and boil them in a droṇa of water;
when that is reduced to one-fourth, one should add half a tulā of jaggery,
and once it has cooled and been cooked, eight palas of honey.
One should consume six *palas* of *tugākṣīrī*, two *palas* of *pippalī*,
and the three aromatics (*trisugandhi*) according to one's digestive strength;
this will destroy cough, dyspnea, fever, hiccup, and asthma.
In this case, based on the observation of practice and the instruction of experienced physicians, four parts of water should be added because the quantity of the *droṇa* of water is small;
and two *palas* of the three aromatic substances (*trisugandhi*) should be added, according to the agreement with the presence of the mental [tradition]. (34–35)
Chapter 13:
First, lukewarm water should be drunk after consuming rice with ghee and jaggery;
in cases arising from pitta, one should untiringly drink clarified butter with milk as an after-drink. 1.
A wise person should drink long pepper (pippalī), long pepper root (pippalīmūla), black pepper (marica), and ginger (viśvabheṣaja) with urine in cases of loss of voice caused by kapha.
In cases of hoarseness arising from fat (medas), the procedure prescribed for kapha is desired.
In cases of disorders born of depletion (kṣayaja) or those arising from all three doṣas (sarvaja), one should perform medical treatment after first declaring the prognosis.

A powder made from equal parts of cavya, sour vetasa, the three pungents (kaṭutrika), tittiḍīka, tālīsa, jīraka, tugā, and dahana, combined with treacle and the three aromatics (trisugandhi), is recommended for hoarseness of voice, chronic rhinitis (pīnasa), phlegm disorders, and loss of appetite.
One should administer this linctus— consisting of the paste of jujube leaves fried in ghee and mixed with rock salt— for hoarseness of voice and cough. Alternatively,
one may use [medicinal herbs] boiled with sweet substances, mixed with sugar and honey.
One whose voice is impaired while speaking loudly should drink milk.
Ghee cooked with the juice of *vyāghrī* and with *rāsnā*, *vāṭyāla*, *gokṣura*, and *vyoṣa* destroys impairment of the voice and the five types of cough.
When fresh juices are unavailable, one should prepare a decoction from dried substances using eight times the quantity of water; it should be taken when reduced to one-fourth. (Adhikāra 14, Verse 8)

When vomiting has occurred due to wind (*vāta*), one should drink the powder of long pepper (*kṛṣṇā*), viḍaṅga, barley ash, reṇukā, bhārṅgī, rāsnā, elā, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), rock salt (*lavaṇottama*), and ginger (*nāgara*) with water boiled with vacā according to the prescribed method, or with oil, warm water, or any kind of wine.
In the case of bile (*pitta*), emesis is recommended with jaggery-water and sweet substances; a linctus made of rock salt, sugar, honey, and ghee is desired.
For a kaphaja type, the post-prandial drink (anupāna) should be neem water mixed with honey and enriched with *dīpyaka*;
or else, one should administer the powder previously mentioned for the vātaja type, or likewise employ all the measures prescribed for all [three doshas] combined. || 2 ||

One should administer enemas for disorders arising from wind (vāta), purgatives for bile (pitta), and emetics for phlegm (kapha); however, for those caused by mental distress, one should employ things pleasing to the heart and methods that bring joy.
But in cases where the afflictions arise from the destruction of desires or from fear, [the following applies].

One should indeed prescribe treatments for existence that are capable of bringing about further existence; furthermore, when matters have transcended their ordinary scope, one should infer the means for rebirth through the ancient paths of the Vedas.
One should [prescribe] various foods that are wholesome and customary to one's own region.

One should consume various foods such as roots, fruits, sweets, syrups, and linctuses, and enjoy diverse juices through various preparations; furthermore, one should eat light, dry, and mentally pleasing meals.
Tamarind with jaggery-water, combined with cinnamon, cardamom, and black pepper, is recommended for gargling in diseases characterized by a loss of desire for food.
[6] Kuṣṭha, sauvarcala salt, cumin, sugar, black pepper, and biḍa salt... [7]
Dhātrī, elā, padmaka, uśīra, pippalī, candana, utpala, lodhra, tejovatī, pathyā, tryūṣaṇa, and yavāgraja,
along with the juice of fresh dāḍima, ajājī, and sugar.
These four gargles, containing oil and honey, destroy the four types of anorexia— those caused by vāta alone, and those arising from all [doshas] combined.
The three pungents (ūṣaṇa), triphalā, and the two types of turmeric (rajanī), powdered and mixed with the awns of barley, [are used as a powder].
One should provide other bitter and pungent medicines mixed with honey for the purpose of cleansing the mouth.
Kārava, jīraka, marica, drākṣā, vṛkṣāmla, dāḍima, sauvarcala salt, jaggery, and honey destroy all types of anorexia.
One should prepare one karṣa each of yavānī, tittiḍīka, nāgara, amlavetasa, dāḍima, and sour badara;
and half a karṣa each of dhānyaka, sauvarcala, ajājī, and varāṅga. || 12–13 ||
One hundred pippalīs, two hundred maricas,
and four palas of sugar should be powdered together.
This powder cleanses the tongue, is pleasing to the heart, and stimulates the appetite for food.

It destroys pain in the heart, spleen, and flanks; it removes constipation and flatulence; it alleviates cough and dyspnea; it is astringent; and it cures disorders of the digestive tract and hemorrhoids.
(15) Chapter 15.

Since all types of vomiting are considered to arise from the agitation of the stomach (āmāśaya), one should first employ fasting, with the exception of that caused by Vāta; or else, one should administer purification therapies that eliminate Kapha and Pitta.
Milk mixed with water, when drunk, destroys vomiting born of Vāta.
One should drink ghee with rock salt to ward off vomiting caused by Vāta;
or a soup of Mudga and Āmalaka with ghee and rock salt;
or one should drink gruel prepared with the five roots (pañcamūlī) mixed with honey.

In the case of a Pitta-dominant condition, for the purpose of downward movement [of the doshas], Trivṛt should be administered with the juices of grapes, Vidārī, and sugarcane; however, if the Pitta located in the seat of Kapha has increased excessively, one should eliminate it upwards using sweet substances.
Once purified, at the appropriate time, one should take a churned drink (mantha) made with honey, sugar, and parched grain, or even a thin gruel (peyā).
Or one should cause [the patient] to drink boiled rice with the juice of *mudgara* or with the juices of wild animals.
Having mixed *āmalakī* juice with an *akṣa*-measure of sandalwood, one should drink it combined with honey; by this, vomiting is brought to an end.

A decoction of roasted mung beans with parched grain (lāja), honey, and sugar is proclaimed as a remedy that destroys vomiting, diarrhea, thirst, burning sensations, and fever. One should also lick the powder of *harītakī* combined with honey.
When the morbid humor (doṣa) has been directed downward, vomiting ceases quickly.
A decoction of parpaṭaka drunk with honey destroys vomiting;
likewise, water boiled with guḍūcī, triphalā, ariṣṭa, and paṭolī [achieves the same].
[This preparation] with honey and sugar destroys vomiting and acid bile.

For vomiting characterized by phlegm (kapha), emesis is recommended using *piṇḍītaka* fruits combined with long pepper (*pippalī*), mustard, and neem water, along with rock salt (*saindhava*), provided it does not conflict with the patient's strength, for the purpose of purifying the phlegm.
One should drink the powder of viḍaṅga, triphalā, and viśva mixed with honey;
or one may cure vomiting born of phlegm by using viḍaṅga, plava, and śuṇṭhī.
Alternatively, one may take the powder of badara along with jāmbava, or karkaṭaka-śṛṅgī combined with mustā.

One should lick *durālabhā* mixed with honey for the purpose of suppressing phlegm and vomiting. Alternatively, one should take a nourishing preparation (*tarpaṇa*) combined with honey as a remedy for these three [conditions]. Furthermore, a decoction prepared from *guḍūcī* according to the prescribed method is known as "the cold infusion" (*himasaṃjñita*).
In all three types [of vomiting], one should drink a wholesome decoction combined with honey;
or a cold decoction of *śrīphala* or *guḍūcī* mixed with honey should be drunk during the three kinds of vomiting; or alternatively, *mūrvā* with rice-water.
For one drinking small amounts of water boiled with jambū, āmra-pallava, gavedhuka, dhānya, sevya, and hrīvera,
along with honey and the three aromatics (trisugandhi), vomiting is pacified.
Durālabhā licked with honey also destroys [vomiting].
A linctus made from the juice of the Jātī fruit combined with long pepper (pippalī) and black pepper (marica), and mixed with honey, destroys even severe vomiting.
Sauvarcala salt, cumin, sugar, and black pepper— this linctus, when combined with honey, is excellent for curing vomiting.
The pulp of the kola fruit, long pepper, dhātrī, parched rice, ginger, and the three myrobalans (phalatrika)—
Śyāmā, añjana, water from a rain cloud, kola-bone, and the excrement of a fly—these five combined [with honey] form one linctus.
Equal parts of kaṇā, uṣaṇa, kapittha-water, tvak, elā, and patra, mixed with honey, form another.
These six linctuses, each containing one-fourth part [of honey], are destroyers of vomiting.
A linctus made from the marrow of *kolānalaka*, honey, beeswax, black pepper, and rice, quickly suppresses vomiting.
[21] A linctus of parched grain (*lāja*), *kapittha*, honey, *māgadhika* (long pepper), and black pepper [achieves the same].

Three electuaries—consisting of honey, harītakī, trikaṭu, dhānyaka, and jīraka; and consisting of pathyā, amṛtā, marica, honey, and pippalī—are for the pacification of all types of vomiting and loss of appetite. (22)
Having licked the powders of cardamom, cloves, nutmeg, the marrow of *kola* fruit, parched grain, *priyaṅgu*, thick sandalwood, and long pepper,
combined with honey and white sugar;
It destroys vomiting born of phlegm, wind, and bile.

Having added honey to water boiled with the tender leaves of *jambu* and mango, and having cooled it well and sprinkled it with parched grain (*lāja*), one should drink it; this is a proven remedy for vomiting and diarrhea. 23–24.
In cases of vomiting that has persisted for a long time, treatments that subdue the wind (vāta) should be employed.

For, due to the continuous occurrence of vomiting, the wind inevitably increases as a result of the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātu); therefore, in long-standing cases, wind-alleviating measures that provide support and nourishment should be administered.

Medicated jaggery with ghee mixed with milk, the Kalyāṇaka, Tryūṣaṇa, and Jīvana formulations, aphrodisiacs, as well as meat broths and electuaries, bring about the pacification of persistent vomiting.
Vomiting born of disgust is cured by most pleasing things, and that born of pregnancy-longing by desired fruits.

One should treat vomiting caused by undigested matter (āma) with fasting and emesis; that arising from unwholesome things with wholesome regimens; and that born of worms in the same manner as heart disease caused by worms.
One should boil [a paste] of padmaka, amṛta, nimba, dhānya, and candana.
A *prastha* measure of clarified butter prepared with the paste and decoction [of these drugs] is a remedy that prevents vomiting,
alleviates thirst and loss of appetite, and is supreme for removing burning sensations and fever.
(29) Chapter 16.
When thirst arises from wind (vāta), curd mixed with jaggery is recommended,
as well as nourishing, cooling juices and the juice of *guḍūcī*.
Or, water boiled with the first of the five groups of five-ingredient formulas that have been mentioned may be used.
A person should drink it lukewarm and in small quantities, never causing an obstruction of thirst; water boiled with Pitta-alleviating drugs, or even milk, destroys the fever arising from Pitta.
[Milk] mixed with *kāśmarya* and sugar, along with sandalwood, *uśīra*, and *padmaka*, [is likewise effective].
One should drink water combined with grapes and licorice for thirst caused by pitta.

Likewise, one should prepare decoctions from the sārivādi group, the tṛṇapañcamūla, or the utpalādi group; or similarly, from the sweet (madhura) group, or from other groups such as those beginning with madhūkapuṣpa.

Oil prepared with *bilva*, *āḍhakī*, *dhātaki*, the five spices (*pañcakola*), and *darbha* destroys vomiting caused by *kapha*; it is beneficial, as is a gargle here with warm water infused with *nimba* blossoms.
[One should also use] *jīraka*, fresh ginger, *śṛṅgavera*, and *sauvarcala* salt, soaked in half their volume of water.
Heart-pleasing and fragrant liquors, when drunk, immediately pacify thirst. One should overcome thirst arising from a wound by warding off the pain through the drinking of meat broths and blood;
that which arises from wasting (kṣaya) should be destroyed by milk-water, or meat-water, or honey-water.
One should conquer all thirst caused by [the consumption of] heavy food, as well as that produced by all [other causes], except for wasting diseases (kṣaya), by using gargles.
A person afflicted by thirst should drink parched grain water mixed with honey, or ghee combined with jaggery, or [water] joined with *kāśmarya* and sugar.
Or one should drink a decoction of *āmra* and *jambū* mixed with honey;
this dispels all vomiting and likewise removes thirst.
[One may also use] *gostana*, sugarcane juice, milk, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, and *utpala*.
Surely our terrible thirst will be quenched by drinking from it through the nose.
Gargles with milk, sugarcane juice, *mārdvīka* wine, honey, rum, molasses-water, and sour fruits such as *vṛkṣāmla* destroy dryness of the palate. 11–12.
Holding honey in the mouth as a gargle produces clarity in the oral cavity, heals wounds, and pacifies burning sensations and thirst.
Cold water mixed with honey, when held until one is satiated to the throat, [provides similar relief]. 13.
One should administer it as an emetic or as a drink; by this, thirst is pacified.
For those who are excessively dry or weak, goat’s milk quickly quenches thirst here, or else a cold, sweet, and heart-pleasing juice [of fruits] fried in ghee. || 14–15 ||
One should quench with jaggery-water the thirst that arises after eating unctuous food.
One should drink the decoction of banyan-leaf buds, sugar, lodhra, pomegranate, and madhuka,
mixed with honey and rice-water, to ward off vomiting and thirst.
In cases of dryness of the palate, one should drink ghee or even the scum (maṇḍa) of ghee.
Those emaciated by fainting, vomiting, thirst, burning sensations, women, wine, or fatigue,
as well as those suffering from internal hemorrhage (raktapitta) or alcoholism (madātyaya), should drink cold water.
Fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla) destroys bad taste in the mouth, impurities, and foul odors;
that same liquid, when cooled and salt-free, is an excellent remedy for dryness of the mouth.
The juice of *kola*, pomegranate, *vṛkṣāmla*, *cukrīkā*, and *cukrikā* [is also used for this purpose].
An application of the five sour fruits (pañcāmlaka) to the face immediately subdues thirst.

One should prepare a pill from the sprouts of the banyan tree (vaṭapraroha), madhuka, kuṣṭha, utpala, and powdered parched grain; when this well-compounded mixture is held in the mouth, it quickly destroys even excessive thirst.
One should feed [the patient] cooled red śāli rice mixed with honey;
by this, vomiting and thirst that have persisted for a long time are pacified.
If one suffering from thirst, emaciated by a previous illness, does not obtain water—
A man may quickly encounter either death or a chronic disease;
therefore, one should again overcome his thirst with wholesome food, drink, and medicine.
Once that thirst is conquered, even other diseases can be successfully treated.
One who is thirsty falls into delusion; through delusion, one gives up one's life.
Therefore, in all circumstances, water is never to be withheld from anyone.
(17.25) Adhikāra 17: Water.
Immersion in water, gems with their strings, cold plasters, the breeze from fans,
fragrant drinks, and cooling beverages are not prohibited in any type of fainting fit (mūrchā).
Furthermore, milk prepared with drugs of the sweet group (madhura-varga) and the meat broths of wild animals (jāṅgala) seasoned with pomegranate are always beneficial.
Likewise, barley, red śāli rice, satīna, and mung beans are recommended for fainting fits.
One should administer decoctions that destroy fever according to the specific doṣa involved;
however, in fainting caused by blood (raktajā), cold treatments are beneficial.
In the case of intoxication caused by liquor, one should vomit the liquor and enjoy sleep as desired;
in the case of intoxication caused by poison, one should administer anti-poisonous medicines.
[One should take] jujube pulp, uśīra, and saffron with cold water.
One should conquer fainting caused by bile (pitta-mūrchā) by licking long pepper (kṛṣṇā) mixed with honey.
In cases of fainting and intoxication, one should drink a decoction of mahauṣadha, amṛtā, kṣudrā, pauṣkara, and granthika, combined with kaṇā.
One should drink a decoction of durālabhā with ghee for the alleviation of vertigo;
or the use of triphalā, or the use of milk, or the elixirs (rasāyana), or the ghee from a jar (kaumbha-sarpiḥ) is recommended. 7.
The application of collyriums, nasal drops, medicinal smoke, blowing [into the nose],
pricking with needles, cauterization, squeezing between the nails,
plucking out the hair of the head and body, and even biting with the teeth are recommended [as methods of torture].
And the crushing of *ātmaguptā* is beneficial for awakening him. (18) Mantha [should be prepared] with dates, grapes, *vṛkṣāmla*, *amlīkā*, and pomegranates.
Combined with *parūṣaka* and *āmalaka*, it removes the disorders caused by alcohol.
Alternatively, one may take *satīna* and *mudga* beans mixed with pomegranate and *āmalaka*, or with the juice of grapes, *āmalaka*, dates, and *parūṣaka*.
One should prepare various kinds of nourishing drinks, broths, and meat soups;
or one should drink ghee prepared with a decoction of harītakī or with the juice of āmalakī,
or even the Kalyāṇaka ghee, which removes intoxication and fainting.
Cold water, when drunk until satiety, immediately cures vomiting, fainting, diarrhea, and intoxication caused by betel nut (pūgaphala).
[This is also cured] by smelling wild cow dung, or by drinking water, or even by eating salt.
The intoxication caused by betel nut is pacified by a gargle of powdered *rujā* and sugar.

When wine has been digested, a small amount of wine mixed with *sauvarcala* salt, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), and water should be administered; this cures the affliction caused by the intake of wind (*vātapānātyaya*).
Mudga soup mixed with sugar, or sweet meat broth, should be administered in cases of *pitta*-dominant alcoholism (*pittapānātyaya*); furthermore, all cooling treatments are to be employed.
In cases of alcoholism arising from *kapha*, fasting (*laṅghana*) should be performed according to the patient's strength.

One should drink wine, composed and focused, combined with drugs that stimulate digestion. In cases arising from all [three] doshas, this entire treatment should be employed. Through these successful therapeutic measures, the disorder of intoxication (madātyaya) attains pacification.
If one does not administer milk following the sequence of wine, but instead employs fasting and other such measures, then once the phlegm has been diminished and weakness and lightness have arisen,
milk— whose qualities are equal to those of *ojas* and opposite to those of wine— should be used. (11)
One should gradually consume milk preparations and wine in very small quantities.
Ghee prepared with the decoction of *punarnavā*, milk, and the paste of *yaṣṭīmadhu* promotes nourishment when drunk by those whose vitality has been impaired by the consumption of wine.
Sauvarcala salt, ajājī, vṛkṣāmla, and amlavetasa, combined with one-eighth part each of cinnamon, cardamom, and black pepper, and joined with a portion of sugar—
this eight-ingredient laghuṇa is supreme for kindling the digestive fire.
In cases of intoxication (madātyaya) where kapha predominates, one should administer a purification of the channels (srotoviśodhana).
A powder consisting of cavya, sauvarcala salt, hiṅgu, pūrakā, and viśvadīpyaka should be drunk with wine; this cures the ailments of alcoholism (pānātyaya). || 15-16 ||

One who is immersed in water, whose limbs are adorned with sandalwood paste, and who wears a garland, may drink liquor accompanied by meat as a side dish along with devotion; such a person shall never incur diseases nor fall into an intoxication that impairs the mind.
A beverage made from grapes, wood-apples, and pomegranates, enriched with honey and sugar, removes the confusion caused by drinking.
Chapter 19:

A wise person should lick that [medicated ghee], which has been washed a hundred times, mixed with barley flour combined with jujube (kola) and emblic myrobalan (āmalaka), along with fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla). 1.
One should cover all his limbs with a cloth moistened with *āranāla*,
and then anoint him with *lāmajja*, sour gruel (*śukta*), and sandalwood paste.
He should be fanned by a palm-leaf fan from which drops of sandalwood water are trickling.
A person afflicted by burning sensations should sleep on a bed of plantain leaves (3).
He should resort to sprinkling with water, immersion baths, and fans, as well as cold water mixed with sugar, for the alleviation of thirst and burning heat (4).
One should alleviate internal burning (antardāha) with milk, milk-decoctions, and very cold sandalwood-infused liquids, as well as with these and other cooling remedies.
[A decoction] prepared with kuśa and other herbs, śāliparṇī, and the jīvaka group [should also be used].
Oil or ghee that alleviates burning sensations and destroys Vāta and Pitta is recommended; furthermore,
whatever [substance] removes Pitta-fever and burning sensations is desired for this purpose,
such as Phalinī, Rodhra, Sevya, water, Hemapatra, and Kuṭannaṭa.
An ointment consisting of *kālīyaka* mixed with resin (*rasa*) is recommended for application in cases of burning sensations.
Even a smooth, dry, and thick paste of sandalwood causes a burning sensation;
however, *aguru* produces a cooling effect because it obstructs the heat residing in the skin, whereas the other acts in the opposite manner.
A person afflicted by burning sensations should immerse themselves in a wooden tub filled with water mixed with the powder of *hrīvera*, *padmaka*, *uśīra*, and sandalwood.
(Adhikāra 20)
In cases of Vātika [apasmāra], the drinking of oleaginous substances (sneha-pāna) should be administered first; in the case of Pittaja, purgation (vireka) should be performed;

and in Kaphaja, emesis (vamana) should be carried out, followed by the sequence beginning with enemas (basti). Furthermore, whatever else is prescribed in the treatment of apasmāra [should also be applied].
In cases of insanity (unmāda), that same treatment should be administered because the doshas and the affected tissues (dūṣyas) are common to both conditions.
The fresh juices of brāhmī, kūṣmāṇḍī fruit, ṣaḍgranthā, and śaṅkhapuṣpikā are seen to remove insanity when used individually, mixed with kuṣṭha and honey.
For the pacification of insanity, one should drink water decocted with the ten roots (daśamūla) mixed with ghee or meat broth,
or with the powder of white mustard (siddhārthaka), or simply fresh ghee;
or else the juice derived from the palm tree branches.
Mustard oil should always be employed for nasal administration (nasya) and for massage (abhyañjana).
Siddhārthaka, vacā, hiṅgu, karañja, devadāru,
mañjiṣṭhā, triphalā, śvetā, kaṭabhī bark, and the three pungents (kaṭutrika) [are the ingredients].
Priyaṅgu, śirīṣa, and the two types of haridrā (rajanī) in equal parts, ground with goat's urine— this medicine is used as a drink,
an ointment, an errhine, an external application, a bath, and likewise for rubbing the body.
It removes epilepsy, poison, insanity, malevolent spells, misfortune, and fever;
it destroys fear of spirits and is praised at the royal court.
Ghee prepared with this [herb], or that same ghee combined with cow's urine, serves the same purpose.
Trikaṭu, asafoetida, salt, vacā, kaṭukarohiṇī, śirīṣa, seeds of naktamāla, and white mustard seeds—
when ground with cow’s urine, these form a medicinal wick (varti) beneficial for use as an eye-salve (añjana).
It subdues quartan fever, epilepsy, and insanity.
One should console the patient with the words of friends joined with matters of dharma, action, and wealth;
or one should speak of the destruction of something desired, or show him wonders.
Having bound it and smeared it with mustard oil, one should place it face upwards in the sun;
or else, one should touch it with heated iron, oil, or water, or strike it with whips while it is firmly bound in a secluded house. || 13 ||
For when the wandering mind is restrained, it proceeds toward that happiness accordingly.
One should terrify him with snakes whose fangs have been extracted, with tamed lions and elephants, with enemies bearing weapons in their hands, and likewise with boars.
Alternatively, the king's men, having led him outside and bound him tightly, might terrify him with threats of execution under the king's command.
For the fear of death is considered even greater than the pain of the body or other fears.

By that means, his mind, which has become agitated in every way, attains tranquility. Furthermore, for one whose mind is afflicted by the loss of a beloved object, one should bring it to peace through consolations and assurances obtained by acquiring something similar to it.
One should bring to pacification those states arising from desire, grief, fear, anger, joy, envy, and greed by means of their very opposites.
Having understood the [individual's] defects, age, suitability, place, time, and strength or weakness, [one should act accordingly].
One should apply this medical treatment for insanity caused by the humors (doṣas) or by spirits (bhūtas).
Furthermore, for one who has become insane due to gods, sages, ancestors, or gandharvas, the wise physician should avoid sharp treatments such as collyrium and cruel procedures.

The physician should conquer adventitious insanity according to the rules with the drinking of clarified butter and other remedies; for adventitious [insanity], the prescribed treatment is desired to consist of mantras and the like, as well as worship, offerings of food (bali), oblations (upahāra), sacrifices (iṣṭi), burnt offerings (homa), mantras, collyrium (añjana), and so forth. || 22 ||
One should employ Kalyāṇaka, or great Vaitasa ghee,
as well as the oil named Nārāyaṇa and likewise Mahānārāyaṇa;
also Jaṭilā, Pūtanā, Keśī, Coraṭī, Markaṭī, and Vacā.
Trāyamāṇā, jayā, vīrā, coraka,
kaṭurohiṇī, kāyasthā, sūkarī, chatrā, sāticchatrā, palaṃkaṣā,
mahāpuruṣadantā, vayasthā, and the two types of nākulī.
Ghee prepared with kaṭaṃbhārā, vṛścikālī, and sthirā,
when duly processed, destroys insanity, possession by spirits, and epilepsy occurring for the fourth time;
this ghee, named Mahāpaiśācika, is like nectar.
It produces intelligence, intellect, and memory, and promotes the growth of the limbs in children.
[This is prepared] with decoctions of two palas each of the five roots (pañcamūla), āvakāśmarī, rāsnā, eraṇḍa, trivṛt, balā, mūrvā, and śatāvarī. || 27–28 ||
That ghee known as Vaitasa, prepared with the ingredients of Kalyāṇaka, is proclaimed as the supreme pacifier of all mental disorders.
A decoction should be made using double the amount of water and one-fourth part of the paste of Pānīyakalyāṇaka.
One *āḍhaka* of ghee, cooked with two *palas* each of asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), sauvarcala salt, and the three pungents (*vyoṣa*) in four times as much cow’s urine, destroys insanity.
(21.31) Adhikāra 21.
The wise physician should treat epilepsy caused by vāta primarily with enemas (basti), that caused by pitta primarily with purgatives (virecana), and that born of kapha with emetics (vamana).
Thereafter, the physician should properly administer a sharp awakening therapy.
For one whose body is completely purified, there shall be a treatment that removes insanity.
Manahśilā, haritāla, and the excrement of a pigeon,
when used as a collyrium, destroy epilepsy and especially insanity.
For epilepsy and insanity, nasal drops and eye-salves should be prepared from yaṣṭī, hiṅgu, vacā, vakra, śirīṣa, and garlic,
along with goat's urine. Likewise, one should use wood-apples, autumnal mudga beans, musta, uśīra, and barley.
One should prepare suppositories by grinding together the three pungents (savyoṣa) with goat's urine.
These are like nectar for those suffering from epilepsy, insanity, snakebite, artificial poisoning, ingestion of poison, or those who have drowned.
The bile of a dog extracted under the Puṣya constellation is an ointment that destroys epilepsy;
that same substance, when combined with clarified butter, is considered an excellent fumigation.
One who suffers from trembling of the heart, pain in the eyes, perspiration, and coldness of the hands and other limbs [should be treated thus].
One should administer water decocted with the ten roots (daśamūlī) and the Kalyāṇājya ghee for him.
He who eats milk-rice and consumes the powder of vacā with honey will certainly conquer even the most terrible epilepsy that has persisted for a long time.
Two palas each of śaṇa, trivṛt, eraṇḍa, daśamūla, śatāvarī, rāsnā, māgadhikā, and śigru should be boiled together.
Likewise, [two palas each of] vidārī, madhuka, the two types of medā, the two types of kākolī, and sugar [should be added]. || 10 ||
One should cook the finest ghee with the ingredients of date palm, abhīru, grapes, muñjāta, and likewise gokṣura, along with the components of reed and ghee;
this is known as Mahāvaitasa, and it destroys all forms of epilepsy.
This [remedy] conquers insanity, catarrh, tertian and quartan fevers, evil, and misfortune; it wards off all planetary influences,
removes asthma and cough, and purifies the semen and the menses.
Having added sixteen parts of water to the substance to be crushed and boiled, it should be reduced to one-fourth; this is known as the procedure for decoction (kvātha).
[This is done] with the juice of brāhmī, along with vacā, kuṣṭha, and śaṅkhapuṣpī.
Ancient clarified butter (purāṇa-sarpiḥ) destroys insanity, possession by spirits, and epilepsy.
One should cook clarified butter with eighteen times its quantity of the juice of *kūṣmāṇḍaka* and a paste of *yaṣṭyāhvā*;
drinking that is the supreme remedy for epilepsy.
Ghee prepared with equal parts of cow dung juice, curd, sour gruel, milk, and urine destroys insanity, possession by spirits, and epilepsy occurring on the fourth day.
[One should take] the two groups of five roots (pañcamūla), the three myrobalans (triphalā), the two types of turmeric, kaṭukā, and vacā.

Having boiled two palas each of saptaparṇa, apāmārga, nīlinī, kaṭurohiṇī, śamyāka, the root of phalgu, pauṣkara, and durālabhā in one droṇa of water, once the liquid has been reduced to a quarter part; ||| 18–19 ||
Bhārgī, pāṭhā, the three pungents (trikaṭu), trivṛtā, nicula,
śreyasī, māḍakī, rāsnā, mūrvā, bhūnimba, citraka, the two types of sārivā, rohiṣa, bhūtīka, and madayantikā.
Having ground these [substances] into portions the size of an akṣa, one should cook one prastha of clarified butter with equal quantities of cow-dung juice,
sour curd, milk, and urine; this is known as the "Great Five Products of the Cow" (Mahāpañcagavya), which is like nectar.

It is [effective] in epilepsy, insanity, swelling, abdominal enlargements, tumors, hemorrhoids, anemia, jaundice, and vitiligo; it destroys misfortune, spirits, and demons, and it eradicates quartan fever. (23)
Chapter 22:
Anointing with oil, fomentation, enemas, nasal therapy, unctuous purgation, and substances that are unctuous, sour, salty, sweet, aphrodisiac, and dispellers of Vata diseases [are beneficial]. 1.
Soup made from the fruits of *paṭola* is aphrodisiac, alleviates *vāta*, and is light;
soup prepared with *vāṭyālaka* is especially effective in destroying *vāta*.
Milk boiled with the *pañcamūla* and *balā* is beneficial for diseases caused by *vāta*.

When a disorder arising from Vāta is not pacified by cold, hot, unctuous, dry, and other such treatments, it should be understood that the blood (śoṇita) itself is vitiated. [The remedies for this are:
Vājigandhā, the three types of Balā, Daśamūlī, and Mahauṣadha.

The two *gṛdhranakhyau* and *rāsnā*—this group is a destroyer of *vāta*. An application (*pradeha*) made with warm fish from marshy lands (*ānūpa*), along with fermented whey (*savesavāra*), will remove wind. An application prepared with the four fats (*sneha*) processed with the ten roots (*daśamūla*) and aromatic drugs (*gandhauṣadha*) is a subduer of *anila* (wind).
Boneless meat, ground and steamed, combined with ghee and jaggery,
and mixed with long pepper (*kṛṣṇā*) and black pepper (*marica*), is known as *vesavāra*. The *Kākolyādi* group, when combined with all sour substances, subdues *vāta*.
Sālvana is described as meat from the buttocks that has been well-boiled, combined with all types of fats,
lukewarm, and distinctly seasoned with salt; one should always apply it as a poultice for those suffering from diseases of Vāta.

The *kākolyādi* group should be taken, combined with the eight groups (*aṣṭavarga*); the *bhadradārvādi* group destroys wind (*vāta*), while the sour group begins with pomegranate (*dāḍima*). All the fats (*sneha*) are included, as well as the four specific fats and salts such as *saindhava*.
The three groups beginning with *kākolyādi* should be processed with the three [groups] beginning with *amlādi*.

When wind (*vāta*) has reached the stomach (*āmāśaya*), this "six-footed" formulation should be administered for seven nights with lukewarm water to one who has undergone emesis in the prescribed order.
Citraka, indrayava, pāṭhā, kaṭukā, ativiṣā,
and abhayā constitute the six-ingredient formulation (ṣaṭcaraṇa) considered to be a pacifier of great diseases.
One karṣa consists of eighteen niṣpāvas, while one dharaṇa consists of twenty-three of them.

By that, the Ṣaḍdharaṇa formulation is administered for seven nights. When the Vāta has reached the colon (pakvāśaya), an unctuous purgative (snehavirecana) should be administered; likewise, cleansing enemas (śodhanīya-vasti), as well as medicinal gruels (prāśa) with a high salt content, should be used. || 13–14 ||

When [the vāta] has entered the bladder, the procedure for purifying the enema (basti) should be performed; when it is provoked in the ears and other sense organs, the sequential treatment (krama) that subdues vāta should be applied. One should also employ oleation, massage, poultices, rubbing, and ointments.
When [the Vāta] has reached the skin, flesh, blood, and vessels, one should perform bloodletting.
When it has reached the tendons, joints, and bones, the wise physician should apply oleation, poultices, thermal cautery, bandaging, and massage. (16–17)
When the Vāta is deeply hidden or located within the bone, the physician, being strong, should apply a tube to the bone after it has been opened with a hand-fan and suck out the air.
When the Vāta has reached the semen, the treatment for seminal disorders should be performed.
Vomiting and nasal medication (nasya) properly administered by a skilled practitioner cure wind (vāyu) located in the chest, the three parts of the neck, or the nape of the neck.
[The paste is made from] māṣa, balā, śukaśimbā, kattṛṇa, rāsnā, aśvagandhā, and urubūka.
A lukewarm decoction, mixed with asafoetida and salt, when inhaled as a nasal drop (nasya),
removes hemiplegia (pakṣavāta), stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha), and pain in the ears; it also certainly conquers even the most difficult-to-cure facial paralysis (arditavāta) within seven days.
One *māṣa* each of asafoetida and rock salt, and one *śāṇa* each of the drugs beginning with *jaraṇā*;
or one should drink *vāṭyālaka* boiled with *māṣa*, *ātma-guptā*, and castor seeds, combined with asafoetida and rock salt, as a remedy for hemiplegia. (23)
One pala or even half a pala of garlic, finely minced,
should be sprinkled with the powdered ingredients— hing, cumin, rock salt, black salt, and the three pungents (kaṭutrika)— each measured at one māṣaka, and then thoroughly stirred.
Just as one who has been consumed by fire is restored by drinking a decoction of *rubūka*,
so too [this medicine] should be administered daily for one month without interruption;
it quickly destroys wind-diseases (*vātaroga*), facial paralysis (*ardita*), and tetanus (*apatantraka*).
It cures those suffering from diseases of a single limb as well as those with diseases of all limbs;
it specifically destroys stiffness of the thighs, sciatica, and disorders caused by worms, and especially cures ailments of the waist and abdomen, as well as abdominal diseases.
Having eaten a preparation made from ground black gram (māṣa) with fresh butter, the patient suffering from ardita should consume milk and meat broth, and then drink a decoction of daśamūlī.
He should be devoted to oleation and massage, and intent upon enemas, nasal therapy, and medicated smoking.
One suffering from ardita (facial paralysis) should drink ghee after the main meal.
For viśvācī and avabāhuka, one should drink a decoction of daśamūla, balā, and māṣa mixed with oil and clarified butter after dinner, and apply it as a nasal drop (nasya).
One should drink the fresh juice of the root of *balā*, or likewise that of *pāribhadra* and *ātmaguptā*;
or one who applies it as a nasal drop (*nasya*) with the juice of *māṣa* for a month will have arms equal to a thunderbolt.
Alternatively, a decoction prepared from the five roots (*pañcamūlī*) or the ten roots (*daśamūla*) [may be used].
Dry fomentation as well as nasal medication (nasya) is recommended for stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha).
In cases of wasting of the upper arm (bāhuśoṣa), one should drink the great Kalyāṇaka ghee after eating;
this is also indicated if the heart or the back is elevated and gradually painful.
When Vāyu moves upward, one should designate that condition as *kubja* (dwarfism).

One should treat a recent case of *kubja* with Vāyu-alleviating drugs and *daśamūlī*, using either medicinal baths or meat soups; however, one should avoid treating it when it has become fully developed.
In cases of *tūnī* and *pratitūnī*, one should drink the powder of the *pippalyādi* group with warm water;

or, in cases of flatulence (*ādhmāna*), one may take unctuous salt with ghee, or alkali and asafoetida. Fasting, fomentation with the palms of the hands, and medicinal suppositories (*phalavarti*) are also indicated.
It acts as a stimulant, a digestive aid, and a purifying enema. With *dāru*, *haimavatī*, *kuṣṭha*, rock salt (*saindhava*), alkali (*kṣāra*), and asafoetida (*hiṅgu*),
ground with sour liquids and applied lukewarm, it cures abdominal distension (*ādhmāna*) and abdominal enlargement (*udara*).

In cases of *pratyādhmāna*, however, emesis, fasting, and digestive stimulants are indicated. For *pratyaṣṭhīlā* and *aṣṭhīlikā*, as well as for abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and internal abscesses (*abhyantaravidradhi*), the same treatments apply; furthermore, the *hiṅgvādi* formulation is especially recommended here.
In cases of *viśvācī*, lameness, and paralysis; in burning and tingling sensations of the feet;

in disorders of the abdomen and head; and in the disorder known as *vātakaṇṭaka*—one should pierce the veins as previously specified, and the treatment should be like that for wind-diseases (*vātaroga*). (41)
In cases of tongue-stiffness (jihvāstambha) and likewise in facial paralysis (ardita), the general treatment prescribed is most excellent;
however, in the case of headache (śirograha), treatments for wind (marut) located in the head should be administered.
[One should use] turmeric, vacā, kuṣṭha, pippalī, and ginger.
One should prepare a fine powder from equal parts of ajājī, ajamodā, yaṣṭīmadhuka, and saindhava.
A person should stir that powder with ghee and consume it every day.
Within twenty-one nights, a man shall become a possessor of the Veda (śrutidhara).
With a voice like the sound of clouds and drums and the resonance of a cuckoo in rut, he shall conquer dullness, stammering, and muteness; this auspicious linctus shall bring victory.
One should drink guggulu with the juice of guḍūcī and triphalā at the head of a jackal, or else take castor oil with milk, or vṛddhadāraka;
or one should administer the śyāmā, samā, ālambuṣā, and other formulations that alleviate vātarakta.
Once the blood has been removed, the entire therapeutic procedure for alleviating Vāta is recommended.
For those suffering from sciatica (gṛdhrasī), lameness (khañja), or paraplegia (paṅgu), one should drink a decoction of Daśamūlī, Balā, Rāsnā, Guḍūcī, and Viśvabheṣaja with castor oil.
Castor seeds should be purified and ground, then cooked in milk;
this milk-porridge (pāyasa) is a supreme remedy for pain in the waist and sciatica (gṛdhrasī).
Alternatively, a decoction of the five roots (pañcamūlī), combined with *rubu* oil and *trivṛt*, [is also effective].
When drunk, it immediately cures sciatica (gṛdhrasī), abdominal tumors (gulma), and colic (śūla).

One should drink either oil or clarified butter, or the juice of fresh ginger and citron mixed with sour gruel (cukra) and jaggery; this is prescribed as a remedy for pain in the hips, thighs, back, and the sacrum (trika), as well as for abdominal tumors, sciatica, and upward movement of wind (udāvarta).
One should take one *pala* of *rāsnā* and five *karṣas* of *guggulu*,
form them into pills with clarified butter, and eat them to overcome *gṛdhrasī*. Alternatively,
one may consume milk-porridge (*pāyasa*) prepared with ground *śuṇṭhī* and *gandharva-bīja*.
When consumed, it undoubtedly destroys pain in the waist and sciatica (gṛdhrasī).

One should not perform the procedure of enema (basti) at the outset as long as the upper tract has not been purified; in that case, the unctuous substance (sneha) is useless, like an oblation poured into ashes.
When intense oleation and fomentation have been applied to the calf of one suffering from *gṛdhrasī*,
and after the area has been thoroughly massaged with the feet, one should gradually draw down the *gṛdhrasī* through a fine channel into the little toe.
Having recognized that the elevated knot (granthi) is situated within the tendon (kaṇḍarā),
one should quickly incise it with a surgical instrument, extract the growth which resembles a coral sprout,
cauterize it with fire, and then apply a plaster of yaṣṭīmadhu and sandalwood.
One should lance the vein four finger-breadths below the indrabasti;
if it does not subside, one should cauterize the little toe of the foot.
Or, a person should drink castor oil mixed with cow's urine.
This regimen for one month removes the seizing pain in the thighs caused by vultures (gṛdhra-sī).
In the case of vātakaṇṭaka, one should frequently perform bloodletting,
drink castor oil, or apply cauterization with needles.
Vāyu, when aggravated and associated with *sāma* (undigested matter), residing in the waist, produces pain;

that is called *kaṭigraha* (waist-stiffness). When it resides in both thighs, it is called *paṅgu* (lameness). One should drink [medicine] with a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*) or with water boiled with *nāgara* (ginger).
In all cases of hip pain, castor oil should be used.

One pala each of the three myrobalans (triphalā) and long pepper (pippalī), along with half a pala each of cinnamon bark and cardamom, should be powdered and saturated with a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla).
Having given five palas of guggulu made into pills, this [remedy],
through the practice of meat broth, destroys wind diseases entirely—
those located in the joints, bones, and marrow— just as Indra’s thunderbolt destroys a tree.
Having stirred this [guggulu] repeatedly with twice its weight of *lehava* (molasses), it should be dried in the sun seven times with water decocted from the ten roots (*daśamūla*).
[The ingredients are: *ābhā*, *aśvagandhā*, *hapuṣā*, *guḍūcī*, *śatāvarī*, *gokṣuraka*, and *samaṅgā*. (66–67)

Śyāmā, śaṭī, ghoṣavatī, yavānī, and nāgara—these powders should be taken in equal parts. To this mixture, an amount of kauśika (mustard oil) equal to the total weight of the powder should be added, along with half that amount of clarified butter (sarpiḥ).
Then, taking a dose of half an akṣa, one should administer it as a remedy followed by a post-drink (anupāna) of wine or vegetable broth.

Whether with wine, or lukewarm water, or even with milk or meat broth—[these are used] in cases of stiffness in the waist, sciatica, pain in the arms or back, lockjaw, or in the knees and both feet; likewise when the *vāta* resides in the joints, has entered the bones, reached the marrow, or is located in the tendons and the abdominal cavity. || 69-70 ||

The perfected ones declare that this thirteen-ingredient formulation conquers diseases associated with vāta and kapha, those provoked by vāta, disorders of the heart, the female reproductive tract, and the doshas; it is also used for fractures, piercing wounds, and lameness caused by vāta.
[It is prepared] in a decoction of daśamūla with one pala each of the jīvanīya drugs.
Ghee cooked with milk is nourishing and conquers the afflictions of wind (vāta).
Ghee cooked with a decoction of aśvagandhā and its paste, using four times as much milk, destroys wind, acts as an aphrodisiac, and increases muscle mass.
One should properly boil goat meat, free from its skin and devoid of horns, hooves, and so forth, along with the two groups of five roots (pañcamūlī), in one droṇa of water.
With that decoction reduced to one-fourth, one should cook one prastha of ghee.
With the drugs of the jīvanīya group, along with yaṣṭyāhva, milk, and śatāvarī—
this preparation known as Chāgalādyam removes all disorders of vāta; it is beneficial for facial paralysis, earache, deafness, muteness, and nasal obstruction.
This clarified butter is recommended for those who are dull-witted, stammering, or lame, as well as for those with clubfoot, gout, or hunchback; it is also praised for facial paralysis and hernia.
Thirty-two palas of *daśamūla* should be added here.
Whatever substance is mentioned again in connection with ghee, oil, or a medicinal formulation, it should be understood here by the noble one as being double the portion.
Elā, murā, sarala, śailaja, dāru, kauntī—
Caṇḍā, śaṭhī, nalada, campaka,
hemapuṣpa, sthauṇeya, gandharasa, pūtidala, mṛṇāla, śrīvāsaka, kunduru, nakha, ambu, varāṅga, and kuṣṭha. || 79 ||
Having obtained as much as possible of kālīyaka, jalada, karkaṭa, candana, śrī, the fruit of jāti together with its blossoms, saffron, spṛkkā, turuṣka, and laghu, one should prepare them.
One should cook oil with the decoction of *balā*, milk, and curd;
this is declared to be beneficial for wind-related diseases (*vātāmaya*), bestowing strength, complexion, and bodily splendor.

Oil cooked with the decoction and paste of *balā*, along with an equal amount of milk, cures all disorders of vāta; likewise, oil prepared with *śaileya* [is effective]. [One should prepare oil] from a decoction of *balā* roots and that of *daśamūlī*.
Take eight auspicious parts each of the decoction of barley, jujube, and horse gram, as well as eight parts of milk and one part of oil; having combined these together,
one should cook them while adding the sweet group of drugs along with rock salt.
Likewise, [he should offer] aguru, sarjarasa, sarala, and devadāru;
mañjiṣṭhā, candana, kuṣṭha, elā, and kālānusārivā;
māṃsī, śaileyaka, patra, tagara, and the two types of sārivā. || 85 ||
Śatāvarī, aśvagandhā, śatapuṣpā, and punarnavā—
having properly prepared these, one should place them in a pitcher made of gold, silver, or likewise of clay, and deposit it well-secured. || 86–87 ||
This oil, known by the name Balā-taila, cures all disorders of Vāta;

therefore, one should administer it to a woman who has recently given birth in a dose according to her strength. It should also be given to a woman desiring conception and to a man whose semen is depleted. (88)

It is beneficial in every way for those whose vital essence (vāta) is depleted, who have been struck in their vital points (marman), who are agitated, or likewise injured; it is also used for those with fractures and those overcome by exhaustion.
It dispels vāta diseases such as ākṣepaka (convulsions) and others.
If one uses this for six months, it cures hiccups, dyspnea, ophthalmia, abdominal tumors, and difficult-to-overcome cough; it removes intestinal hernia (antravṛddhi),
and the person becomes possessed of fresh bodily constituents and stable youthfulness.
For this indeed should be performed by a king, as well as by those men who are royal ministers, and by those men who are happy, delicate, and wealthy. [The trees are:
Bilva, Agnimantha, Syonāka, Pāṭalā, and Pāribhadraka. (92)
Prasāriṇī, aśvagandhā, bṛhatī, kaṇṭakārikā,
balā, atibalā, śvadaṃṣṭrā, and punarnavā— one should boil ten-pala portions of each of these in four droṇas of water. || 93–94 ||
Having strained the remainder of the decoction, one should cause a vessel of oil to be prepared with *śatapuṣpā*, *devadāru*, *māṃsī*,
*śaileyaka*, *vacā*, *candana*, *tagara*, *kuṣṭha*, and the four types of *elāparṇī*.
Rāsnā, turagagandhā, saindhava, and punarnavā—
having ground two-pala portions of each of these, one should add them and provide an equal amount of śatāvarī juice along with oil. || 96–97 ||
One should administer four times the amount of milk, whether from a goat or a cow,
for drinking, enemas, massage, food, and nasal drops;
this is recommended for a horse, an elephant, or even a human who has been shattered by wind (vāta).
The lame and those who crawl on their haunches are cured by this oil.

It also cures the downward-moving winds (vāta) and those located in the head, as well as stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha), lockjaw (hanustambha), dental diseases, and throat obstruction (galagraha). || 99-100 ||

For those whose single limb withers, whose gait is unsteady, whose senses are decayed, whose semen is lost, and who are emaciated by fever; for those who are deaf, whose tongues are stammering, and whose intellect is very slight.
For women who have few offspring or those who do not conceive at all; for those whose testicles are afflicted by wind (vāta) or who suffer from severe enlargement of the intestines (antravṛddhi)—
for them, this oil is excellent, and it is known by the name Nārāyaṇa.
The roots of śatāvarī, aṃśumatī, pṛśniparṇī, sahā, balā, and eraṇḍa, as well as those of bṛhatī,
pūtika, gavedhuka, and sahacara. || 104 ||
One should boil ten-pala portions of these [drugs] in one droṇa of water; when reduced to one-fourth and strained, one should add the medicinal paste (garbha) consisting of punarnavā,
vacā, dāru, śatāhvā, candana, and aguru.
One should employ half a pala each of śaileya, tagara, kuṣṭha, elā, māṃsī, sthirā, balā, aśvagandhā, saindhava, and rāsnā;
and one should add two prasthas each of cow's milk and goat's milk. (107)
One should cook one *prastha* of *śatāvarī* juice with one *prastha* of oil.
Listen now to the potency of this prepared oil for horses broken by wind (*vāta*), as well as for elephants and men. (108–109)
This oil should be administered to those suffering from all disorders of vāta;
having drunk it, that man will certainly become long-lived and firm. A mule would even conceive a fetus, how much more so a human woman?
It destroys heart pain, side pain, as well as hemicrania,
scrofula, goiter, gout, throat obstruction,
jaundice, anemia, and even epilepsy.
This [oil] was proclaimed by the Blessed Viṣṇu as the auspicious "Nārāyaṇa" oil, which brings an end to wind-disorders.
Having boiled one hundred [palas] of Aśvagandhā in a droṇa of water until one-eighth remains, [one should proceed].
Having strained [the decoction], one should cook the oil, adding four times as much milk and a paste made of lotus stalks (mṛṇāla),
lotus tubers (śālūka), lotus filaments (visa-kiñjalka), mālatī flowers, vībera, madhuka, sārivā, and padmakesara. || 114–115 ||
Medā, punarnavā, drākṣā, mañjiṣṭhā, the two types of bṛhatī,
elā, elavāluka, triphalā, musta, candana, and padmaka— [a decoction] prepared with these cures vāta residing in the blood, as well as raktapitta and asṛgdara. || 116 ||

It destroys [diseases], promotes nourishment, and bestows strength; it increases the flesh of the emaciated, cures disorders of the semen and the female reproductive tract, and removes defects of wounds.
Through drinking, massage, and oil enemas, it makes even eunuchs virile.
When [the disease] is localized in the *saṃkucita* [muscle], an oil massage (*abhyaṅga*) prepared with black gram (*māṣa*) and rock salt (*saindhava*) should be applied;
when it has reached the arms and head, nasal drops (*nasya*) and drinking [of oil] after meals should be administered.
[The oil should be prepared with] black gram, *ātmaguptā*, *atirasā*, and castor root (*urubūka*).
Oil prepared with well-ground rāsnā, śatāhvā, and salts, along with four times as much of a decoction of māṣa and balā, destroys pakṣavāta.
Having added one *prastha* of black gram (*māṣa*) and cooked it properly in one *āḍhaka* of water, when the liquid has been reduced to one-fourth, one should add four times as much milk.
Then, adding one *prastha* of sesame oil and a paste (*kalka*) measuring one *akṣa*, [one should cook it].
The eight life-sustaining drugs (jīvanīya), along with śatapuṣpā,
rock salt, rāsnā, ātmaguptā, madhuka, balā, vyoṣa, and trikaṇṭaka, [are used] for hemiplegia, facial paralysis, and severe earache caused by vāta.
It is recommended for dull hearing, deafness, cataracts caused by the three doṣas,
tremors of the hands, tremors of the head, viśvācī, avabāhuka, kalāyakhaja, and [related conditions], when administered as a drink, anointment, or enema.
Known as *māṣataila*, it removes diseases of the area above the clavicle.
[It is prepared] with the decoctions of *māṣa*, *atasī*, barley, *kuraṇṭaka*, *kaṇṭakārī*, *gokaṇṭa*, *tuṇṭuka*, *jaṭā*, and *kapikacchu*.
With a decoction of cotton seeds, hemp seeds, horse gram, jujube, and kola, or even with the broth of goat meat,
along with ginger, pippalī, and śatapuṣpā. || 126 ||
This oil known as Māṣākhya, cooked with the roots of Sairaṇḍa and Sapunarnavā, along with Saraṇī, Rāsnā, Balā, Amṛtalatā, and Kaṭuka, removes Avabāhuka (sciatica). || 127 ||
Hemiplegia (ardhāṅgaśoṣa), apatānaka, āḍhyavāta, ākṣepaka, as well as tremors of the arms and shaking of the head—
these are [treated] by means of nasal medication (nasya), enema therapy (basti), and affusion (pariṣecana).
It destroys pains in the waist, hips, and knees, as well as disorders of the wind (vāta),

when taken separately in a decoction of black gram (māṣa), in a decoction of balā, in a decoction of rāsnā, in a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla), or in the meat broth of goat, along with barley, jujube (kola), and horse gram (kulattha). || 128–129 ||
Having added one *prastha* of oil and four times as much milk, one should cook it with one *akṣa* each of *rāsnā*, *ātmaguptā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *śatāhvā*, castor root (*eraṇḍa*),
*mustaka*, the *jīvanīya* group, *balā*, and the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*).
In cases of trembling of the hands, trembling of the head, withering of the arms, and avabāhuka;
in deafness, earache, and terrible ringing in the ears; in viśvācī, ardita, kubja, gṛdhrasī, and apatānaka—[these are cured].
One should employ this excellent Māṣa oil for enemas, massages, internal drinks, and nasal drops; it removes diseases of the regions above the clavicle.
Having boiled the two groups of five roots (the daśamūla) in sixteen times the quantity of oil, [one should proceed as follows].
Having prepared an āḍhaka of māṣa beans and having taken four times that amount of the decoction,
the wise physician should cook one prastha of oil with an equal quantity of goat’s milk, adding half a karṣa of the medicinal paste ingredients.
Aśvagandhā, śaṭhī, devadāru, balā, rāsnā, prasāraṇī,
kuṣṭha, parūṣaka, bhārṅgī, the two types of vidārī, punarnavā, the fruit of mātuluṅga, jīraka, hiṅgu, and śatapuṣpā. || 136 ||
Having collected śatāvarī, gokṣuraka, pippalīmūla, citraka, the entire jīvanīya group, and rock salt,
one should recognize this great māṣa oil as being properly prepared. || 137–138 ||
In cases of hemiplegia, lockjaw, facial paralysis, and apatantraka;
in avabāhuka and viśvācī, as well as in lameness and clubfoot;
in tremors of the hand, tremors of the head, and in both kyphosis and dwarfism. || 139 ||
One should prescribe this medicine for Hanumannya-graha, Sādhimantha of the Vāta type, loss of semen, ringing in the ears, severe earache, and for the alleviation of Kalāya and Khañja.
One should employ [this] in enemas, ointments, drinks, and nasal drops.
Having added half an āḍhaka of māṣa and half a tulā of daśamūla,
one should boil thirty palas of goat meat in one droṇa of water.
When the decoction has been strained and cooled, and one-fourth part has been removed,
one *prastha* of sesame oil should be added along with four times as much milk, as well as *ātmaguptā*, *uruvūka*, *śatāhvā*, and the three salts. || 143–144 ||
The vitalizing (jīvanīya) drugs, mañjiṣṭhā, cavya, citraka, kaṭphala,
the three pungents (vyoṣa), pippalīmūla, rāsnā, madhuka,
saindhava, devadāru, amṛtā, kuṣṭha, vājigandhā, vacā, and śaṭhī. || 145 ||
One should prepare this with these equal parts of medicinal pastes over a mild fire for the treatment of hemiplegia,
wind-afflictions, deafness, lockjaw, pain in the ears, neck, and head, and tridoṣa-induced blindness. (146–147)
In cases of wandering of the hands, feet, head, and neck; in slow gait;

in the *kalāya*, *khañja*, and *pāṅgulya* disorders; in *gṛdhrasī*, *āmavāta*, and *bāhuka*; as well as in drinking, enemas, massage, nasal therapy (*nasya*), and filling the ears or eyes [with medicinal oil].

They praise this oil as a remedy that cures all diseases caused by wind (vāta). Oil cooked with a large quantity of the juice of *ketakī* root, *balā*, and *atibalā*, and prepared with an abundant amount of *tuṣodaka* (fermented rice-water), destroys wind that has entered the bones.
Oil prepared with *vājigandhā*, *balā*, *viśvā*, and the ten roots (*daśamūlī*) ground into a paste with water is recommended for consumption and for enemas in cases of *gṛdhrasī*.
One afflicted by diseases of the wind (*anila*) should drink oil cooked with the paste and the fresh juice of garlic (*rasona*).
Indeed, his wind-related diseases (vātaroga) quickly perish, like large knots that have been incorrectly grasped.
Having boiled one *tulā* each of *prasāraṇī*, *aśvagandhā*, and *daśamūla* separately in a *droṇa* of water, and when reduced to one-eighth [of its original volume]... (152–153)

One āḍhaka of oil, four parts of milk, an equal amount of curd, and two parts of kāñjika, along with two palas each of granthika, kṣāra, prasāraṇī, akṣa, and saindhava; and one pala each of mañjiṣṭhā, agni, yaṣṭyāhva, and the jīvanīya group [of drugs]. || 154 ||
Having added five pieces of ginger and thirty bhallātaka fruits, one should cook [the mixture] with basti and other liquids;
this destroys vāta located in the joints, channels, and bones, and serves to increase virility, enthusiasm, memory, intelligence, strength, complexion, and digestive fire. (155–156)

One should boil one hundred *prasāraṇī* plants that have been crushed in one *āḍhaka* of pure water until reduced to one-fourth; then one should add an equal amount of oil, curd, and sour gruel (*kāñjika*), along with twice as much milk and two-pala portions of the following pastes: prasāraṇīṃ tathā rāsnāṃ suradāru tathaiva ca | bṛhatīṃ ca vacāṃ caiva śatapuṣpāṃ sasaindhavam || 158 || etaiḥ kalkaiḥ samāyuktaṃ tailametat vipācayet | etattailavaraṃ nityaṃ vātavyādhiṣu yojayet || 159 || pānābhyañjanasekeṣu vastau caiva prayojayet | apasmāragṛhītānāṃ gadgadānāṃ tathaiva ca || 160 || śuṣkakāse tathā śoṣe bādhirye mūkatāsu ca | etattailavaraṃ nityaṃ praśastaṃ vātarogiṣu || 161 || It should be cooked with these pastes: *prasāraṇī*, *rāsnā*, *suradāru*, *bṛhatī*, *vacā*, *śatapuṣpā*, and rock salt (*saindhava*). This excellent oil should be employed constantly in cases of wind-diseases (*vātavyādhi*); it should be applied for drinking, massage, affusion, and enemas. It is highly recommended for those afflicted by epilepsy, stammering, dry cough, consumption, deafness, and muteness. This excellent oil is always praised for those suffering from wind-disorders.
Citraka, pippalīmūla, madhuka, saindhava, vacā,
śatapuṣpā, devadāru, rāsnā, vāraṇapippalī, the root of prasāraṇī, māṃsī, and bhallātaka. (158–159)
One should cook this oil over a mild fire; it removes diseases caused by vāta and kapha,
and it dispels eighty types of vāta disorders occurring in men and women,
including kubja (kyphosis), stiffness, lameness, gṛdhrasī (sciatica), and khuḍuka (contracture).
It quickly cures stiffness of the jaw, back, head, and neck.
Having uprooted the Prasāraṇī plant along with its roots and leaves during the autumn season,
one hundred [parts] should be taken from Sahacara and likewise one hundred from Śatāvarī.
The physician should boil one hundred parts each of balā, aśvagandhā, ātmaguptā, and ketakī in four times as much water; then, with liquids consisting of one āḍhaka each of curd-whey,
meat broth, sour gruel, and milk, he should cook one āḍhaka of oil.
One should cook it with one āḍhaka of curd over a gentle fire; the quantity of each of these ingredients to be added should be half a pala. [The ingredients are:
tagara, madana, kuṣṭha, kesara, mustaka, and tvak.
Rāsnā, rock salt (saindhava), long pepper (pippalī), spikenard (māṃsī), mañjiṣṭhā, liquorice (yaṣṭika),
as well as medā, mahāmedā, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, śatapuṣpā, vyāghranakha, dry ginger (śuṇṭhī), and devāhva. || 166–167 ||
Having ground together kākolī, kṣīrakākolī, vacā, and bhallātaka, one should prepare prasāraṇī;
once it is cooked— neither overdone nor cold— it should be strained and set aside.
Listen as I declare where it is to be applied:
for those who are hunchbacked, for the lame, and likewise for the dwarfs;
for one whose single limb withers, and for those whose bones and joints are broken. (169–170)
This is the supreme aphrodisiac for those with vitiated wind-blood (vāta-śoṇita), those whose minds are afflicted by wind, and those whose semen is diminished by sexual indulgence;
it should be administered as an enema, for drinking, for massage, and with food. (171)
When consumed, it quickly pacifies various disorders born of Vāta.
[One should take] three *tulās* of the branches, roots, and leaves of *prasāraṇī*, one *tulā* each of *kuraṇṭa*, *chinna-ruhā*, *rubuka*, *rāsnā*, and *śirīṣa*.

Having boiled one hundred *ghaṭas* of water with *devadāru*, *sahadevā*, and *ketaka*, and having added one *taila-ghaṭa* (one jar of oil), two jars of fermented grain-water (*tuṣāmbu*), and one *āḍhaka* of whey;
then having added one *āḍhaka* each of vinegar, goat’s meat-broth, sugarcane juice, and milk— (173)
With *spṛkkā*, *karkaṭa*, *jīvaka*, *ādyavikasa*, *kākolikā*, and *kacchurā*;
with small cardamom (*sūkṣmailā*), camphor (*ghanasāra*), *kundu*, *sarala*, saffron (*kāśmīra*), *māṃsī*, and *nakha*;
and with *kālīya*, blue lotus (*utpala*), *padmaka*, *āhva*, the two types of *niśā*, *kaṅkolaka*, and *granthika*. || 174 ||
With *cāmpeya*, *abhaya*, *coca*, betel nut (*pūga*), *kaṭuka*, nutmeg (*jātīphala*), and *abhīru*;
with *śrīvāsa*, *amaradāru*, sandalwood (*candana*), *vacā*, *śaileya*, and rock salt (*sindhūdbhava*);
and with oil, water, *kaṭambharā*, *aṅghri*, *nalikā*, *vṛścīvaka*, and *kaccoraka*.
With water infused with musk, the ten roots (*daśamūla*), *ketakī*, *tālīśa*, *yamānī*, and *aśvagandhā*; and with *kauntī*,

*tārkṣya-ja* (mustard), *śallakī* fruit, the three mild drugs (*laghu-traya*), *śyāmā*, *śatāhvā*, *maya*, combined with *bhallātaka*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), lotus filaments, *mahāśyāmā*, and cloves (*lavaṅga*).
One should cook it with Triphalā and the three pungents (Savyoṣa) in a large vessel over a mild fire;

by means of drinking, massage, enemas, and nasal administration, it destroys that Vāta located in the entire body, in half the body, or in specific limbs, as well as that which has taken refuge in the joints, bones, and marrow. (176)
It pacifies various diseases arising from phlegm and bile,
nourishes the bodily constituents (dhātus), makes them firm, bestows new youth upon men,
provides great strength even to the aged, and grants conception to barren women. (177)

Having drunk this oil, even an old woman gives birth to a son; trees sprinkled with it, though withered, become fruit-bearing, glossy, and firm; and men, cows, horses, and elephants whose limbs are broken become perfectly strong again. (178)
That which carries the fragrance of *ketakī* flowers, which is yellowish-brown in color, bitter or pungent in taste, light when weighed, smooth when crushed,
which does not turn to ash when burnt, and which emits a crackling sound and a smell like leather in the fire— [such is the nature of the *guggulu* resin].
That pure, beautiful daughter of a noble deer, declared fit for a king,
was placed by the great ones in the midst of water held in the palm of the hand;
then, for a moment, it must be contemplated once again in that very state.
If that water becomes reddish but not yellow in color, it is not musk; this is an artificial transformation.
[Take] two palas of rock salt, five of ginger, and [five each] of granthika and chitraka. || 180 ||
Two pairs of *bhallātaka* seeds, twenty [of the same], and two *āḍhakas* of fermented gruel (*āranāla*)—
one should cook one *prastha* of oil with these; it bestows progeny,
cures the pain of *gṛdhrasī* and thigh-contraction, and removes all disorders of *vāta*.
Chapter 23:
Vāta-śoṇita (blood vitiated by wind) is of two kinds: superficial and deep-seated.
That which resides in the skin and flesh is superficial; that which resides in the internal tissues is deep-seated. || 1 ||

Anointing with solid fats, oils, and the like; drinking bitter ghee (sarpiḥ); affusions, ointments, and bloodletting; and purification (śodhana) are beneficial for both [types of fever]. In cases of severe fever, the drinking of ghee, purification, and venesection (śirāvyadha) are especially recommended. || 2 ||

Wheat flour, goat's milk, and a paste of *rubu* seeds mixed with goat's milk should be applied as an ointment; for sprinkling, clarified butter washed a hundred times (*śatadhautasarpiḥ*) is prescribed, and sheep's milk alone is recommended.
A digestive decoction (*pācana*) is prepared by boiling three *karṣas* each of *amṛtā*, *nāgara*, and *dhānyaka*.
The decoction derived from *vatsādani*, when drunk combined with *guggulu*, conquers blood-impregnated *vāta* and all types of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*) without exception;
it thoroughly restores the blood that has become vitiated by *samīraṇa* (wind).
One should drink a decoction of rāsnā, guḍūcī, and caturaṅgula with castor oil;
in this manner, one will gradually conquer entirely even that disorder of blood and vāta which has arisen in all the limbs.
Alternatively, having eaten three or five pathyā fruits with jaggery, one should drink a decoction of chinnaruhā.
Indeed, this [Guḍūcī] necessarily pacifies even severe Vātarakta that has spread as far as the knees.
When combined with ghee, it subdues Vāta; with jaggery, constipation; with sugar, Pitta; with honey, Kapha;
when mixed with castor oil, severe Vātāsra (Vātarakta); and with ginger, it pacifies Āmavāta. (7–8)
Amṛtā (Guḍūcī) destroys wind and bile, dries up phlegm and fat,
pacifies vātarakta, and cures scabies and erysipelas.
[One should take] the fresh juice, paste, powder, or decoction of Guḍūcī.
By consuming this for a long period, one is liberated from vātaśoṇita (gout).
Milk boiled with the ten roots (daśamūlī) immediately destroys pain; likewise, a lukewarm affusion with ghee is beneficial when vāta predominates.
By drinking a decoction prepared with *paṭola*, *kaṭukā*, *abhīru*, and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) along with *amṛtā*, a person shall conquer vāta-śoṇita accompanied by burning sensations.
Alternatively, when phlegm (*kapha*) is predominant, one should take a decoction of *dhātrī*, *mustā*, and *haridrā*.
One who eats wholesome food should drink Pippalī according to their strength in a decoction of Kokilākhyā and Amṛtā; within three weeks, they will be freed from Vātaśoṇita (gout/rheumatism).
This [remedy] pacifies Kapha and blood, and destroys scabies and erysipelas.
Jaggery and ghee are known to pacify vātarakta and are beneficial for the heart.

In all cases, one who is well-composed should habitually consume either harītakī with jaggery, or a decoction of guḍūcī, or the "increasing-quantity-of-pippalī" regimen (pippalī-vardhamāna). || 15–16 ||
A decoction made from nine karṣas each of triphalā, nimba, mañjiṣṭhā, vacā, kaṭukarohiṇī, vatsādanī,
and dāruniśā [is used for] vātarakta, as well as kuṣṭha, pāmā, and raktamaṇḍala.
It removes the severe leprosy known as Kapālikā simply by being drunk.
From one Karṣa up to one Pala, one should add sixteen times the amount of water;
thereafter, up to one Kuḍava, the water should be eight times the quantity.
Having carefully extracted the root of *lāṅgalī*, which is equal to nectar, one should combine it with the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), iron filings, and the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*);
or [one may add] *guggulu*, *amṛtavallī*, and the juice of grapes and citron.
One should eat pills the size of jujube fruits (kola), mixed with the juices of the three myrobalans (triphalā) and stirred with honey; hear now what fruit they produce:
[they cure] the most terrible cracking of the feet and the cracking of all the limbs. (21)
It quickly destroys all of that, even blood that is otherwise incurable.
Ghee boiled with the decoction and paste of guḍūcī along with milk cures vāta and blood disorders, and conquers even difficult-to-cure leprosy (kuṣṭha).
One should prepare a liquid medicinal preparation using one, two, or three liquid substances, with four parts of liquid in total.
One should add milk equal in quantity to the oil, and water four times the amount of the milk.
This should contain a paste of *śatāvarī* within it, and [the resulting decoction] should be four times the volume of that [milk].

Ghee cooked with an equal amount of milk destroys vātaśoṇita (gout). Oil prepared with the decoction and paste of balā, along with four times the amount of milk and processed ten times, conquers vātāsṛj (hemorrhagic disorders) and vātapitta.
