This [mixture] is auspicious, promotes virility, increases semen in men, cures disorders of the seminal fluid and the female reproductive tract, and alleviates disorders of the wind (vāta).
It consists of sārivā, sarja, mañjiṣṭhā, yaṣṭīmadhu, and beeswax, combined with milk.
In cases of vāta-śoṇita (gout), cooked oil known as piṇḍa-taila should be administered;
alternatively, castor oil prepared with sārivā, sarja, yaṣṭīmadhu, and beeswax combined with milk should be used to alleviate the pain of gout.

One should cook one *tula* of purified *nāgabalā* in water until reduced to a quarter-remnant decoction; [this, along with] beeswax, *mañjiṣṭhā*, resin (*sarjarasa*), and *sārivā*, is known as *piṇḍataila*, which destroys the pain of *vātarakta*.
Having drained [the bladder], one should add one āḍhaka of oil mixed with goat’s milk;
having cooked it with five palas each of the pastes of nata and yaṣṭīmadhuka separately, this indeed pacifies even aggravated vātarakta within seven nights by means of administering an enema.

This excellent oil, prescribed by the Aśvins, when drunk for ten days, indeed renders one free from disease. One should take a *prastha* of guggulu, which has a color resembling the eye and the interior of a fine buffalo's hide,
and throw it into a body of water along with *triphalā* in the quantities previously specified.
Thirty-two palas of chinnaruhā should be given and boiled with care; being vigilant,
one should stir it repeatedly with a ladle until half the water has been consumed through contact with the fire.
Having poured it out and filtered it through a cloth, one should pour it back again into an iron vessel.
When that has become thickened, resembling a piece of ice, one should pour into it half a *pala* of powdered *triphalā* and six *akṣas* of powdered *trikaṭu*.
Having carefully powdered half a pala of kṛmiripu (karañja) seeds, one karṣa each of trivṛt and dantī, and one pala of guḍūcī,
one should administer it with a post-digestive vehicle (anupāna) of vegetable broth, water, or fragrant water.
One who follows this regimen of diet and conduct, having employed this medicine at all times,

conquers vāta-śoṇita (gout) that is localized in the body, whether it arises from a single humor or from a combination of two, even when it has been long-standing, flowing, dried up, or cracked, extending even down to the knees. (39–40)

It quickly destroys ulcers, cough, leprosy, abdominal tumors, swelling, ascites, anemia, urinary disorders, weak digestion, constipation, and the pustules of prameha. When consumed continuously, it destroys all diseases in the course of time.
Having overcome the defect of old age, one attains the form of youth.
(42) One *prastha* of *guḍūcī*, half a *prastha* of *guggulu*, and one should prescribe the same measure for each of the three fruits (*triphalā*). (43)
Having crushed everything together, one should boil it in water that is not salty until a quarter remains; having strained it, one should place it again on the fire.
One should cook that decoction until it reaches a thick consistency.
Take one pala each of dantī, vyoṣa, viḍaṅga, guḍūcī, and the bark of the three myrobalans (triphalā);
then, having strained them, one should take half a pala of each.
Furthermore, one should take one karṣa of trivṛt for each [of the other ingredients] and grind everything together into a powder. || 45-46 ||
Having ascertained that it is well-cooked, the wise physician should place it while still lukewarm;
then, having assessed the strength of the patient's digestive fire, he should administer the appropriate dose.
It cures vātarakta, as well as leprosy (kuṣṭha), hemorrhoids, and the impairment of the digestive fire.

This Guggulu, beginning with Amṛtā, which was fashioned by the Aśvins in ancient times, dispels malignant ulcers, urinary disorders (prameha), rheumatism (āmavāta), fistula-in-ano, sinus ulcers, and swelling— all of these.
Two *prasthas* of *amṛtā*, one *prastha* of *guggulu*,
one *prastha* each of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and one *prastha* of *varṣābhū*—
having crushed all these together, one should boil them in water that is not salty.
One should cook it again until only a quarter remains and it has reached a thick consistency. Then,
one should add half a pala each of the roots of dantī and citraka, pippalī, viśva, and triphalā, as well as guḍūcī, tvak, and viḍaṅga.
One should powder one *trivṛt* root and all [the other ingredients] together in one place; once prepared, one should add one *pala* of *amṛtā-guggulu* to that while it is still warm.
One who suffers from *amlapitta* should eat it especially according to the strength of their digestive fire.
It destroys vātarakta, as well as leprosy (kuṣṭha), hemorrhoids, loss of digestive fire,
malignant ulcers, urinary disorders (prameha), rheumatism (āmavāta), fistula-in-ano, sinus tracts,
and edema caused by wind; indeed, it cures all diseases.
For this Amṛtāguggulu was indeed fashioned by the two Aśvins in ancient times. [The ingredients are:
śatāvarī, nāgabalā, vṛddhadāraka, uccaṭā, punarnavā, amṛtā, kṛṣṇā, vājigandhā, and trikaṇṭaka.
One should have ten *pala* each of these made into a fine powder.
The wise man should mix that powder with half as much sugar, knead it together, and place it in a very strong vessel combined with half an *āḍhaka* of honey.
Having stirred it with one *prastha* of clarified butter and three *palas* of the "three aromatics" (*trisugandhi*),
a man should eat it as his desired food according to the strength of his digestive fire.
It cures *vātarakta*, consumption, leprosy, and cough arising from *pitta*.
Having destroyed diseases arising from wind, bile, and phlegm, as well as others of that kind,
this elixir named *Yogasārāmṛta* makes a person free from wrinkles and grey hair, increasing fortune and splendor.

One should avoid daytime sleep and similar causes of distress, as well as physical exertion, sexual intercourse, pungent, hot, heavy, obstructive, salty, and sour foods. (62) [No verses of the *Siddhayoga* appear on this page.]
