Chapter 24:
Oleation, bloodletting, emesis, enema therapy, and purgation.
One should avoid rich foods and drinks because they are antagonistic to those [therapies].

Therefore, in this condition, one should always employ sudation, fasting, and drying treatments, while protecting the wind (vāta) from the excess of undigested matter (āma), fat (medas), and phlegm (kapha).
Therefore, whatever pacifies kapha without aggravating vāta should always be employed as the medicine for ūrustambha.
One should consume old śyāmāka, kodrava, uddāla, and śāli rice.

If there is an aggravation of Vāta due to the dryness [of the diet]— indicated by insomnia and pain— one should employ a regimen of oleation and sudation to alleviate the Vāta disorders, using wholesome meat from wild animals that is free of ghee, along with saltless vegetables.
One should cause him to swim repeatedly against the current of a river with cool, auspicious water, and again and again across a clear, cool lake of still water; thus,
when his phlegm has dried up, the seizing pain in the thighs will subside.
This therapeutic procedure should be performed while protecting the strength of the body and the digestive fire.
In cases of *ūrustambha* (stiffness of the thighs), one should drink either *śilājatu*, *guggulu*, *pippalī*, or *nāgara* with urine or with a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*).
Bhallātaka, amṛtā, śuṇṭhī, dāru, pathyā, punarnavā, combined with the two types of pañcamūla, destroy ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs).
Pippalī, pippalīmūla, and the fruits of bhallātaka [are likewise effective].
Having drunk the paste mixed with honey, one is freed from ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs).
For the destruction of ūrustambha, one should lick a compound of triphalā, cavya, kaṭuka, and granthika with honey, or drink puruṣa (pippalī) with urine.
Or one should lick the powder of triphalā mixed with kaṭukā and honey;
or a person may drink the powder known as ṣaṭcaraṇa with lukewarm water;
or the pippalī-vardhamāna preparation with honey or jaggery.
In cases of thigh-stiffness (ūrustambha), they highly recommend Gaṇḍīra and Ariṣṭa.

A paste made from two Palas each of Pippalī root and Nāgara, combined with eight parts of Katvara and one Prastha of oil mixed with an equal amount of curd, cures sciatica and stiffness of the thighs.
Saindhavādya oil is beneficial, as indeed is Amṛtādya guggulu.
Chapter 25:
Fasting, sudation, bitter, digestive, and pungent [substances].
Purgation, the internal administration of fats (sneha-pāna), and enemas (basti) are indicated for Āmavāta.
A decoction of śaṭhī, śuṇṭhī, abhayā, ugrā, devāhvā, ativiṣā, and amṛtā is a digestive (pācana) remedy for Āmavāta; it should be accompanied by a dry diet (rūkṣa-bhojana).
A person suffering from āmavāta should drink a paste of śaṭhī and viśvauṣadhī combined with a decoction of varṣābhū for seven nights in order to digest the āma.
[One should also use] daśamūla, amṛtā, eraṇḍa, rāsnā, nāgara, and dāru.
A decoction [of these] with castor oil destroys heavy Vāta accompanied by undigested matter (āmā).
Alternatively, one should drink castor oil with a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūlī) or with water boiled with ginger, in cases of pain in the abdomen, bladder, and waist.
One should drink a decoction of rāsnā, guḍūcī, eraṇḍa, devadāru, and mahauṣadha when vāta is localized in all the limbs, or when it is associated with āma and has reached the joints,
bones, and marrow. [6] [A decoction] of rāsnā, amṛtā, āragvadha, devadāru, trikaṇṭaka, eraṇḍa, and punarnavā...
One suffering from pain in the calves, thighs, knees, groin, or back should drink a decoction mixed with powdered ginger (nāgara).
A decoction of ginger and gokṣuraka, consumed every morning,
is digestive and a destroyer of pain in cases of vāta with āma and hip pain.
Combined with barley-alkali (yavakṣāra), it destroys dysuria.
One should drink a decoction of mahauṣadha and guḍūcī mixed with long pepper (pippalī) in cases of abdominal distension accompanied by pain and swelling, especially in cases of lumbago.
In cases of āmavāta, one should drink water decocted with daśamūla mixed with kaṇā,
or eat abhayā and viśva, or guḍūcī with nāgara;
or a person should consume harītakī combined with castor oil according to the prescribed method.

One who is afflicted by the pain of undigested matter (āmānila) and constantly tormented by the increase of *gṛdhra-sī* should always drink one *karṣa* of powdered *nāgara* with sour gruel (*kāñjika*).
This is a supreme remedy that pacifies *āmavāta* and removes *kapha-vāta*.

One should drink the powder of the five pungents (*pañcakola*) with warm water; it destroys weak digestion, colic, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), anemia (*āmaya*), phlegm disorders, and loss of appetite.
A powder made from *amṛtā*, *nāgara*, *gokṣura*, *muṇḍitikā*, and *varuṇaka* [is likewise effective].
Drinking curd-whey with sugar-cane juice is renowned for destroying undigested matter (āmadoṣa) and wind disorders.
14. Two parts of maṇimantha, two parts of yavānī, three parts of ajamodā, and five parts of nāgara [are taken]. 15.
Twelve auspicious *harītakī* fruits, finely powdered, when drunk with whey (*mastu*),
sour gruel (*āranāla*), buttermilk (*takra*), ghee, or warm water, conquer *āmavāta*, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and diseases arising in the heart and bladder.

This Vaiśvānara powder is known to cure splenic disorders, glandular swellings, colic, and the like, as well as hemorrhoids, abdominal distension, constipation, diseases of the stomach, and ailments arising in the hands and feet; it restores the downward movement of the bodily winds (vāta). || 17-18 ||
One should prepare a fine powder of Alambuṣā, Gokṣuraka, Guḍūcī, Vṛddhadāraka, Pippalī, Trivṛt, Mustā, Varuṇa, Punarnavā,
Triphalā, and Nāgara. || 19–20 ||
Taken with whey, sour gruel, buttermilk, milk, or meat broth, it quickly destroys *āmavāta* and swelling located in the joints.
Equal parts of *śatapuṣpā*, *viḍaṅga*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and black pepper [should be used].
This powder, when drunk with warm water, is a supreme stimulant for the digestive fire.
Asafoetida, chavya, biḍa salt, ginger, black cumin, and puṣkara root— this powder, taken in increasing proportions, becomes a conqueror of wind-born colic.
Citraka, pippalīmūla, yavānī, kāravī, as well as viḍaṅga, ajamodā, jīraka, and suradāru; cavya, elā, saindhava, kuṣṭha, rāsnā, gokṣura, and dhānyaka.
One should prepare a fine powder of triphalā, mustaka, vyoṣa, tvak, uśīra, yavāgraja,
tālīsapatra, and patra; and one should take an amount of guggulu equal in measure to all these substances combined.
Having thoroughly kneaded it with clarified butter, one should place it in a greasy vessel;
from this, one should administer the dose even while eating food according to one's desire.
This formulation, known as Yogarāja, is like nectar.
It destroys disorders such as āmavāta and āḍhyavāta, as well as worms, malignant ulcers, splenic enlargement, abdominal tumors, abdominal distension, flatulence, and hemorrhoids;
it kindles the digestive fire and likewise increases vitality, luster, and strength.
This conquers wind diseases (vātaroga), even those located in the joints and marrow.
Alambuṣā, gokṣuraka, triphalā, nāgara, and amṛtā are taken in increasing proportions by one part each respectively; the powder of śyāmā is equal to the total of these.
One should drink it with *surā*, *takra*, *kāñjika*, or warm water;
when drunk, it conquers *āmavāta* accompanied by swelling, as well as *vātaśoṇita* located in the spine, knees, thighs, and joints, and it destroys fever and loss of appetite. (31)
This powder, beginning with Alambuṣā, is a destroyer of the host of diseases.
Triphalā is well-known as consisting of Harītakī, Akṣa, and Dhātrī respectively;
from each of these, there is an increase of one part in successive order.
One should drink an equal powder of *pathyā*, *viśva*, and *yavānī* with buttermilk,
warm water, or even sour gruel (*kāñjika*).
This quickly destroys *āmavāta*, as well as swelling and weak digestion.
One pala each of ajamoda, marica, pippalī, viḍaṅga, suradāru, citraka, śatāhvā,
saindhava, and pippalīmūla— these nine ingredients should consist of one pala each. There should be ten palas of śuṇṭhī and as many palas (ten) of vṛddhadāra.
One should prepare a powder by combining five palas of pathyā with all [the other ingredients] together.

Having made boluses (vaṭaka) with an equal amount of jaggery, or drinking the powder with warm water, all diseases of the digestive tract arising from undigested matter (āma) and wind (anila) are destroyed. || 37-38 ||
Viśvācī, pratitūnī, tūnī, and diseases such as gṛdhrasī—terrible ailments arising from the waist, bladder, knees, and anus—as well as the cracking of the bones and shanks with intense pain;
swelling in all the limbs and joints, and whatever other conditions are born of āmavāta. || 39 ||
All [these ailments] go to destruction, like darkness destroyed by the rays of the sun.
One should cook one prastha of ghee with the decoction and paste of nagara,
using either four times that amount of the same [decoction] or with plain water alone.
Ghee prepared with ginger is said to be the supreme pacifier of wind and phlegm, an excellent stimulator of the digestive fire, and a destroyer of pain in the waist.
[This is prepared] with the decoction and paste of amṛtā and mahauṣadha.
Ghee prepared over a mild fire is a supreme remedy for vātarakta;
when administered, it quickly destroys āmavāta, āḍhyavāta, and other such disorders, as well as worms, skin diseases, ulcers, hemorrhoids, and abdominal tumors.
Having made a paste of one pala each of hiṅgu, the three pungents (trikaṭuka), cavya, and likewise maṇimantha, one should cook one prastha of ghee with one āḍhaka of fermented rice-gruel (āranāla);
that ghee destroys abdominal diseases.

It destroys colic, constipation, flatulence, āmavāta, and stiffness of the waist; it cures disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī-doṣa) and is a supreme stimulant for weak digestion. It should be prepared with milk for nourishment, or with curd in cases of retention of feces and urine.
This is proclaimed by the wise for the purpose of kindling the digestive fire (dīpana).
Ghee prepared with a paste of ginger and four times as much sour gruel (sauvīraka) is excellent; it stimulates the fire and is supreme in curing āmavāta.

Having washed one *prastha* of *siddhārthaka* (white mustard seeds) well in water to remove the husks, one should place it along with one *prastha* of *maṇḍa* (scum of boiled rice) and let it sit for three days. Then, having ground them into powder, one should add one *pala* each of the following to a heap of grain: ||| 49-50 ||
Alambuṣā, gokṣuraka, śatapuṣpā, punarnavā, prasāraṇī, the bark of varuṇa, śuṇṭhī, and likewise madana—
having ensured they are properly cooked, this preparation is perfected when mixed with rice. || 51 ||
Fried in mustard oil and combined with asafoetida and rock salt,
or taken with salt, it conquers diarrhea accompanied by great pain—
whether it be of single origin, caused by two humors, curable, or even arising from the combination of all three humors.

This gruel, which cures wind in the hips, thighs, and knees, as well as flatulence and wind in the sacrum (trika), removes upward-moving wind (udāvarta) and promotes strength, complexion, and digestive fire.
[One should take] one hundred palas of garlic and one kuḍava of sesame.
The wise man [should take] asafoetida, the three pungents (tri-kaṭuka), the two alkalis, the five salts,
as well as śatapuṣpā, kuṣṭha, pippalī, urine, citraka, ajamodā, yavānī, and coriander. || 55–56 ||
One should have each of these made into a fine powder— one *pala* for each— and place them in a sturdy vessel of ghee for sixteen days,
having added one *āḍhaka* of oil and half a *prastha* of fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*).
One should consume a karṣa measure of it and drink liquor afterwards;
this is for cases of āmavāta, vāta located in the whole body or a single limb,
epilepsy, weak digestion, cough, asthma, and poisons.
It is recommended for those suffering from insanity, wind-disorders, and colic.

One hundred crushed bulbs of garlic and half that amount of dehusked sesame seeds should be placed in a vessel of cow's buttermilk along with an equal quantity of the ground medicinal ingredients. 59–60.
One pala each of coriander, the three pungents (ginger, black pepper, and long pepper), cavya, citraka, gajapippalī, ajamodā, cinnamon, cardamom, and granthika;
eight palas of sugar and half a pala of black pepper.
Four [palas] each of kuṣṭha and ajājī, as well as one kuḍava of honey;
four [palas] of fresh ginger, eight palas of ghee,
and twenty [palas] of white sesame oil.
Four *siddhārthaka* seeds and likewise four *rājikā* seeds, one *karṣa* measure of asafoetida, and the five salts—
having combined these, one should place them inside a sturdy jar in the midst of grain.
Having extracted [the medicine] after twelve days, one should eat it in the morning according to one's strength. Afterward, the person should drink liquor, *sauvīraka*, *sīdhu*, or *madya*.
Once that has been digested, one may eat whatever food is desired, with the exception of curd and flour-based foods.
Through its consumption for one month, this [remedy] subdues all diseases:
eighty diseases born of vāta, forty born of pitta,
twenty born of śleṣman, and twenty types of prameha.
It is supreme for removing abdominal enlargement, hemorrhoids, and the five types of gulma;
it is the best remedy for the eighteen types of skin diseases and consumption.
It quickly dispels trembling, the pain of gulma, and stiffness.
It effects the healing of broken joints and bones that have fallen apart;
it improves the complexion of the eyes, acts as an aphrodisiac, promotes longevity, and increases strength.
[One should take] one hundred palas of crushed garlic and fifty palas of black sesame seeds.
One should prepare this in curd of equal measure placed in a vessel smeared with ghee.
Twenty palas of *cukra*, along with an equal amount each of jaggery, ginger, and *mātuluṅga*, as well as that much sesame oil and that much ghee, should be added here.
Śatapuṣpā, gaja-pippalī, pomegranate, vṛkṣāmla, dhātakī, musta,
trikaṭu, kuṣṭha, jayā, grapes, ela, and the two types of jīraka;
suradāru, sindhu, biḍa, sauvarcala, romaka, and sāmudra salt.
Having made them equal in size to a *palāśa* leaf, the wise man should have them ground into a fine powder.

After stirring it, he should place it within a heap of grain for three periods of seven days while maintaining protective rites (*rakṣā*). Thereafter, on an auspicious lunar day, at a favorable moment (*muhūrta*), and under a propitious asterism (*nakṣatra*), he should extract the perfected substance.
A person should eat a bolus weighing two *pala*s, made fragrant with the powder of cinnamon bark, cardamom, saffron, camphor, cloves, and nutmeg;
avoiding excessively hot food and when thirsty, one should drink wine as desired.

This medicinal bolus of garlic, called Amṛta, is declared by Parāśara to be nectar itself. For men whose bodies have bones that are crushed, fallen out, displaced, fractured, or dislocated at the joints,
there is indeed no other medicine superior to this.
It generates strength, complexion, and digestive fire; it increases memory, intellect, and wisdom; it is auspicious;
and it pacifies all disorders that have remained unvanquished by hundreds of other medicines.
[One should avoid] curd, fish, molasses, milk, *potakī*, black gram, and flour-based foods.
One afflicted by āmavāta should avoid meat from marshy regions (ānūpa), as well as those foods that cause secretions (abhiṣyandi) and others that are heavy and slimy;
these must be diligently avoided by men suffering from āmavāta. (71–72)
Chapter 26: Emesis, fasting, sudation, digestive stimulants, medicinal suppositories, alkalis, powders, and pills are recommended for the alleviation of colic. (1)
For the wind (vāyu) is swift-acting; therefore, one should conquer it with haste.
Indeed, sudation alone brings relief to one afflicted by colic.
Soup made of horse gram (kulattha), combined with unctuous substances, destroys colic of the windy nature in no time.

One should drink [this powder] with warm water in cases of colic (śūla) and when the digestive tract has been emptied of food; it consists of Saindhava salt, Vyōṣa, and Lāva, enriched with Hiṅgu, Sauvarcala salt, and pomegranate.
Alternatively, one should drink a powder of Hiṅgu, Prativiṣā, Vyōṣa, Vacā, Sauvarcala salt, and Abhayā with warm water.
Balā, punarnavā, eraṇḍa, the two types of bṛhatī, and gokṣura, when drunk together with asafoetida and salt, will instantly conquer the pain of vāta.
Tumburu, abhayā, asafoetida, puṣkaramūla, and the three salts [likewise act as a remedy].
One suffering from wind-pain, abdominal tumors, or convulsions should drink [this] with barley-water.
Having boiled water with the roots of *viśva* and castor plant (*eraṇḍa*), one should drink it combined with asafoetida and *sauvarcala* salt; this immediately wards off pain.
A decoction of *hiṅgu*, *puṣkaramūla*, or *hiṅgu* with *sauvarcala* salt,
along with *viśva* and *eraṇḍa*, when drunk, alleviates colic. Likewise, a decoction of *rūbūka* and barley, combined with *hiṅgu* and *sauvarcala* salt, [achieves the same].
Yavānī, hiṅgu, sindhūttha, kṣāra, sauvarcala,

and abhayā should be drunk with the scum of wine (surāmaṇḍa) as a remedy for wind-pain (vātaśūla). [Likewise, a preparation] with sauvarcika, āmlīkā, jīraka, and marica, each succeeding one being double the amount of the preceding, [is also effective].
A pill made by grinding these with the juice of *mātuluṅga* removes wind-pain (*anila-śūla*).
[The formulation consists of] *hiṅgu*, *amlavetasa*, *kṛṣṇā*, *āmalaka*, *yavānī*, alkali, *abhayā*, and *saindhava*, each taken in equal parts.
One should drink the powder mixed with the scum of varuṇī liquor for the relief of increased pain born of vāta;
or, having made a pill from sesame seeds, one should roll it over the abdomen.
The pill quickly pacifies even the most unbearable colic. By applying a plaster of *madana* mixed with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) to the navel, one conquers colic;
or else, a paste of *jīvantī* root combined with oil destroys pain in the flanks.
Jaggery, śāli rice, barley, milk, drinking ghee, purgatives,
and the meat of wild animals are the remedies for those suffering from pitta-type colic (pitta-śūla).
In cases of pitta-type colic, however, emesis should be induced with milk, water, sugarcane juice, as well as paṭola and nimba.
Plunging into cool waters, pleasant breezes, bronze vessels submerged in water, other excellent cooling things, moonbeams with sandalwood paste— these are very cold.
There are also vessels made of bronze, silver, and copper on all sides.
One should place full vessels of water upon a trident.

Purgatives that remove pitta are recommended, as are the juices of rabbits and quails; nourishing food prepared with parched grain and honey is advised, along with very cold medicinal formulations mixed with honey.
In cases of vomiting, fever born of pitta, severe colic, burning sensations, or excessive thirst,
a person seeking relief should drink a very cold gruel of barley mixed with honey.
[One may also take] the juice of āmalakī or vidārī with trāyamāṇā and cow’s milk.

One should drink wine mixed with sugar to destroy pitta-type colic. A person should drink the juice of śatāvarī mixed with honey in the morning for the purpose of pacifying burning sensations and colic, and to remove all diseases caused by pitta.
One should drink water boiled with śatāvarī, yaṣṭyāhva, vāṭyāla, kuśa, and gokṣura, and then cooled, mixed with jaggery, honey, and sugar;
this destroys pitta-blood disorders, burning sensations, and colic, and immediately removes burning fever. || 22 ||
One should cause [the patient] to drink a decoction prepared with triphalā, nimba, yaṣṭīmadhu, kaṭukā, and āragvadha, mixed with honey, for the alleviation of burning sensations and pain.
[Likewise, one may use] the two types of bṛhatī, gokṣura, eraṇḍa, kuśa, kāśa, and ikṣuvālikā.

Yellow [substances] would instantly destroy even the most dreadful colic arising from bile (pitta). One should lick the powder of *dhātrī* (myrobalan) mixed with honey to alleviate colic caused by bile. In cases of phlegm (kapha), one should employ fasting, emetics, head-purgatives (nasal evacuations), and the drinking of honey and *sīdhu* liquor.
One should consume honey, wheat, barley, and *ariṣṭa* liquors, as well as all dry and pungent substances.
One should administer *pañcakola* combined with the three salts and asafoetida, along with lukewarm water, to be drunk in cases of pain caused by *kapha*.
The roots of *bilva*, *eraṇḍa*, *citraka*, and *viśvabheṣaja* (ginger),
combined with *hiṅgu* and rock salt, are an excellent remedy that instantly removes colic. Alternatively, the juice of *mātuluṅga* or a decoction of *śigru* is even more effective.
Sakṣāra (alkaline preparation) drunk with honey relieves pain in the flanks, the heart, and the bladder.
The juice of vidārī and pomegranate, combined with trikaṭu, salt, and honey, quickly conquers pain arising from the three doṣas.

One should drink water boiled with equal parts of castor seeds and roots, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *gokṣura*, the *parṇinīs*, *sahadevā*, *siṃhapucchī*, and *ikṣuvālikā*, combined with *yavakṣāra*. || 31 ||
It cures colic arising from individual doshas as well as that arising from all of them together. Maṇḍūra purified with cow’s urine and combined with the powder of triphalā,
when licked with honey and ghee, destroys colic born of the three doshas.
Conch-shell powder combined with salt, asafoetida, and the three pungents (vyoṣa), when drunk with warm water, destroys colic born of the three doṣas.
In the case of colic caused by undigested matter (āma), treatment that destroys kapha-induced colic should be administered.
Whatever increases the digestive fire (agni) should all be consumed while being served.
A decoction prepared from castor root, bilva, the two types of bṛhatī, mātuluṅga, pāṣāṇabheda, the three pungents (tri-kaṭu), and radish [is likewise beneficial].
Alkali, cinnabar, and salt, mixed with *rubū* oil,
should be drunk for pains in the hips, shoulders, penis, heart, and breasts.
[Also] asafoetida, *tumburu*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *yavānī*, *citraka*, and *abhayā*.
One should drink this powder, containing alkali and salt, in the morning with warm water.
It destroys disorders of feces, urine, and wind, relieves colic, acts as a digestive, and stimulates the digestive fire.
[Likewise,] *citraka*, *granthika*, *eraṇḍa*, *śuṇṭhī*, and *dhānya* boiled in water [should be used].

In cases of colic, abdominal distension, and constipation, a powder made of asafoetida, viḍalavana, rock salt, dīpyaka, saindhava, pathyā, and ginger in equal parts quickly conquers pain and stimulates a sluggish digestive fire. (39)
In a condition characterized by both pitta and vāta, one should drink the *bṛhatyādi* group of drugs mixed with honey;
or, in the case of pain arising from vāta and pitta, one should employ a combined therapeutic regimen.
One should drink a decoction of *paṭola*, *triphalā*, and *ariṣṭa*, combined with honey.
For the pacification of fever, vomiting, burning sensations, and colic caused by pitta and kapha:
one should employ, combined together, those treatments which have been described separately for pitta-born and kapha-born disorders in cases of colic arising from both kapha and pitta.
Having observed the strength and weakness of the *doṣas*, the physician should administer emesis and purgation as appropriate, using the remedies prescribed for *kapha* and *pitta*.
A powder made from equal parts of *rucaka* salt, *hiṅgu*, and *mahauṣadha* [should be used].
It should be drunk with ginger-water in cases of colic (viṣūcikā) arising from phlegm and wind, as well as pain in the heart, flanks, back, and abdomen;
likewise, it should be taken with barley-juice in cases of constipation.

In cases where there is the drinking of powder with a decoction, the decoction is predominant; therefore, the "four liquids" rule does not apply here with respect to the powder. (45) Because only a small quantity of asafoetida is mentioned, the word "sama" (equal) carries the sense of "together with. (46)

One should drink the powder of the two alkalis, asafoetida, the three salts, and puṣkaramūla, along with water boiled with viśva, ubūka, daśamūla, and barley, for the relief of constriction in the heart, flanks, and waist, as well as for colic.
One suffering from severe pain in the colon, flesh, fever, abdominal tumors (gulma),
and colic should drink a powder of asafoetida, sauvarcala salt, harītakī, viḍa salt, rock salt, tumburu, and puṣkaramūla with a decoction of daśamūla and barley.
It is recommended for pain in the sides, heart, waist, back, and shoulders, as well as for drowsiness, tetanus, swelling, excessive salivation due to phlegm, and diseases of the throat.
One who desires [recovery] should drink garlic mixed with wine in the morning.
This powder, which kindles the digestive fire and destroys colic born of wind and phlegm,
consists of asafoetida, the three pungents (trikaṭuka), kuṣṭha, alkali of barley, and rock salt, combined with the juice of citron; it removes splenic pain.

The excellent powder of triphalā combined with sharp iron filings should be administered with honey and ghee; it wards off all types of pain. [One should take] that which has been boiled in urine, dried, and mixed with iron filings.
One should eat Abhayā with jaggery today for the pacification of all types of colic (śūla).
In cases of Vāta, non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) combined with purgatives are indicated;
in Pitta, milk applications and sweet substances are used.
Bitter, astringent, and pungent substances, as well as emetics, are indicated when colic is associated with kapha.
Long pepper root (nāgara), long pepper (pippalī), wood-apple (bilva), caraway (kāravī), chaba pepper (cavya), and leadwort (citraka) [are also used].
Asafoetida, pomegranate, wood sorrel, vacā, alkali, and sour vetasa;
marsh mallow, black salt, cumin, and citron; with three parts of curd and ghee—this prepared mixture is known as *dādhika*.

This preparation with curd is remembered as the best for pacifying the humors; it is excellent for curing abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, pain in the heart and flanks, and diseases of the female reproductive organs. (57) For one whose body is wrapped in a blanket while performing breath control (prāṇāyāma), [this is beneficial].
Incense made from roasted flour (saktu) smeared with pungent oil is the supreme remedy for removing colic (śūla). Pain, thirst, fainting, constipation, heaviness,
loss of appetite, cough, dyspnea, and hiccups are known as the complications (upadrava) of colic.
One suffering from colic should avoid physical exertion, sexual intercourse, wine, salt, pungent substances, suppression of natural urges, grief, and anger. (Chapter 27)
Fasting, emesis, purgation, unctuous enema (anuvāsana),
non-unctuous enema (nirūha), and enemas prepared with vājigandhā and others, as well as honey-oil enemas (mādhutailika), are recommended.
[One should also administer] viḍaṅga seeds, trikaṭu, trivṛt, dantī, and citraka.
Having gathered all these together, one should have them made into fine powders.
Having prepared modakas with jaggery, one should eat them upon rising in the morning;
one should also take warm water as an after-drink, which increases the digestive fire.
It conquers colic born of the three doṣas and that arising from the digestive transformation (pariṇāma).
If a man eats a bolus made from the paste of ginger and sesame seeds prepared with milk,
his severe colic of digestion will depart within seven nights.
Having burnt equal parts of castor root, *vahni*, *śambūka*, frog, and *gokṣura* inside [an earthen vessel], one should drink it with warm water for the pacification of colic.
Ashes produced from *śambūka*, when drunk with warm water, [provide relief] at that very moment.
This destroys colic born of digestion, just as Viṣṇu destroyed the Asuras.
Having made a pill of equal parts of Śambūka, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), and the five salts, [one should take it] with the juice of Kalamba.
Or one may consume it at the time of the morning meal according to one's strength;
the person is suddenly liberated from colic born of the digestive transformation (pariṇāma). He who drinks barley-gruel alone with pea-soup for seven nights [is likewise freed].
It conquers chronic pain resulting from transformation (pariṇāma), let alone that which is newly arisen. Iron powder combined with *varā*, when licked with honey and clarified butter,
pacifies colic of the digestive tract (*pakti-śūla*) or its associated impurities.
One should lick a powder of *kṛṣṇā*, *abhayā*, and iron mixed with honey and sugar; this immediately destroys even the most severe colic arising from indigestion (*pariṇāma-śūla*).
A powder of *pathyā*, iron filings, and *śuṇṭhī* [should be taken] with honey and ghee.
It destroys the pain arising from the transformation [of the humors], whether it be of the nature of vāta, pitta, or kapha.
(12) Sea salt, rock salt, kṣāra, rucaka,
romaka, viḍa, (13) dantī, iron filings and dross, trivṛt, and sūraṇaka— [these] in equal parts.
Having been cooked over a gentle fire with curd, cow’s urine, and milk,
one should drink that powder with warm water according to the strength of one's digestive fire.
After each dose has been digested, one should eat a meal of black gram and other grains prepared with ghee.
It certainly removes pain in the navel caused by abdominal tumors (gulma) and the spleen;
likewise, it destroys abscesses (vidradhi) and stone-like growths (aṣṭhīlikā) arising from phlegm and wind. There is no medicine superior to this for all types of colic pains.
It is considered especially effective for curing disorders arising from the transformation of food (pariṇāma).
One should cook ghee with long pepper and jaggery in four times the amount of milk;
this destroys acid bile (amlapitta) and colic born of the transformation of food. || 17–18 ||

Ghee prepared with a decoction and a paste of *pippalī*, combined with honey and followed by the consumption of milk, certainly destroys even severe colic known as *pariṇāma-śūla*. [19] Powdered *kola*, *granthika*, ginger, *capalā*, and alkali, taken in equal parts—
Having boiled iron rust (maṇḍūra) in eight times its quantity of fragrant water until it has become thick, one should eat it at the beginning,
middle, and end of meals, generally while consuming milk and rice,
to conquer diseases of wind and phlegm, as well as chronic colic and various types of pain. || 20 ||

One should take one *prastha* of iron rust powder mixed with powdered *viśvauṣadha*, *māgadhī*, *yavakṣāra*, *kolāgranthika*, and one *pala* each of the other ingredients; having combined these, one should bring the entire mass to a solid consistency by gradual heating with eight times its weight of urine.
Three pills, each the size of a jujube fruit, should be taken at the beginning, middle, and end of a meal;

by eating with meat broth, clarified butter, vegetable soup, milk, or meat, a person wards off the colic caused by the displacement of food, as well as abdominal tumors, splenic disorders, and loss of digestive fire. (22–23)
One should cook eight palas of maṇḍūra in half an āḍhaka of cow urine along with one prastha of milk; once prepared, this cures digestive colic (pakti-śūla) in men.
One should cook eight palas of maṇḍūra in eight times its quantity of cow urine.

When it has reached consistency, one should add one *pala* each of powdered *capalā*, *nāgara*, *kṣāra*, *pippalīmūla*, and *pippalī*. From this, one should prepare pills that alleviate colic caused by digestive disorders (*pakti-śūla*).
Having thoroughly purified it and reduced it to powder, take eight *pala*s of *maṇḍūra*,
eight *pala*s of the juice of *śatāvarī*, as well as eight *pala*s of curd and milk,
and four *pala*s of cow’s clarified butter.
One should cook everything together until it reaches the consistency of a ball.
When prepared, one should eat it in the middle of the meal or even before the meal;
it cures colic caused by wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and that which arises from indigestion (pariṇāma).
Indeed, this yoga undoubtedly destroys [the impurities] of the iron rust (maṇḍūra);
its taste is pungent, its smell is auspicious, and it becomes a solid mass through intense rubbing after digestion.
Viḍaṅga, citraka, cavya, triphalā, and the three acrids (tryūṣaṇa) [are used].
These nine parts are like iron dross.
Having added twice as much cow urine and half as much jaggery, one should cook it slowly over a mild fire until it is well-cooked and has attained the consistency of a solid mass. || 31-32 ||
Having placed it in a greasy vessel, one should consume it in the measure of a jujube fruit (kola), administered at the beginning, middle, and end of the meal;
this formulation quickly pacifies even the most severe colic of the digestive tract.
It destroys jaundice, anemia, edema, and even weak digestion; it eliminates hemorrhoids,
disorders of the duodenum, worms, abdominal tumors, and abdominal enlargements,
as well as acid gastritis and obesity.
One should avoid dried vegetables and those that are burning-hot, sour, or pungent; for this jaggery known as Maṇḍūra indeed puts an end to colic during digestion.
Out of compassion for those afflicted by colic, it has been proclaimed by Tārā. (36)
If one consumes fine iron powder cooked with the fresh juices of *akṣa*, *āmalaka*, and *śivā*, along with jaggery, one who suffers from colic is freed from pain arising from the three *doṣas*.
[37] Eight *palas* of *dhātrī* powder and four *palas* of iron powder [are used]. [38]
One should take two palas of yaṣṭīmadhuka powder and rub it on a cloth;
this powder should then be saturated with a decoction of amṛtā for seven days.
Having dried it in the fierce heat of the sun and ground it once more, it should be placed in a new jar.

Combined with ghee and honey, one should eat it three times— beginning, middle, and end of the meal. This regimen, according to the persistence of the humors, destroys at the beginning of the meal the humors arising from bile and wind.
Eaten during the meal, it overcomes constipation in men; eaten at the end of the meal, it conquers the disorders caused by food and drink, and the food does not burn.
Thus, even a very severe colic in men subsides once the food has been digested.
When properly administered, this yoga quickly removes aged bile;
it is beneficial for the eyes, destroys graying hair, overcomes diseases arising from phlegm and bile, clarifies the blood, and conquers anemia and jaundice.

From half a *tulā* of steamed and pressed *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourds, one should fry it in half a *prastha* of clarified butter; then, adding an equal amount of sugar, one should cook it with the juice of *āmalaka*.
While stirring, one should add one *prastha* of well-steamed *kūṣmāṇḍa* juice and another *prastha*.
When that has reached the state of being cooked, one should grind [the following] into powder and add it with a ladle:
two palas each of long pepper (*kaṇā*), cumin (*jājī*), and ginger (*śuṇṭhī*);
one pala of black pepper (*marica*); and tālīśa, coriander (*dhānyaka*), the four spices (*caturjātaka*), and musta. || 46–47 ||
One *karṣa* each of [the aforementioned ingredients] and half a *prastha* of honey,
when taken, destroys colic arising from the three *doṣas*,
as well as vomiting, acid dyspepsia, fainting, asthma, cough, and loss of appetite. (48)
This excellent elixir known as Khaṇḍāmalaka destroys heart pain, internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), and back pain.
Take two parts of powdered kalāya and one part of iron powder.
One should thoroughly rub [the ingredients] with the juice of *kāravella* and *palāśa*.
Then, a person should consume one pill weighing one *karṣa*;
taken with a drink of rice-gruel (*maṇḍa*), it destroys even severe chronic bile disorders (*jaratpitta*).
One should lick the powder of the three myrobalans (triphalā) combined with iron powder, or one should lick it mixed with the powder of liquorice (yaṣṭīmadhu) along with honey for that disease.
Having induced emesis until the bile (pitta) is eliminated, and purgation until the phlegm (kapha) is eliminated. 52–53.

Regarding the liquid food, that which was prescribed for aged pitta should be administered; once the stomachs of undigested matter (āmāśaya) and digested matter (pakvāśaya) are purified, the liquid food will reach a state of equilibrium. A steamed cake made of black gram (māṣa) and lotus seeds (indīvarī), along with husks, mixed with ghee, is beneficial.
In that condition, wheat porridge mixed with ghee and jaggery, or with sugar and cooled milk, or well-mashed, is considered beneficial.
A great disease arising from the liquid part of food is difficult to diagnose and difficult to treat.
Therefore, one should exert the greatest effort toward its pacification.
Since the digestive fire becomes weak when pitta is digested within the liquid food,
one should therefore prepare the food and drinks in moderate quantities.
"That which has been prescribed for food and liquids is also beneficial in the case of decaying bile (jaratpitta)"— thus has the treatment for food and liquids been briefly described.
(58) Chapter 28.

One should eat barley-based food prepared with the juices of *trivṛt*, *sudhā*, leaves, sesame, and other vegetables—whether cultivated, aquatic, or marshy—as well as with other substances that promote the passage of wind, urine, and feces; one should also drink clear wine, molasses, and *sīdhu* liquor.
In cases arising from Vāta, a non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*) is recommended after the patient has been lubricated and fomented.

In cases of fecal obstruction (purīṣaja), the procedure prescribed for intestinal distension (ānāhika) should be performed; in that situation, the physician should administer the milk-Vaitaraṇa enemas. [The ingredients are:
Śyāmā, Dantī, Dravantī, Snuh, Mahāśyāmā, Snuhī, and Trivṛt.
Saptalā, śaṅkhinī, śvetā, rājavṛkṣa, satilvaka, kampillaka, karañja, and hemakṣīrī—this is the group [of drugs]. It should be used with any one of these: ghee, oil, powder, decoction, or paste.
It destroys upward-moving wind (udāvarta), abdominal enlargement (udara), flatulence (ānāha), poison, and abdominal tumors (gulma).
Trivṛt, kṛṣṇā, and harītakī, taken in two, four, and five parts respectively, made into pills with an equal amount of jaggery, remove diseases caused by the obstruction of feces and flatus.
This powder—consisting of *harītakī*, *yavakṣāra*, *pīlunī*, and *trivṛt*—should be drunk with ghee; it destroys *udāvarta*.
[The next formulation consists of] *hiṅgu*, *kuṣṭha*, *vacā*, *svarjikā*, and *biḍa*, each increasing by two parts.
That powder, when drunk with wine, is an excellent remedy for upward-moving wind (udāvarta).
A wise person should lick one *viḍālapadaka* measure of finely ground powder— consisting of one *pala* of sugar and an equal amount of *trivṛt* along with *upakulyā*— mixed with honey before a meal.
This sweet powder, known by the name Nārācaka, is suitable for kings and should be administered in cases of deep-seated constipation, as well as in disorders of bile and phlegm.
Having cooked asafoetida, honey, and rock salt together, one should roll them into a well-formed suppository.
One should apply [this] smeared with ghee to the anus; it destroys upward movement of wind (udāvarta).
Madana, pippalī, kuṣṭha, vacā, and white mustard seeds, combined with jaggery and alkali, are recommended as a medicinal suppository (phalavarti).
A wise person should insert into the swollen anus either radish mixed with sour gruel and combined with house-soot, rock salt, and oil, or crushed leaves of *nirguṇḍī*.
In the case of a urinary injury, one should drink wine enriched with *sauvarcala* salt along with urine.
Or the wise man should drink ela with wine, or milk-water, or the fresh juice of duḥsparśā, or a decoction of kakubha;
or he should drink the seed of īrvāru with water, rendered salt-free.

One should employ milk boiled with the five roots (pañcamūlī) or even grape juice in every way according to the procedure for dysuria and urinary calculi. One should treat upward-moving wind (udāvarta) caused by suppressed yawning with oleation therapies and sudations.
In cases of lacrimation caused by tears, one should diligently apply oleation and sudation;
in cases caused by sneezing, one should induce sneezing using a "sneezing-leaf" held at the nose;
and in cases caused by eructation, one should administer unctuous medicated smoke according to the prescribed sequence.

One should overcome vomiting and distress according to the specific dosha by means of nasal drops, oleation, and other therapies. Milk boiled with four times its quantity of water and the ingredients for purifying the bladder should be given to the patient who has drunk it to his heart's content until the liquid is fully digested. || 19 ||
Beloved women should delight a man suffering from the upward movement of semen (śukrodāvarta).
In this condition, massage, immersion baths, wine, cocks, rice, milk, decoction enemas (nirūha), and sexual intercourse are beneficial.
For the alleviation of hunger, food that is unctuous, warm, and taken in small quantities is beneficial;
for the quenching of thirst, one should drink *mantha* or even cold gruel (*yavāgū*).
A person afflicted by fatigue and labored breathing should eat broth once he has fully recovered his rest.
In cases of suppressed sleep, a person should drink milk and engage in pleasant conversation;
in cases of constipation (ānāha) as well, one should employ treatments that alleviate upward-moving wind (udāvarta).

Twice the amount of hiṅgu, along with vacā, kuṣṭha, suvarcikā, and the powder of viḍaṅga, taken with warm water, destroys abdominal distension, colic pain, heart disease, gulma, and upward-moving wind. [1] Vacā, abhayā, citraka, yavaśūka, pippalī, ativiṣā, and kuṣṭha— [these should be used].
By drinking warm water and eating wholesome rice, one quickly conquers abdominal distension and obstructed wind.
(2) One should saturate Trivṛt, Harītakī, and Śyāmā with the milky sap of Snuhī;
these pills, when taken with urine, are excellent for breaking up abdominal distension. (3)

A suppository (varti) prepared by cooking together rāḍha, dhūma, viḍa, vyōṣa, jaggery, and cow’s urine, and shaped like a thumb, should be inserted into the rectum; it cures abdominal distension and colic.
A suppository may also be made from trikaṭu, saindhava salt, mustard seeds, house-soot (gṛhadhūma), kuṣṭha, and madanaphala.
This suppository, the size of a thumb, made of honey or jaggery and smeared with clarified butter, when inserted slowly into the anus, has proven results;
it pacifies abdominal distension and upward movement of wind (udāvarta) and removes abdominal tumors and swellings (jaṭharagulma). || 5-6 ||
Radish, both dried and fresh, the five roots of *varṣābhū*,
and the fruit of *ārevata*— having boiled these in water, one should cook ghee with it. When that [ghee] is drunk, it pacifies *udāvarta* entirely.
Chapter 30:
Light food is digestive, unctuous, hot, and promotes the downward movement of Vata; it is nourishing and beneficial for all those suffering from abdominal tumors (gulma). 1.
In cases of gulma, the pacification of vāyu should be carried out in every way according to the prescribed rules;
once the vāyu here has been conquered, even a minor procedure will destroy any other aggravated doṣa.
Having brought softness to the channels and having subdued the excessive vāyu, [the treatment succeeds].
Fomentation applied after oleation removes a gulma by breaking up its obstruction;

this is especially true for a person who has first been well-oleated and fomented in the case of a vātika gulma, and subsequently purified by unctuous enemas, purgatives, and decoction enemas with oil.
A wise physician should treat [the patient] with careful discernment regarding dosage and timing.

(4) Meat broths from wild animals that are pleasantly warm, well-oiled, seasoned with rock salt, and combined with the three pungent spices (kaṭutrika) are beneficial for those suffering from gulma when used as drinks. (5)

A skilled physician should apply poultices (kumbhī), boluses (piṇḍa), bricks (iṣṭakā), and fomentation (sveda). Warm compresses (upanāha) such as sālvana and others should also be applied. Bloodletting should be performed by pouring blood from the site or by venesection in the middle of the arm.
Sudation and downward movement of the bowels (anulomana) are indeed recommended for all those suffering from gulma.
The juice of mātuluṅga, asafoetida, pomegranate, viḍa salt,
and rock salt should be drunk with the scum of wine (surāmaṇḍa) to alleviate the pain of vāta-gulma.
Or one should drink castor oil mixed with the scum of *vāruṇī* wine;
a man suffering from wind-type abdominal tumors (*vātagulma*) should drink that same oil with milk.
Alternatively, an alkali made from *ketakī* stalks, combined with *svarjikā* and *kuṣṭha*, may be used.
When drunk with oil, it pacifies gulma arising from Vāta.
When Kapha becomes aggravated during the treatment of Vāta-gulma, emesis is recommended there, as well as powders and other remedies that remove Kapha.
If the pitta becomes aggravated, purgation is the remedy there;
however, if the gulma is not pacified even by those [purgatives] that destroy the doshas, bloodletting should be performed.
One should treat a patient with pitta-type gulma using the Kākolyādi, Mahātiktaka, and Vāsādi groups [of drugs].
After the patient has been lubricated, one should induce purgation and subsequently apply the treatment of enemas (basti).
In the case of a pitta-type gulma arising from unctuous and hot factors, one who desires purgation should lick kampilla with honey,
or drink the juice of grapes mixed with jaggery.

One should recognize that gulma as being "burning" (vidahyamāna) when it is accompanied by distress such as burning sensations and pain, disturbances such as nightmares, loss of appetite, and fever; one should then apply poultices (upanāhana) to it.
When it is ripe (pakva), however, it is characterized by pressure sensitivity, elevation, external protrusion, and slight pain.
In that case, the wound is dark brown, resembling the color of a goat's bladder; it requires both cleansing and healing.
If that morbid humor (doṣa) is expelled spontaneously through either the upper or lower channels, one should wait for twelve days while guarding against complications with appropriate foods.
However, clarified butter is the supreme purifier; once purified, it should be taken with honey and bitter herbs (18).
One should treat phlegm-induced gulma with oleation, poultices, sudation, sharp emetics, enemas, and formulations prescribed for vata-gulma (19).

A person suffering from *kapha*-type abdominal tumors (*gulma*) should drink water boiled with the five roots (*pañcamūlī*), or aged *vāruṇī* liquor, or even aged *ārdvīka* wine at the appropriate time. One should also take buttermilk mixed with powdered *yavānī* and seasoned with *viḍa* salt.
One should drink this digestive stimulant, which promotes the downward movement of wind, urine, and feces; in cases of mixed humors, this very same therapeutic procedure is applied.
When a gulma arises from the combination of all three humors (saṃnipāta), a regimen that subdues the three humors is beneficial.
Vacā, abhayā, viḍaṅga, śuṇṭhī, hiṅgu, kuṣṭha, agni, and dīpyaka, taken in parts of two, three, six, four, one, eight, seven, and five respectively, form a powder which,
when drunk with wine or other liquids, removes abdominal tumors (gulma), flatulence, and enlargement of the abdomen (udara).
It destroys colic, hemorrhoids, dyspnea, and cough, and is an excellent stimulant for the digestive fire in cases of malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī). 24.
Yavānī, hiṅgu, rock salt, kṣāra, sauvarcala salt, and abhayā should be drunk with the scum of wine (surāmaṇḍa) to eradicate abdominal tumors (gulma) and colic. 25.
Having burned *pūtīka* leaves, *gajacirbhaṭa*, *cavya*, *vahni*,
and the three pungents (*vyoṣa*) arranged as a bed with salt as a pillow,
one should grind them into a powder and administer it mixed with curd-whey.
In cases of gulma, abdominal enlargement, edema, anemia, and diseases arising from the rectum,
[one should use] asafoetida, puṣkaramūla, tumburu, harītakī, śyāmā, viḍa salt, rock salt, yavakṣāra, and mahauṣadha (ginger). || 26–27 ||
One should cause him to drink this, fried in ghee and mixed with barley-decoction water; by that, his gulma—along with its pain and its spreading—is broken up.
[The powder of] vacā, harītakī, hiṅgu, rock salt, and amlavetasa [is used].
One should drink barley-alkali and yavānī with warm water.
For this, within seven nights, breaks up the entire mass of gulma along with its pain and complications, and increases the digestive fire.

Surā (fermented liquor) mixed with long pepper (pippalī), long pepper root (pippalīmūla), cumin (ajājī), leadwort (citraka), and rock salt (saindhava), when drunk, quickly destroys even the most difficult-to-cure gulma.
[Likewise, a preparation of] nādeyī, kuṭaja, arka, śigru, bṛhatī, snuh, bilva, and bhallātaka...

Having burned *vyāghrī*, *kiṃśuka*, *pāribhadraka*, *jaṭā*, *pāmārga*, *nīpa*, *agnikā*, *vāsā*, *muṣkaka*, and *pāṭalā* along with salt, and having boiled them in water, this [decoction] with the addition of *hiṅgu* and other ingredients is prescribed for abdominal tumors (*gulma*), abdominal enlargements (*udara*), and *aṣṭhīlā*. || 32 ||
Asafoetida, ugragandhā, viḍa salt, ginger, cumin, harītakī, puṣkaramūla, and kuṣṭha— this powder,
prepared with each subsequent ingredient in increasing proportions, is desired for abdominal tumors, abdominal enlargements, indigestion, and choleraic disorders (visūcikā).
[33] Triphalā, kāñcanakṣīrī, saptalā, nīlinī, and vacā—

One afflicted by all types of gulma, abdominal enlargements, splenic disorders, skin diseases, hemorrhoids, and consumption should drink a powder of trāyantī, hapuṣā, tiktā, trivṛt, saindhava salt, and pippalī, mixed with urine, warm water, meat broth, or similar liquids. || 34–35 ||
A paste (kalka) made from śatāhvā, the bark of cirabilva, dāru, bhārgī, and kaṇā,
when drunk with a decoction of sesame, removes gulma born of blood.
A decoction of sesame, combined with jaggery, vyoṣa, hiṅgu, and bhārgī, may likewise be used.
For women who have blood-born gulma and whose menses have ceased,
the juice of the *dhātrī* (myrobalan), prepared with the alkali of *kiṃśuka* flowers, should be drunk according to the proper method;
likewise, wine combined with alkali and the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*) destroys blood-born gulma.
Listen also to another specific remedy for purifying the blood:
she should drink ghee prepared with the alkaline water of *palāśa*.
Or, one may cause it to be broken up with hot [substances]; once it is broken, the regimen prescribed for *asṛgdara* is beneficial. || 39 ||
One should cook ghee with hapuṣā, vyōṣa, pṛthvīkā, cavya, citraka, saindhava, ajājī, pippalīmūla, and dīpyaka,
along with the juices of kola and mūlaka, as well as milk, curd, and pomegranate.

That supreme ghee destroys vāta-gulma, and it relieves colic, distension, and constipation; it also eliminates disorders of the female reproductive tract, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī-doṣa), dyspnea, cough, anorexia, fever, and pain in the flanks, heart, and bladder. (41–42)

Where there are five or more liquids in a preparation involving fats, they say the fat should be equal [in measure] to those liquids; however, if there are fewer, the fat should be four times [the quantity of the other liquid].
Twenty-five *abhayā* fruits should be boiled in one *droṇa* of water.
Take as many palas of dantī as there are of citraka; likewise,
when the decoction is reduced to one-eighth, one should cook jaggery equal in weight to the dantī,
along with three palas each of the powder of abhayā and trivṛt, and four palas of oil.
Once the linctus is prepared, one should add one pala each of long pepper and dry ginger when it has cooled;
then, add half a kuḍava of honey and likewise one pala of the four aromatics (cāturjātaka).
Then, having licked one pala of the linctus and eaten one harītakī, [one should take the medicine].
The unctuous person is purged of the morbid humors; one should then consume a *prastha* of meat broth with rice.
Splenomegaly, edema, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, heart disease, anemia, disorders of the digestive tract, nausea, irregular fevers, skin diseases, and anorexia are pacified.
Ghee prepared with the paste of trikaṭu, triphalā, dhānyaka, viḍaṅga, cavya, and citraka, along with milk, cures vāta-gulma. [Also,
ghee prepared with] drākṣā, madhuka, kharjūra, vidārī, and śatāvarī...
One should cook *parūṣaka* fruits and *triphalā*, each weighing one *pala*, in one *āḍhaka* of water until reduced to one-quarter.
Then, adding the juice of *āmalaka*, ghee, sugarcane juice, and milk, along with a paste of *abhayā* equal to one-quarter [of the total liquid], [one should prepare this medicated ghee].
One should prepare this ghee; once prepared, it should be mixed with one-quarter part each of sugar and honey.
This medicated ghee removes pitta-type gulma and cures all diseases caused by pitta.
Ghee boiled with the ten roots (daśamūla) along with trikaṭu, alkali, and salt [is also recommended].
This quickly removes *kapha*-type gulma when combined with asafoetida, *viḍa* salt, and pomegranate.
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with one *pala* each of long pepper, long pepper root, *cavya*, *citraka*, and dry ginger, along with alkali from barley (*vaya-kṣāra*).
That ghee, prepared with one prastha of milk, cures gulma caused by kapha;
it also removes disorders of the grahaṇī, anemia, heart disease, splenic enlargement, cough, and fever.
One should cook six-ingredient (ṣaḍaṅga) ghee in the fresh juice of āmalaka fruits.
Combined with sugar and rock salt, this is beneficial for all those afflicted with abdominal tumors (gulma).
One should boil vṛścīva, urubūka, varṣābhū, the two types of bṛhatī,
and citraka in one droṇa of water until it is reduced to one-fourth.
One should place it in a jar smeared with Māgadhī, Citraka, and honey;
having added one prastha of honey and combined it with half a part of powdered Pathyā,
a person who has finished his meal should drink that which has been steeped for ten days in husks.

This Arishta will conquer Gulma caused by indigestion, which is otherwise very difficult to overcome. One suffering from Gulma should not eat dried meat, radishes, fish, dried vegetables, pulses, Vāluka, or sweet fruits.
Chapter 31:
When the heart is afflicted by vāta, one should cause the patient, who has been treated with oleation,
to vomit using a decoction of the two groups of five roots (daśamūla) together with unctuous substances and salt.
Long pepper, cardamom, sweet flag, asafoetida,

alkali of barley, rock salt, black salt, ginger, and ajamodā— these, when powdered and mixed with fruit juices, fermented grain-liquors, horse gram decoction, curd, wine, and āsava, [are used as a snuff].
One should cause the person whose body has been purified to drink one of the various types of unctuous substances (sneha).
Or, one should drink warm ginger decoction (nāgara-kāṣāya), which increases the digestive fire,
removes cough, dyspnea, and wind, and destroys colic and heart disease.

When the heart is afflicted by pitta, one should induce vomiting with water mixed with śrīparṇī, madhuka, honey, sugar, and jaggery; one should consume ghee boiled with sweet drugs, and employ the astringent decoctions prescribed for the destruction of pitta-fever.
Cold plasters, as well as sprinkling treatments, and purgation are indicated when the heart is afflicted by pitta.
Once purified, the diet and drink should consist of pitta-alleviating substances such as grapes, sugar, honey, and *parūṣaka*.
One should also drink sugar ground with water along with *yaṣṭīmadhu* and *tiktakarohiṇī*.
Milk processed with the bark of *arjuna* should be administered for heart disease,
along with sugar, or with the five roots (*pañcamūlī*), or with *balā*, or with *madhuka*.
Those who drink the powder of *kakubha* bark with ghee, milk, or molasses-water [are likewise benefited].

Having destroyed heart disease, chronic fever, and hemorrhagic disorders caused by pitta, they shall become long-lived. When heart disease arises from kapha, one should induce vomiting with decoctions of *vacā* and nimba,
and then administer the *pippalyādi* powder, which cures wind-type heart disease.
In cases arising from the three doṣas, fasting should be administered first; furthermore, food that is beneficial for all [three types] should be prescribed.
Having considered whether the condition is mild, excessive, or moderate, the appropriate treatment for all three should be performed.
One should lick a powder of *puṣkara* root mixed with honey.

This powder, prepared with oil, ghee, and jaggery, destroys heart-pain, dyspnea, and cough, and wards off consumption and hiccup. Furthermore, the man who drinks this powder made from wheat and *pārtha* (calotropis) along with milk shall become a conqueror of all heart diseases. || 12-13 ||
Wheat and *kakubha* flour, cooked with goat’s milk, cow’s ghee,
and combined with honey and sugar, pacifies severe heart disease in men.
One should cause the powder of the root of *nāgabalā* to be drunk with milk.
The bark of the *kakubha* tree destroys heart disease, cough, and asthma;
it is a supreme elixir (*rasāyana*), strengthening and subduing wind (*vāta*) when used for a month.
By employing it for a year, one will certainly live for a hundred years.

One should drink asafoetida, ugragandhā, biḍa salt, viśva, kṛṣṇā, kuṣṭha, abhayā, citraka, and yavaśūka, enriched with sauvarcala salt and pauṣkara, along with barley water; this destroys colic and heart disease.
Furthermore, a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla) combined with salt and alkali [is beneficial].
It destroys dyspnea, cough, heart disease, abdominal tumors, and colic.
One should feed a patient suffering from heart disease caused by worms unctuous rice and meat, along with curd and minced meat, for three days; thereafter, one should administer a purgative.
One should cause [the patient] to drink fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla) mixed with a strong dose of viḍaṅga, along with fragrant substances, salt, cumin, and sugar; this is most beneficial.
In cases born of worms, one should drink urine combined with viḍaṅga and iron.
Thus, the worms situated in the heart of men fall downward.
Thereafter, one should give him barley-food along with viḍaṅga;
furthermore, fifty of the best harītakīs and two palas of sauvarcala salt.
Ghee prepared with these is known by the name Vallabhaka; it destroys heart-disease, dyspnea, abdominal tumors, abdominal enlargement, and wind disorders.
Śvadaṃṣṭrā, uśīra, mañjiṣṭhā, balā, kāśmarya, kattṛṇa, the root of darbha, pṛthakparṇī, palāśa, ṛṣabhaka, and sthirā—[these are the ingredients]. 23–24.
One should cook their juice with four times as much milk,
along with the pastes (kalka) of *svaguptā*, *ṛṣabhaka*, *medā*, *jīvantī*, *jīvaka*,
*śatāvarī*, *ṛddhi*, *mṛdvīkā*, sugar, *śrāvaṇī*, and lotus stalks (*bisas*).
One *prastha* of this prepared preparation, taken with ghee, cures diseases of the heart caused by vāta and pitta, as well as colic;
it removes dysuria, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, cough, asthma, and consumption; and it bestows strength and flesh upon those exhausted by archery, women, wine, heavy loads, or travel. (26–27)
Ghee prepared with *balā*, *nāgabalā*, and the decoction of *arjuna*, along with a paste of *yaṣṭīmadhu* constituting one-fourth part,
pacifies severe heart disease, colic, consumption, internal hemorrhaging (*raktapitta*), cough, and blood disorders caused by *vāyu*.
Ghee prepared with the juice of the paste of *pārtha* (arjuna) is recommended for all diseases of the heart.
Regarding Chapter 32:

Having carefully examined those methods for the pacification of urinary calculi (aśmarī) that have been described, one should apply them according to the specific dosha, as well as the sequential regimen beginning with oleation (sneha).

In cases of dysuria caused by Vāta, one should administer massage, oleation, non-unctuous enemas (nirūha), unctuous enemas (basti), fomentation (sveda), poultices (upanāha), urethral/vaginal enemas (uttara-basti), and affusions (sekāḥ), prepared with the Sthirādi group and other Vāta-alleviating drugs; one should also provide meat soups (rasa) prepared with the same.
[One should also use] Amṛtā, Nāgara, Dhātrī, Vājigandhā, and Trikaṇṭaka.

One afflicted by diseases of Vāta, suffering from colic, or having difficulty in urination, should drink [this]. Cold affusions, immersions, and plasters [are indicated], as well as the summer regimen, enemas, milk, and purgatives.

In cases of urinary distress (kṛcchra) arising from pitta, one should administer [medicines] with grape juice, vidārī juice, sugarcane juice, and ghee. Kuśa, kāśa, śara, darbha, and ikṣu constitute the group derived from grasses.

This *pañcamūla*, which alleviates the distress caused by *pitta* and cleanses the bladder, when boiled and drunk with milk, destroys blood [disorders] located in the penis. [The same applies to] *śatāvarī*, *kāśa*, *kuśa*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *vidārī*, *śālī*, *ikṣu*, and *kaserukā*.
One should conquer urinary distress caused by pitta (*paittika-mūtrakṛcchra*) by drinking a well-cooled decoction mixed with honey and sugar.

(6) In cases of painful and burning urinary distress accompanied by constipation, one should drink a decoction of *harītakī*, *gokṣura*, *rājavṛkṣa*, *pāṣāṇabhida*, and *dhanvayavāsaka*, combined with honey. (7)
An āmalaka fruit with jaggery is aphrodisiac, removes fatigue, is refreshing, and is pleasing;
it destroys pitta, blood disorders, burning sensations, and colic, and prevents dysuria.
[It may be taken] with urine, wine, or the fresh juice of plantain.
For the destruction of dysuria caused by *kapha*, one should drink *truṭi* ground finely.
One should drink the seeds of *śitimāraka* ground with buttermilk for the destruction of dysuria;
likewise, one should drink coral powder with rice-wash water in cases of *kapha*-related dysuria.

In all diseases arising from the three doṣas, however, one should act after carefully considering the sequence of the locations of vāyu; when one doṣa is more predominant than the other three, emesis should first be administered if kapha is the primary factor.
In cases of pitta, purgation is indicated; in cases of vāta, however, enema (basti) is prescribed.
The group beginning with bṛhatī—namely bṛhatī, dhāvanī, pāṭhā, yaṣṭīmadhu, and liṅgaka—is digestive (pācanīya); it removes the three doṣas and cures dysuria (kṛcchra).
One should drink lukewarm milk mixed with jaggery according to one's desire;
it cures all types of dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra) and removes urinary gravel and diseases caused by Vāta.
Likewise, in cases arising from injury, one should apply it immediately as a healer of wounds.
In cases of dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra), Vāta-alleviating treatment should always be administered for him.
When the condition is born of feces (purīṣaja), sudation, powder-preparations, massage, and enemas (basti) should be employed.
One should drink a decoction of Gokṣura seeds combined with Yava-kṣāra.
When drunk, it quickly wards off dysuria and disorders arising from feces;
it destroys sugar-gravel and urinary stones in cases of gravel and stone-induced dysuria; and as a linctus with honey, it cures obstruction caused by the suppression of semen.
Excellent women should be enjoyed by one whose bodily tissues have been nourished with aphrodisiacs.
A man should drink milk mixed with cardamom and asafoetida and combined with ghee;
this serves to purify urinary disorders and removes defects of the semen. 18
Trikaṇṭaka, āragvadha, darbha, kāśa, durālabhā, parvatabheda,
and pathyā, when drunk with honey, destroy urinary calculi.
Even for one whose death has arrived,
there is relief from dysuria by drinking the powders of cardamom, *aśmabheda*, bitumen, and long pepper, stirred with rice-water.
Alternatively, by licking these together with jaggery,
even one who is near death and suffering from dysuria may live.
Iron powder, finely ground and mixed with honey, [is likewise effective].
It quickly destroys dysuria through three linctuses; of this there is no doubt.
(21) Yava-kṣāra (barley-alkali) equal in measure to sugar destroys all forms of dysuria;
or else, the juice of Nidigdhikā with honey is a destroyer of dysuria. (22)
Ghee or milk prepared with śatāvarī, kāśa, kuśa, śvadaṃṣṭrā, vidārī, ikṣu, and āmalaka, mixed with sugar, [is beneficial].
This should be employed for difficult urinary disorders arising from pitta.

Ghee prepared with the fresh juices of *trikaṇṭaka*, castor root, *kuśa* grass, and others, along with *abhīru*, *karkāruka*, and sugarcane, and mixed with half a part of jaggery, should be drunk for the disorders of painful micturition, urinary stones, and urinary obstruction.
Chapter 33:
For one who has undergone oleation and sudation, unctuous purgation is beneficial;
thereafter, for one whose body has been thoroughly cleansed, urethral/vaginal enemas (uttarabasti) are beneficial. || 1 ||
One should drink wine prepared with *pāṭalī*, *yavaśūka*, *pāribhadra*, and sesame, along with an alkaline solution and combined with cinnamon,
cardamom, and black pepper; or one may lick these same substances individually, using jaggery as a vehicle.
One should cause [the patient] to drink salt mixed with the paste of triphalā,
or one should have them drink the fresh juice of nidigdhikā strained through a cloth;
or [one may give] saffron paste mixed with honey, which has been steeped overnight in water.
Ash of *pāṭalā* mixed with oil, or strained alkaline water, or a paste of *īrvaru* seeds the size of an *akṣa* combined with rock salt and fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*),
when drunk, liberates one from urinary obstruction (*mūtrāghāta*).
A man suffering from urinary obstruction should drink liquor mixed with *sauvarcala* salt.
Having drunk liquor with salt combined with pomegranate juice, cardamom seeds, and ginger, he is liberated from urinary obstruction.
One should drink śilājatu in a decoction of the vīratarādi group,
or the juice of durālabhā, or the decoction of vāsaka;
or ghee prepared with trikaṇṭaka, eraṇḍa, śatāvarī, and the tṛṇapañcamūla.
Milk thickened with jaggery and mixed with ghee is recommended for diseases such as dysuria (kṛcchra) and others.
One who consumes boiled and cooled milk with rice should drink sandalwood paste with sugar-water; this is excellent for hot winds accompanied by blood.

For one whose blood is excessively discharged due to overindulgence with women, and for whom sexual intercourse has ceased, a nourishing regimen is beneficial; likewise, the fat and oil of a cock (tāmracūḍa) are beneficial when used in urethral enemas (uttaravasti). || 11 ||
Take equal parts of the fruit of *svaguptā*, raisins, black sugarcane juice, and powdered sugar, along with half-parts each of milk, honey, and ghee;
having thoroughly churned all these together, one should lick a portion the size of an *akṣa* fruit and drink milk.
It destroys the disorders arising from the depletion of semen and bestows a son upon the barren woman.
Citraka, Sārivā, Balā, Kālānusārivā,
Drākṣā, Viśālā, Pippalī, and likewise Citraphalā— [these constitute the formulation].
In the same manner, one should add madhuka and āmalakas;
one should cook an āḍhaka of ghee with these pastes, each weighing one akṣa, along with one droṇa of milk and one droṇa of water, and once it is prepared, one should remove it from the heat.
The wise physician should mix together cold, strained [juice], one *prastha* of sugar, and *tugākṣīrī*; then,
at the appropriate time, he should drink it in measured doses according to the specific humor (*doṣa*) and the patient's strength.
One who has semen characterized by vāta, pitta, or kapha,
as well as one whose semen is bloody or nodular, should drink this highly efficacious ghee, which is both life-prolonging and aphrodisiac, if they desire freedom from disease. || 18-19 ||
A woman who employs this ghee— which is beneficial for progeny, auspicious, a destroyer of all diseases, and propitious— will soon obtain a pregnancy;
it also conquers blood disorders and combined defects of the female reproductive tract.
In all disorders of the urine, one should employ this treatment.
(Chapter 34) The excellent bark of *varuṇa*, combined with *śuṇṭhī* and *gokṣura*, [should be used].
Having added barley-alkali and jaggery, one should boil and drink this beneficial [decoction];
it destroys even long-standing urinary calculi born of Vata.
This group, known as the Vīratarādi, alleviates disorders of Vata.

A wise physician should prepare a decoction with ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), *agnimantha*, pomegranate (*pāṣāṇabheda*), drumstick tree (*śigru*), *varuṇa*, *gokṣura*, chebulic myrobalan (*abhayā*), and the fruits of *āragvadha*; this removes urinary calculi, gravel, dysuria, and pain caused by urinary obstruction. (2–3)
A person should drink [this] powder of asafoetida, alkali, and salt;
it destroys urinary calculi and dysuria, is a supreme digestive stimulant and carminative,
and subdues Vata located in the abdominal cavity as well as that affecting the waist, thighs, anus, and penis.
Pāṣāṇabheda, vasuka, vaśira, aśmantaka, śatāvarī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, bṛhatī, kaṇṭakārikā,
kapotavaṅkā, ārtagala, kāñcana, uśīra, and gucchaka.
Vṛkṣādanī, bhallātaka, varuṇa, and the fruit of śāka;
barley, kulattha, kola, and the fruits of kataka—
clarified butter boiled with a decoction of these and with the addition of ūṣaka and other ingredients [is a remedy].
It quickly breaks up urinary stones produced by Vāta.
The Ūṣakādi group destroys Kapha, dries up fat,
and cures urinary stones, gravel, dysuria, and Kaphaja abdominal tumors.
In this group of wind-alleviating substances, one should prepare alkaline preparations, barley gruel, thin gruel, decoctions, milks, and foodstuffs.
Kāśa, kuśa, śara, guccha, itkaṭa, moraṭa, and aśmabhid [are included]. 10–11.
Darbha, vidārī, vārāhī, śāli-root, trikaṇṭaka, bhallūka, pāṭalī, pāṭhā, pattara, and kuraṇṭikā,
along with punarnavā and śirīṣa— [an oil] prepared by boiling [these] with that [decoction].
Ghee infused with the seeds of śilāhvā, madhuka, indīvara, trapusa, vāruka, and other such [plants] is auspicious; when administered,
it quickly breaks up stones (aśmarī) produced from bile.
One should prepare alkaline preparations, barley gruels, thin decoctions, milks,
and foods within this group that destroys pitta;
one should prepare the alkaline substances and so forth by boiling them with decoctions and adding medicinal additives.
The technical definitions (paribhāṣā) apply according to their occurrence within each group as they are found.
16. Śilājatu is called śilāhvam; puṇḍraka and gundra are synonyms for gucchaka.
Madhuka is so called because its [Sanskrit] name has been shortened; it is also called bījaka because of its seeds. 17.
In the group beginning with varuṇaka, however, [the medicated ghee] is prepared with guggulu, elā, hareṇu, kuṣṭha, musta, marica, citraka, and surāhvaya; and with these,
along with the ūṣakādi group, goat’s ghee is processed.
It quickly breaks up stones produced from phlegm.
One should prepare alkalis, barley gruels, thin porridges, decoctions, milks, and meals using this group of phlegm-destroying substances. || 19–20 ||
Indeed, this group beginning with Varuṇa wards off phlegm and fat; it destroys headache, abdominal tumors, and internal abscesses.
Regarding seminal calculi, however, the general procedure for destroying stones [is prescribed].

One should drink the juice derived from flowers and fruits mixed with barley-alkali and jaggery; it removes urinary obstruction and destroys gravel and stones. A decoction made from ginger, varuṇa, gokṣura, pāṣāṇabheda, and kapotavaṅkā [is also effective].
Drunk mixed with jaggery and *yavaśūka*, it destroys even severe urinary calculi (23).
A decoction prepared from the bark of *varuṇa*, *śilābheda*, dry ginger, and *gokṣuraka*, combined with alkali, breaks up even gravel (24).
One should drink a decoction of the bark of *varuṇa* root combined with its paste;
likewise, a slightly warm decoction derived from the root of *śigru* causes the passage of stones.
One should drink a decoction of *varuṇa* root bark mixed with jaggery.
It quickly causes the stone to fall and destroys pain in the bladder.

(26) One should drink a concentrated decoction of *elā*, *kulyā*, *madhuka*, *aśmabheda*, *kauntī*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *vṛṣaka*, and *rubūka*, along with *aśmajatu* and sugar, in cases of gravel and painful urination accompanied by stones. (27)
The powder of *trikaṇṭaka* seeds mixed with honey and drunk with sheep’s milk for seven days breaks up urinary calculi.
Likewise, *kulattha*, rock salt, the essence of *viḍaṅga*, sugar, *śītali*, and *yavaśūka* [are effective].
One should cook ghee with the seeds of *kūṣmāṇḍaka* and *gokṣura* in the water of *varuṇa*.
This quickly destroys all difficult-to-cure urinary stones, dysuria, urinary obstruction, and retention of urine— just as the fall of a thunderbolt destroys fully grown trees.
Alternatively, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee with a decoction of the five roots beginning with *śara*, along with a paste of *gokṣura*. When prepared, it should be consumed with sugar;
it destroys urinary calculi and dysuria, and cleanses the seminal passage. || 31 ||
One should boil the crushed *varuṇa* weighing one *tulā* in a *droṇa* of water until reduced to one-quarter; having strained it, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee [with this decoction].

Amṛtā, stone-derived [substance], and the seed of the trapuṣa should be given;

A person should drink [this] in a dose of one *akṣa*, taking into account the place, time, and other factors.

This destroys urinary calculi (*aśmarī*), gravel (*śarkarā*), and painful urination (*mūtrakṛcchra*).
And as for the oil known as Saindhavādya which has been proclaimed by the sages,

it is likewise praised in every way for urinary retention (mūtrāghāta), painful urination (mūtrakṛcchra), piercing pain, and exhaustion from physical trauma; it is also recommended for fractures and for those overcome by fatigue.
The substances such as rock salt (saindhava) and others specified in the section on *vardhma* are intended here [as well].
[Adhikāra 35] Śyāmāka, kodrava, uddālaka, wheat, chickpeas, and *āḍhakī*.
Old horse-gram (kulattha) is always beneficial for those suffering from urinary disorders (mehin). For those with such disorders, bitter vegetables, meat of wild animals, deer, and birds,
preparations of barley, mung beans (mudga), and śāli and ṣaṣṭika rice are recommended.

From the separate recitation of the *pārijāta*, *jaya*, *nimba*, *vahni*, and *gāyatrī* mantras, along with *aguru*, yellow *sindūra*, and *śārada* [incense]; and from eating water, sugarcane, liquor, sand, salt, and flour— || 3 ||
These eight decoctions, when taken with honey, gradually destroy the various types of thick urine (sāndrameha).
Dūrvā, kaseru, pūtīka, kumbhīka, plava, and śaivala,
boiled together with water and drunk, are an excellent remedy for the disease of seminal urine (śukrameha).
A decoction of triphalā, āragvadha, and drākṣā, when drunk mixed with honey,
invariably destroys the urinary disorder known as phenaprameha in men.
[Likewise, a decoction] of rodhra, abhayā, kaṭphala, mustaka, viḍaṅga, pāṭhā, arjuna, and dhanvana...
These four decoctions—of kadamba, śāla, arjuna, and dīpyaka; and of viḍaṅga, dārvī, dhava, and śalyaka—should be consumed with honey for the various types of kaphaja prameha.
[7] [The decoctions] of rodhra, arjuna, uśīra, and kucandana; and of ariṣṭa, sevya, āmalaka, and abhayā. [8]

These four decoctions—of dhātrī, arjuna, ariṣṭaka, and vatsaka; and of nīlotpala, elā, tiniśa, and arjuna—are prescribed mixed with honey for the treatment of pitta-type urinary disorders (pittaprameha).
[Also prescribed are] the three fruits of aśvattha, caturaṅgula, and nyagrodha.
The five decoctions of *saraktasāra*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and honey, taken in sequence,
destroy the urinary disorders known as *nīla*, *hāridra*, *śukta*, *kṣāra*, and *gaṇḍīrika*; and this same preparation, when combined with honey, conquers *raktameha*.
A decoction made from dates (*kharjūra*), *kāśmarya*, the stones of *tinduka*, and *amṛtā* [should be used]. Having powdered *chinnā*, *vahnikaṣāya*, *pāṭhā*, *kuṭaja*,
*rāmaṭha*, *tiktā*, and *kuṣṭha*, one should drink it with ghee in the morning for urinary disorders (*mehe*).
One should drink a decoction of *kadara*, *khadira*, and *pūga* with honey in cases of *kṣaudra-meha*;
however, one should employ a decoction of *agnimantha* in *vasā-meha*.
[In *śīta-meha*, one should use] *pāṭhā*, *śirīṣa*, *dusparśā*, *mūrvā*, *kiṃśuka*, and *tinduka*.
The physician should administer a decoction of *kapittha* fruits in cases of elephantiasis (*hastimeha*).

One suffering from urinary disorders caused by *kapha* and *pitta* should lick the powders of *kampilla*, *saptacchada*, *śāla*, *vaibhītaka*, *rauhītaka*, *kauṭaja*, and *kapittha* flowers mixed with honey.
To one who has been treated with unctuous therapy, emesis, purgation, or non-unctuous enema, one should administer meat broth prepared from the *dhātrī* (myrobalan) fruit,
combined with *niśā* (turmeric) and honey, in all types of prameha; or alternatively, a decoction boiled with *dāru*, *triphalā*, and *mustaka*.
A decoction of triphalā, dāru, dārvī, and abda, taken with honey, destroys urinary disorders (meha).
Alternatively, a decoction derived from kuṭaja, asana, dārvī, abda, and the three fruits (triphalā), or the fresh juice of guḍūcī, should be drunk with honey; these cure all types of meha.
One should drink one akṣa each of the pastes of śāla, muṣkaka, and kampilla with the juice of dhātrī and honey; this is the supreme remedy for all types of meha.
[One should also take] triphalā, dāruniśā, and viśālā...
Having boiled Musta and adding a paste of Niśā,
one should drink the decoction mixed with honey when all types of prameha have arisen. (20)

To alleviate urinary disorders, one should lick either the powder of triphalā, or that derived from *aśmajatu*, or that produced from iron (*lohaja*), or that originating from *abhayā*, mixed with honey.
