The mango, the wood-apple, the rose-apple, the priyāla, the kakubha, and the dhava;
the madhūka, the madhuka, the rodhra, the varaṇa, and the pāribhadraka;
the paṭola, the meṣaśṛṅgī, the dantī, the citraka, and the āḍhakī. || 22-23 ||

One should prepare a fine powder of equal parts of karañja, the three myrobalans (triphalā), indra-vṛkṣaka, and bhallātaka fruits. This powder, known as nyagrodhādya-cūrṇa, should be licked with honey.
One should also drink the juice of the three fruits followed by urine;
thus, the twenty types of urinary disorders (prameha) and those conditions characterized by painful urination (mūtrakṛcchra) are pacified by this application, and pustules do not arise. || 25-26 ||
With *trikaṇṭaka*, *aśmantaka*, *somavalka*, *bhallātaka*, *ativiṣā*, *rodhra*, *vacā*, *paṭola*, *arjuna*, *nimba*, *musta*, *haridrā*, *padmaka*, *dīpyaka*,
*mañjiṣṭhā*, *aguru*, and *candana*— all these together [are used] for disorders arising from *kapha* and *vāta*.
One should cook oil in cases of kapha (meheṣu) and clarified butter in cases of pitta; when all three symptoms are present,
one should prepare a pill by mixing guggulu with equal parts of the powder of trikaṭu and triphalā,
combined with a decoction of gokṣura— so says the physician.
One should consume it in a manner that is harmonious with the humors, the season, and one's strength;
there is no restriction here, and one may perform activities as desired.
It conquers urinary disorders (prameha), diseases of Vata, urinary obstruction, and abdominal enlargements.
Ghee prepared with a decoction that cures *kapha*-type urinary disorders is beneficial for *kapha*;
ghee prepared with a decoction that destroys *pitta*-type urinary disorders is beneficial for *pitta*.
[The ingredients are: *daśamūla*, the two types of *karañja*, *devadāru*, and *harītakī*.
Varṣābhū, varuṇa, dantī, citraka, and punarnavā; sudhā, nīpa, kadamba, bilva, and bhallātaka;
as well as śaṭhī, puṣkaramūla, and pippalīmūla. || 33–34 ||
One should boil these ten parts of ten palas each separately in a water-pot,
adding one prastha each of barley, jujube, and horse-gram.
When reduced to one-fourth, one should cook one prastha of ghee with that decoction.
Nicula, triphalā, bhārgī, rohiṣa,

gajapippalī, śṛṅgavera, viḍaṅgas, vacā, and likewise kampillaka— with this as the internal medicinal addition (garbha), it should be prepared and administered according to the patient's strength. || 36-37 ||
This indeed is the celebrated and excellent ghee known as *Dhanvantara*;
it [cures] skin diseases, abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, edema, and gout; as well as splenic enlargements, hemorrhoids, abscesses, and pustules. (38)
This ghee cures epilepsy as well as insanity;

alternatively, water boiled with eight times the quantity of the decoction should be used here. And bitumen (śilājatu) should be processed by being saturated with the water of the śālasāra group of drugs.

Having thus purified the body by drinking that very [mixture], one should drink the flour-paste according to one's strength along with the juices of wild animals; once that has been digested, one should take food.
In this manner, a person should continue the use [of the medicine] until one *tulā* has been consumed.

Having abandoned madhumeha, as well as śarkarā and aśmarī, he— endowed with bodily vigor, complexion, and strength— lives for a hundred years free from disease. (42) [No verses of the Siddhayoga appear on this page.]

A physician should treat pustules such as *śarāvikā* and others like swellings; once they have suppurated, one should treat them like ulcers. For these [pustules], drinking [this preparation] is recommended.
A decoction of *vanaspati* and cow's urine is a sharp purifier;
one should prepare an oil with *elā* and other ingredients for the healing of wounds. One should also prepare a decoction and medicinal ointments (*udvartana*) with *āragvadha* and other such drugs.
One should perform sprinkling with *śālasāra* and other such substances, and [use] food and the like mixed with *kaṇā* (long pepper) and so forth.

One should avoid fermented gruel (*sauvīraka*), wine (*surā*), sour gruel (*sukta*), oil, milk, molasses, clarified butter, non-sour sugarcane juice, flour-based foods, and the meat of animals from marshy regions.
When the urine of a patient suffering from prameha is no longer turbid, non-viscid, clear, and bitter or pungent, then it is declared that health has been restored.

Old *śāli* rice, mung beans, horse gram, wild millet, and common millet, as well as emetic enemas, should always be consumed by one who is obese. Furthermore, anxiety, anger, smoking [of medicinal smoke], physical exercise, and bloodletting [are beneficial].

Fasting, an uncomfortable bed, magnanimity of spirit, and the conquest of darkness ward off the harmful onset of excessive sleep. One who is constant in physical exercise, eats sparingly, and consumes barley and wheat [is likewise protected].
By abandoning greed, one is liberated from the defects caused by over-nutrition.
A diet of barley and śyāmāka grain, which one enjoys through physical exertion, mental concern, sexual intercourse, travel, honey, and staying awake, inevitably destroys excessive corpulence.
Water mixed with honey, consumed in the morning, destroys obesity.
A formulation consisting of viḍaṅga, ginger, alkali, iron filings, honey, barley,
and āmalaka powder is an excellent destroyer of excessive corpulence.
One should drink the warm scum of boiled rice or become emaciated in body.
Barley meal mixed with cavya, jīraka, vyōṣa, hiṅgu, sauvarcala salt, anala, and honey, when drunk, destroys fat and stimulates the digestive fire.
Vyoṣa, viḍaṅga, śigru, triphalā, kaṭurohiṇī,
the two types of bṛhatī, the two types of haridrā, pāṭhā, ativiṣā, sthirā, hiṅgu, the root of kembuka, yavānī, dhānya, and citraka.
One should powder together sauvarcala salt, ajājī, and hapuṣā.
The portions of the powder, oil, ghee, and honey should be equal in measure;
with sixteen times that amount of roasted grain flour (saktu), one should drink this as a nourishing potion (saṃtarpaṇa).
Through its application, diseases arising from over-nutrition (saṃtarpaṇa) are pacified,
as are urinary disorders (prameha), obstructed winds (mūḍhavāta), skin diseases (kuṣṭha), hemorrhoids (arśas),
jaundice (kāmalā), splenic disorders, anemia (pāṇḍvāmaya), swellings (śotha), dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra), and anorexia (arocaka). || 11 ||
Heart disease, consumption, cough, asthma, throat obstruction, worms, disorders of the duodenum, excessive whiteness, and extreme obesity [are cured];
the digestive fire of men is kindled, and memory and intellect increase. || 12-13 ||
With triphalā, ativiṣā, mūrvā, trivṛt, citraka, vāsaka, nimba, āragvadha, ṣaḍgranthā, saptaparṇa, and the two types of niśā;
with guḍūcī, indrasurā, kṛṣṇā, kuṣṭha, sarṣapa, and nāgara.
Oil cooked with these [drugs] in equal parts and saturated with the juice of the surasādi group,
when employed for drinking, massage, gargling, nasal administration, and enemas,
overcomes diseases caused by kapha such as obesity, lassitude, itching, and others.
A rubbing powder made of śirīṣa, lāmajjaka, and hemarodhra removes skin disorders and excessive sweating.
An ointment consisting of patra, ambu, loha, abhayā, and candana removes foul body odor.
A plaster made from the juice of half a vāsā leaf combined with powdered conch shell [removes skin diseases].
Or even the juice of bilva leaves destroys bodily foul odors.
(18) Harītakī, lodhra, ariṣṭa leaves, mango bark, and pomegranate rind—this is declared to be a cosmetic paste for women, and a leg-paste for kings. (19)
Ground with cow’s urine, it destroys leprosy; when combined with cow’s milk, it produces a radiant complexion.
When prepared with milk, it removes foul odors from the armpits and other areas; it is highly recommended for subjugation when combined with the two types of *rajanī*.
Equal parts of *vyoṣa*, *agni*, *musta*, *triphalā*, *viḍaṅga*, and *guggulu* [should be used].
Eating this, one conquers all diseases born of fat, phlegm, and wind.

Red rice, barley, mung beans, and the meat broths of wild animals are beneficial.
Purgation and non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana) are recommended for all types of abdominal enlargements (jaṭhara).
One should treat vātodara in a strong patient with oleation and sudation; once the body has been lubricated and fomented, one should administer unctuous purgation (snehavirecana).

If a man who has been well-purged by oil therapy nevertheless suffers from flatulence, the physician should treat him with non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) that are very unctuous and possess sour and salty tastes.
[One should use] sea salt, sauvarcala salt, saindhava salt, alkali of barley, and ajamodā.
One should take equal parts of long pepper (*pippalī*), leadwort (*citraka*), fresh ginger (*śṛṅgavera*), asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), and biḍa salt.
These powders, saturated with ghee, should be consumed; it is highly recommended to take a mouthful first.
This cures abdominal enlargement due to wind (*vātōdara*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), indigestion, the provocation of wind, and disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī*).
It instantly destroys hemorrhoids, skin diseases, anemia, and fistulas.
One suffering from Vata-type abdominal enlargement should drink buttermilk mixed with long pepper and salt;
one suffering from Pitta-type abdominal enlargement should drink sweet buttermilk combined with sugar and black pepper.

One suffering from *kapha*-type abdominal enlargement or *sannipāta*-type abdominal enlargement should consume buttermilk mixed with *yavānī*, rock salt (*saindhava*), cumin (*ajājī*), and the three pungents (*vyoṣa*).
One who eats milk should take long peppers (*pippalī*) that have been saturated with the milky sap of the *snuhī* plant.
One suffering from abdominal disease should consume a thousand [units] according to one's capacity.
The administration of bitumen (śilājatu), urines, guggulu, the three myrobalans (triphalā),
and the milk of the snuhī plant pacifies abdominal disease.
A cake made from rice flour saturated with the milk of *snuk* causes the belly to swell greatly; this application brings about [this result] within seven nights.
Alternatively, one should employ the "increasing dose of *pippalī*" (*pippalī-vardhamāna*) as prescribed in the medical compendium (*kalpa*).
There is nothing on earth equal to this for the destruction of abdominal enlargements (jaṭhara).

A decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla), ginger (nāgara), chinnaruhā, punarnavā, and abhayā conquers dropsy (jalodara), edema (śotha), elephantiasis (ślīpada), goiter (galagaṇḍa), and diseases of wind (vātaroga).
One should powder the root of *paṭola*, *rajanī* (turmeric), *viḍaṅga*, the bark of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*),
*kampillaka*, *nīlinī*, and *trivṛt*. Of these, the first six [drugs] should be taken in one *karṣa* each, while the last three should be taken in two, three, and four *karṣas* respectively.
Having made a powder of that [plant], a person should drink a handful with cow's urine;
once purged, he should eat soft rice with the broth of wild animals.
Or, having drunk the scum (maṇḍa) or thin gruel (peyā) with the three pungents (vyoṣa), he should drink milk for six days.
One should drink the decoction and then drink the powder; in this manner, one should do so again and again.
This powder destroys all types of abdominal enlargements (udara), including those accompanied by ascites, and it removes jaundice, anemia (pāṇḍuroga), and edema (śvayathu).
Yavānī, hapuṣā, dhānyaka, triphalā, along with upakuñcikā,
kāravī, pippalīmūla, ajagandhā, śaṭhī, vacā, śatāhvā, jīraka, vyoṣa, svarṇakṣīrī, and citraka. || 18 ||
Two parts each of the two types of alkali (kṣāra), puṣkaramūla, kuṣṭha, and the five salts;
one part each of viḍaṅga and likewise three parts of dantī; trivṛt and viśālā in double the amount, and sātalā four times that amount. || 19–20 ||
This powder named Nārāyaṇa destroys hosts of diseases; having encountered it, diseases do not survive, just as the Asuras did not survive Viṣṇu.
It should be drunk with buttermilk by those suffering from abdominal enlargements, and with the decoction of jujube fruits by those suffering from abdominal tumors.

In cases of *ānāha* (abdominal distension) and wind-diseases (*vātaroga*), [one should use] *surā* liquor; with *prasannā* (the clear supernatant of wine) for piercing pains in the limbs; with pomegranate juice for hemorrhoids (*arśas*);
with *vṛkṣāmla* (tamarind) for cutting pains; and with warm water for indigestion (*ajīrṇaka*).
In cases of fistula-in-ano, anemia, cough, dyspnea,

throat-obstruction, heart disease, disorders of the small intestine, leprosy, weak digestion, and fever; in cases of venom from fangs, root-poison, natural poison, and artificial poison— [this [remedy] is effective].
This purgative should be drunk by one whose digestive tract is softened according to what is appropriate.

One should cook two *prasthas* of ghee with half a *palika* each of long pepper (*pippalī*), long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*), chaba pepper (*cavya*), leadwort (*citraka*), and dry ginger (*nāgara*), along with alkali (*kṣāra*). (25–26)
Having added an āḍhaka of whey (dadhimanda) to the decoction of half a tula of the paste of the two pentads of roots (dvipañcamūla), one should prepare this ghee;
it cures abdominal enlargements, edema, flatulence due to vāta, abdominal tumors, and hemorrhoids. || 27 ||

One who suffers from abdominal enlargement (jaṭhara) should drink one *prastha* of ghee prepared with four parts water, two parts urine, and one *pala* each of the paste of *citraka* and alkali (*kṣāra*).
[28] Likewise, one may take three *palas* of ginger (*nāgara*), one *prastha* of ghee, and one *āḍhaka* of oil. [29]

Having prepared this from *mastu* (buttermilk), one should drink it; it removes all types of abdominal enlargements (*udara*) and is recommended for tumors (*gulma*) arising from phlegm (*kapha*) and wind (*vāta*).
[The recipe: two *pala* of *arka* (calotropis) milk and six *pala* of *snuhī* (spurge) milk.
Pathyā, kampillaka, śyāmā, śamyāka, girikarṇikā, nīlinī, trivṛtā, dantī, śaṅkhinī, and likewise citraka—
one should cook one prastha of ghee with one-pala portions of each of these. || 31-32 ||
Then, one should administer a single drop into his impure bowel;
for as many drops as he drinks, so many times will he be purged with force.
This cures leprosy, abdominal tumors, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), swelling, and fistula-in-ano.
It pacifies the eight types of abdominal enlargements (udara), just as Indra’s thunderbolt destroys a tree.
This is known by the name Bindughṛta; one who is anointed with it is purged.
It should be employed for drinking and for sprinkling in the case of those suffering from the eight types of abdominal enlargements.

Having drunk Devadruma, Śigru, or Mayūraka ground with cow’s urine, or alternatively Aśvagandhā ground with cow’s urine, one quickly destroys increased abdominal enlargement (udara), all types of worms without exception, and vitiated abdominal disorders.
[One may also use] a paste of one karṣa each of Snuk-milk, Dantī, Triphalā, Viḍaṅga, Siṃhī, Trivṛt, and Citraka.

Having drunk one *akṣa* (two karṣas) of well-cooked ghee measuring one *kuḍava*, along with half that amount of water, one should drink warm water after it has been purged; then, the expert in the procedure should administer lukewarm *peyā*.
This "Nārāca" [formula] is prescribed as a pacifier for abdominal diseases when administered with due care.

This powder of *yavānikā*, *citraka*, *yāvaśūka*, *ṣaḍgranthi*, *dantī*, and *magadhodbhavā* destroys enlargement of the spleen when taken with warm water, or with whey (*mastu*), *surā* liquor, or *āsava*.
Pippalī is auspicious when processed by soaking it in a solution of *palāśa* alkali.
It is known to pacify the pain of abdominal tumors (gulma) and splenic enlargement, and to stimulate the digestive fire.
Having burnt vidanga, arka, agni, rock salt, and barley flour together with vacā, one should drink them as a powder mixed with milk; this removes abdominal tumors, splenic disorders, and dropsy.

For the pacification of the spleen and liver disorders, one should drink alkali mixed with *viḍa* salt and *kṛṣṇā* (long pepper), or the acidic secretion of *pūtika*, according to one's strength, in the morning.
One should burn the leaves of *arka* with salt inside a smokeless fire.
Or one may drink alkali with mastu (curd-whey); this dispels splenic disease.
Alkali derived from sea-shells or oyster-shells should be drunk according to the proper method, or long peppers (pippalī) should be administered with milk for the pacification of splenic enlargement.
This bolus (modaka) made of bhallātaka, abhayā, and jīraka, together with jaggery,
destroys even a severe enlargement of the spleen within seven nights. [One should take] a decoction of saubhāñjana combined with rock salt, agnika, and kaṇā.
Or one should employ barley-alkali (yavakṣāra) combined with the alkali of Palāśa.

Likewise, one should administer sesame seeds with salt and ghee containing six palas; one should apply the entire therapeutic procedure prescribed for splenic enlargement (plīha) to the liver (yakṛt).
One should consume garlic, long pepper root, and abhayā,

and drink a mouthful of cow’s urine, for the sake of being freed from the disease of splenic enlargement (plīharoga). For one who consumes a paste of śarapuṅkhā with buttermilk according to the strength of their digestive fire, [the spleen is cured].
If the spleen were not conquered, then even a mountain would float upon the water.
(49) A decoction of śārṅgeṣṭā mixed with rock salt and tamarind is a formulation for the subsiding of the spleen; or else, the juice of ripe mangoes with honey [is effective]. (50)

Urine or water infused with the powdered seeds of *rohitaka* and *abhayā*, when drunk, cures all types of abdominal enlargements (*udara*), splenic disorders (*plīha*), urinary disorders (*meha*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), worms, and abdominal tumors (*gulma*).
After one has eaten with curd, the physician [should apply] a vein at the middle of the left arm.
One should lance [the spleen] on the left for the destruction of the spleen, and on the right for the destruction of the liver (yakṛt).
One should massage the spleen firmly to induce the flow of vitiated blood.
[This should be done] with a prastha of decoction of *nikumbha* mixed with its paste.

One should cook one *prastha* of ghee in a decoction of one *tulā* of *citraka* to cure splenic disorders, jaundice, and anemia. One should likewise cook one *prastha* of ghee with double the amount of fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*) and four times the amount of whey (*dadhi-maṇḍa*).
With the five pungents (pañcakolaka), the four alkalies (tālīsa-kṣāra), and combined with salt, one should add two types of jīraka, the two types of niśā, and black pepper;
[this cures] splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, flatulence, anemia, loss of appetite, and fever. || 55-56 ||

When drunk, it destroys pain in the bladder, heart, flanks, waist, and thighs, as well as upward-moving wind (udāvarta) and chronic rhinitis; it cures hemorrhoids, alleviates swelling, kindles the digestive fire, promotes strength and complexion, and also subdues morbid consumption (bhasmaka). || 57 ||
One should cook ghee mixed with the paste of *pippalī* along with four times as much milk; this is an excellent remedy for splenic disorders, weak digestion, and diseases of the liver.
Twenty-five palas of the best *rohitaka* bark [should be used].
One should prepare a decoction combined with two *prastha*s of the five pungent fruits (*pañcakola*).
Then, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee with all those [ingredients] along with one *pala* each of the five pungent fruits and an equal amount of crushed *rohitaka* bark.
When administered promptly, this quickly pacifies excessive enlargement of the spleen, as well as abdominal tumors (gulma), fever, dyspnea, worms, anemia, and jaundice.
One should grind one hundred palas of rohītaka and one āḍhaka of jujube fruits. 61–62.
Having prepared [the decoction] in a droṇa of water until one-fourth remains,
one should add a prastha of ghee and four times as much goat's milk;
into that, one should put all these pastes, each measuring one akṣa.
Vyoṣa, triphalā, hiṅgu, yavānī, tumbaru,
biḍa salt, ajājī, black salt, pomegranate, devadāru, punarnavā, viśālā, yavakṣāra, and pauṣkara. (64–65)
One should cook ghee with viḍaṅga, citraka, hapuṣā, cavikā, and vacā; once prepared, one should place it in an auspicious vessel.
One should then administer a dose of three palas, having regard for the strength of the disease.
Then one should feed [the patient] with meat broth, vegetable soup, or even milk.
When that ghee has been consumed, it destroys these many diseases:
enlargement of the liver (yakṛt), enlargement of the spleen (plīhodara), splenic colic (plīhaśūla), and likewise liver disease (yakṛt).
It pacifies pain in the abdomen, pain in the heart, pain in the flanks, loss of appetite, and obstructive colic; it cures anemia accompanied by jaundice,
alleviates vomiting and diarrhea, and destroys drowsiness and fever.
The medicine named Mahārohitaka is the best for destroying the spleen. (70) Chapter 38: A decoction of Harītakī, Nāgara, Devadāru, Punarnavā, and Chinnaruhā.
Guggulu mixed with urine should be drunk; this is the most excellent treatment for dropsical abdominal enlargements (śothodara).
Castor oil mixed with daśamūla, or the juice of triphalā combined with cow’s urine, or a decoction of daśamūla taken with urine, destroys vātodara, swelling, and colic.
A decoction of punarnavā, nimba, paṭola, śuṇṭhī, tiktā, amṛtā, dārvī,
and abhayā destroys jaundice accompanied by swelling of all limbs, abdominal enlargement, cough, pain, and dyspnea.
(3) One should drink punarnavā, dārvī, abhayā, and guḍūcī along with cow’s urine and mahiṣākṣa.
In cases of skin diseases, swelling, abdominal enlargements, anemia, obesity, excessive salivation, and disorders of upward-moving phlegm,
one should drink buffalo milk mixed with cow’s urine, or cow’s milk mixed with the three myrobalans (triphalā). Alternatively,
for those suffering from edema and abdominal enlargements, one may drink only cow’s urine after consuming a diet of milk-rice.
Having ground old *māṇaka* seeds and cooking them with double the amount of rice in milk and water, one should consume that prepared *pāyasa*.
It destroys wind-belly (*vātōdara*), swelling, malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), and even jaundice (*pāṇḍutā*).
This proven application, declared by physicians, is free from adverse effects.
Punarnavā, dārvī, amṛtā, pāṭhā, bilva, śvadaṃṣṭrā, the two types of bṛhatī, the two types of rañjanī, pippalī, citraka, and vṛṣa [are the ingredients]. 8.
Having powdered these in equal parts, a person should drink them with cow’s urine;
this destroys swelling of many kinds that spreads through all the limbs, as well as the eight types of abdominal swellings (śothodara) and even deep-seated ulcers.
Chapter 39:
Water boiled with ginger (śuṇṭhī), punarnavā, castor root (airaṇḍa), and the five roots (pañcamūla) is recommended for swelling caused by vāta, both for drinking and as an adjunct to food. 1.

In a swelling caused by pitta in one who subsists on a milk diet, one should drink a decoction of *trivṛt*, *guḍūcī*, and *triphalā* mixed with cow’s urine; or else, a powder of the three fruits (*phalatrika*) in a dose of one *akṣa*.
Or [one may take] a paste of *punarnavā*, *viśva*, *trivṛt*, *guḍūcī*, *śamyāka*, *pathyā*, and *amaradāru*.
In swelling arising from phlegm (kapha), one should drink water mixed with the urine of a buffalo and these [substances].
In cases of phlegm, however, an ointment of *kṛṣṇā*, sand, old oil-cake (*piṇyāka*), *śigru* bark, and *umā* should be applied;
there should also be sprinkling with a decoction of horse-gram (*kulattha*) and ginger, along with urine, and anointing with *caṇḍā* and *aguru*.
Ajāji, pāṭhā, ghanā, pañcakola, vyāghrī, and rajanī, when drunk with lukewarm water, destroy swelling that is increased, chronic, and caused by the three doṣas; so too do bhūnimba and mahauṣadha.
This [formula] is taught in the Caraka Saṃhitā under the name "Pippalyādi-cūrṇa" (the powder beginning with pippalī).
In this case, at the place where *cavikā* is required, *mātaṅgapippalī* should be taken.
If one consumes the juice of fresh ginger mixed with old jaggery while subsisting on goat's milk, it will quickly remove all swelling.
Guggulu taken with a decoction of punarnavā, dāru, and śuṇṭhī, or with cow’s urine alone,
or with a decoction of daśamūla, destroys swelling. Bilva leaf juice, combined with pāṇḍu and black pepper, [is used] for swelling caused by the three doṣas.
One should also administer it in cases of vit-saṅga, durnāman (hemorrhoids), and kāmalā. The powder of jaggery, pippalī, and śuṇṭhī destroys swelling,
pacifies indigestion due to undigested matter (āma), relieves colic, and cleanses the bladder.
For those suffering from swelling (śotha), one should consume the city [of Haridrā] with urine, or Pippalī mixed with milk, or Abhayā in equal parts with jaggery,
or Viśva; or else, jaggery with Ārdraka, or jaggery with Nāgara, or jaggery with Abhayā, or jaggery with Pippalī.
Increasing by one *karṣa* daily, a person should consume a dose of three *palas* for either a fortnight or a month;
this cures edema, catarrh, diseases of the throat and mouth, as well as asthma, cough, loss of appetite, chronic rhinitis, and other such ailments.
It destroys chronic fever, hemorrhoids, disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī),
as well as other diseases of kapha and vāta.
One should administer a paste made of sthalapadma, stirred with milk.
It also cures diseases of the spleen and conquers swelling (śotha) of the entire body or of a single limb.
Milk boiled with dāru, varṣābhū, and nāgara removes swelling; alternatively, milk prepared with citraka, vyoṣa, and vṛddhadāru should be drunk.
By drinking a decoction of *siṃhāsya* and *amṛtabhaṇṭākī* mixed with honey,
a person may conquer dysuria, edema, asthma, cough, fever, and vomiting.
Having consumed a paste of *bhūnimba* and *viśva*, a decoction of *punarnavā* should then be drunk.
It certainly and quickly removes swelling affecting all parts of the body in men.
A paste of Triphalā, iron powder, and alkalis, or the juice of Triphalā, along with liquorice, milk, sesame seeds, and fresh butter, conquers swelling.
It destroys swelling caused by *āruṣkara* (marking-nut) or by the stalks of *śāla* leaves.
In the case of swelling caused by poison, however, the treatment prescribed for poison is recommended.
[This applies to a paste] of *punarnavā*, *citraka*, *devadāru*, the five pungents (*pañcoṣaṇa*), alkali (*kṣāra*), and *harītakī*.
Ghee cooked with a paste [of drugs] in a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla) is the best for destroying swelling (śotha).
One should cook ghee in the decoction of the five spices (pañcakola) and horse gram (kulattha), along with a paste of punarnavā; this ghee destroys swelling.
Sacrificial grains (yava),
pāṭhā, dīpyaka, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), vetasāmla, the fruit of bilva, pomegranate, and yāvaśūka— these are used with citraka.
Having ground one akṣa each of long pepper root and cavya,
one should cook them with one āḍhaka of water and then consume one prastha of ghee.
It destroys hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, and all types of swelling, and it kindles a bright digestive fire.
Having placed milk in a jar smeared with the paste of *citraka*, one should curdle it properly, churn it well, and [use] that...

Clarified butter produced from that [milk], containing the root of *citraka* and prepared with buttermilk, is a powerful destroyer of swelling; it cures hemorrhoids, diarrhea, wind-disorders, abdominal tumors, and urinary diseases, and it increases the digestive fire.
One should cook one *prastha* of clarified butter with the decoction and paste of *māṇaka*.
It cures swelling caused by a single humor, by two humors combined, and that arising from all three humors (tridoṣa). [This is prepared with:
śaileya, kuṣṭha, aguru, dāru, kauntī, tvak, padmaka, elā, ambu, palāśa, musta, priyaṅgu, thauṇeyaka, hema, māṃsī, tālīsa, patra, plava, and dhānyapatra. || 25–26 ||

For a condition characterized by Vāta, they recommend an oil massage prepared with śrīveṣṭaka, dhyāmaka, pippalī, spṛkkā, and nakha, as available; furthermore, a paste made from these well-ground ingredients is also advised.
[27] [This is also prepared with] dried radish, varṣābhū, dāru, rāsnā, and mahauṣadha.
Oil cooked with this [decoction] and applied as an ointment destroys swelling along with its root.
One should boil a *kaṃsa* measure of the decoction of the two *pañcamūlas* with one hundred *abhayās*.
When the linctus is well-cooked, one should add jaggery, and once it has reached the proper consistency, add the powder of *vyoṣa* and the three aromatics (*trisaugandhya*). || 28–29 ||
One *prastha* measure of honey, well-cooled, along with a small amount of *yavaśūka* powder and a single *abhayā*, when consumed as a linctus, destroys even advanced swelling (*śvayathu*),
as well as dyspnea, fever, anorexia, urinary disorders, abdominal tumors, splenic enlargement, diseases of the three *doṣas*, and anemia. (30)

[It cures] emaciation, consumption, wind, blood disorders, acidity, bile, discoloration, defects of urine, and defects of semen. Due to the presence of honey, there is no fixed measure; however, for a combination of trikaṭu (vyoṣa) and other ingredients, "karṣa" is a synonym for a small amount. A *śukti* is considered to be half a *pala*.
Regarding the measure of *kaṃsaharītakī*, Jaijjaṭa states in the Caraka-saṃhitā that it is equal to ten roots (*daśamūlī*) and harītakī;
therefore, one should boil one hundred *pathyā* (harītakī) fruits in a *kaṃsa* of the decoction of the ten roots.
One *tulā* (ten *prasthas*) of jaggery, four *palas* each of sugar, *vyoṣa*, and *yavakṣāra*,
one *suvarṇa* part of *trijātaka*, and half a *prastha* of honey, when cooled, [mixed together];
this preparation of *daśamūla* and *harītakī* destroys even the most difficult swellings (*śotha*).

One should cook one *āḍhaka* of water from *punarnavā*, *amṛtā*, *dāru*, and the ten roots (*daśamūla*), along with one *prastha* of fresh ginger juice and one *tulā* of jaggery, to treat fever, anorexia, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, skin diseases, anemia, and abdominal ailments. (36–37)
When that [mixture] has been prepared, one should add one karṣa each of powdered vyōṣa, patra, elā, tvak, and cavya; once it has cooled, one should mix in one kuḍava of honey and lick it.
This electuary, named Paunarnava, destroys swelling and colic.
It relieves cough, dyspnea, and anorexia, and increases strength, complexion, and digestive fire.

One who desires to destroy swelling (śopha) should avoid flour-based foods, sour substances, salts, wine, clay, daytime sleep, non-forest meat, women, ghee, oil, milk, heavy foods, and [excessive] water. || 39–40 ||
Village-dwelling animals, meat from marshy regions, salt, dried vegetables, fresh grain, molasses-based foods,

flour-based foods, curd, rice-and-pulse porridge, slimy substances, wine, sour items, parched grains, dried meat, eating in equal proportions [of incompatible foods], as well as heavy, unwholesome, and burning-to-the-stomach food.
One suffering from swelling should avoid sexual intercourse at night and during dreams.
[Adhikāra 44] A person should drink either *guggulu* or *rubu* oil with cow’s urine.
It quickly destroys an increase of Vāta that has persisted for a long time. Alternatively, one should drink castor oil with milk for a month;
or Nārāyaṇa oil should be employed for drinking, massage, and enemas.
An external application (pradeha) made of sandalwood, madhuka, lotus, uśīra, and blue water-lily ground with milk will alleviate burning sensations, swelling, and pain.
An ointment consisting of the paste of the five barks mixed with ghee should also be applied.
In cases arising from blood (raktaja), all Pitta-alleviating measures should be employed, along with bloodletting.
However, for an increase in Kapha, one should apply a plaster made of drugs with hot potency ground with urine;
furthermore, one should drink a decoction of Pītadāru combined with urine.
One should apply a warm poultice of the surasādi group or drugs used for head-purgation (śirovirecana), mixed with urine, to an abscess arising from fat that has been fomented.
Having fomented an abscess originating from urine, one should wrap it with a cloth bandage.
The wise physician should pierce [the swelling] below the suture on the side with a vrīhimukha instrument, provided it has not reached the scrotal sac; in cases of *antra-vṛddhi* (intestinal hernia),
one should apply the procedure for *vāta-vṛddhi* (flatus-induced enlargement) and perform cauterization there with fire as is beneficial.
Having carefully avoided the sīvanī vein at the end of the ear above the conch-shell [of the ear],
one should pierce the vessel either directly or by inversion to cure inguinal hernia (antravṛddhi).
Alternatively, having incised the skin midway between the thumb and forefinger, one should cauterize it when the condition is reversed in its location.
A decoction prepared with rāsnā, yaṣṭīmadhu, amṛtā, eraṇḍa, balā, and gokṣura,
when mixed with rubu oil, quickly destroys inguinal hernia (antravṛddhi).
Having drunk castor oil processed with balā and combined with milk...
A person shall conquer enlargement of the spleen (antravṛddhi) accompanied by flatulence and colic.
One should consume Harītakī every morning, prepared with urine, mixed with oil and salt, which removes diseases caused by Kapha and Vāta.

A person should eat a myrobalan (harītakī) prepared with cow’s urine and fried in castor oil, combined with powdered rock salt, followed by a drink of lukewarm water; this destroys even long-standing and greatly increased *vṛddhi* (enlargement).
One should drink the decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) mixed with cow’s urine in the morning, remaining alert and unwearied.
It destroys swelling arising from phlegm and wind located in the testicles.
Sarala, aguru, kuṣṭha, devadāru, and mahauṣadha,
ground with urine and fermented gruel (āranāla), destroy swelling and conquer phlegm and wind.
A paste made from *pathyā* fried in castor oil,
combined with *kṛṣṇā* and rock salt, is an excellent remedy for the disease of enlargement (*vṛddhi*).
Cow’s ghee mixed with rock salt and carefully stored in a conch-shell vessel [is likewise beneficial].
Matured for seven days by the rays of the sun, it destroys even the most advanced *kauraṇḍa*.
An ointment made from a paste of *vacā* and mustard seeds destroys swelling.
Having reached a state of accumulation due to the consumption of excessively moist, heavy, and unwholesome foods—
When the *doṣa* produces a swelling like a knot at the joints of the groins, accompanied by fever, pain, and prostration of the limbs, one should designate that as *vardhma*.
[The roots] of *bilva*, *kapittha*, *aralu*, *agni*, and the two types of *bṛhatī*...

A powder made from *śyāmā*, *pūtikarañja*, *śigru*, and *kataru*, combined with *viśvauṣadha*, *aruṣkara*, black pepper (*kṛṣṇā*), *granthika*, *cavya*, the five salts, alkali, and *ajamodā*, ground into a fine powder and drunk with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) or warm water, conquers *vardhma*.
A lukewarm plaster made from wheat paste and *kunduruka* mixed with fresh cow’s milk is an excellent remedy for removing swelling and pain.
Immediately upon the death of a crow, one should insert [the paste] once it has been dissected.
A wise person should apply this for a moment, and it shall become free from pain in that very instant.
Saindhava salt, madana, kuṣṭha, śatāhvā, nicula, vacā, hrīvera, madhuka, bhārgī, devadāru, and nāgara [are the ingredients]. || 23–24 ||
Kaṭphala, pauṣkara, medā, cavikā, citraka, śaṭhī,
viḍaṅga, ativiṣā, śyāmā, reṇukā, nīlinī, sthirā, bilva,
ajamodā, kṛṣṇā, dantī, and rāsnā— [these] in equal parts. || 25 ||
Castor oil, or any oil that subdues *kapha* and *vāta*, when used as an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*), cures abdominal enlargement,
upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, urinary diseases, undigested matter (*āmamāruta*),
flatulence (*ānāha*), and urinary stones (*aśmarī*). It accomplishes what is to be achieved.
Ghee prepared with *sūreśvara* should be administered to prevent the increase of the *vardhma*.
(Adhikāra 41) Food such as barley, mung beans, and *paṭola*, which is pungent and dry, [should be consumed].
One should employ emesis and bloodletting in the case of *galagaṇḍa*.
Alternatively, a lukewarm plaster made of *nicula*, seeds of *śigru*, or even the *daśamūla* is highly recommended for a wind-induced (*vāta*) goiter.

For a goiter caused by phlegm (*kaphagaṇḍa*) that is as large as a *devadāru* tree, one should apply a plaster; when smeared with the root of *hastikarṇapalāśa* ground with rice-water, the goiter (*galagaṇḍa*) is pacified. 3.
One should grind mustard seeds, *śigru* seeds, hemp seeds, flax seeds, barley, and radish seeds with sour buttermilk;
this cures swellings, glandular knots, and erupting *gaṇḍamālā*.
By means of this application as a paste, [the ailments] are pacified or go to dissolution before long.
The juice of ripe karkāruka, combined with viḍa salt and rock salt, destroys even a recent goiter when used as a nasal medication; of this there is no doubt.

One should drink the burnt ashes of *jalakumbhīka*, processed by boiling and strained through cow’s urine, while subsisting on *kodrava* grain and buttermilk, for the pacification of goitre (*galagaṇḍa*). Iron dross mixed with buffalo urine should be kept in a jar for one month.
One should lick [the paste of] *antardhūma* burnt with honey for *galagaṇḍa*. An external poultice (*upanāhana*) made from *sūryāvarta* and garlic causes the eruption of blisters;
through the discharge of these blisters, *galagaṇḍa* is undoubtedly pacified.
One should drink oil prepared with amṛtavallī, nimba, haṃsāhvaya, vṛkṣaka, pippalī,
the two types of balā, and devadāru for the constant benefit of those suffering from the disease of galagaṇḍa (goiter).
Twelve veins are described as being located on the sides below the tongue.
Among those, the wise physician should gradually cut the two black *sthūlaśiras* vessels after seizing them with a hook and [cutting] with a *kuśa* leaf;
once the blood has flowed from that wound, he should apply ginger with jaggery.
And as food, a non-obstructive soup made from *kulattha* beans is recommended.
One should incise three veins in the goiter (*galagaṇḍa*), located respectively at the external junction of the two ears, in the middle, and near the base.
Sesame oil cooked with viḍaṅga, kṣāra, sindhūgra, rāsnā, agni, vyoṣa, dāru,
and the juice of kaṭutumbī fruit destroys even long-standing galagaṇḍa when used as a nasal medication (nasya). || 15 ||
Oil prepared with four times as much juice of *kaṭutumbī* (bitter gourd), along with *viḍaṅga*, *anala* (citraka), rock salt (*sindhūttha*), *rāsnā*, *ugrā*, alkali (*kṣāra*), and *dāru* (devadāru),
is an excellent remedy for *gaṇḍamālā* and a supreme cure for *galagaṇḍa*.
A decoction made from the roots of *varuṇa*, rich with honey and drunk once,
quickly destroys even long-standing *gaṇḍamālā*.
The auspicious bark of *kāñcanāra* should be ground with the water of the month of Jyeṣṭha and consumed.
Combined with Viśvabheṣaja, these are supreme for removing Gaṇḍamālā. One should drink two palas of the fresh juice extracted from Alambuṣā leaves;
this destroys Apacī, Gaṇḍamālā, and Kāmalā.

One should eat a *pupūlikā* (a type of cake) prepared by cooking the root of *vanakārpāsikā* together with rice, for the purpose of destroying *apacī* (scrofulous swellings). Furthermore, *saubhāñjana* and *devadāru* ground with *kāñjika* [should be used].
A lukewarm medicinal paste will destroy even the most difficult apacī.
Having quickly ground the root of āragvadha with rice-water, one may eradicate gaṇḍamālā through both nasal administration and external application.
For those suffering from the disease of *gaṇḍamālā*, one should properly apply as a nasal medication (*nasya*) the root of *nirguṇḍī* well-ground with water;
likewise, a nasal medication may be prepared with the fresh juice of *kośātakī* or *tumbī*, combined with long pepper (*pippalī*).
Or one may prepare [a remedy] with oil derived from *ariṣṭa*, along with *vacā*, *upakulyā*, and honey.
In cases of unripe (*āma*) glandular swellings (*granthi*), the physician should apply treatments for swelling;
once they have suppurated, he should drain them, purify the area, and heal it with wound-healing medicines.
Hiṃsrā, sarohiṇī, amṛtā, bhārgī, śyonāka, bilva, aguru, and kṛṣṇagandhā, ground with cow bile and mixed with tālapatrī, should be applied as a paste for a swelling caused by vāta.
For a swelling caused by pitta, leeches are beneficial, and sprinkling with milk and water is also recommended. || 27 ||
One should drink cooling decoctions of the *kākolī* group mixed with sugar;
or one may drink a powder of *harītakī* with grape juice or sugarcane juice;
or one may apply plasters made from the barks of *madhūka*, *jambu*, *arjuna*, and *vetasa*.

Once the humors have been removed in the proper sequence, the physician should perform scarification (*vimlāpana*) on a tumor arising from phlegm (*śleṣman*) on a patient who has undergone sudation, using the thumb, bamboo, or stones;
[specifically] with the roots of *vikaṅkata*, *āragvadha*, *kākaṇantī*, *kākādanī*, and *tāpasavṛkṣa*.
A wise person should apply a paste of *alābu*, *bhārgī*, *karañja*, *kālā*, and *madana* to this [stone].
A plaster consisting of the roots and bark of *dantī* and *citraka*, the milky sap of *saudha* and *arka*, jaggery, the seeds of *bhallātaka*, and *kāsīsa* would split even a rock.

Having extracted the unripened granthis arising from the vital spots (marmas), the physician should apply fire; furthermore, having repeatedly scarified them according to the instructions, he should rub them with alkali (kṣāra).
Since there is no distinction between granthis and arbudas in terms of location, cause, shape, dosha, and the affected tissue (dūṣya), [the same treatment applies].
Then the physician, who knows the prescribed methods, should treat the arbudas according to the treatment for granthi.
In the case of a vata-arbuda, one should apply poultices made of unctuous meats or vesavāra; the skillful physician should administer fomentation via a tube and repeatedly extract blood with a horn.

In the case of a pitta-arbuda, mild sudation and poultices are beneficial, as is purgation of the body; furthermore, after rubbing the growth, one should apply a thick plaster made of finely ground leaves of udumbara, śāka, and gojī, mixed with honey, along with sarjarasa, priyaṅgu, patrāṅga, lodhra, arjuna, and yaṣṭimadhu.

An ointment made with conch-shell powder together with the ashes of radish roots should be applied to remove tumors caused by phlegm (kapha), especially in cases of glandular swellings (granthi) and the like. [37] Furthermore, one may use a paste of flat beans (niṣpāva), oil-cakes (piṇyāka), and horse gram (kulattha), enriched with meat and mixed with curd. [38]
One should apply a medicinal paste so that worms may release their offspring there, or flies [may deposit theirs];
then, once only a small remnant remains devoured by the worms, one should scrape it away and subsequently apply fire.
That which has few roots should be wrapped with leaves of tin, copper, lead, or even iron.

One should repeatedly apply alkaline substances, fire, and surgical instruments while constantly observing the patient's vital strength (prāṇa). Those tumors that have arrived spontaneously at the stage of suppuration should be treated according to the prescribed method of managing suppurating wounds; for if one leaves any residual morbid humors (doṣas) in the tumors, they will quickly recur.

Therefore, one should extract them entirely; for if they remain with a residue, they will kill like poison or fire. (41) When smeared with the juice of *upodakā* and wrapped in its leaves, various types of boils and tumors on people quickly perish. (42)

Upodakā ground with sour gruel (kāñjika) and buttermilk (takra), mixed with salt, is seen by some as a poultice for the daily pacification of tumors (arbuda) arising in vital spots (marman) during the nights. Furthermore,
the fomentation of Snuhī and Gaṇḍīrī destroys tumors.
Alternatively, fomentation with salt or likewise with lead [is prescribed].
This plaster, consisting of turmeric, lodhra leaves, asafoetida, soot from a house, and realgar,
mixed with a large amount of honey, is supreme for removing fat and swelling.
One should perform this very same procedure in its entirety for *śarkarārbuda* (gravel-like tumor).
Having burnt mustard seeds and *ariṣṭa* leaves together with *bhallātaka* fruits, this paste, ground with goat’s urine, is a plaster that destroys *apacī* (scrofula).
One should burn the stem of the *aśvattha* tree, *nicula*, and the tusk of a cow for seven days along with *āluka*; this ash destroys *apacī* (scrofulous swellings) in an instant.
[The distance] from the heel is twelve finger-breadths.
Having properly incised the mitvendra-basti while avoiding it, the physician should extract the net-like structures resembling fish-eggs and apply fire [cauterization]. || 49 ||

"Or the physician should make three lines above the wrist (*maṇibandha*)."
For the complete pacification of apacī, [an ointment] with a finger's breadth [of space] between [the fingers] is prescribed. Oil prepared with the bark of the śākhoṭaka tree removes gaṇḍamālā;
alternatively, nasal drops (nāvana) prepared with bimbī, aśvamāra, and nirguṇḍī may also be used.
Oil prepared with the juice of *nirguṇḍī* and the paste of the root of *lāṅgalī*, when used as a nasal drop (*nasya*), quickly destroys even the most difficult-to-overcome *gaṇḍamālā*.
Furthermore, this excellent oil, cooked with *chucchundarī*, certainly [effects a cure] in an instant.
Through massage, one may destroy even the most dreadful gaṇḍamālā of men.
Oil boiled with sandalwood, abhayā, lac, vacā, and kaṭukarohiṇī, when drunk, conquers apacī along with its very root.
Oil boiled with vyoṣa, viḍaṅga, madhuka, saindhava, and devadāru, when used as a nasal drop (nasya), may remove even difficult cases of apacī. (55) Adhikāra 42
One should generally treat elephantiasis (ślīpada) with fasting, plasters, sudation, purgation, bloodletting, and predominantly hot therapies that alleviate kapha.
[One may also use] dhattūra, eraṇḍa, nirguṇḍī, varṣābhū, śigru, and sarṣapa.
This ointment destroys elephantiasis, even that which is long-standing and severe.
(2) The bark of the *rūyikā* root, ground with fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*), destroys elephantiasis through application as an ointment, even when it is deeply rooted and firm. (3)
The root-fiber of the *vandāka* plant, which grows on the *piṇḍāraka* tree, conquers severe elephantiasis when drunk with clarified butter;
it certainly cures it when tied with a thread around the calf.
Moreover, *citraka* and *devadāru* are always beneficial as an external ointment.
Alternatively, a paste of *siddhārtha* and *śigru*, ground with urine and applied lukewarm,
may be used. Having performed oleation, sudation, and poultices for elephantiasis caused by Vāta, the physician should pierce a vein four finger-breadths above the ankle.
In cases of ślīpada caused by pitta, one should pierce the vein below the ankle and perform pitta-subduing treatments, as in the case of pitta-type arbuda and visarpa.
[One should apply] mañjiṣṭhā, madhuka, rāsnā, sahiṃsrā, and punarnavā.

This paste, ground with fermented rice-water (āranāla), is for the pacification of pitta-type elephantiasis (pitta-ślīpada). In kapha-type elephantiasis (śleṣma-ślīpada), one should carefully pierce a vein in the thumb;
furthermore, the person should frequently drink astringent decoctions mixed with honey.
Or one should drink a paste of abhayā with any one of the urines;
likewise, one should drink guḍūcī, or nāgara, or devadāru.
One should drink [these] with mustard oil for the cessation of elephantiasis (ślīpada).
Or one may take the juice derived from the leaves of the *pūtīkarañja* according to one's strength; likewise,
a wise physician who understands the distinctions of time and suitability should administer the juice derived from *putrajīvaka* by this very same procedure.

One should drink the fresh juice of *palāśa* roots mixed with an equal amount of oil; or, those suffering from elephantiasis (*ślīpada*) should consume *pathyā*, *suradāru*, and *viśva* along with *guggulu* and cow's urine.
One should drink the powder derived from *vṛddhadāruka* with sour gruel (*kāñjika*).
A person who drinks long pepper (rājanī) mixed with jaggery and cow’s urine destroys elephantiasis (ślīpada) that has arisen within a year, and especially ringworm and skin diseases (dadru-kuṣṭha).
He who drinks Harītakī fried in Gandharva oil with cow’s water [achieves the same].
One becomes free from the constriction of elephantiasis within seven nights.
Fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla) mixed with oil destroys phlegm and wind;
it is digestive, cures disorders of undigested matter (āmadoṣa), and is a destroyer of elephantiasis.
One should powder equal parts of the three pungents (trikaṭu), the three myrobalans (triphalā), cavya, dārvī, varuṇa, gokṣura, alambuṣā, and guḍūcī;
having collected the powder of all these, one should add an equal amount of vṛddhadāru.
That should be drunk with sour gruel (kāñjika) in a dose of one akṣa by measure; once it is digested, there should be no restriction on food, which may include anything desired.
It destroys elephantiasis (ślīpada), obesity, and severe rheumatism (āmavāta).
It removes skin diseases, abdominal tumors, and loss of appetite, and it alleviates pain caused by Vāta and Kapha.
(20) Two palas each of Pippalī, Triphalā, Devadāru, Nāgara, and Punarnavā, along with an equal amount of Vṛddhadāruka— (21)

One should drink one *karṣa* measure of the powder with fermented gruel (*kāñjika*). Once it has been digested, there are no dietary restrictions; one may eat whatever food one desires. This cures elephantiasis (*ślīpada*), wind diseases (*vātaroga*), and even splenic enlargement (*plīhāna*).
It kindles a fierce digestive fire and subdues *bhasmaka* (the condition of excessive digestion).
Take one *karṣa*, half a *pala*, and one *pala* respectively of black pepper, *citraka*, and *dantī*; twenty *harītakī* fruits; and two *palas* of jaggery.
One should eat a sweetmeat (modaka) with honey; it destroys even difficult-to-cure elephantiasis (ślīpada). [The ingredients are:
surasā, granthika, vyoṣa, viḍaṅga, vacā, śaṭhī, pāṭhā, elā, hapuṣā, śyāmā, cavya, dāru, varā, and puru. (24–25)
One should cook a *prastha* of clarified butter with one *karṣa* each of the five salts and alkaline substances;

then, a person should drink one *akṣa* of that [mixture] for a month along with fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*), *daśamūla* decoction, and whey. This destroys even difficult-to-cure elephantiasis (*ślīpada*).
The ghee named Saurēśvara cures enlargement of the spleen, hemorrhoids, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, goiters, tumors, scrofula, elephantiasis, and worms.
[It is prepared] with *viḍaṅga*, black pepper, *arka*, ginger, and *citraka*. 28.
For the cure of elephantiasis (ślīpada), one may also drink oil cooked with bhadradāru, elūka, and all types of salts.
(Chapter 43, Verse 29)
The application of leeches is recommended for every type of abscess (vidradhi), except when pitta is predominant; [in such cases], mild purgation, light food, and fomentation are advised.
[For other types, one should apply] pastes of wind-alleviating roots saturated with muscle fat, oil, and ghee.
A thick, lukewarm plaster should be applied in the case of a Vata-type abscess (vātavidradhi).
Fomentations and poultices should be administered using the roots of the *śigru* tree;
one should also apply a plaster made of barley, wheat, and mung beans that have been cooked and ground into a paste.
In this way, even an unripened abscess dissolves in an instant.

Furthermore, for a wind-induced abscess (vāta-vidradhi), one should drink either guggulu or *rubu* oil with a decoction of *punarnavā*, *dāru*, *viśva*, and the ten roots (*daśamūla*), along with *abhayā*.
In cases of the Pitta-type [fever], one should apply a plaster made of sugar, parched rice, madhuka, and sārivā ground with milk;
or alternatively, a plaster of payasyā, uśīra, and candana ground with milk.
Or, one should drink a decoction of triphalā combined with the paste of trivṛt and ghee.

One should apply a plaster made from the paste of the five barks mixed with ghee, and one should constantly foment a kaphaja abscess using bricks, sand, iron filings, cow dung, husks, and dust, all ground with urine.

One should sprinkle a swelling or an ulcer that is accompanied by pain with a lukewarm decoction of the ten roots (daśamūlī) mixed with oil, or with meat broth. All therapeutic measures for a pitta-type abscess (pittavidradhi) should be applied here without exception.
One skilled in the treatment of abscesses should apply [remedies] for those caused by blood and external factors.
A decoction of *Saubhāñjana* combined with asafoetida and rock salt,
when consumed every morning, destroys an abscess before long.
One should wash the root of the *śigru* tree with water and grind it with water; by drinking its juice mixed with honey, a person destroys internal abscesses (*antarvidradhi*).
[Likewise,] the root of white *varṣābhū* and the root of *varuṇaka* [are used similarly].

Water boiled with [the drugs of] the Varuṇādi group, when drunk while still unfermented (uncooked), conquers internal abscesses (vidradhi). Indeed, for the pacification of an internal, unripened abscess, one should drink a decoction of the Varuṇādi group with the addition of the Uṣakādi group as a medicinal adjunct.
This [treatment] is prescribed for the unripe stage; however, once it has ripened, treatment should be like that for an ulcer.
The root of *pāṭhā* taken with honey and rice-water pacifies an internal abscess that has arisen deeply within a person, as if it were torn out, very quickly.
Oil should be cooked with *priyaṅgu*, *dhātakī*, *lodhra*, *kaṭphala*, and the bark of *tiniśa*; this is for healing wounds in cases of abscesses (*vidradhi*).
(16) Chapter 44.
First, one should perform debridement; second, irrigation; third, the application of a poultice; and fourth, the procedure of incision.
Fifth, one should perform cleansing; the sixth is desired as healing.
These stages of the ulcer have been described; the seventh is that which removes deformity.
Mātuluṅga, agnimantha, devadāru, mahauṣadha, ahiṃsrā, and rāsnā, when applied as a paste, conquer swelling caused by vāta.
A paste made by grinding the bark of the *śākhoṭaka* tree with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) is unctuous and destroys wind-swelling (*vāta-śotha*), just as Suparṇa destroys serpents.
Likewise, *dūrvā*, the root of *nala*, *madhuka*, and *candana* [are used].
All these cooling groups [of drugs] constitute a paste that destroys swelling caused by pitta.
A paste made from the bark of nyagrodha, udumbara, aśvattha, plakṣa, and vetasa, mixed with ghee, is the supreme means for quenching swelling.
Ajagandhā, aśvagandhā, kālā, along with saralā, ekaiṣikā, and ajaśṛṅgī— this application as a paste destroys swelling caused by kapha.
[7] With punarnavā, dāruśigru, daśamūla, and mahauṣadha...
For a swelling caused by phlegm (kapha) and wind (vāta), a lukewarm plaster is prescribed.
One should not apply a plaster at night, nor one that has fallen off,
nor one that is stale, nor indeed one that is drying.

One should ignore the plaster as it dries during the process of compression; nor should one smear the face with it, for by that, the morbid humors (doṣas) are discharged. Having anointed and fomented [the area], one should then apply pressure slowly using a bamboo tube.
One should massage with the palm or the thumb for the purpose of softening [the swelling].
A wise physician should perform bloodletting at the very outset in the case of a large, inflamed, or painful ulcer.
That swelling which does not subside through the application of plasters, fomentations, affusions,
and depleting therapies, even that quickly goes to destruction by the letting out of blood. On one side are all other treatments, and on the other side is bloodletting alone.
For blood indeed turns into pus; if that [blood] is absent, there is no pain.
A swelling that does not subside through the application of plasters and other treatments, one should apply digestive (pācanīya) substances as a poultice (upanāhana) therein.
A bolus made of sesame seeds, linseed, sour curd,
barley meal, yeast, kuṣṭha, and salt is recommended for use as a poultice (upanāhana).
[Likewise,] the roots and fruits of hemp and śigru, linseed, sesame, and mustard [are also used].
Barley flour, fermenting agent (kiṇva), and warm substances— these constitute a digestive preparation.
A lukewarm bolus made of barley flour mixed with either oil, ghee, or both, is recommended for poulticing (upanāha) to promote the suppuration of swelling.
Elephant tusk rubbed in water, when applied as a mere drop,
causes suppuration and bursting even of an extremely hard swelling.
Regarding slimy substances, however, the bark and roots are used for squeezing out the contents.
In brief, the powders of barley, wheat, and mung beans;
cirabilva, agnika, dantī, citraka, and hayamāraka;
and the excrement of pigeons, herons, and vultures—these constitute a powder for causing fissures.
Alternatively, there are alkaline substances, or alkali itself, which is the supreme agent for incision;

thereafter, a wash consisting of a decoction of *paṭolī* and neem leaves is used, while if the area is not yet purified, a wash derived from the bark of the *nyagrodha* group of trees is employed once it has been purified. || 22 ||
The two groups of five roots (pañcamūlī) should be used for vāta disorders; the nyagrodhādi group for pitta disorders;
and the āragvadhādi group should be employed in all procedures for kapha disorders.
This applies to those whose putrid flesh has been removed, whose flesh is established, and who are not regenerating.
A paste made of sesame seeds combined with madhuka should be used for healing (saṃropaṇa). A paste combined with nimba leaves and honey is known as purifying (saṃśodhana).
Furthermore, when combined with the two aforementioned substances or with ghee, it is also used for secondary healing (uparopaṇa).
