Some wise men, however, say that it is a paste of sesame and barley.
One should pacify an undigested [abscess], ripen one that is ripened, burst one that is ripe, and once burst, one should cleanse it and promote healing.
A paste made of neem leaves and sesame seeds with honey cleanses the ulcer.
This same procedure applies to a paste of barley mixed with ghee for the purpose of healing.
A suppository composed of neem leaves, ghee, honey, daruharidra, and madhuka, or a paste of sesame seeds, shall cleanse and heal the ulcer.
Nimba leaves, sesame, danti, trivṛt, rock salt,
and honey constitute a plaster that pacifies malignant ulcers and acts as a lion among purifiers.
Sesame paste with salt, the two types of haridrā, trivṛt, and ghee [are likewise used].
A paste of madhuka and nimba leaves serves as a purifier for wounds.
A decoction of triphalā, khadira, dārvī, nyagrodha and the rest, balā, kuśā, and the leaves of nimba and kola is beneficial for purification.
Yashṭīmadhu and sesame seeds, well-ground and mixed with ghee, heal wounds; or alternatively, the root of Sārivā alone purifies all types of wounds.
(33) A paste made from the milk of the Saptaparna tree pacifies malignant wounds when applied as an ointment.

Śarapuṅkhā mixed with honey is said to heal all wounds. One should cleanse narrow-mouthed wounds located in joints or vital spots (marmans) by means of a suppository (varti) prepared from trivṛt, dantī, lāṅgalī, honey, and rock salt.
Suṣavī leaves, dhattūra, karṇamoṭa, and kuṭhāraka— these, applied individually as a paste, heal deep wounds;
or alternatively, with the powders of the five barks (pañcavalkala) combined with the powder of oyster shells.
Or by means of the powders of dhātakī and lodhra, those wounds heal. Those wounds which are accompanied by burning, painful, and dominated by vāta (wind),
for them [one should apply] sesame seeds and marrow fried and cooled in milk.
Having ground that very substance with milk, the physician should apply it as an ointment;
this application and other treatments pacify pitta-type abscesses and erysipelas, and the practitioner should employ them properly on wounds caused by fire.
One should fumigate those afflicted by wind (vāta), who have secretions (sāsrava), and who suffer from intense pain,
with barley, clarified butter (ājya), *bhūrja* bark, *madana*, *śrīveṣṭaka*, and *surāhvaya*.
Those [patients] should be fumigated with *śrīvāsa*, *guggulu*, *aguru*, and the resin (*niryāsa*) of *sāla*.
The wounds become firm, and the discharge and pain vanish.
(41) Sesame seeds, milk, sugar, honey, oil, madhuka, and sandalwood—by means of an ointment made from these, one should pacify swelling, pain, burning, and bleeding in the wounds. (42)
The juice of karañja, ariṣṭa, and nirguṇḍī destroys worms in wounds.

Filling the wound with the leaves of kalāya and vidalī and the stone of the kośāmra fruit, or irrigating it with the juices of the surasādi group, or applying a plaster of garlic, [is also effective].
Nimba, śamyāka, jāti, arka, saptaparṇa,
and aśvamāraka, combined with urine, act as vermin-killers when used for irrigation, as ointments, or for washing; or,
by covering the wound with a strip of flesh, one may eliminate the worms from the ulcer.
Alternatively, one should apply a plaster of garlic (laśuna) to destroy worms.
Those large ulcers that are characterized by discharge, suppuration, foul odor, pain, and swelling,
attain relief when [guggulu] mixed with the decoction of triphalā is drunk.

Guggulu combined with the powder of triphalā and formed into pills (vaṭaka) acts as a free-flowing remedy that destroys constipation and cleanses and heals ulcers. Amṛtā-guggulu is recommended, and Vajraka oil is also beneficial. 48–49.
Having prepared pills from the powder of viḍaṅga, triphalā, and vyoṣa together with guggulu and clarified butter, one should consume them while eating wholesome food;
this purifies malignant ulcers, apacī, prameha, and kuṣṭha, as well as sinus tracts. || 50 ||
Take equal parts of the powders of *amṛtā*, *paṭola* root, *vāsa*, *triphalā*, *trikaṭu*, and *kṛmighna*; the portion of *guggulu* should be equal to the total of all these.
One should eat one pill daily, measuring one *akṣa*.
To conquer wounds, wind-disorders, blood disorders, abdominal tumors, edema, anemia, and other such ailments:
realgar, together with madder, lac, and the two types of turmeric, applied as a plaster with ghee and honey, is a supreme purifier of the skin. (52–53)
A paste made of iron filings, green vitriol (kāsīsa), and the flowers of the three myrobalans (triphalā) produces blackness instantly on fresh skin.
[This is achieved] with kālīyaka, latā, copper, bone, gold, and the finest kālā-rasa.
An ointment made with cow-dung juice is the best means for restoring the natural color [of the skin].
55. Chapter 45:
A physician should irrigate a fresh wound that is accompanied by pain.

Having recognized an accidental wound (āgantuvraṇa), the physician should apply a cooling treatment that destroys the heat of pitta and rakta, using ghee mixed with liquorice (yaṣṭīmadhuka) and slightly warmed,
combined with ghee and honey.
A single application of *kāntakrāmuka*, ground very finely with cow’s ghee, certainly pacifies an exogenous wound through its topical application; of this there is no doubt.
This is for the purpose of suppressing the heat of the injury and the spreading that occurs at that time.
Astringent decoctions that are cold-sweet and unctuous are beneficial when applied as ointments and the like.
When blood is located in the stomach (āmāśaya), emesis is said to be the wholesome treatment;
when it is located in the large intestine (pakvāśaya), purgation should undoubtedly be administered.
A decoction made from bamboo bark, eraṇḍa, śvadaṃṣṭrā, and aśmabhida, taken with asafoetida and salt, causes the blood located within the abdominal cavity to flow out;
likewise, one may use the unsalted broth of barley, jujube, and horse gram.
One should eat food or drink gruel mixed with rock salt (saindhava).
For when blood flows excessively from a wound,
the wind (vāyu) generally becomes aggravated due to that loss of blood, causing intense pain.
One should administer the drinking of fats (sneha-pāna), affusion (pariṣeka), unctuous ointments (snigdha-lepa), poultices (upanāhana),
and oil enemas (sneha-basti) prepared with Vāta-alleviating drugs.
Thus has been described the seven-day regimen beneficial for fresh wounds.
After seven days, the treatment should be performed as for a physical wound.
Gaurī, haridrā, mañjiṣṭhā, māṃsī, madhuka, prapauṇḍarīka, hīvera, bhadramusta, and candana [are the ingredients].
One should cook one prastha of ghee with jātī, nimba, paṭola, karañja, kaṭurohiṇī,
madhūcchiṣṭa, madhūka, and likewise mahāmedā,
using the decoction of the five barks (pañcavalkala). || 12 ||

This Gaura is of great power and is the purifier of all wounds. It quickly cleanses wounds— whether they are exogenous, congenital, or long-standing— and it also rapidly clears even the most tortuous channels.
The young leaves and fruits of the *naktamāla*,
the leaves of the *sumanā*, as well as those of the *paṭola* and *ariṣṭa*;
the two types of *haridrā*, beeswax (*madhūcchiṣṭa*), *madhuka*, and *tiktarohiṇī*.

One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with one *karṣa* each of these: mañjiṣṭhā, candana, uśīra, utpala, sārivā, and trivṛt. This [medicinal ghee] pacifies malignant ulcers and likewise purifies sinus tracts (*nāḍī*).
This Karañjādi ghee is for those with fresh incised wounds.
[It is prepared] with equal parts of Jātī, Nimba, Paṭola leaves, Kaṭukā, Dārvī, Niśā, Sārivā, Mañjiṣṭhā, Abhayā, beeswax, Tuttha, Madhuka, and the seeds of Naktāhvā.

Ghee prepared with these [herbs] causes wounds that have narrow openings, those located in vital spots (marmas), those that discharge, those that are deep, those accompanied by pain, and those with sinus tracts, to become purified and heal.
[The herbs used are: Prapauṇḍarīka, Mañjiṣṭhā, Madhuka, Uśīra, and Padmaka.
Clarified butter prepared with turmeric and milk heals wounds.
Likewise, one should cook clarified butter after grinding together beeswax, licorice, *lodhra*, resin (*sarjarasa*), *mañjiṣṭhā*, sandalwood, and *mūrvā*.

This planting is prescribed for all those who have been consumed by fire. Powder made from the dried bark of the *aśvattha* tree, along with the application of the ashes produced by burning it, destroys the wound caused by an internal burn from an axe, as does its dusting [over the area].
Oil prepared by grinding earthworms destroys all [skin diseases] when used as an ointment after massage; likewise, sand submerged in water [destroys them] through application.
So too does mustard oil prepared with *pāṭalī* and astringent decoctions [achieve this].
It destroys the pain of burnt wounds, discharge, burning sensations, and eruptions.
Sandalwood, banyan shoots, mañjiṣṭhā, madhuka, prapauṇḍarīka, dūrvā grass, pattraṅga, and likewise dhātakī [are used for this]. || 22–23 ||
Oil should be cooked with these [ingredients], combined with ghee and milk;
it is excellent for wounds scorched by fire, acting as a supreme application for immediate healing.
One hundred palas of kuṭhāraka should be boiled in non-saline water.
Then, one should cook one *prastha* of oil with the remaining foot [of the decoction] along with the pastes (*kalka*) of *kuṭhārā*, *apāmārga*, *proṣṭhikā*, and *makṣikā*.
This oil of *kuṭhārā* cleanses and heals wounds.
The supreme application of oil massage should be performed upon the channels, both those that are innate and those that are adventitious.
Alternatively, oil prepared with the fresh juice of *dūrvā* grass, or with *kampillaka*, or with the paste of *dārvī* bark, is a primary means for healing wounds.
One should prepare ghee using the same procedure as for oil; having recognized that blood and bile (raktapitta) predominate, one should administer ghee alone.
When the wound has healed or is just beginning to heal, the patient may eat all types of meat soups.

When the wind (vāta) encounters a moist or unbound ligament, or a struck limb, it dries up the vitiated blood that has not been discharged and produces a knotted wound characterized by burning and excessive itching;
this is known as *vraṇagranthi* (wound-nodule).
One should employ the procedure for applying an alkaline thread (kṣārasūtra), which removes malignant ulcers.
Chapter 46:
Having first identified a fracture, one should sprinkle it with cold water.
One should apply a plaster of mud and perform a bandage provided with *kuśa* grass.
One should raise what is depressed, press down what is elevated, pull out what is protruding, and turn upward what has gone downward.
For the purpose of anointment, a paste of mañjiṣṭhā and madhuka ground with sour liquids,
mixed with ghee washed a hundred times, and rice flour should be applied as an ointment;
furthermore, a very cool decoction of the nyagrodhādi group should be used for pouring over the area.
In cases of pain, the wise physician should administer milk boiled with the five roots (pañcamūlī), or apply lukewarm oil from a revolving machine (cakrataila).
Meat, meat broth, milk, clarified butter, and soup made from satīna beans [are also beneficial].
One who understands [the nature of healing] should provide nourishing food and drink to one with a fracture.
Generally, a substance that is heavy, cold, soft, unctuous, abundant, coarse, slimy, slow-acting, stable, and smooth is called nourishing (bṛṃhaṇa).
A person with a fracture should drink in the morning the milk of a cow that has calved for the first time, mixed with ghee, boiled with sweet medicinal herbs, cooled, and combined with lac; likewise,
one should take asthisamhāra with ghee, lac, wheat, and arjuna.
A person suffering from a dislocated joint or a fractured bone should drink a paste made of garlic,
honey, lac, ghee, and sugar with milk.
For those whose bones are severed, split, or displaced, the rejoining of the joints will occur without delay for one who consumes this.
One who desires well-being after a fracture should drink milk with lac and madhuka, or ghee prepared with the jīvanīya herbs; one should drink the bark of arjuna with milk, or wheat flour with ghee.
Furthermore, lac, asthisamhṛt, kakubha, aśvagandhā, powdered nāgabalā, and puru [should be used].
It destroys pain in fractured, dislocated, or unstable joints and makes the limbs as firm as a thunderbolt.
Guggulu, equal in measure to all these ingredients—Ābhā, Triphalā, and Vyōṣa—should be administered; it heals fractured joints.

In the case of a fracture with an open wound, one should rub the wound with decoctions mixed with a predominance of ghee and honey; thereafter, one should treat the remainder as in the case of a simple fracture.
One should also apply the oleaginous substances prescribed for wind-diseases (vātavyādhi) here as well.
One who has suffered a fracture should avoid salt, pungent substances, alkaline matter, sourness, sexual intercourse, exposure to the sun, physical exercise, and dry food. (15) Chapter 47.

Having sought out the course of the sinus channels and incised them with a surgical instrument, the physician skilled in the procedure should perform the entire regimen for ulcers, including cleansing, healing, and so forth.
Once a sinus caused by Vāta has been properly incised, the physician should apply an ointment.
One should apply a paste made of ground sesame seeds combined with *pratyakpuṣpī* and its fruit for [a bile-related] condition;
for a bile-conditioned [abscess], one should use sesame, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *nāgadantī*, and the two types of *niśā*;
for a phlegm-conditioned [abscess], one should use sesame, *yaṣṭyāhva*, *nikumbha*, *ariṣṭa*, and rock salt.
A wound caused by a splinter that has been incised and cleansed should be smeared with sesame, honey, and clarified butter.

A wick made from a thread and combined with the powder of *āragvadha*, *niśā*, and *kālā*, along with clarified butter and honey, should be applied to the ulcer; it is a purifier and eliminates the sinus tract.

The fruit and bark of *ghoṇṭā*, the fruit of *madana*, the bark of betel nut (*pūga*), and the best salt— this paste, mixed with the milky sap of *sruhī* and *arka* and formed into a wick, destroys sinus (*nāḍī*) in no time. Alternatively, the best salt, combined with honey and formed into a wick, is said to destroy sinus.
The oil prescribed for malignant ulcers, when used, quickly destroys the [sinus] track.

A wick made from *jāti*, *arka*, *śamyāka*, *karañja*, *dantī*, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), black salt (*sauvarcala*), and *yāvaśūka*, ground with the milky sap of *snuh* and *citrika*, destroys the sinus in no time.
For those who are emaciated, weak, or fearful, and for a vein that rests upon a vital point (marman), one should cut it with an alkaline thread and never with a surgical instrument;
having sought its course with a probe, one should follow it with an alkaline thread.
One should insert the needle with care, then raise it quickly and remove it; having brought the end of the thread together, one should apply a firm tie.
Then, observing the strength of the caustic, one should introduce another thread.
The wise physician should apply an alkaline solution until the path [of the disease] is severed;

this same procedure should be performed by a knowledgeable physician even in cases of fistula-in-ano (bhagandara). Furthermore, in cases such as tumors (arbuda), one should lift [the growth] and place a thread at its base.
Or, if it is covered all over with needles having tips like barley grains, one should bind it at the base with a thread; and once it has been excised, one should treat the wound.
Guggulu, the three myrobalans (triphalā), and the three acrids (vyoṣa) in equal parts, combined with clarified butter, [should be applied].
This oil, prepared with svarjikā,
sindhu, dantī, agni, tryūṣaṇa, anala, nīlikā,
and the seeds of kharamañjarī, cooked in cow’s urine, cures fistulas caused by vitiated channels and destroys hemorrhoids (bhagaṃdara).
This pacifies malignant ulcers and removes ulcers caused by kapha and sinus tracts (nāḍīvraṇa).

Having prepared a decoction from the category of unripe fruits (*śalāṭu*) of the *kumbhīka*, *kharjūra*, *kapittha*, *bilva*, and forest trees (*vanaspati*), one should cook oil therein, adding *mustā*, *saralā*, and *priyaṅgu*. || 15–16 ||
Having applied the powders of *saugandhika*, *amocara*, *ahi-puṣpa*, and *dhātakī*,
a sinus tract originating from a foreign body will indeed heal, and the wound will certainly close quickly and with ease.
[Likewise, one may use] *bhallātaka*, *arka*, *marica*, and the best salt.
An oil prepared with Viḍaṅga, the two types of Rajanī, Citraka, and the juice of Mārkava is effective; it destroys sinus tracts caused by Kapha and Vāta, as well as scrofula and ulcers. || 18 ||
Having squeezed *nirguṇḍī* along with its roots and leaves, one should prepare an equal quantity of oil with that juice; this cures fistulas and malignant ulcers,
and is beneficial for scabies and scrofula when used as a drink, an ointment, or an errhine.
In various types of sphota (eruptions) as well as in malignant ulcers,
the physician should apply those wicks (varti) prescribed in the chapter on the treatment of two types of ulcers (dvivraṇīya) to all sinus tracts.
(20–21) Chapter 48.
Having observed swelling of the rectum, one should dry it and then cleanse it; bloodletting should be performed so that suppuration does not occur. [The following are used:
banyan leaves, brick, ginger, guḍūcī, and punarnavā.
Having ground it well into a paste-like consistency, an ointment is recommended for fistula-in-ano (bhagandara).
For unripened abscesses (piḍakā), one should first employ depleting therapies and then perform treatments ending with purgation; the procedure for those that have burst will be described hereafter.

Having performed the sequence of probing, incision, cauterization with alkali, application of fire, and so forth, one should treat it like a wound according to the specific humor (doṣa) and in the proper order.
[The paste consists of] trivṛt, sesame seeds, nāgadantī, and mañjiṣṭhā, together with clarified butter.
This [application] combined with rock salt and honey serves as a debriding agent (utsādana).
A paste made of rasāñjana, the two types of haridrā, mañjiṣṭhā, nimba leaves,
trivṛt, tejovatī, and dantī destroys sinus ulcers (nāḍīvraṇa).

The group of drugs beginning with *nyagrodha*, which is beneficial for cleansing and healing, should be cooked into either oil or clarified butter (*ghṛta*); when prepared thus, it destroys fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṃdara*). [Likewise,] *kuṣṭha*, *trivṛt*, *tila*, *dantī*, *māgadhī*, and rock salt (*saindhava*) mixed with honey [are used].
Rajanī, triphalā, and tuttha are beneficial for the purification of wounds. Having prepared a wick with the milks of snuhī and arka along with dārvī, the wise physician,
having ascertained the depth of the fistula-in-ano, should diligently fill it with this.
This [mixture] undoubtedly destroys the sinus (nāḍī) located within the entire body.
Sesame, harītakī, kuṣṭha, leaves of mariṣṭa, the two types of niśā, vacā, lodhra, and soot—
this is a purifying and healing agent for fistula-in-ano, sinus, venereal sores, and malignant ulcers.
An ointment made from cat bones combined with the juice of triphalā quickly destroys fistula-in-ano (bhagandara) and is supreme for healing malignant ulcers.
A pill composed of three parts of triphalā, five parts of puru, and one part of kṛṣṇā [is likewise effective].
It is said to be a purifier of leprosy, fistula-in-ano, sinus tracts, and malignant ulcers.
(12) One who avoids indigestion and eats the meat of a jackal in various ways, such as with side dishes and the like, shall be freed from fistula-in-ano within a month. (13)
The *pañcatikta* ghee is recommended, as is that prepared with *guggulu* and other ingredients.
[One should take] *citraka*, *arka*, *trivṛt*, *pāṭhā*, *malayū*, *hayamāraka*, *sudhā*, *vacā*, *lāṅgalakī*, *haritāla*, and *suvarcikā*.
A wise person should cook oil with crushed jyotiṣmatī;
this oil, named Viṣyandana, should be administered for fistula-in-ano (bhagandara), as it is a supreme purifier, healer, and restorer of natural skin color. || 16 ||
One should cook oil with *karavīra*, *niśā*, *dantī*, *lāṅgalī*, salt, and *agni*, along with *mātuluṅga*, *arka*, and *vatsāhva*, for the treatment of fistula-in-ano (*bhagandara*).
One should avoid physical exercise, sexual intercourse, combat, riding on the back of animals, and heavy foods.
A man whose wound has healed should avoid [sexual intercourse] for one year.
Chapter 49:
For one who has been lubricated and fomented, venesection should first be performed in the middle of the penis.
Either leeches should be applied, or there should be purification from above and below;
however, the healing process must be protected with great effort, for it causes emaciation of the penis.
Alternatively, one should drink a decoction of *paṭola*, *nimba*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and *guḍūcī*, along with *khadira* and *asana*.
The application of guggulu combined with triphalā is a practice that removes all types of secondary infections (upadaṃśa).
One should apply a plaster made of prapauṇḍarīka, madhuka, rāsnā, kuṣṭha, punarnavā, sarala, aguru, and bhadrākhya for conditions arising from vāta.
One should apply a smooth paste composed of red ochre, collyrium, madder, madhuka, ushira, padmaka, sandalwood, and blue lotus for the treatment of pitta-type [fever].
[Regarding the trees: among nimba, arjuna, ashvattha, kadamba, shala, jambu, vata, udumbara, and vetasa...
One should apply washes, ointments, medicated ghees, and powders for upadaṃśa arising from pitta and blood (5).
For that arising from kapha, one should apply a warm plaster made of the barks of śālāñjaka, karṇa, aśvakarṇa, and dhava, ground with surā liquor and mixed with oil (6).
One should perform the washing of the ulcer with a decoction of triphalā or with the juice of bhṛṅgarāja for the pacification of upadaṃśa.
One should burn triphalā in a cauldron; that soot, when combined with honey, [is used as a collyrium].
This ointment for *upadaṃśa* heals the ulcer instantly.
For the treatment of inflammation of the penis (*meḍhrapāka*), one should employ a decoction made from the leaves of *japā*, *jāti*, *aśvamāra*, *arka*, and *śamyāka* separately for washing.

Ghee prepared with a paste (kalka) and decoction (kaṣāya) of karañja, nimba, arjuna, śāka, jambu, vaṭa, and other such trees, cures the disorder of upadaṃśa accompanied by burning, suppuration, discharge, and redness. [10] House-soot, haridrā, and the dregs of wine—by means of these three [one may also treat it]. [11]
One should cook oil with these ingredients in increasing proportions; it removes itching, swelling, and pain, and acts as a purifier, healer, and restorer of natural skin color.
For hemorrhoids that have been excised or cauterized, the treatment should be performed as in the case of upadaṃśa (syphilis).
Chapter 50:
Drinking ghee is beneficial, as is purgation which is wholesome;
bloodletting is beneficial, as is a light diet. || 1 ||
One should apply a plaster of finely ground *sarṣapī* seeds mixed with astringent decoctions;
with those same ingredients, one should prepare an ointment oil for the healing of the wound.
This same procedure should also be applied in the case of *avamanyaka*, and blood should likewise be let from both [the *sarṣapī* and *avamanyaka*].
When blood has been removed from an aṣṭhīlā, one should treat it like a phlegm-granule (śleṣmagranthi).

In the case of a kumbhikā, one should extract the blood; once it has suppurated and the ulcer has been cleansed, an ointment made of tinduka, triphalā, and lodhra should be applied, and oil should be used for healing.

In this very same therapeutic sequence for *alajī* when its blood has been removed, the wise physician should constantly foment the conglobate mass with *nāḍīsveda* (tube-fomentation) and apply very unctuous poultices that are comfortably warm. || 5 ||
Having excised the carbuncle known as *uttamā* after it has been removed with a hook,
one should treat it with pastes and powders of astringent decoctions mixed with honey.
The regimen prescribed for *pittavisarpa* is beneficial for *puṣkarī* and *mūḍha*.
In cases of suppuration of the skin and loss of sensation, one should again sprinkle the area with lukewarm *balā*-oil and apply a poultice (*upanāha*) made of drugs belonging to the sweet group.
When the *śatapottaka* ulcer has been scarified, the procedure for *rasakriyā* should be performed.
Immediately thereafter, oil prepared with *pṛthakparṇī* and other herbs should be administered.

Furthermore, the treatment for a blood-born (*śoṇitaja*) tumor (*arbuda*) is the same as that for a blood-born abscess (*raktavidradhi*); [this includes] decoctions, pastes, medicated ghees, oils, powders, and medicinal extracts.
One should apply [medicines] for cleansing and healing only after careful and repeated examination.
Having declined to treat them, a physician should then perform the remedial measures for arbuda, māṃsapāka, vidradhi, and tilakālaka.
Chapter 51:
In cases of kuṣṭha where vāta is predominant, ghee [is indicated]; where kapha is predominant, emesis;
and where pitta is predominant, bloodletting and purgation should be administered first.
Venesection is recommended for both minor and major kuṣṭha when it is concealed;
however, a kuṣṭha patient with an abundance of doṣas should be purified repeatedly while carefully protecting their life-force.
For if the doṣas are removed in excessive measure, vāyu may quickly destroy the strength.
When the heart is afflicted by the humors (doṣas), emesis is indicated in cases of skin diseases (kuṣṭha) located in the upper part of the body.
A decoction of vacā, vāsā, paṭola, nimba, and the bark of phalinī,
mixed with honey and madana fruit, when drunk, induces vomiting.
Purgation should be administered using *trivṛt*, *dantī*, and the three myrobalans (*phalatrika*).
A medicinal paste (*pradeha*) consisting of realgar, yellow orpiment, black pepper, castor oil, and the milk of the *arka* plant is a destroyer of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*).
Furthermore, another medicinal paste consists of *karañja* seeds, *eḍagaja*, and *kuṣṭha*, ground with cow's urine.
Having ground the leaves of *caturaṅgula* and the leaves of *kākamācī* with buttermilk,
one should apply them as an ointment for the leprosy of a man whose body has been anointed with oil, using also the leaves of *aśvahan*.
[One may likewise use] *eḍagaja*, *kuṣṭha*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *sauvīraka*, mustard seeds, and *kṛmighna*.
This ointment destroys worms, sidhma, circular skin lesions, and leprosy (kuṣṭha).
One should also apply here the ointments for kuṣṭha and other diseases mentioned in the section on koṭha. One should grind the leaves of āragvadha with sour gruel (āranāla).
It destroys ringworm, kiṭibha, kuṣṭha, and even sidhma. 9.
Sthauṇeya, ruṅniśā, dūrvā, saptaparṇa, and tāla, when ground with the juice of dhattūra and applied as a paste, destroy itching, scabies, and other such ailments. 10.
The root of *kāsamarda* ground with sour gruel (*sauvīra*) conquers ringworm, *kiṭibha*, and leprosy through the application of this ointment.
Alternatively, the seeds of radish and mustard, lac, the two types of *rajanī*, and the seed of *prapunāṭa* [may be used].
Having ground together śrīveṣṭaka, vyoṣa, viḍaṅga, and kuṣṭha with urine,
this ointment shall destroy ringworm (dadrū), vitiligo (sidhma), kiṭibha, scabies (pāmā), kapālakuṣṭha, and malignant poisons (viṣama).
[12] With viḍaṅga, eḍagaja, kuṣṭha, niśā, rock salt (sindhūttha), and mustard seeds...
This plaster made from grains ground with sour gruel (dhānyāmla) is a destroyer of ringworm and skin diseases (dadrū-kuṣṭha).
Dūrvā grass, abhayā, rock salt, cakramarda, and kuṭheraka, ground with sour gruel and buttermilk,
destroy even deeply rooted ringworm and itching through three applications of this plaster.

A paste made by grinding equal parts of *śāla* tree resin, *tuṣa*, *cakramarda*, and *abhayā* with water and rice-gruel, when applied as an ointment, is a lion for the elephant-king of ringworm (*dadru*).
Furthermore, there is the great medicine known as *tṛṇa*, which arises from the *varendrī* plant.
Through rubbing and consuming it, leprosy (kuṣṭha) is quickly pacified.
Radish seeds well-ground with the juice of ginger, when applied as a paste,
or with the alkali of the plantain tree mixed with turmeric, destroys sidhma.
Sidhma (vitiligo) is quickly destroyed when treated with a plaster of yavakṣāra mixed with gandhapāṣāṇa and combined with kaṭutaila.
Likewise, [a plaster of] the seeds of kāsamardaka and of radishes [is effective].
Sulphur mixed with fragrant stones is the supreme medicine for *sidhma*.
The juice of *dhātrī*, resin of *sarja*, *pākya*, ground *sauvīra* salt, and that which has been infused with these, when used as an ointment, ensures that the *sidhma* lesions do not recur. (19–20)
Patra, koṣaṇa, kāsīsa, oil, tāpya, and manaḥśilā,
having been kept for seven days in a bronze vessel, destroy sidhma and vitiligo.
[Likewise, a preparation] with dhātrī, akṣa, pathyā, krimiśatru, vahni, bhallātaka, avalguja, iron, and bhṛṅga...
This electuary, increased by its own weight and mixed with sesame oil, destroys all types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
(22) Śaśāṅkalekhā, combined with viḍaṅga, kuṣṭha, pippalī, and the root of hutāśa, along with iron-rust, āmalaka, and oil—when licked, it destroys all types of skin diseases. (23)
Āragvadha, saiḍagaja, karañja, vāsā, guḍūcī, madana, the two types of haridrā, śyāhva, surāhva, khadira, dhava, nimba, viḍaṅga, karavīraka,
granthi, bhūrja, garlic, śirīṣa, sālomaśa, guggulu, and kṛṣṇagandha. || 24 ||
Phaṇijjaka, vatsaka, saptaparṇa, pīlu, kuṣṭha, and the young shoots of sumana;
vacā, hareṇu, trivṛtā, nikumbha, bhallātaka, gairika, añjana, manaḥśilā, āla, gṛhadhūma, elā, kāsīsa, lodhra, arjuna, musta, and sarja. || 25–26 ||
These six, prepared in the form of powders and plasters, smeared with cow-bile and ground once again, are highly effective when combined with mustard oil;
they should be applied by the physician for severe skin diseases, fresh leucoderma, alopecia (surendralupta), kiṭibha, and ringworm (dadru). || 27 ||
When properly applied, these quickly destroy fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, scrofula, and scabies in men.

Having thoroughly burnt elephant dung in an alkaline solution, one should add ten parts of *avalguja* seed to one *droṇa* measure of elephant urine that has been repeatedly strained. Then, one should cook [the mixture]. 29.
When this attains a sticky consistency, one should then prepare a well-prepared pill;
having rubbed a vitiligo spot with it, that [spot] will then quickly attain the same color as the surrounding skin.
A pill made from vājigandhā, iḍagaja, kuṣṭha, and kṛṣṇā [is likewise effective].
Ground with goat’s urine, this [paste] destroys vitiligo when applied as an ointment.

(31) The tender leaves of *pūtīka*, *arka*, *snuh*, and *narendradruma*, along with those of *saumana*, ground with urines and used as an ointment, destroy vitiligo, ringworm, ulcers, leprosy, hemorrhoids, and malignant sinus ulcers. (32)
One *kuḍava* of *avalguja* seeds mixed with a fourth part of yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), ground with cow’s urine, is the supreme remedy for making leucoderma (*śvitra*) disappear.
Having drunk a decoction of *dhātrī* and *khadira* combined with *avalguja*, [one attains this result].
It undoubtedly and quickly destroys white leprosy (śvitra) as white as a conch shell or the moon.

A plaster made of *cakrāṅka* seeds, saturated with the milky sap of the *snuhī* plant, mixed with urine, heated in the sun, and combined with fermenting agent (*kiṇva*), removes *kiṭibha* skin lesions.
One should cook mustard oil with the seed of *unmattaka* and the alkaline water of *māṇaka*; it quickly destroys *vipādikā*.
Rice placed inside a coconut shell becomes putrid.
As an ointment, it destroys chronic eczema (vipādikā) that has persisted for a long time.
[One should take] āvalguja, kāsamarda, and cakramarda combined with niśā, in equal parts with māṇimantha, ground with honey and sour gruel (kāñjika). || 37-38 ||
This proven king of formulations conquers severe itching and skin eruptions (kacchū). A tender *siṃhāsya* leaf, ground with *surabhī* water along with salt,
certainly destroys itching within three days when applied as an ointment.
A man who acts according to his desire should drink two *palas* of cow’s urine mixed with a paste of turmeric; this destroys scabies and *pāmā*.
It also cures swelling and anemia (*pāṇḍu*), and removes abdominal tumors (*gulma*), urinary disorders (*meha*), and phlegm (*kapha*).

One suffering from *kacchū* (scabies) or *pāmā* (eczema) should drink half a *pala* of powdered *gandhapāṣāṇa* (sulphur), processed with cow’s urine and mixed with pungent oil, after it has been thoroughly heated by the rays of the sun. || 42 ||
Sprinkled with that [mixture] for three days and subsisting on a diet of milk, a man quickly becomes endowed with the luster of gold and possessed of desire. [The ingredients are:
night-blooming jasmine, *ragvadha*, and *kākamācī*...
An ointment made from the leaves of *sadārvī* and the seeds of *prapunāṭa*, ground with *sauvīra* alkali and mixed with pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*),
is recommended for conditions such as scabies (*pāmā*). || 44 ||
This group of drugs— consisting of māṃsī, candana, śamyāka, karañja, ariṣṭa, sarṣapa, śaṭhī, kuṭaja, dārvī, and abda— destroys diseases characterized by itching (kaṇḍūmaya).
One who resorts to heat [therapies] should drink bākucī with lukewarm water.
One who eats only milk for three weeks is liberated from the disease of leprosy (kuṣṭha).
Eḍagaja, tila, mustard, kuṣṭha, māgadhikā, and the two types of salt, when prepared with sour gruel and fermented liquid (pūti), destroy ringworm, eczema,
and leprosy within three days.
Having cooked bhallātaka, dvīpī, sudhā, the root of arka, guñjā fruit, tryūṣaṇa, powdered conch-shell, tuttha, kuṣṭha, the five salts, the two types of alkali (kṣāra),
and lāṅgalikā in the milky sap of snuhī and arka, one should place the thickened mass in an iron vessel and apply it as a paste with a probe.
In cases of leprosy (kuṣṭha), vitiligo (kilāsa), freckles (tilakālaka), all types of malignant growths (durnāman), and warts (carmakīla), one should use poison,
varuṇa, turmeric (haridrā), leadwort (citraka), soot (agāradhūma), fire (anal), black pepper (marica), dūrvā grass, milk, arka, and snuhī.
It burns away all varieties of leprosy as soon as it is applied,
like the thunderbolt released from the hand of an enraged Śakra.
[This is prepared] with triphalā, paṭola, rajanī, mañjiṣṭhā, rohiṇī, vacā, and nimba.
This decoction, when practiced regularly, destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha) born of kapha and pitta.
Alternatively, one may consume the fresh juice of *chinnā* according to one's strength; once it is digested, one should eat with ghee, along with a small amount of vegetable broth or water.
Even a man whose body is excessively putrid shall become possessed of a divine form.
One who eats bitter food should drink a decoction of *paṭola*, *khadira*, *ariṣṭa*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and black cane; by this, a leper removes his leprosy.
Sesame, clarified butter, the three myrobalans, honey, the three pungents (vyoṣa), bhallātaka, and sugar—
this "sevenfold" preparation is aphrodisiac, promotes intelligence, cures skin diseases, and is suitable for those who indulge in their desires.
Powdered viḍaṅga, the three myrobalans, and long pepper, licked with honey, [is likewise beneficial].

Having ascertained the movement of the *doṣas*, the physician should administer either cooling or hot food and drinks in cases of *śītapitta*, according to the specific *doṣa* involved.
(14) Chapter 53.

After emesis, one should administer mild purgation there; once the patient has been properly vomited and purged and is well-lubricated, an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) and a decoction enema (āsthāpana) should be given for a long-standing condition, taking into account the nature of the doshas and other factors.

For one whose digestive fire has been purified, a pacifying treatment should be administered; however, depending on the sequence of factors such as the underlying cause and associated conditions, a medicinal formulation of food and drugs must be prepared to address any residual morbid humors.
The wise physician should eliminate upward-moving disorders with emetics and downward-moving disorders with purgatives.
One should prepare food and drink that are predominantly bitter.
One should consume preparations of barley and wheat devoid of pungent seasonings,
or drink parched grain flour or barley meal mixed with sugar and honey according to one's constitution.

A decoction of dehusked barley, vṛṣa, and dhātrī, mixed with the three aromatics (trisaugandhya), honey, and sugar, when drunk while eating with mung bean soup, removes acid bile (amlapitta) and destroys phlegm-bile disorders,
vomiting, itching, fever, eruptions, and burning sensations.
A decoction of *śṛṅgavera* (ginger) and *paṭola* is digestive and appetizing.
Having boiled *paṭola*, *nāgara* (ginger), and *dhānya* (coriander) together, one should drink the water;
it destroys itching, skin eruptions, and severe colic, and overcomes phlegm, bile, and weak digestion.

One should drink water prepared with *paṭola*, *nimba*, *amṛtā*, and *rohiṇī* when there is an excess of *pitta* and *kapha*; for that indeed wards off colic, vertigo, anorexia, low digestive fire, burning sensations, fever, and vomiting.
One should drink a decoction of *yava*, *kṛṣṇā*, and *paṭola* mixed with honey.
It destroys acid bile (amlapitta), as well as loss of appetite and vomiting. A decoction made from vāsā, amṛtā, parpaṭaka, nimba, bhūnimba,
mārkava, triphalā, and kulaka, taken with honey, cures acid bile.
A bitter decoction of the three fruits (triphalā), paṭola, and klītaka, mixed with sugar and honey,
when drunk, destroys fever, vomiting, and acid bile (amlapitta). A preparation combined with vāsā, nimba, paṭola, triphalā, asana, and yāsa conquers [fever].
Guggulu administered in the prescribed sequence [is beneficial] for excessive kapha and acid pitta;
or alternatively, water boiled with chinnā, khadira, yaṣṭīmadhu, and dāru, mixed with honey;
or one should eat abhayā together with grapes, honey, and jaggery.
A linctus of *kaṭukā* and sugar, or *paṭola* and *viśva* combined with honey, should be used;
and for the discharge of blood, *khaṇḍa* and *kūṣmāṇḍaka* are excellent when applied appropriately.
One should drink *paṭola*, *triphalā*, and *ariṣṭa* boiled together and mixed with honey.
For the pacification of fever caused by *pitta* and *kapha*, vomiting, burning sensations, and skin disorders, one should drink a decoction of *siṃhāsya*, *amṛta*, and *bhaṇṭākī* mixed with honey;
thereby a person conquers *amlapitta*, cough, dyspnea, fever, and vomiting. (15–16)
One should skillfully consume Vāsā-ghṛta or Tikta-ghṛta, or lick Māgadhikā mixed with plenty of honey; or whatever other ghee possesses such qualities will pacify the aggravated Amlapitta.
One part of Pañcanimba and double that amount of Vṛddhadāraka [should be used].
Ten times the amount of parched grain flour (saktu), sweetened with sugar, should be given;
when drunk with cold water, it destroys colic arising from pitta and kapha.
This powder, taken with honey, also overcomes even the most difficult acid bile (amlapitta).
Having ground ajājī (cumin) together with dhānyāka (coriander), one should cook it with one prastha of ghee;
this cures kapha, pitta, and anorexia, and overcomes weak digestion and vomiting.
[This may be prepared] with the pastes of paṭola and śuṇṭhī, or with kulaka alone.
One *prastha* of ghee should be cooked [with the aforementioned ingredients] to effectively eliminate *kapha* and *pitta*.
Having risen in the morning, one should drink ghee prepared with a decoction and paste of *pippalī*, mixed profusely with honey, for the cessation of *amlapitta*.
One should cook ghee with a paste made of grapes, amṛtā, śakrapaṭola leaves, uśīra, dhātrī, ghanasāra, candana,
trāyantikā, padmaka, kirātatiktaka, and dhānya. The physician should administer this in appropriate doses along with meals, or prescribe it for drinking during all seasons.

This ghee, when properly administered, quickly destroys aggravated vāta-sthāpitta, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), cough, loss of digestive fire, fever, and acid dyspepsia (amlapitta); indeed, it is like nectar.
[One should prepare this] with a paste of śatāvarī root, one prastha of ghee, and an equal amount of milk.
One should cook it properly over a mild fire, having added four times as much milk.
It destroys acid bile (amlapitta) and diseases arising from wind and bile (vātapitta),
as well as hemorrhagic fever (raktapitta), thirst, fainting, dyspnea, and burning heat.
In cases of amlapitta, a regimen that alleviates kapha and pitta should be employed,
as well as jaggery-pumpkin preparation and sugar-āmalakī. In this condition, one should also administer ghee prepared with jaggery, milk, and kaṇā.
A bolus (modaka) prepared with equal parts of jaggery, long pepper (pippalī), and chebulic myrobalan (pathyā) is said to remove pitta and kapha, and it kindles even a sluggish digestive fire.
This is especially for one suffering from sour bile (amlapitta) who feels as though his very self is ablaze.
Purification is wholesome for that [condition]; there is no pacification without purification.
Whether it has arisen recently or long ago, one should administer emesis in that case.
(Adhikāra 54)

One should treat the types of visarpa according to the specific dosha involved by means of purgation, emesis, ointments, affusions, and bloodletting, using non-burning (avidāhin) remedies such as paṭola,
picumanda, pippalī, and madana.

In cases of visarpa (erysipelas), emesis is recommended, as well as [the use of] indrayava. Ghee combined with the juice of triphalā and trivṛt should be administered for the purpose of purgation to pacify visarpa and fever.
Or one should administer the juice of āmalaka fruits mixed with ghee.
In cases of visarpa caused by vāta, the four groups of the five roots (pañcamūla) should be applied, excluding the grasses, along with ointments, affusions, and medicated ghees.

Kuṣṭha, śatāhvā, suradāru, mustā, vārāhī, kustumburu, kṛṣṇagandhā, arka, vaṃśa, and ārtagala should be employed in affusions, ointments, and likewise in medicated ghees for [the treatment of] vāta. [These are to be used with] prapauṇḍarīka, mañjiṣṭhā, padmaka, uśīra, and candana.
In cases of Pitta-type visarpa, an external application (pralepana) made of liquorice and blue lotuses ground with milk should be applied.

Furthermore, for Pitta-induced visarpa, very cold pastes consisting of kaśeru, śṛṅgāṭaka, padma, gundrā, śaivala, and utpala-kardama, mixed with ghee and placed between layers of cloth, should be applied.
Plasters and affusions made with the five barks (*pañcavalkala*),
or with *padmaka*, *uśīra*, *madhuka*, and *candana*, are recommended. In the case of Pitta-type [fever], however, *śaṅkha* and *śaivala* ground with the mud of a lotus pond is praised.
Either the root of *gundra*, or oyster shell, or red ochre, mixed with clarified butter;
or the roots of *nyagrodha*, *gundra*, and the inner core of a plantain tree,
together with a knot of lotus fiber— this should be used as a plaster soaked in clarified butter that has been washed a hundred times.
Hareṇu, masūra, mudga, and śāli rice—
each of these individually, or all together with clarified butter, should be used as a paste.
[Likewise, one may use] drākṣā, āragvadha, kāśmarya, triphalā, maṇḍa, and pīlu.
Purification with *trivṛt* and *harītakī* is beneficial for visarpa.
For visarpa arising from phlegm (*śleṣman*), an ointment made of *gāyatrī*, *saptaparṇa*, *aragvadha*, *vāsā*, *āragvadha*, *dāru*, and *kuṭannaṭa* should be applied. (12–13)

A paste made from aja, aśvagandhā, saralā, kālā, saikeṣikā, and ajaśṛṅgī, ground with cow’s urine and applied as a poultice after removing the husks of grain, very quickly destroys erysipelas caused by kapha. (14) Madana, madhuka, nimba, and the fruits of vatsaka [are also used].
Emesis should be administered in cases of visarpa arising from kapha.
A paste composed of triphalā, padmaka, uśīra, samaṅgā, karavīra, the root of nala, and anantā destroys kaphaja visarpa.

The leaves of *āragvadha*, the bark from *śleṣmātaka*, and *śirīṣa* flowers, when applied as a paste or used for dusting, are beneficial for those afflicted by desire. A decoction of *mustā*, *ariṣṭa*, and *paṭola* destroys all types of erysipelas (*visarpa*).

Alternatively, [a preparation] of *dhātrī*, *paṭola*, and *mudga* combined with clarified butter [is effective]. Or, a decoction of *amṛtavṛṣa*, *paṭola*, and *nimba* mixed with the pastes of *triphalā* and the heartwood of *khadira*, along with an equal amount of *vyādhighāta*, boiled together and combined with a portion of *guggulu*, conquers all forms of poison and erysipelas (*visarpa*), as well as the eighteen types of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*).

Amṛtavṛṣa, paṭola, mustaka, saptaparṇa, khadira, asitavetra, nimba leaves, and the two types of haridrā remove various poisons, visarpa, kuṣṭha, visphoṭaka, and itching, as well as masūrī, śītapitta, and fever. (20) Chapter 55.
A decoction made from *paṭola*, *amṛta*, *bhūnimba*, *vāsaka*, *ariṣṭa*, *parpaṭa*, *khadira*, and *abdayuta* (musta) removes the pain of eruptive boils (*visphoṭa*) and fever.
[1] A decoction made from *paṭola*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *ariṣṭa*, *guḍūcī*, *musta*, and *candana* [is likewise effective].
One should cause this decoction— consisting of *samūrvā*, *rohiṇī*, *pāṭhā*, *rajanī*, and *durālabhā*— to be drunk; it removes fever caused by *kapha* and *pitta*,
and destroys itching, skin disorders, eruptions, poison, and erysipelas (*vīsarpa*).
A decoction prepared with bhūnimba, vāsā, kaṭukā, paṭola, triphalā, candana, and nimba cures erysipelas,
burning sensations, fever, dryness of the mouth, eruptions, thirst, vomiting, and nausea.
When pitta is associated with kapha, one should add triphalā and purging drugs.
One should drink either *durālabhā*, *parpaṭaka*, *paṭola*, and *kaṭukā* with warm water mixed with *guggulu*, or the *khadirāṣṭaka* decoction;
or else water boiled with *kuṇḍalī* and *picumanda*, or water boiled with *khadira* and *indrayava*.
It quickly destroys the eruptions, just as the wind disperses the clouds.
Sandalwood, nāgapuṣpa, taṇḍulīyaka, sārivā, the bark of śirīṣa, and jasmine— this ointment shall be a destroyer of burning sensations.
Equal parts of *śukataruṇa*, *tamāla*, *māṃsī*, *rajanī*, and *padma* should be ground with cold water; this ointment is effective for all types of eruptive boils (*visphoṭa*).
[9] *Śirīṣa* root, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *cavyā*, *āmalaka*, and *yaṣṭikā*—[these should be used]. [10]
Gargles consisting of the tender leaves of *sajātī* and honey are beneficial for eruptive boils (*visphoṭa*).
*Śirīṣa*, *udumbara*, and *jambū* are suitable for sprinkling and as external plasters; likewise, the bark of *śleṣmātaka* is beneficial when used as a paste or for eye-drops (*añjana*).

An ointment consisting of ten ingredients— śirīṣa, yaṣṭī, nata, candana, elā, māṃsī, the two types of haridrā, kuṣṭha, and vāla— mixed with ghee, is prescribed as a remedy that removes visarpa, kuṣṭha, graha, and consumption.
Through the application of an ointment made from śirīṣa, uśīra, nāgāṅka, hiṃsrā, and bhallātaka, [the affliction] is quickly [removed].
Visarpa, poison, and eruptive boils are undoubtedly pacified.

This fresh ghee, quickly cooked with the decoction and paste of the leaves of vṛṣa, khadira, paṭola, and nimba, along with the bark and amṛtā and āmalakī, conquers visarpa, intoxication, blood disorders, skin diseases, and abdominal tumors.

Ghee cooked with *paṭola*, *saptacchada*, *nimba*, *vāsā*, *phalatrika*, and *chinnaruhā*— this "Five Bitter" (*pañcatikta*) ghee quickly destroys the itching of eruptions, erysipelas, and skin diseases caused by the three *doṣas*.
When the *doṣa* is aggravated in the limbs, it produces swelling similar to erysipelas.

Having thus pierced it, once the wound has formed there, the heat (uṣman) dries up the flesh and creates a thread-like cord. This [cord] should be removed gradually with boluses made of buttermilk and barley meal; otherwise, from the tearing, it may lead to an aggravation of the disease.
From its falling away, there is subsidence of the swelling, but it may recur in another location; this is known as *snāyuka*, and its treatment is said to be like that of *visarpa*.
Having drunk cow’s ghee for three days, one should then drink the fresh juice of *nirguṇḍī* for three days.
Having drunk this extremely potent [remedy], one certainly kills the *snāyuka* [disease]; of this there is no doubt.

An ointment made from the roots and leaves of *saubhāñjana*, ground with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) and mixed with salt, destroys the disease of *snāyuka*; or else, an ointment made from the bark of the *moca* tree [effects the same].
Chapter 56:
For all [types of poisoning], emesis should first be induced using decoctions of *paṭola*, *ariṣṭa*, and *vāsaka*, along with a paste made from *vacā*, *vatsaka*, and *yaṣṭyāhvaphala*.
One should cause the patient to drink the juice of *brāhmī* with honey, or the juice of *hailamocikā*.
Once he has vomited, a purgative should be administered; however, for a weak man, a palliative treatment should be given.
[One may also give] the exudate of *suṣavī* leaves combined with the powder of *haridrā*.
One should drink [this] for the pacification of horripilation, fever, eruptions, and smallpox (masūrī).
For one whose morbid humors have been removed by both [methods], the masūrikā eruptions become purified;
they appear without deformity, with little pus, and suppurate with little pain.
The root of *kaṇṭākī*, sweetened with sugar and prepared by boiling, taken with a single *māṣa* of asafoetida;

or the seed of *jayā* drunk with ghee; or the foot of *śakaṭī* that has been soaked; or the root of *pathyā*, or its fibrous stalk (*śiphā*), born from the flower of *damanaka*, mixed with pungent spices (*uṣaṇa*) or even putrid substances—[these are used for the purpose].
When a disease caused by the sins of previous lives first appears, these medicinal applications should be employed.
Incense made from *ugrā*, ghee, bamboo, indigo, barley, poison, cotton, bone, *brāhmī*, *surasā*, *mayūraka*, and lac removes itching and other such ailments.
If administered at the very outset, the *masūrikā* eruptions are pacified;
some do not even take up the poison here, according to the scriptural injunctions as they may be obtained.
On the first day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, one should place a *snuhī* plant together with a red flag at the house.
A vessel placed upon a white-painted pinnacle wards off the affliction of sin from afar.
For a disease born of wind (vāta), one should first perform a libation with parched grain flour mixed with sugar;
as for the meal, it should consist of bitter soups or the meat broth of gallinaceous birds.
The two groups of five roots (dvipañcamūla), rāsnā, dāru, uśīra, durālabhā, amṛtā, dhānyaka, and musta shall conquer [the fever] arisen from vāta.
[Likewise, it is conquered] by drākṣā, kāśmarya, kharjūra, paṭola, ariṣṭa, and vāsaka.
In the case of Pitta-type [visarpa], a plaster made of parched grain, āmalaka, and dūsparśa, combined with sugar, should be used.
A plaster consisting of śirīṣa, udumbara, aśvattha, śelu, nyagrodha, and vatsaka, mixed with ghee, quickly destroys the burning sensation of wounds and visarpa.
One should administer *durālabhā*, *parpaṭaka*, *bhūnimba*, and *kaṭurohiṇī* as a decoction for drinking in cases of fever born of *kapha* or *pitta*.
[Likewise, one may give] *nimba*, *parpaṭaka*, *pāṭhā*, *paṭola*, and *kaṭurohiṇī*.
Vāsā, durālabhā, dhātrī, uśīra, and the two types of candana—
this decoction of the nimbādi group, when drunk with sugar,
destroys masūrikā caused by the three doṣas and arising from fever or visarpa.
If she who has risen should enter again, one should lead her back outside once more.
Water boiled with paṭola, kuṇḍalī, mustā, vṛṣa, dhanvayavāsaka, bhūnimba, nimba, kaṭukā, and parpaṭa [should be administered]. (15–16)
It pacifies *masūrī* when unripe and purifies it when ripe; there is nothing superior to this for the alleviation of eruptive boils and fever.
One should drink the root of *paṭola* and red *taṇḍulīyaka* combined with a paste of *haridrā* and *āmalaka*.

For the pacification of the burning sensation caused by *masūri* eruptions, as well as for removing horripilation, vomiting, and fever—one should drink water that has been well-decocted with the roots of *paṭola*, red *taṇḍulīyaka*, and likewise *dhātrī* combined with *khadira*, and then cooled thoroughly; this is the supreme destroyer of the disease of *masūrikā*. 18–19.
The decoction known as Aṣṭaka, prepared from khadira, triphalā, ariṣṭa, paṭola, amṛta, and vāsaka, conquers measles and smallpox,
as well as skin diseases, erysipelas, boils, itching, and other ailments when consumed.
A decoction of *amṛtā* and other herbs, however, conquers that which is composed of *pitta* and *kapha*.
The filaments of *mātuluṅga*, ground with *sauvīra* vinegar, quickly cause suppuration through application as a paste and also pacify burning sensations.
A carbuncle arising on the foot causes a burning sensation in the foot;
in that case, they highly recommend frequent sprinkling with rice-water.
However, at the time of suppuration, the wind dries up all of them.

Therefore, nourishing therapy should be performed, and not a wholesome regimen that causes drying. At the time of cooking, medicinal ingredients such as *guḍūcī*, *madhuka*, grapes, *moraṭa*, and pomegranates, combined with jaggery, should be added.
By this means, [the humors] quickly reach the state of maturation, yet the wind (vāyu) does not become aggravated.
Or, for the purpose of ripening, one should lick jujube (bādara) powder with molasses; by this, those [diseases] consisting of wind, bile, and phlegm are quickly matured.
For one afflicted by colic and flatulence, and trembling due to the bodily wind (vāyu),
the juices of desert meat are recommended, mixed with a small amount of rock salt (saindhava).
Soups prepared with the sour juices of pomegranate are beneficial for those suffering from loss of appetite.
Spreading, accompanied by eruptions, moist, and exuding discharge—

such [a wound] is pacified when dusted with the powder of the ten-ingredient paste (daśāṅgalepa). One should drink water that has been heated and then cooled, having been infused with khadira and asana.
For purification, one should employ water produced by reciting the Gāyatrī many times.
[One should also use] Jātī leaves, mañjiṣṭhā, dārvī, betel nut, and śamī;
these, along with āmalaka fruit and madhuka, should be boiled and mixed with honey.
In diseases of the mouth and diseases of the throat, it is recommended for use as a gargle.
They praise the irrigation of the eyes with water decocted from *gavedhu*, *madhuka*, *madhuka*, *triphalā*, *mūrvā*, the bark of *dārvī*, and blue lotus (*nīlotpala*). (32–33)
Pastes of uśīra, lodhra, and mañjiṣṭhā are beneficial for use as an ointment or an eye-drop;
by this means, disorders of vision are destroyed and cataracts (masūrya) do not arise.
One should dust a moistened area with the powder of the five barks (pañcavalkala).
Some desire [to cover] with ashes, others with cow-dung dust;

and out of fear of the falling of insects, one should fumigate with sarala and other woods for the sake of pacifying pain and burning sensations, and for the purification of those [wounds] that have exuded.
One should administer a decoction of Varā with guggulu, or the Khadirāṣṭaka formulation.
For the purification of the throat, one should lick the powder of Kṛṣṇā and Abhayā with honey;
likewise, the Aṣṭāṅga electuary or gargles made from ginger and other ingredients may be used.
One should employ the "five-bitter" (pañcatikta) formulation through drinks, ointments, and food;

one should also perform the treatment for ulcers and avoid oils and similar substances for a long time. [The bark of] nimba, atimuktaka, kāsphota, bimbī, and vetasa— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with the list of medicinal plants.]
That which has been boiled and then cooled should always be used for draining and washing wounds.

An external application (pradeha) made with the two types of niśā, uśīra, śirīṣa, mustaka, lodhra, bhadraśrī, and nāgakeśara removes excessive sweating, eruptive boils, erysipelas, skin diseases, foul odors, and hair loss.
Chapter 57:
Likewise, one should treat ajagallikā and māṃsārbuda with leeches, and one should repeatedly apply a paste made from the ashes (kṣāra) of oyster shells and saurāṣṭrī. || 1 ||

The physician should treat *anuśayī*, *vivṛtā*, *indravṛddhā*, *gardabhī*, *jālagardabhī*, *irivellī*, and *gandhanāmā* according to the procedure for phlegmatic abscess (*śleṣmavidradhi*); one should treat them like a bile-type erysipelas (*pittavisarpa*).
One should heal the ulcer with ghee prepared with sweet medicinal herbs.
One should conquer Vidārikā by means of numerous bloodlettings, fomentations, depletions, and plasters made from Śigru and Devadruma.
By this same method, the physician should treat *panasikā*, *kacchapikā*,
and other hard swellings arising from the humors (*doṣa*).
Likewise, [one should treat] *andhrālajī*, *kacchapikā*, and *pāṣāṇagardabha*.
Having fomented [the area] with *suradāru*, *śilājatu*, and *kuṣṭha*, one should apply a plaster.
This plaster destroys phlegm, wind, and swelling in the case of *pāṣāṇagardabha*.
For *pāṇḍuraṅga*, there should be a plaster and the letting out of blood.
Having excised the anthill with a surgical instrument, one should treat it with alkaline and thermal cauterization,
using realgar, *bhallātaka*, small cardamom, agallochum, sandalwood,
jasmine buds, and *vakra*. One should also cook neem oil with these ingredients.
For that indeed destroys the anthill, which has many openings and much exudation.
In cases of cracking feet (pādadārī), one should pierce the vein that cleanses the sole; furthermore, the feet, having been treated with oleation and sudation, should be repeatedly anointed.
With beeswax, fat, marrow, ghee, and milk mixed together, and having churned the powder of *sarja* and rock salt combined with honey and ghee, it is smeared with pungent oil;
this foot-cleansing application is beneficial. (10–11)

Oil cooked in an alkaline solution made from *upodakā*, mustard, *nimba*, *moca*, *karkāruka*, and *ervāruka*, combined with a portion of salt, destroys *pādadārī* (cracking of the feet) when applied as an ointment.
In the case of *alasa*, one should sprinkle the feet with sour liquids for a long time and then apply an ointment.
With *paṭola*, *ariṣṭaka*, *kāsīsa*, and *triphalā* used repeatedly;
or with *karañja* seeds, *rajanī*, *kāsīsa*, *madhuka*, honey, *rocanā*, and *haritāla*— this ointment is beneficial for those suffering from alasa.
An application of lac, chebulic myrobalan, and *rasāñjana* should be made, or bloodletting should be performed.
Having anointed [the area] with oil prepared with the juice of *bṛhatī*, the wise physician should rub it with the powders of realgar, yellow orpiment, and *kāsīsa*.

One should extract the *kadara* and cauterize it with oil or fire; or, having fomented it with hot water, one should extract it, apply an ointment to the wound, and after applying a powder of *sārjarasa*, bandage it and treat it like a common ulcer. || 17 ||
Having ground *abhayā* with the natural juice of turmeric in a black iron vessel, one should repeatedly smear the ulcer with the resulting paste.
Emesis induced with neem water is beneficial for *padminī-kaṇṭaka*. (18–19)
Clarified butter prepared with nimba water and mixed with honey is recommended for drinking;
alternatively, frequent rubbing with a paste of nimba and āragvadha is beneficial.
In the case of ahipūtana, one should first purify the breast milk of the mother.
Washing wounds with decoctions of triphalā and khadira is beneficial.
Ghee prepared with karañja, triphalā, and tiktas is beneficial for an infant;
rasāñjana, in particular, is beneficial both when drunk and as an external application.

In the case of a prolapse of the rectum (gudabhraṃśa), one should quickly lubricate the rectum with unctuous substances and push it back in; once it has entered, if it remains constricted, one should apply intense fomentation using a cow's dewlap.
One who eats tender lotus leaves mixed with sugar [is also benefited].
Having determined this, it is prescribed that there is no discharge from the anus [in this case].
One suffering from prolapse of the rectum should regularly consume vṛkṣāmla, anala, cāṅgerī, viśva, pāṭhā, and barley sprouts with buttermilk; this kindles the digestive fire.
One should, without hesitation, smear the anus with cow’s fat;
the prolapse of the rectum, which is difficult to re-enter, will undoubtedly enter back in quickly.
Alternatively, one may apply a thorough ointment to the anus using the fats of mice.
Alternatively, one should apply fomentation to the prolapsed rectum using well-steamed rat meat.
Ghee boiled with cāṅgerī, kola, sour curd, ginger, and alkali should be drunk; this cures the pain of rectal prolapse.
Having boiled the great five roots (mahat-pañcamūla) and a female rat that has been freed from its mantra in milk, one should cook oil in that [milk] combined with wind-alleviating herbs.
This oil cures prolapse of the rectum through drinking and massage. || 29 ||

In the case of *parivartikā*, one should apply fomentation and poultices, then anoint it with ghee, and subsequently insert the skin flap slowly; once it has entered, one should apply a warm poultice of flesh.
One should treat *avapāṭikā* in the same manner with oleation and sudation therapies.
Having excised with a surgical instrument cutaneous warts, sebaceous cysts, moles, freckles, and dark spots, one should cauterize them completely with alkali or fire.
The same applies to pimples of youth, flat moles, blue-black spots, facial blemishes, and pitted skin.
One should conquer [these ailments] with bloodletting, medicinal pastes, and likewise with ointments.
A paste of *lodhra*, *dhānya*, and *vacā* removes pimples of youth;
similarly, black pepper combined with *gorocanā*, when applied as a facial paste, has the same effect.
An ointment made of siddhārthaka, vacā, lodhra, and saindhava,
along with emesis, quickly destroys pimples arising from youth (35).
For facial freckles (vyaṅga), either the bark of arjuna or mañjiṣṭhā mixed with honey [should be applied].
A plaster of fresh butter, or soot produced from the hooves of a white horse,
[is used for the face]. Red sandalwood, mañjiṣṭhā, kuṣṭha, lodhra, priyaṅgu, banyan sprouts, and lentils destroy freckles and bestow beauty upon the face.

An ointment for those with impaired limbs is recommended using either the blood of a rabbit or the sharp thorns of the *śālmali* tree ground with milk alone; by being smeared with this for three days, the face becomes like a lotus. (38)
If the face is smeared with *masūra* seeds ground with ghee and mixed with milk,
after seven nights it becomes as radiant as the petal of a white lotus. [Likewise,] the root of a *mātuluṅga*, ghee, realgar, and the juice of cow dung [achieve the same].
This ointment produces a radiant complexion and conquers pustules, moles, and freckles. Indeed,
a face smeared with kālīyaka, blue lotus, āmaya, the cream of curd, the pith of jujube stones, and phalinī becomes as brilliant as the moon within seven nights.

A face anointed with a preparation prepared from *rakṣoghna*, the two types of *śarvarī*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, red ochre (*gairika*), clarified butter, and goat’s milk, shines like the rising orb of the autumnal moon.
[42] With *pariṇatadadhi*, *śarapuṅkha*, blue lotus petals, *kuṣṭha*, sandalwood, and *uśīra*...
With rays that enhance the beauty of her lotus-face, she conquers the decorative mark of the frown.
[She is adorned] with two types of turmeric, licorice, kālīyaka, and kuca-candana;
with prapauṇḍarīka, mañjiṣṭhā, padma, padmaka, and saffron. || 43–44 ||
One should apply a plaster made from the leaves of *kapittha*, *tinduka*, *plakṣa*, and *vaṭa* mixed with milk, or one should cook an ointment oil with these same ingredients as a paste.
This cures moles (*piplu*), dark spots (*nīlikā*), freckles (*vyaṅga*), and unsightly marks on the face (*tilaka*).
One who uses this constantly will quickly conquer [the disease] and make the face beautiful.
One should cook one *kuḍava* of oil with a decoction of *madhuka* and the pastes of *priyaṅgu*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, sandalwood, blue lotus, and *kesara*.
The oil known as Kanaka is supreme for producing radiance on the face; it is highly esteemed for cleansing the skin of eruptions, dark spots, and freckles.
[Its ingredients are: mañjiṣṭhā, madhuka, lākṣā, mātuluṅga, and yaṣṭikā.
With these [ingredients] measuring one *karṣa* each,
along with one *kuḍava* of oil and double the amount of goat's milk, one should cook it slowly over a mild fire;
by mere massage, it destroys dark spots, pustules, and facial freckles.
The face becomes serene, full, and free from the blueness and roughness [of old age];
through application for seven nights, it becomes like gold. [The ingredients are:
saffron, sandalwood, lac, madder, and liquorice.
Kālīyaka, uśīra, padmaka, and blue utpala; the roots of nyagrodha, the shoots of plakṣa, and the filaments of the lotus— each of these,
together with the two sets of five roots (the daśamūla), [should be prepared] as decoctions in portions of one pala each.
One *āḍhaka* of water should be boiled down until one-fourth remains; then,
one should cook one *kuḍava* of oil with one *karṣa* each of *mañjiṣṭhā*, *madhuka*, *lākṣā*, *pattāṅga*, and *madhuyaṣṭikā*.
One should slowly cook that [oil] with twice as much goat’s milk over a mild fire.
When properly cooked, this is indeed excellent for clarifying the complexion of the face;
it destroys dark spots, pustules, and freckles merely by its application as an ointment.

Within seven nights, the face becomes like a lotus through this excellent oil made of saffron and other ingredients, prepared by Vaidehī. In cases of scabies (aruṃṣikā), after blood has been let either by venesection or by leeches, [this oil should be applied].
When the head has been sprinkled with nimba water, an ointment made from horse dung, ghee, and rock salt should be applied.
Alternatively, an ointment consisting of old oil-cake and chicken excrement ground with urine will quickly destroy arūṃṣikā (scaly patches on the scalp).
This oil, prepared with the two types of *haridrā*, *bhūnimba*, *triphalā*, *ariṣṭa*, and *candana*, is beneficial when used as an ointment for the cure of *aruṃṣī*.
However, in the case of *dāruṇa* [arūṃṣī], one should perform venesection on a vein located on the forehead after the patient has been treated with oleation and sudation.
One should administer nasal compresses (avapīḍa), head-poultices (śirobasti), and massages (abhyaṅga). For washing the head, one should use water mixed with the alkaline ash of *kodrava* straw.
[The head should be rubbed] with a mixture of *priyāla* seeds, *madhuka*, and *kuṣṭha*, combined with rock salt (*saindhava*).

In cases of *dāruṇaka*, an application mixed with honey should be made upon the head. Oil boiled with *mālatī*, *karavīra*, *agni*, and *naktamāla* is recommended for massage; it is an excellent remedy for curing *indralupta*.
For this [mixture] certainly and swiftly destroys the terrible [poison] of men:
the milk of the *snuhī* plant, the milk of the *arka*, *mārkava*, *lāṅgalī*, and *viṣa*; goat's urine with cow's urine, *raktikā*, and *indravāruṇī*. (64–65)
One should cook *siddhārtha* (white mustard) with sharp oil (*tīkṣṇataila*), adding the embryo [of the plant] and heating it over a gentle fire; this cooked oil destroys baldness (*khālitya*).
Even that which is as hard as the back of a tortoise grows [hair], and it restores hair that has been stolen away.
She would become smeared by him like a hairy female bear;
[to treat this], one should cook oil with triphalā, iron powder, māṃsī, mārkava, utpala, sārivā, and rock salt; anointing with this will conquer arūṃṣikā.
Having ground into a paste *citraka*, the root of *danti*, and *kośātaki*, one should cook oil that destroys the enemies of the hair.
Oil boiled with *guñjā* fruits and the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* [is likewise effective].

This oil, prepared with *bhṛṅgarāja*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), blue lotus (*utpala*), *sāri*, iron filings, and cow dung, destroys itching, skin diseases, heart ailments, and ailments of the skull;
it removes harshness and makes the hair curly, thick, and firm.

One kuḍava of oil should be prepared with one karṣa each of prapauṇḍarīka, madhuka, pippalī, candana, and utpala, along with twice that amount of āmalaka juice; this constitutes a pratimarśa that cures all diseases of the head.

In cases of Indralupta (alopecia), one should pierce the veins and apply a paste made of śilāja, kāsīsa, and tutthaka all around; furthermore, an oil prepared with kuṭannaṭa, śikhī, jātī, karañja, and karavīraka is beneficial for massage.
Alternatively, having repeatedly applied a paste that has penetrated deeply,
one should smear the entire scalp for a long time with the roots of *guñjā*.
This ointment, consisting of the juice of *bṛhatī* mixed with honey, removes *indralupta* (alopecia).

The root and fruit of *guñjā* ground with the juice of *bṛhatī* fruit should always be applied to one suffering from *indralupta* (alopecia) after it has been rubbed with gold and prepared for treatment.
By applying a paste of *madhuka*, *indīvara*, *mūrvā*, sesame, clarified butter, cow’s milk, and *bhṛṅgarāja*, [hair grows].
Soon the hair becomes thick, firm-rooted, long, and straight.
Oil cooked in the sun with the powder of *vaṭāvaroha* and *keśinī*, along with the fresh juice of *guḍūcī*, causes the growth of hair when used as an anointing massage.
Candana, madhuka, mūrvā, triphalā, blue utpala, kāntā, the aerial root of the vaṭa tree, guḍūcī, and lotus stalk;
likewise iron powder, keśī, and the two types of sārivā. || 80 ||
One should cook oil with the juice of *mārkaava* over a gentle fire.
By this, hair that has fallen out on the head grows back thick,
curly, firmly rooted, glossy, and resembling the color of a bee.
This excellent oil destroys premature graying when used as a nasal drop (nasya).
Oil boiled with yaṣṭīmadhuka, milk, and āmalaka fruits,
when administered as a nasal drop, produces hair or even facial hair.
Having prepared ink from elephant tusks and the finest *rasāñjana*, hair grows even on the palms of the hands by means of this application.
[Likewise,] *triphalā*, *nīlinī* leaves, iron, and *bhṛṅgarāja* in equal parts [are used].

Combined with sheep’s urine, this is the supreme means for blackening. One should add iron powder mixed with the powder of the three myrobalans (triphalā) into a slightly ripened coconut filled with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*.
Having left it for one month, he should properly extract it from the womb. Then, having shaved the head and applied an ointment, the excellent physician,
having wrapped it with plantain leaves, should release it on the seventh day.
One who eats milk and meat broth should wash [the head] with decoctions of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*);
this is a supreme method for coloring the skull and turning it black.
One should bury blue lotus (*utpala*) together with milk in the ground for one month.
The blackening and nourishing of the hair is prescribed [as follows]:

by using the paste of iron rust (*lohamala*) and *āmalaka* fruit together with *japā* flowers, a man who bathes regularly here shall not see gray hairs, just as one who bathes in the Gaṅgā does not see the hells.

The seeds of *nimba* and *āsana*, processed with the juice of *bhṛṅga*, along with their oil, when administered as nasal drops (nasya) by one who consumes milk and rice, destroy gray hair along with its very roots.
Alternatively, pure *nimba* oil may be used for nasal administration according to the prescribed ritual.

For a man who subsists on milk for one month, this destroys gray hair, the foremost messenger of old age. (93) Two *prasthas* of milk, one *prastha* of the juice of the excellent *mārka* plant, one *pala* of *madhuka*, and one *kuḍava* of oil—when cooked together, this nasal medication (*nasya*) removes gray hair. (94)
This ointment, made from *kāsīsa*, *rocanā*, *tuttha*, *haritāla*, and *rasāñjana* ground with acidic liquids, cures scabies and snake-bite.
[95] [Oil] boiled with *paṭola* leaves, *triphalā*, and *rasāñjana*...
Drinking clarified butter destroys even severe *ahipūtana*.
Equal parts of *rajanī* and the root of *mārkava*, ground with cold water and applied as a paste, destroy the terrible *visarpa* known as *varāhadaśana*.
Chapter 58:
In the case of inflammation of the lips caused by Vāta, one should apply a poultice (upanāhana) with Sālvaṇa;
likewise, oil boiled with Vāta-alleviating drugs should be used for both cerebral application (mastishka) and nasal medication (nasya).
Fomentation, oil massage, the internal administration of fats (sneha), and the drinking of meat broth are also recommended.
One should apply a powder of śrīveṣṭaka, sarjarasa, guggulu, devadāru, and yaṣṭīmadhuka as a rubbing agent (pratisāraṇa).
In cases where the lower parts are afflicted by pitta, one should employ venesection, emesis, purgation, the drinking of bitter decoctions, a diet of meat broth, cold plasters, and affusions.
In cases arising from pitta, blood, or trauma, one should treat with leeches.
One should perform the entire therapeutic procedure exactly as for a pitta-type abscess (pittavidradhi).

Once blood has been removed, head-purgation (śirovirecana), medicated smoking (dhūma), fomentation (sveda), and gargling (kavaladhāraṇa) should be employed in cases of lip disease caused by phlegm (kaphātma oṣṭhakopa).
The three pungents (trikaṭu), svarjikākṣāra, and the alkali derived from barley awns, combined with honey, should be applied as a rubbing paste (pratisāraṇa).
In cases of tumors arising from fat (medoje), after they have been fomented, incised, and purified, the application of fire (jvalana) is beneficial.
A rubbing with *priyaṅgu*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and *lodhra*, mixed with honey, is beneficial;
likewise, an application of the powder of the three myrobalans combined with honey is wholesome.
In the case of *śītāda* after blood has been removed, [one should apply] ginger and mustard seeds in water.
One should also prepare a decoction of triphalā and hold it as a gargle (gaṇḍūṣa).
A paste should be applied consisting of priyaṅgu, musta, and triphalā.
[The following are also used: kuṣṭha, dārvī, lodhra, abda, samaṅgā, pāṭhā, tiktā, tejinī, and pītikā.
A powder is recommended for rubbing; it destroys bleeding from the gums as well as itching and pain.
(10) For loose teeth, the chewing of *bakula* flowers should be performed to stabilize them.
(11) In the case of a fresh swelling of the gums (*dantapuppuṭaka*), bloodletting should be carried out.
A rubbing (pratisāraṇa) with the five salts, alkali, and honey [is prescribed].
When throbbing and hypersensitivity of the teeth arise due to Vāta,
gargles (kavalagraha) consisting of warm oil, clarified butter (ājya), and decoctions of Vāta-subduing herbs should be used.
One should hold honey mixed with long pepper and ghee in the mouth;
this is declared to be the preeminent medicine for removing toothache.
When the gums have been drained, one should rub the ulcerated area.
For a mouth-rinse (gaṇḍūṣa), the powders of *lodhra*, *pattūra*, *yaṣṭimadhu*, and *lākṣā*, with honey as the predominant ingredient, should be applied;
for a *kṣīrin* [type of ulcer], they should be combined with honey, ghee, and sugar.
However, in the case of *sauṣira* after blood has been extracted, [the powder] should be prepared with *lodhra*, *musta*, and *rasāñjana*.
An application with honey is recommended; for gargles, the milky trees are beneficial. (16) A wise physician should perform the treatment prescribed for Śītāda in the case of Paridara.
(17) In Upakuśa, one should first purify both the body and the head.
The physician should cause drainage with the leaves of *kākodumbarikā* and *gojī*,
and should rub [the area] with salts combined with honey and *vyoṣa*.
Long pepper, mustard, white [mustard], ginger, and the fruit of *naicula* [should be used].
Having mixed it with lukewarm water, one should apply a gargle for him.

Then, in the case of dental abscesses (dantavaidarbha), one should cleanse the roots of the teeth with a surgical instrument; thereafter, one should apply alkali (kṣāra) and all other cooling treatments.
Having extracted the supernumerary tooth, one should then apply fire;
in this case, the wise physician should perform the procedure as in the treatment for caries (krimidantaka).
After excising the excess flesh, one should treat it with these powders mixed with honey.
Pippalī mixed with honey is prescribed as a gargle along with pāṭhā, vacā, tejavatī, svarjikā, and yāvaśūka. Furthermore,
a decoction of paṭola, nimba, and triphalā is recommended for rinsing the mouth.
Head-purgation (śirovireka), as well as purgative smoking (dhūma), are beneficial;
one should perform the treatment for sinus ulcers (nāḍīvraṇa) on the dental canals.
One should extract that tooth upon which the sinus has arisen.
Having cut away the flesh with a surgical instrument, if the growth does not emerge above,
one should cleanse it and then cauterize it with either alkali or fire. For if the jawbone is neglected during the process of extraction, it will cause destruction.
Therefore, one should extract a broken tooth along with its root, as well as a fractured bone.
When an upper tooth is extracted, blood flows profusely;
and due to this excessive loss of blood, the terrible diseases previously mentioned arise.
Therefore, the physician should not extract even a loose upper tooth.
[One should use] a decoction prepared from *jāti*, *madana*, *kaṭuka*, *svādukaṇṭaka*,
*lodhra*, *khadira*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and *yaṣṭyāhva*.
Oil is indeed a purifying agent; for it destroys the disease located in the teeth.
Having prepared a decoction and observed [the condition], one should apply a paste of *lodhra* and other ingredients, as well as *kaṇṭakī*, *madana*, *svādukaṇṭā*, and *vikaṅkata*.
Lukewarm oil-gargles of clarified butter or of *traivṛta* ghee,
decoctions of wind-alleviating herbs that crush tooth-aversion, as well as unctuous smoking and unctuous nasal therapy (*nasya*), are beneficial. (32)
The physician, without injuring the roots of the teeth, should extract the calculus;
thereafter, he should rub the area with powdered lac mixed with honey.
Furthermore, one should perform the treatment for sensitive teeth (danta-harṣa) in its entirety.
The *kapālikā* type is difficult to cure; even in that case, this treatment is beneficial.

One should conquer the immobile *kṛmidanta* (worm-infested tooth) by means of fomentation and bloodletting, as well as by the application of *avapīḍa* drops, Vāta-alleviating [medicines], and the holding of oil gargles (*snehagaṇḍūṣa*).
