The wise physician should administer asafoetida with warm substances, along with emollient foods such as *bhadradāru* and the roots of *varṣābhū*.
A decoction of *bṛhatī*, *bhūmikadamba*, *pañcāṅgula*, and *kaṇṭakārikā* [is also used for worm-inflicted dental disease].

A gargle mixed with oil alleviates the pain of carious teeth (kṛmidanta). Alternatively, having extracted the loose tooth, one should cauterize its socket; then, [one should apply a paste] of vidārī, yaṣṭyāhva, śṛṅgāṭaka, and kaseru.

Oil prepared with ten times its quantity of milk is highly recommended for use as a nasal drop (nasya). In cases of jaw dislocation (hanumokṣa), one should perform the same treatment prescribed for facial paralysis (ardita). Sour fruits, cold water, dry food, and the cleansing of the teeth [are also advised].
Likewise, one suffering from dental disease should avoid very hard foods.
Regarding the treatment for wind-born swelling of the lips that was previously mentioned, that indeed should be administered by the physician for thorns arising from wind.

In cases arising from pitta where [the area] has been rubbed and the vitiated blood has been drained, sweet substances used as a powder for rubbing (pratisāraṇa), gargles (gaṇḍūṣa), and nasal drops (nasya) are beneficial.
In cases of thorny eruptions (kaṇṭaka) arising from kapha, once they have been scraped and the blood has been depleted, [the same treatments apply].
A rubbing (pratisāraṇa) should be performed with the Pippalyādi group mixed with honey;
one should also take a gargle (kavala) made of white mustard and rock salt,
and one should eat food with soups of *paṭola*, *nimba*, and *vārtāka* prepared with alkaline water.
Having scraped the upajihvā (ranula), one should rub it with an alkaline preparation and treat it with head-purgatives, gargles, and medicated smokes.
This powder consisting of the three pungents (vyoṣa), alkali, abhayā, and vahni (citraka) is for rubbing.
One should cook oil with these [drugs] for the purpose of pacifying upajihvā (ranula).
Galashuṇḍikā (uvulitis) arises at the root of the palate from kapha and blood;
having excised it, one should rub the area with a paste of vyōṣa, rock salt, ugrā, and honey.
Galaśuṇḍī is cured by applying an ointment made from Vajrī and milk;
furthermore, the physician should perform friction-massage (pragharṣaṇa) on the galaśuṇḍī using Kuṣṭha, Aruṇā, Vacā, Saindhava, Kṛṣṇā, Pāṭhā, and Plava, mixed with honey. 49.
Having decocted vacā, ativiṣā, pāṭhā, rāsnā, kaṭukarohiṇī, and picumanda, one should add [these] alone to it.
A soup made from mung beans prepared with alkali is also beneficial for food.
In cases of Tuṇḍikerī, Dhruṣa, Kūrma, Saṃghāta, and Tālupuppuṭa, this same procedure should be performed; however, there is a specific distinction regarding surgical intervention (śastrakarman).
In the case of Tālupāka, however, a treatment that destroys pitta (pittanāśana) must be administered.
In cases of dryness of the palate, oleation, sudation, and treatments that subdue Vāta should be employed.
For the curable types of Rohiṇī, bloodletting is beneficial, as are emesis,
the inhalation of medicinal smoke, gargles, and nasal therapy.
When the blood has flowed out in the case of a vātika [disease], one should rub the area with salts.
One should also repeatedly hold lukewarm oil-gargles (tailakavala).
In the case of a paittika [disease], one should rub it with patraṅga, sugar, and honey.
A decoction of grapes (*drākṣā*) and *parūṣaka* is beneficial as a gargle (*kavalagraha*).

One should rub away [the disease] caused by *kapha* with house-soot (*āgāradhūma*) and pungent substances (*kaṭuka*). Oil prepared with *śvetā*, *viḍaṅga*, *dantī*, and rock salt (*saindhava*) [is also effective].
In cases of excessive phlegm, nasal therapy (nasya) and gargling (kavala) should be administered.
A physician should treat Rohiṇī caused by blood in the same manner as Pittaja disorders; having drained Kaṇṭhaśālūka, one should treat it like Tuṇḍikerī.
One should eat barley-gruel once a day, in small quantities and with oily substances; one should treat adhijihvikā just as one would upajihvikā.
Having lifted the tongue and pulled out the adhijihvikā with a hook...
One should excise it with a circular blade (maṇḍalāgra) using sharp, hot methods such as friction and so forth;
having drained the mass, one should perform purification according to the prescribed procedure.
Furthermore, whatever disease is a "fleshy growth" (gilāyu), that too should be treated with a surgical instrument.
One should lance a galavidradhi (throat abscess) that is not located on a vital spot and is fully matured.
In diseases of the throat, bloodletting, sharp nasal therapy (nasya), and other procedures should be employed,
along with the drinking of a decoction made from the bark of *darvī*, *nimba*, *tārkṣya*, and *kaliṅga*.
Alternatively, a decoction of *harītakī* mixed with honey should be drunk.
Or, *kaṭukā*, *ativiṣā*, *pāṭhā*, *dāru*, *mustaka*, and *kaliṅgaka*, boiled in cow’s urine, should be drunk; these destroy diseases of the throat.
House-soot, barley-alkali, pāṭhā, the three pungents (vyoṣa), rasāñjana, tejohvā, the three myrobalans (triphalā), iron, and citraka— these,
powdered together and mixed with honey, should be held in the mouth; this destroys diseases of the throat.
The powder known as Kālaka indeed cures diseases of the teeth, mouth, and throat.
Manahshila, yavakshara, haritala, saindhava, and the bark of darvi—this powder, when combined with honey, [is used for these purposes]. (66–67)
One should hold clarified butter mixed with its scum for throat diseases; this is celebrated as the excellent preparation known as Pītika.
[One should also use] Yavāgraja, Tejavatī, Pāṭhā, Rasāñjana, Dāruniśā, and Kuṣṭha.
One should prepare a pill with honey and hold it in the mouth for all diseases of the throat.

One should drink warm decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla), or soup made from mung beans and horse gram, along with milk, sugarcane juice, cow’s urine, curd-whey, sour gruel, or fermented rice-water.
Having examined the specific humor (doṣa), one should administer boluses even with oils or clarified butter.
[The following ingredients should be used: the five spices (pañcakola), tālīsa, patra, elā, marica, and tvac; and the alkalis of palāśa and muṣkaka, along with yavakṣāra—all powdered together.
When old jaggery has been boiled down to twice its original volume, pills the size of the *karkandhu* fruit should be made. Kept for seven days in the ashes of the *muṣkaka* tree,
they become like nectar when applied in all diseases of the throat.
In the case of *sarvasara* caused by *vāta*, one should rub the area with powders containing salts; oil prepared with *vāta*-alleviating drugs is beneficial for gargling and nasal administration.
In the case of *sarvasara* caused by *pitta*, for a person whose body has been purified [by emesis and purgation]—

Every procedure that removes pitta should be performed with sweet and cooling measures. In the case of sarvasara caused by kapha, one should employ scraping (pratisāraṇa), gargles (gaṇḍūṣa), medicated smoke (dhūma), purificatory treatments (saṃśodhana), and all therapies that eliminate kapha.
In cases of stomatitis (mukhapāka), venesection, head-purgation, and body-purgation should be performed; furthermore, one should constantly and repeatedly chew the leaves of the *jātī* jasmine.
[A decoction] made from *jātī* leaves, *amṛtā*, grapes, *vāsā*, *darvī*, and the three fruits (*phalatrika*) [is also beneficial].
The decoction, when drunk mixed with honey or used as a mouth gargle, cures inflammation of the mouth (mukhapāka).
The fresh sprouts of *paṭola*, *nimba*, *jambu*, *āmra*,
and *mālatī* constitute the "five sprouts" (*pañcapallava*), which is an excellent astringent for rinsing the mouth.
In cases of mouth ulcers (mukhapāka), a decoction of the five barks or a decoction of the three myrobalans (triphalā) mixed with honey should be used for rinsing the mouth.
The juice of *darvī* boiled down until it becomes a thick extract constitutes a medicinal paste (rasakriyā).
Taken with honey, it cures diseases of the mouth, blood disorders, sinus ulcers, and wounds.
One should drink a decoction made of *saptacchada*, *uśīra*, *paṭola*, *musta*, *harītakī*, *tiktakarohiṇī*, *yaṣṭyāhva*, *rājadruma*, and *candana* to eliminate suppuration of the mouth.
The decoction of paṭola, śuṇṭhī, triphalā, viśālā,
trāyamāṇā, tiktā, the two types of niśā, and amṛtā, when drunk with honey, destroys [fever].
And when [the disease] is located in the mouth, it destroys all oral ailments.
Boiled triphalā, pāṭhā, mṛdvīkā, and jasmine buds should be consumed or eaten; triphalā destroys inflammation of the mouth.
Sesame seeds, blue lotus, ghee, sugar, and milk, along with honey,
used as a gargle for one whose mouth is burnt, removes burning and suppuration.
One should properly boil one *tulā* of *nīlasahācara* in a *droṇa* of water.
Having strained the oil into a decoction consisting of one-fourth its weight,
one should cook it slowly with a paste (kalka) of *anantā*, *khadira*, *eriṇa*, *medā*, *jambu*, *āmra*, and *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, each weighing half a *pala*.
That oil, when applied to the mouth, immediately bestows stability upon the teeth.
Having crushed one hundred fresh pieces of *irimeda* bark into small fragments and boiled them with four *āḍhakas* of water, when reduced to a quarter,
the wise physician should slowly cook half an *āḍhaka* of oil with that decoction.
With one *akṣa* part each of the pastes of mañjiṣṭhā, lodhra, madhuka, irimeda, khadira,
kaṭphala, lākṣā, nyagrodha, musta, sūkṣmailā, karpūra, agaru, padmaka, lavaṅga, kaṅkola, and jātī; || 89–90 ||
A physician should administer this prepared formulation of *phala*, *pattra*, *aṅga*, *gerika*, *varāṅga*, *gajakesara*, *kusuma*, and *dhātakī* for diseases arising in the mouth,
such as loose teeth, abscesses (*vidradhi*), *sauṣira*, *śītāda*, and *dantaharṣa*.
This oil should be used for worms, toothache, the loosening of advanced gum tissue, decayed teeth, foul breath, and the aforementioned diseases.
One should cook one *prastha* each of lac-resin and milk separately [with the base oil]. 92–93.
Oil prepared with a decoction of these four-fold ingredients and one *pala* each of *lodhra*, *kaṭphala*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *padmakesara*, *padmaka*,
*candana*, *utpala*, and *yaṣṭyāhva* should be held as a gargle (*gaṇḍūṣa*).
It destroys toothache, looseness of the teeth, falling out of teeth, and the condition known as *kapālikā*; it cures *śītāda*, putrid breath, loss of appetite, and a bad taste in the mouth.
It overcomes these ailments located in the mouth and makes the teeth firm. (95–96)
The paste and decoction of bakula fruit, lodhra, vajrivallī, kuraṇṭaka, caturaṅgula, babbūla, vājikarṇa, and erimāsana—
oil cooked with these, when applied to the mouth, [cures diseases]. || 97 ||
Indeed, by means of this nasal medication (nāvana), it stabilizes loose teeth.

One should properly boil one *tulā* of *khadira* wood in one *droṇa* of water; when reduced to one-eighth, one should add the following as an after-throw (*prativāpa*) into that very [decoction]: || 98–99 ||
Jātī, karpūra, pūga, and the fruits of kaṅkola— this pill should be prepared to increase the beauty of the mouth,
and for diseases of the teeth, lips, and mouth, as well as ailments of the tongue and palate. (100)

Having boiled two and a half *tulās* of *gāyatrī* bark together with four jars of water on a scale equal to the essence of the *gāyatrī*, and having reduced it until one-quarter remains, it should be filtered through a fine cloth.

Then one should cook it again slowly with a mild fire. When that [mixture] has attained consistency, one should add the fine powder of those substances belonging to the portion for the mouthfuls (kavalagraha).

Elā, lotus-stalks, white sandalwood, sandalwood water, *śyāmā*, *tamāla* leaves, *ghanasāra*, iron rods, the juice of *lajjālu*, the three myrobalans, *rasāñjana*, and *dhātakī*— [The text continues: ...the ichor of elephants, honey, sugar, and the like, along with the various juices of fruits and flowers, were prepared as a cooling bath for the Lord. (Note: This is a partial translation of a passage describing medicinal and aromatic substances used for a ritual bath. The full list includes various herbs, woods, metals, and fruit juices.)
Of *śrīpuṣpa*, *gairika*, *kaṭaṅkaṭī*, and *kaṭphala*; of *padmākāṣṭha*, *lodhra*, *vaṭa-roha*, and *yavāsaka*; combined with *māṃsī*, *niśā*, and the bark of *surabhi*.
One should prepare one *pala* each of powdered *kaṅkola*, nutmeg, cardamom, and cloves; then,
having removed it from the heat while still cool, add four *palas* of camphor.
Having cast [the powder], one should make pills resembling peas;
when dried and placed in the mouth, they ward off diseases arising from the throat, lips, tongue, teeth, and palate. (105)
They produce fragrance, sharpness, and relish in the mouth, as well as supreme firmness of the teeth and lightness of the tongue. (106) Section 59.
To alleviate earache, one should fill the ear with the auspicious, pleasantly warm juices of *kapittha*, *mātuluṅga*, and *śṛṅgavera*.
[Likewise,] the juice of *śṛṅgavera*, honey, rock salt (*saindhava*), and oil [may be used].
This, when lukewarm, should be applied to the ears; it removes pain.
The fresh juice of garlic, ginger, śigru, muraṅgī, radish, and plantain is excellent for filling the ears when used lukewarm.
Or one may sprinkle it with sea-foam powder according to the prescribed method.
The fresh juices of ginger, *sūryāvarta*, *saubhāñjana* root, and radish—
each combined separately with honey, rock salt, and oil, and applied while warm— remove earache.
The resin of *Saubhāñjana* mixed with sesame oil,
applied warm as a filling in the ear, serves to alleviate earache.
[It may also be prepared] with any one of the eight urines.
One should fill the ear with lukewarm [oil] for the alleviation of earache.
Alternatively, having prepared a shallow cup from a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree provided with many leaves, one should smear it with oil, heat it over coals, and place it over the ear.
The oil that drips from that ear-cup heated by charcoal reaches the auditory canal and immediately causes pain.
[One should apply] the stalks of the great *pañcamūla*, eight finger-breadths in length.
Having wrapped [the ear] in linen and sprinkled it with oil, one should then set it on fire.
The oil that drips from those [wick-wicks), lukewarm, should be applied;
that is to be known as *dīpikā-taila*, which relieves earache.
A leaf of the *arka* plant, yellowed by ripening, smeared with clarified butter (*ājya*), and heated over a fire, is pressed to extract its juice;
when poured into the ear, it destroys pain and excessive affliction.
[11] This applies to an ear afflicted by intense pain, accompanied by ringing sounds, and discharging moisture.
The physician should add goat's urine, lukewarm and combined with rock salt,
along with bamboo scrapings; or he may cook oil with the urine of a goat or a sheep, and with that [oil] he should fill the ear of one suffering from earache.
One should hold [the oil] in the ear while massaging the root of the ear until the pain becomes mild; this should be done for a hundred measures (mātrā) or until there is no longer any pain.
Mustard oil should be prepared with asafoetida, tumburu, and dry ginger.
In cases of earache and ringing in the ears, filling [the ear] is said to be beneficial.
[The ingredients are]: the alkali of hair, radish, and ginger; asafoetida with dry ginger; *śatapuṣpā*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, *dāru*, *śigru*, and *rasāñjana*. (15–16)
Sauvarcala salt, yavakṣāra, svarjika, udbhida, saindhava, bhūrjagranthi, viḍa salt, musta, and honey-vinegar in a fourfold quantity,
as well as the juice of mātuluṅga and the juice of kadalī; || 17 ||
Oil should be cooked with these; it is the supreme remedy for earache.
By filling the ear with this oil, deafness, tinnitus, and even severe purulent discharge, as well as worms residing in the ear, are cured.
By the instruction of Kṛṣṇātreya, this excellent caustic oil (kṣārataila), which removes the disease of facial suppuration (mukhapāka), quickly brings about their destruction.
Having taken one part of *cheda* and honey, [one should add] four parts of fermented gruel (*śuktaka*) and so forth.
Others, however, write that there is one part of oil for each; they also record *madhuśukta*.
That which is combined with barley-water and honey, and contains ginger and jaggery, and has been kept for three nights upon a heap of grain, is declared to be *madhuśukta*.

In cases of ringing in the ears (*karṇanāda*) or deafening noise in the ears (*karṇakṣveḍa*), one should fill the ears with mustard oil; for deafness caused by such ringing, one should administer the medicine prescribed for vāta-type earache.
Oil derived from sesame seeds, processed with alkaline water from the *mārga* plant and its medicinal paste, [is also beneficial].
It removes tinnitus and also deafness through filling [the ear].
One should cook one *prastha* of oil with a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūlī*);
this should be administered into the ear as the supreme medicine for deafness.
Having ground the fruit of the *bilva* with urine, one should cook oil with milk; in that [oil], one should administer ear-filling for deafness (*bādhirya*).
In the same manner, this procedure should be performed for ringing in the ears (*praṇāda*), preceded by nasal therapy (*nasya*).
An errhine (nasya) made from jaggery and ginger mixed with water may be used for both [types].
For ear discharge (karṇasrāva), they praise the filling of the ear with a powder of the five astringents (pañcakapāya) combined with the juice of wood-apple (kapittha) and honey.
Tinduka, abhayā, lodhra, samaṅgā, and āmalakī—
these should be understood here by the term "the five decoctions" (pañcakaṣāya).
The juice extracted from the fruit of the karpāsī plant, combined with the powder of sarja bark, [is used].
Mixed with honey, this excellent [preparation] is highly recommended for ear discharge (karṇasrāva).
Fresh leaves of Jambu and Āmra, along with equal parts of fresh Kapittha and cotton fruit, should be chewed;
those experts declare that the juice mixed with honey removes such discharges.

Oil of *nimba* and *karañja*, boiled with these [herbs] along with mustard oil, is prescribed for removing ear discharge (32). The juice of elephant dung and *kuṭaja*, steamed by the method of *puṭapāka*, combined with oil and rock salt (*saindhava*), is an excellent remedy for ear discharge (33).
One should cook mustard oil with the meat of a *śambūka* (a type of snail);
by the mere filling of it, an ear-tract disorder (*karṇanāḍī*) is pacified.
[This is done] with the powder produced from sulphur, realgar, and turmeric.
Eight *pala* of pungent oil, together with one-sixteenth part of *muṣṭi*, cooked until it is equal in quantity to the juice of *dhattūra* leaves,
shall conquer even long-standing sinus infections (*nāḍī*) arising in the ear. (35)
Now, in the case of ear-obstruction (karṇapratīnāha), one should employ oleation and sudation; thereafter, once the head has been purged, one should perform the appropriate treatment.
For ear-inflammation (karṇapāka), one should apply the same remedies as for ulcerative erysipelas (kṣatavisarpa).
Nasal fomentation (nāḍī-sveda), emesis, medicated smoking (dhūma), head-purgation (mūrdha-virecana),
and all procedures that remove phlegm (kapha) eliminate itching of the ears.
Having moistened [the area] with oil and liquefied it with fomentation, [one should proceed].
The physician should properly clean the earwax with a probe.
The juice of nirguṇḍī, oil, rock salt, soot, powder, and jaggery, combined with honey, when used as a filling, pacify foul-smelling ears (pūtikarṇa).
Oil cooked with the juice of *jātī* leaves conquers *pūtikarṇa*.
Alternatively, oil prepared with the tender leaves of *varuṇa*, *arka*, *kapittha*, *āmra*, and *jambū*, or the juice of *jātī* leaves, removes *pūtikarṇa*.

One should fill the ear infested with worms with the fresh juice of *sūryāvartaka*, the juice of *sinduvāra*, and the juice of the root of *lāṅgalī*, sprinkled with the powder of the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*); this is a supreme destroyer of parasites. (42)
For the purpose of destroying worms in the ear, one should employ an anthelmintic procedure (kṛmighna-vidhi).
Fumigation with eggplant (vārtāka) is beneficial, as is the use of mustard oil (sārṣapa-sneha).
Furthermore, filling [the ear] with yellow orpiment (haritāla) mixed with cow's urine is recommended.
For foul odor in the ears, fumigation with *guggulu* is said to be best;
for killing worms, it should be used with yellow orpiment (*haritāla*) mixed with cow’s urine,
or with the decoction of the *rājavṛkṣa* group, or with water from the *surasā* group.
One should perform irrigation of the ear with these powders and fill it with them;
one should also apply the treatment prescribed for abscesses (vidradhi) in cases of an abscess.
Rubbed *rasāñjana* mixed with honey and a woman’s milk [should be used].
This is commended even for long-standing, purulent otitis (pūtikarṇaka) accompanied by discharge.
Oil prepared with kuṣṭha, hiṅgu, vacā, dāru, śatāhvā, viśva, and saindhava, along with goat's urine, cures pūtikarṇa. || 47-48 ||
Oil cooked with *śatāvarī*, *vājigandhā*, *payasyā*, and castor seeds, along with milk, is the supreme means for nourishing the ears.
Oil prepared in milk with the paste (*kalka*) of the *jīvanīya* group [of herbs] is likewise beneficial.
The nourishment and growth of the *pālī* [flesh] occurs with the decoction of the meat of marshy animals (*ānūpa*).
Chapter 60:
Milk boiled with the five roots (*pañcamūlī*) and *citraka* and *harītakī* [is beneficial].

Ghee-jaggery confection (sarpirguḍa) and the six-ingredient soup (ṣaḍaṅgayūṣa) are for the alleviation of chronic rhinitis (pīnasa). [One should take] vyoṣa, citraka, tālīsa, tamarind, and amlavetasa, along with cavya and ajājī in equal parts, with cardamom (elā), cinnamon bark (tvak), and cinnamon leaves (patra) added in one-fourth the quantity of those.
This powder, beginning with *vyoṣa* (the three pungents) and combined with old jaggery, destroys chronic rhinitis, dyspnea, and cough, and is an excellent promoter of appetite and voice.
[3] With *pāṭhā*, the two types of *rajanī*, *mūrvā*, *pippalī*, and *jātipallava*...
Oil prepared with *dantī* as a nasal medication (*nasya*) leads to the pacification of chronic rhinitis (*pīnasa*).
Oil cooked with *vyāghrī*, *dantī*, *vacā*, *śigru*, *surasa*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), and rock salt, when used as a nasal drop (*nāvana*), removes the disease of putrid nose (*pūtināsā*).
Oil prepared with trikaṭu, viḍaṅga, rock salt (saindhava), the fruit of bṛhatī, śigru, surasa, and dantī, boiled with cow’s urine, should be used as a nasal drop (nasya) for pūtināsā.
Kaliṅga, hiṅgu, marica, lākṣā, surasa, and kaṭphala [are also used].
An *avapīḍa* (nasal drop) made from *kuṣṭha*, *ugrā*, *aśigru*, and *jantughna* is highly recommended.
One should cook *kaṭutaila* with those same ingredients combined with urine;
this is proclaimed as the supreme remedy for *apīnasa* and fetid nose (*pūtināsa*).

In the case of inflammation of the nose (nāsāpāka), all Pitta-subduing measures—both external and internal—should be employed; after bloodletting, the barks of milk-exuding trees mixed with clarified butter should be used for irrigation and as a paste.
Decoctions that destroy pus, blood, and blood-bile (raktapitta) should also be used as nasal drops (nāvana).

Oil or clarified butter prepared with a paste and decoction of *śuṇṭhī*, *kuṣṭha*, *kaṇā*, *bilva*, and *drākṣā*, used as a nasal drop (*nasya*), cures the disease of sneezing (*kṣavathu*). In the case of a burning sensation, one should employ all Pitta-alleviating measures that are sweet and cooling.

In the constriction of the nose, the drinking of unctuous substances is primary, as are unctuous medicated smokes and daily nasal enemas (mūrdhabasti). In cases of vātika coryza, one should drink ghee prepared with the five salts or with the first group of drugs (vīratarādigaṇa) according to the prescribed sequence.
One should observe the entire procedure for nasal therapy (nasya) and other treatments as proclaimed by Ātreya.
For those [types of headache] arising from pitta and blood, ghee processed with the sweet drugs (madhuraka) should be drunk;
furthermore, one should apply cooling affusions (pariṣeka) and plasters (pradeha).
In cases born of kapha, after having administered oleation with ghee or having induced emesis with gruel cooked with sesame and māṣa, one should follow the therapeutic regimen that subdues phlegm.
[This is done] with dārvī, iṅguda, nikumbha, kiṇihī, and surasa.
Then, various wicks (vartis) should be prepared separately for inhalation according to the prescribed rules.
A person should inhale the smoke of roasted barley flour mixed with ghee and oil;
this is declared to cure coryza and to alleviate cough and hiccup. (16-17)
Alternatively, the physician should administer smoke to those suffering from acute catarrh by placing roasted barley flour mixed with ghee inside a hollowed-out shell.
Or, he may use jayā leaves cooked in a closed vessel (puṭapāka) combined with sea salt and oil.
In all types of catarrh, habitual practice [of oleation] is the supreme medicine.
One should treat them according to their respective conditions with head massage, fomentation, the consumption of pungent and sour foods, emesis, and the drinking of ghee.
A pungent preparation combined with jaggery, along with a diet of unctuous and sour curd,
cures acute coryza and especially promotes the digestion of kapha.
Then, once the kapha is known to have matured, one should eliminate it by means of head-purgatives (nasyas).
Pippalī, śigru seeds, viḍaṅga, and marica—
this expressed juice (avapīḍa) is praised for warding off coryza (pratiśyāya). These aforementioned treatments, ground with urine, should be employed against worms (kṛmi).
The wise [physician] should employ purgatives, anthelmintic medicines,
and the respective treatments for the remaining disorders.
[One should also use] the flowers of red karavīra, jasmine, āsana, and mallikā.
Oil prepared with these together is the best for destroying hemorrhoids of the nose.
Having added one hundred palas each of the juices of *citraka*, *āmalakī*, *guḍūcī*, and *daśamūla*, along with one *āḍhaka* of powdered *pathyā* and jaggery, [one should prepare the medicine].
One should cook [the mixture] for a hundred [times];

when it has become solid, one should add twelve palas of the three pungents (vyoṣa) and the three aromatics (trijātaka), half a pala of alkali (kṣāra), and on the following day, half a prastha of honey; then one should consume it according to one's digestive fire.
This elixir (rasāyana) increases the digestive fire and destroys wasting, cough, difficult-to-cure rhinitis, worms, abdominal tumors, upward-moving wind (udāvarta), hemorrhoids, and asthma.
[It is prepared with] soot from a house, kaṇā, devadāru, alkali, naktāhva, and rock salt.
Oil prepared with *śikharī* seeds is proven effective and beneficial for hemorrhoids of the nose.
(Adhikāra 61) [Treatment] should be carried out by means of fasting, medicinal plasters, sudation, venesection, and purgation.
One should treat [the patient] with eye-salves, collyriums, eye-drops, and other such remedies. Diseases arising in the eyes and abdomen, as well as catarrh, ulcers, and fever—
these five diseases are destroyed by fasting for five nights.
Sudation, medicinal paste, bitter food, affusion for four days, and fasting—
these six are the digestive remedies for the undigested humors (āma) in eye diseases.
[3] With fragrant resin (śrīvāsa), ativiṣā, lodhra, and a small amount of rock salt, powdered together—
When the eye disease is unmanifest, one should apply a poultice made of *guṇḍa* leaves externally.
Collyrium, filling the eye with medicine, and the drinking of decoctions are not recommended for the undigested (āmaja) stage;
however, if one considers the eye disease to be painful and its symptoms manifest, [these treatments may be applied].
However, for the purpose of restraining pain, one should always perform eye-drops (āścotana).
For an eye disease born of wind (māruta), lukewarm decoctions of bilva and others, along with eraṇḍa, bṛhatī, tarkārī, and madhuśigru, are beneficial as eye-drops.
Goat’s milk boiled with the sprouts, roots, and bark of *eraṇḍa*,
as well as with the roots of *kaṇṭakārī*, is beneficial when applied as a lukewarm irrigation. Then, once the morbid humors have been fully ripened, one should apply the appropriate collyrium.
Collyrium is desired at midday during the winter and the cool season;
it is also desired in the forenoon or the afternoon during the summer, the autumn,
and indeed always during the spring, provided it is not cloudy and not excessively hot during the rainy season.
The physician should prepare a wick for sharp eye-salve (tīkṣṇāñjana) the size of a mustard seed;
for moderate [salve], the measure should be one and a half times that, and for mild [salve], it should be double.
However, the smallest dose is the size of a viḍaṅga fruit, the medium is two, and the best is three.
The standard measure for wicks used in the preparation of *rasakriyā* has been proclaimed. For a purgative powder, two *śalākā*s are prescribed;
for a mild [purgative], it should be three *śalākā*s; and for an unctuous collyrium, four [are required].
Salaka probes made of gold, silver, copper, iron, bell-metal, stone,
or bone are recommended for the application of collyrium; they should be auspicious, eight finger-breadths in length, shaped like a bud at the tip, and as thick as a pea in circumference.
Placing a wet touchstone in his left palm and taking collyrium with his right hand, he should gently rub it upon the stone. With that paste, the wise man should smear the tip of the probe.
Having lifted the upper eyelid with the joint of the left thumb,
one should skillfully insert the small probe between the eyelid and the white of the eye;
first one should apply the collyrium to the left eye, and afterwards to the right.

One should not touch the inner eye with a probe, the thumb, or the forefinger. A medicinal wick (varti) made from the bark of the *bṛhatī* and castor roots, the root of *śigru*, and rock salt (*saindhava*),
ground together with goat’s milk, cures wind-related eye diseases.
One should grind together haridrā, madhuka, drākṣā, and devadāru with goat’s milk; this is an excellent collyrium for abhiṣyanda.
[Likewise, one may use] prapauṇḍarīka, yaṣṭyāhvā, niśā, āmalaka, and padmaka.
Boiled with cold water and mixed with honey, it cures pitta-type eye diseases.
Milk boiled with grapes, madhuka, mañjiṣṭhā, and the jīvanīya group [of herbs], when used as an eye-drop in the morning, is beneficial for those suffering from swelling and pain in the eyes.

In cases born of *kapha*, one should administer fasting (*laṅghana*), sudation (*sveda*), nasal medication (*nasya*), and a diet consisting of bitter and other such [pungent] substances; one should also perform sharp blowing (*pradhamana*) and apply sharp poultices (*upanāhana*).
[These poultices should be made] from *phaṇijjaka*, *āsphota*, *kapittha*, *bilva*, *pattūra*, *pīlu*, *surasa*, *arjaka*, and *bhaṅgā*.
One should apply sudation or an ointment made of *barhiṣṭha*, ginger, *suradāru*, and *kuṣṭha*.
Alternatively, a lukewarm poultice consisting of ginger, neem leaves, and a small amount of rock salt should be applied to the eye; in brief, this removes swelling, itching, and pain. (23–24)
The bark of the pārijāta tree, when combined with oil, sour gruel (kāñjika), and rock salt, destroys eye pain born of phlegm, just as the thunderbolt destroys trees.
Furthermore, lodhra mixed with rock salt, fried in clarified butter, ground with sauvīra, and bound in a white cloth [is likewise effective].
One should apply this as an eye-drop; it destroys burning, itching, and pain of the eye.
Lodhra, ground on a stone and mixed with ghee, along with khadira, ajāji, mustard, ginger, ariṣṭa, and rock salt, [should be used]. || 26–27 ||
One should place that bound [powder] on a cloth and apply it with clear, sour *kāñjika* juice;

by this, one should perform an irrigation of the eyes, which conquers itching, disease, tearing, and friction. Lodhra, having been smeared with nimba leaves, should then be heated by fire to produce either a powder or a paste.
Eye-drops mixed with human milk are said to be capable of curing vāta, pitta, and blood disorders.
Vāta-born [eye disease] is cured by unctuous, hot [substances]; that born from pitta and blood by mild and cool ones;
and that consisting of kapha by sharp, dry, hot, and clear ones. (29–30)
The sāṃnipātika [type of eye disease] arises from the reversal of sharp, hot, mild, and cold [qualities].
Its time is throughout the day and the first watch of the night.
Alternatively, it is that which a person can endure while being administered as an āścotana [eye-drop].
That [medicine] should be administered once, twice, or thrice during the day and night.
For scarification, seven or eight drops are prescribed; for oleation, ten;
for instillation, twelve should be used; and for healing, likewise twelve.
When applied correctly, eye-drops result in clarity of the eyes,
the subsiding of pain, the cessation of disease, and lightness of vision. If applied incorrectly, they cause an increase in the disease, heaviness, and turbidity of the eyes.
If the eyes are excessively treated with eye-drops (āścyotana), there occurs an outflow of blood and morbid humors (rāgadoṣaparisrava).
An irrigation (seka) with water cooled by grinding together tirīṭa, triphalā, yaṣṭīmadhu, sugar, and bhadramustaka destroys redness and congestion of the eyes (raktābhiṣyanda).
A powder made from kaseru and madhuka, enclosed within a cloth and placed in rainwater, serves as a beneficial eye-drop (āścotana).
The drinking of bitter ghee and frequent purgation are also recommended. (37–38)

The application of leeches around the eyes as well as the prescribed procedure for curing *pittābhiṣyanda* (ophthalmia caused by bile) has been set forth. Sprinkling with the juice of *śigru* leaves removes all eye diseases.
The resin of the *śigru* leaf, well-ground and fumigated with ghee inside a copper vessel, destroys swelling, itching, lacrimation, and pain. [Likewise,
a preparation] made from equal parts of *pathyā*, *gairika*, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), *dārvī*, and *tārkṣya* [is effective].
An external application ground with water cures all eye diseases.
A highly effective pill, containing within its core finely ground neem leaves mixed with jasmine and rock salt,
should be roasted with powdered lodhra.

Enveloped on all sides with cotton from Sauvīra that is thick and exceedingly soft, it causes the long-term subsiding of eye irritation when moved over the eyes. (42) One should take the appropriate medicinal powder in a dose equal to a jujube fruit. (43)
Having tied a clean, soft linen cloth [around the eye], one should touch it again;
by this, burning, lacrimation, suppuration, redness, and swelling are pacified.
Filtered bilva leaf juice, combined with ghee, rock salt, and long pepper, [is likewise beneficial].
Rubbed on a cord and fumigated over a fire of cow dung,
it should be stirred with milk and used as a filling for the eyes; this removes swelling and pain, and is recommended in cases of *abhiṣyanda*, *adhimantha*, and blood discharge from the eyes.
Salt, pungent oil, and sour gruel, thickened in a bronze vessel, well-ground with a stone, and fumigated over a fire of cow-dung,
when sprinkled with goat's milk, pacifies the agitation of wind and phlegm.
It conquers eye-pain, discharge, swelling, and redness.
(47) This entire procedure is also recommended for the Mantha and other such conditions;
if there is no relief at all, one should cauterize the area above the eyebrows during the Mantha treatment. (48)

In cases of netrapāka (inflammation of the eye), one should apply leeches to the joint of the eyelid, administer purgation, or perform venesection; furthermore, one should apply irrigations and plasters as prescribed for śukra (corneal opacity). [One may also use] vibhītaka, śivā, dhātrī, paṭola, ariṣṭa, and vāsaka.
The decoction should be drunk with guggulu; it destroys swelling, pain, and ophthalmia (akṣipāka).
It also cures pilla, ulcerated śukra, and discolorations (rāga) and other such ailments.
Ghee cooked with these [drugs] likewise destroys those many diseases.
The group beginning with vāsaka— consisting of āṭarūṣa, abhayā, nimba,
dhātrī, mustā, akṣa, and kūlaka— destroys bleeding and phlegm and is beneficial for the eyes.
Three pathyās, six vibhītakas, and twelve dhātrīs [are likewise used].

Having drunk a decoction boiled in half a *prastha* of water and reduced to one-eighth, one shall conquer ocular exudation (*abhiṣyanda*), discharge (*āsrāva*), redness, and darkness of vision (*timira*); it destroys inflammation, redness, pain, and tearing, and clarifies the sight. (53–54)

If the eyes are struck, one should apply cold eye-drops and other such treatments; one should quickly perform procedures that produce clarity of vision, using unctuous, cooling, and sweet applications. || 55 ||
Even if [the patient] is afflicted by the distress of sweating, fire, smoke, fear, grief, disease, or heat, the physician should treat them in that same manner.
Having carefully examined the nature of the external affliction, one should first apply fomentation using the heat from the mouth.
Eye-drops with breast milk will immediately alleviate [eye diseases] caused by pitta and blood.

For one whose vision is impaired by looking at a solar eclipse, fire, lightning, and so forth, nourishing treatments such as unctuous and cooling substances should be administered; furthermore, the application of triphalā should be consumed in the evening. || 57–58 ||

An ear-drop (pūraṇa) consisting of niśā, triphalā, dārvī, sitā, and madhuka, combined with human breast milk, destroys eye pain caused by trauma; likewise, an ear-drop of the juice or the powder of itkaṭā sprouts [is effective]. || 59 ||
Having ground goat's ghee, milk, madhuka, blue lotuses, and both jīvaka and ṛṣabhaka, one should cook this into medicated ghee;
this ghee is highly recommended for all injuries to the eyes. (60)
In the first stage (paṭala), the disorder caused by injury is curable;
in the second stage it is manageable (yāpya); and in the third stage it is not cured. [The remedy consists of] rock salt, deodar, ginger, citron juice, and ghee.
When the preparation has dried, that collyrium should be mixed with half its weight of breast milk or water.
In cases of vāta-abhiṣyanda and other disorders of vāta, or in the complication of māruta, ghee or milk taken before a meal is beneficial during the course of eating.
One should drink ghee prepared with milk and the juice of *karkaṭa*, along with *vṛkṣādanī*, *kapittha*, and the five roots (*pañcamūla*) of both the small and large varieties.
To pacify the condition caused by sour substances that have been stored overnight, one should apply cooling medicinal plasters.
One should drink either Tailvaka-ghee or Traiphala-ghee, or even aged ghee alone;
the therapeutic procedure for curing Pittaśyanda should be carried out without venesection.
Ghee and honey should be used as an ointment (añjana) for the treatment of Śirotpāta.
Similarly, rock salt (saindhava) rubbed with breast milk is highly recommended;

one should apply this as a collyrium (añjana) for the condition known as sirāharṣa. Alternatively, one may use treacle mixed with honey, or antimony (tārkṣyaśaila), or ferrous sulfate (kāsīsa) combined with honey.
Cane-sugar mixed with sour gruel and breast milk, or molasses with rock salt,
as well as clarified butter produced from cow's milk, are prescribed for nourishment;
they are excellent for clarifying the vision and removing cataracts.

In cases of excessive lacrimation (abhiṣyanda) and inflammation of the eye (adhimantha), one should apply a strengthening [collyrium] to the eye; it quickly expels the humors and likewise checks the tearing.
This should be done while the patient lies on his back, remaining motionless and as comfortable as possible. 70–71.
In a house free from the glare of the sun and fire, devoid of dust, smoke, and wind, pleasant and undisturbed, for one who is free from anger and fear,
having made a firm support out of bean-flour paste so that it does not leak; || 72 ||
The width at the base should be half a finger-breadth, and at the root, exactly two finger-breadths;
it should be of such a measure for the eye-socket that it does not obstruct the eyes, so that the eyelashes may reach as far as the eyebrows.
Then, having covered the eyes with a yellow, blue, or green cloth, or with leaves, one should thereafter look as comfortably as possible;
or, in the case of wind-related disease, one should practice breath-retention for a thousand measures of speech.
In cases arising from pitta and blood, there are eight; in those arising from kapha, six hundred;
in those of the nature of sannipāta, seven; and likewise five in the procedure for maintaining health (svasthavidhi).
Then, having caused the oleaginous substance (sneha) to flow out from the outer corner (apāṅga), one should cleanse the eye.
One should cleanse his phlegm with medicated smoke prepared through application. In the regimen for maintaining health, nourishing therapy (tarpaṇa) should be administered every second day;
however, in cases arising from Vāta, Pitta, or blood, it should be given daily or on alternate days respectively.
In cases arising from *saṃnipāta*, the saturation should be given every two days; in cases of *kapha*, every three days.
It should be lukewarm for *kapha* and *vāyu*, but cold for *pitta* and blood disorders.
[It results in] easy sleep and awakening, clarity, and proficiency of complexion. (79–80)
Cessation of pain, alleviation of disease, and lightness of action—these are the signs of proper satiation; one should observe them correctly.
For the purpose of pacifying ulcerous discharges and seminal impurities, one should drink *guggulu* with its six adjuncts.
A conch shell, *tinduka* fruit,
and silver rubbed together with bell-metal and breast milk overcome diseases caused by injured semen. Sandalwood, red ochre, lac, and jasmine buds [are likewise used].
This medicinal wick (*varti*) removes ulcerous discharges and purifies the blood.
One may also extract blood from the eye using a needle or leeches;
alternatively, a single *puṇḍarīka* [flower] may be consumed with goat’s milk.

One should destroy the discharge of tears caused by passion by means of treatments for wounds, inflammation, and complications. A decoction made from *dhātrī* fruit, *nimba* leaves, *kapittha* leaves, *yaṣṭyāhva*, *lodhra*, *khadira*, and sesame seeds,
when well-cooled and poured into the eyes, destroys all types of *śukra*.
Tutthaka mixed with water destroys semen when used to fill the eyes.
A wick made from sea-foam, dakṣāṇḍa, bark, and rock salt, combined with honey and the seeds of *śigru* and soaked in *śigru* water, destroys semen. (87)

This collyrium formulation, consisting of equal parts of *dakṣāṇḍatvak*, stone, conch shell, glass, sandalwood, and red ochre, scrapes away [affections of] the *puṣpa* and *arman* stages. It may also be prepared with *śirīṣa* seeds, black pepper, long pepper, and rock salt.
Alternatively, the friction of the semen should be performed with rock salt (saindhava).
Having taken the well-impregnated powder of the fruit of *naktamāla*,
the wise one [should use it] with the juice arising from the flowers of *palāśa*.
A wick (varti) composed of all flowers except for the *kusumbha* should be applied as an ointment for the eyes.
A wick made from rock salt (*saindhava*), the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), long pepper (*kṛṣṇā*), *kaṭukā*, conch-shell navel (*śaṅkhanābhi*),
and copper dust (*tāmra-rajas*), ground together, destroys cataracts (*śukra*).

Sprinkling with water infused with crushed *puṃnāga* leaves, or with the decoction of *śyāmāka* grain, removes the flowers [of the plant]. Four parts of conch shell and half that amount of realgar [are used].
Half a part of realgar, half a part of black pepper, and half a part of rock salt—
this powder-collyrium is excellent and supreme for clearing the eyes and promoting the secretion of semen;
it should be applied with honey in cases of *piccaṭa* and with whey in cases of *arbuda*.
The essence of *madhuka* or the seed of the *akṣa* tree combined with rock salt— these four medicinal collyriums, used with honey, are for the pacification of *śukra*.
Finely ground camphor dust mixed with the milky sap of the *vaṭa* tree [is also used].
By quickly applying this collyrium, one destroys even thick and elevated semen.
Having prepared and strained the lye from the pith of the palmyra, the coconut, the marking-nut, the bamboo shoot, and bamboo, [one should apply it]. 97–98.
One should prepare a fine powder made from the bones of a young elephant, saturated with alkali seven or eight times;
this is the best means for blackening the eyes when they have become white due to incurable disorders of the *śukra*.
For those white [discharges] that are curable, this is the supreme collyrium:
one pala each of *paṭola*, *kaṭukā*, *dārvī*, *nisva*, *vāsā*, the three fruits (*phalatrika*), *durālabhā*, *parpaṭaka*, and *trāyantī*. (100–101)
One should boil one *prastha* of *āmalaka* fruits in water that is not salty until one-fourth remains; into that decoction,
one should cook one *prastha* of ghee with the pastes of *bhūnimba*, *kuṭaja*, *musta*, *yaṣṭimadhu*, and *candana*.
This [oil], prepared with long pepper (pippalī), is beneficial for the eyes and wholesome for the two ears;
it removes diseases of the nose, ears, eyelids, skin, and mouth, as well as ulcers, and is an excellent remedy for jaundice, fever, erysipelas, and scrofula.
This oil of goat, prepared with milk and the medicinal herbs kṛṣṇā, viḍaṅga, madhuyaṣṭikā, sindhujanman, and viśvauṣadha,
[cures] timira, śukra, and eye-pain in the head of men.
Saindhava salt, vājipāda, and gorocana, combined with the juice of the bark of the *selu* tree and applied as a nasal medication (*nasya*) during the treatment for complications of suppuration,
destroys the *ajakā* disease. (105–106)
One *kuḍava* of ghee cooked with the paste of a rabbit's head and water in which the remaining parts have been boiled cures elephantiasis (*ajakā*).
One should cook one *kuḍava* of ghee with the decoction of a rabbit.
By filling [the ear] with a paste of yaṣṭīmadhu and prapauṇḍarīka mixed with an equal amount of goat’s milk, one cures disorders of semen, injuries,
and suppuration;
it also destroys pain in the eyebrows and temples, and especially burning sensations and redness.

Without blood, there can be no semen, wounds, suppuration, or disorders of digestion; therefore, one should extract blood from these [afflicted parts] using leeches. Timira is declared to be the root cause of the destruction of vision.
Therefore, the sages say that one should quickly provide medical treatment for it.
Whatever defect remains concentrated in one part of the vision,
in whatever shape it exists, one sees things in that very form because of it.
In the third stage it is called *kāca*, and in the fourth it is named *nīlikā*.

That which has not yet reached the stage of redness (*rāga*) is curable for one who undergoes treatment; *timira* is likewise [curable]. That which has reached the stage of redness is palliable (*yāpya*), while that which has reached the state of *paṭala* must be rejected as incurable.
Triphalā-ghṛta, honey, barley, foot-massage, śatāvarī, and mung beans— this group, which is beneficial for the eyes, has been described in brief by physicians.
Jīvanti-śāka, suniṣaṇṇaka, taṇḍulīya, and excellent vāstuka [are also beneficial].

Cillī, as well as mūlakapotikā, and the meat of birds and wild animals are beneficial for the eyesight. Vegetables derived from paṭola, karkoṭaka, kāravella, vārtāka, tarkārī, karīra, śigru, and ārtagala, when prepared with ghee, are likewise beneficial for the eyesight. (115–116)
Timira turns into rāga; from rāga it becomes kāca; from kāca, nīlī is produced; then the man becomes blind. One should always consume the well-powdered triphalā.

In cases of Timira caused by pitta or vāta, one should administer [the collyrium] enriched with ghee; in that caused by kapha, it should be prepared with oil and honey, applied according to the appropriate method. || 118 ||
The paste, decoction, or powder of triphalā,
when consumed with honey or clarified butter, brings an end to all types of cataracts (timira).
He who avoids unwholesome food and consumes the powder of triphalā in the evening with clarified butter and honey [attains the same result].
He is freed from ocular disorders, just as a man whose wealth is exhausted is freed from his servants.
One suffering from the disease of *timira* should regularly consume either ghee or a decoction of *varā*.
By washing the eyes in the morning with a decoction of *triphalā*, [the disease is cured].

Diseases that have arisen perish and never occur again. By filling the cavity of the mouth with water and rinsing it many times in the morning, one who mercilessly sprinkles the eyes with those waters instantly destroys all forms of cataracts (timira).
If, after eating, one rubs the palms of the hands together and applies that water to the eyes, it will very quickly dispel cataracts (timira),
just as clarified butter (sarpiḥ) applied to the eyes destroys darkness situated on the ground, like the sun.
The *kaṭhina* (formal robe) remains in effect for a hundred years; however, after seven days of applying collyrium, it is certainly [lost].
Kataka fruit, conch shell, rock salt, the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), sugar, sea-foam, *rasāñjana*, honey, *viḍaṅga*, and realgar—[these are the ingredients]. 125–126.
Having made all these equal, one should grind them with goat's milk;
this [formula] called Sukhāvatī removes timira, paṭala, kāca, arma, and śukra, and it quickly destroys itching, discharge, arbuda, and impurities. 127.
Harītakī, vacā, kuṣṭha, pippalī, and black pepper (marica), along with the marrow of the bibhītaka fruit, conch-shell navel (śaṅkhanābhi), and realgar (manaḥśilā)—
having made all these equal in measure, one should grind them with goat’s milk.
It destroys cataracts, itching, films, tumors, and excess flesh, as well as the condition where one cannot see at night;
even a flower three years old it can destroy in a single month.
The wick known as Candrodayā purifies the vision of men.
However, strong collyrium should not be applied to the eyes during the day;
for the eye, weakened by purgation, suffers when it encounters the sun.
Therefore, it is desired that collyrium be applied at night, for the eye, having been drawn upon by the collyrium, thrives during the night due to the quality of sleep.
Just as [the luster of] gold and various kinds of gems [is enhanced by polishing]. // 133 //
The cleansing of washed items is of various kinds, performed with oils, brushes, and so forth. Likewise, when the eyes of mortals are treated with collyrium, eye-drops, and other such means,
their vision shines undisturbed like the moon in a cloudless sky.

A collyrium made of *harītakī*, *haridrā*, *pippalī*, and salts conquers itching and cataracts (*timira*) and is never obstructed in its action. [Likewise, a collyrium of] *triphalā*, the shell of a hen’s egg, *kāsīsa*, and iron filings [is effective]. 136.
Having ground blue lotus, viḍaṅga seeds, and the foam of the lord of rivers with goat’s milk, one should saturate it in a copper vessel;
after it has stood for seven nights, one should grind it again with milk and form it into pills.
This wick bestows vision upon the blind who have not yet opened their eyes.
(138) Eighty sesame flowers, sixty grains of *pippala*, fifty *jātī* flowers, and sixteen black peppercorns. (139)
This collyrium made from *kusumikā* shall turn back [the effects of] lost vision.
This collyrium, ground with water using sandalwood, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), betel nut (*pūga*), and the sap of the *palāśa* tree, removes all cataracts (*timira*).
A wick (varti) prepared from vyoṣa, utpala, abhayā, kuṣṭha, and tārkṣya removes arbuda,
paṭala, kāca, timira, arma, and the discharge of tears.
Tryūṣaṇa, triphalā, vakra, saindhava, and realgar [are also used].
This medicinal wick (varti), which destroys moisture, exudation, and itching, is praised for removing phlegm.
Made from one part of Pippalī and two parts of Harītakī ground with water, this wick is pleasant for the eyes and removes cataracts, pterygium, opacities, films, and tearing.
Collyrium, white pepper, long pepper, liquorice, the marrow of the *vibhītaka* fruit, conch-shell navel, and realgar—
these should be taken in equal parts and ground with goat’s milk.
One should apply a wick that has been dried in the shade to the eyes; it cures tumors (arbuda), film (paṭala), cataracts (kāca), darkness of vision (timira), red streaks (raktarājikā),
fleshy growths (adhimāṃsa), and impurities, as well as night-blindness.
The wick named Candraprabhā would purify even one who is blind from birth.
(147) Triphalā, Vyoṣa, Sindhūttha, Yaṣṭī, Tuttha, Rasāñjana, Prapauṇḍarīka, Jantughna, Lodhra, and Tāmra as the fourteenth. (148)
Having ground these substances together, a wick (varti) should be prepared with rainwater;
it was written by Nāgārjuna for the purpose of paralyzing [the eyes] at Pāṭaliputra.
It destroys cataracts (timira) as well as the layers of the eye (paṭala).

The sudden inflammation caused by breast milk is certainly conquered by [the juice of] *kiṃśuka*. Furthermore, jaundice and redness of the eyes are overcome by the juice of flowers; one should conquer imminent cataracts (*timira*) with collyrium made from *lodhra* water.
If the eyes have been covered for a long time, they open without difficulty when treated with goat's urine, and clarity is regained.
One should prepare a medicinal wick (varti) from pippalī, tagara, utpala leaves, madhuka, and haridrā.
One who desires eyes equal to those of Suparṇa should constantly apply this collyrium.
This pill, prepared from the powder of vyoṣa, rock salt, triphalā, and añjana, ground with water, is called Kokilā; it removes cataracts (timira).
A wick made from turmeric, *āmalakī*, black *ketaka*, and white mustard seeds, combined with rainwater, removes all eye diseases.
[155] A [wick] made from *vyāghrī*, *mustā*, and *yaṣṭimadhu* (liquorice), combined with long pepper and rock salt...
A wick soaked in goat’s milk and placed in copper cures all eye diseases.
(156) Turmeric, nimba leaves, long pepper, black pepper, (157) viḍaṅga, bhadramusta, and the seventh, ginger— these [are used].
One should grind all these ingredients in equal parts with cow urine.
One should administer pills the size of a jujube stone, dried in the shade;
they destroy *timira* when taken with water, and likewise *paṭala* when taken with honey.
One should apply Sindhu salt-water for itching, breast-milk for pain, milk for immediate irritation, and Kiṃśuka for *paiccaṭa*. [The following are used:
the three pungents, two fruits of *karañja*, the two types of *rajanī*, and *saindhava* salt.
They declare the roots of the *bilva* tree, of *varuṇa*, and the tenth, the water-holding (*vāridhara*), to be [the best].
It destroys darkness, deep gloom, cataracts, *piccaṭa*, and *śukra* [disorders], as well as *arjunaka* and *añjanaka*; it delights the people, and one's sight does not perish for a hundred years.
Blue lotus, viḍaṅga, long pepper, red sandalwood, collyrium,
and rock salt destroy cataracts instantly.
Leaf, red ochre, camphor, liquorice, blue lotus, and collyrium [likewise act as a remedy].
Combined with *nāgakeśara*, this removes all darkness (cataracts); the application of collyrium is threefold: as a pill, a liquid, and a powder.
Having gathered [the ingredients] and rubbed them with the juice of lac, one should apply them like earthworms... [164]
Having lit a wick made of cotton dyed with alkaline salt and mixed with madhūka honey,

using the finest clarified butter, the soot produced from the continuous stream of flames is declared to be a destroyer of the dense darkness of both day and night, whether one is far away or nearby. 165.

Rubbing collyrium with a finger that has been rubbed on the ground is a pacifier for those two [eyes], removing cataracts, corneal opacities, and skin diseases, and destroying the "smoky" vision (dhūmikā).
[One should also apply it] with triphalā, bhṛṅga, mahauṣadha, honey, ghee, goat's milk, and cow urine. || 166 ||
One makes the eye like a Garuda, having sevenfold sprinkled upon a Naga;
[this is done] with the water of Triphala, the juice of Bhringaraja, clarified butter, a paste of poison, goat’s milk, and excellent honey. || 167 ||
Then, having heated a single piece of lead seven times every day, one should subsequently have a probe fashioned from it;
at the time of sunrise, it may be applied with collyrium or without collyrium.

When employed, this probe removes eye diseases arising from black and white [humors], those accompanied by *karikari* and *karika*, those caused by excessive unctuousness (*paicchilya*), and those located in the joints and the eyelids. 169.
One should add powdered *kaṇa* and rock salt to a decoction of *uśīra*.
Once it has been strained, honey should again be added along with ghee until the mixture is thick.
When this has cooled, it is beneficial as a collyrium (*añjana*) for all types of *timira*.

A medicinal extract (rasakriyā) prepared with the juice of *dhātrī*, *añjana*, honey, and clarified butter destroys eye diseases caused by *pitta* and *vāta*, and removes cataracts (*timira*) and opacities (*paṭala*).
Ginger and *bhṛṅgarāja* mixed with *yaṣṭī* oil [is likewise beneficial].
This [medicine] should be administered as a nasal drop (nasya) to destroy severe ophthalmia (mahāpaṭala).
When blindness (liṅganāśa) has arisen from phlegm (kapha), one should, according to rule and with full awareness, pierce the opening made by fate and irrigate the eye with breast milk.
Then, once the forms have been seen, one should slowly remove the probe; having anointed the eye with clarified butter, one should bandage it with a cloth strip.
Thereafter, the patient should lie down on his back in a place free from disturbances.
At that time, one should not perform belching, coughing, sneezing, spitting, or shaking; thereafter, one should observe the same restrictions as one who has drunk medicated oil (sneha).
Every three days, one should wash with decoctions that pacify the wind (vāta).
After three days, due to the fear of wind, one should foment the eye as previously described.

Having thus restrained it for ten days, that which is beneficial for clarifying the vision should be applied; thereafter, one should employ the subsequent treatment and consume light food in moderation.
Redness, swelling, tumors, suppuration, blisters, squinting eyes,
and other diseases such as *adhimantha* may arise from improper piercing or from unwholesome conduct.
One should treat each of these according to its specific requirements.
(179) Now learn from me further formulations for cases of pain or eye disease:
dūrvā grass, barley, gairika, and sārivā, ground into a paste and mixed with clarified butter. (180)
These should be applied as a facial paste for the subsiding of pain and redness.
Furthermore, a lukewarm paste made from *payasyā*, *sārivā*, leaves, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and *madhuka*, combined with goat’s milk, is said to be beneficial.

Ghee prepared in four times the quantity of milk processed with wind-alleviating (vātaghna) drugs, with the addition of the Kākolyādi group as a paste, should be employed in all therapeutic procedures.
If the pain is not thus pacified, one should administer purgation to the patient after he has been lubricated and fomented.
Then the wise man should cauterize the vein as prescribed.
Therefore, O auspicious lady, listen to me regarding collyrium for the sake of clarifying the vision:
[the flowers] of the ram's horn, of the śirīṣa, and of the dhava.
Having ground together equal parts of *mālatī*, pearls,
and lapis lazuli with goat’s milk, the physician should place them in a copper vessel for seven days, then prepare a wick from that mixture and apply it as a collyrium.
One should prepare wicks from *srotoñjana*, coral, sea-foam, realgar, and black pepper, or else as previously described; likewise,
one may use *rasāñjana* along with honey, *tālīsa*, and *svarṇagairika*.
Combined with the liquid of cow dung, it is for one whose vision is impaired by bile (pitta).
The filaments of the red and blue lotuses combined with the liquid of cow dung— this pill-collyrium is beneficial for those who are blind by day and by night.
The three pungents (*tri-kaṭu*) grown in riverbeds, along with *añjana*, realgar (*manaḥśilā*), the two types of *niśā* (turmeric and *dāruharidrā*),
and cow liver mixed with *candana*— this pill, or an ointment made from these, is recommended for those who do not see during the day and night.
Pippalī seeds cooked inside goat liver and ground with its own juice [should be used].
In the same way, *ūṣaṇa* (black pepper) taken with honey quickly cures night-blindness.
One should cook a well-prepared goat liver thoroughly filled with *māgadhikā* (long pepper) over a fire;
when consumed or used as an ointment, that liver undoubtedly destroys night-blindness.

Ghee boiled with the decoction and paste of triphalā along with milk, when drunk at the onset of night, will quickly destroy cataracts (timira). One prastha of the juice of triphalā and one prastha of the juice of bhṛṅgarāja [should be used].
One *prastha* of the juice of *vṛṣa* and an equal amount of *śatāvarī*,
one *prastha* each of goat’s milk, *guḍūcī*, and the juice of *āmalaka*— having collected all these, one should cook ghee with them. (195–196)

The paste consists of *kaṇā*, sugar, grapes, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), licorice (*madhuka*), *kṣīrakākolī*, *madhuparṇī*, and *nidigdhikā*. Once it is known to have been properly prepared, one should store it in a clean vessel.
Drinking [the medicine] upwards, drinking it downwards, and drinking it in the middle are recommended.
It removes all eye diseases simply by being drunk, even when blood is present, when the blood is vitiated, and even when there is excessive bleeding.
In cases of night-blindness, timira, cataract (kāca), nīlikā, paṭala, arbuda, abhiṣyanda, adhimantha, and the severe pakṣmakopa,
as well as in all eye diseases caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha.
It cures loss of vision and weak sight caused by the vitiation of *kapha* and *vāta*,
as well as the discharge from the eyes due to *vāta* and *pitta*; it provides near and far vision,
bestows the vision of a vulture, and immediately increases strength, complexion, and digestive fire.
The great ghee known as Triphalādya destroys all diseases of the eyes.
[It consists of] Triphalā, Tryūṣaṇa, Drākṣā, Madhuka, Kaṭurohiṇī, Prapauṇḍarīka, Sūkṣmailā, Viḍaṅga, and Nāgakesara.

One *karṣa* each of blue lotus, the two types of *sārivā*, sandalwood, and the two types of turmeric, along with an equal amount of milk and three times as much decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), should be cooked with one *prastha* of ghee;
this cures all eye diseases. || 204–205 ||
Timira, defects, discharges, jaundice, cataracts, tumors, erysipelas, menorrhagia, itching, blood disorders, and swelling;
as well as baldness, graying of the hair, and the falling out of hair. || 206 ||
It quickly dispels irregular fevers, vital points (marmas), and semen;
furthermore, it swiftly destroys many other diseases arising in the eyes or in the vital points, just as the sun destroys darkness. (207–208)

And indeed, no other means for clarifying the vision has been seen by the sages, such as Kaśyapa and others, that is as effective as the "three-fruit ghee" (traiphalaṃ ghṛtam). This ghee is prepared with a decoction of the three fruits and abhīru, combined with a paste (kalka) containing an equal portion of yaṣṭīmadhuka.

Clarified butter mixed with a fourth part of honey destroys the three doṣas and cures existing cataracts (timira). A kuḍava of oil cooked with one prastha of the juice of bhṛṅgarāja, along with yaṣṭīmadhu and palāśa, immediately clarifies the vision.
Through nasal administration for one month, this undoubtedly destroys wrinkles and graying hair (211).
Oil cooked with a decoction of cow dung is excellent and beneficial when used as a nasal drop for cases of *timira*;
likewise, clarified butter alone is beneficial in the Pitta-type, while *Aṇutaila* is beneficial in those arising from Vāta and blood (212).
Jīvaka, Ṛṣabhaka, Medā, Drākṣā, Aṃśumatī, Nidigdhikā, Bṛhatī, Madhuka, Balā, Viḍaṅga, Mañjiṣṭhā, Śarkarā, Rāsnā,
Nīlotpala, Śvadaṃṣṭrā, Prapauṇḍarīka, Punarnavā, and Lavaṇa. || 213 ||
Having added oil or clarified butter along with four times the amount of milk, one should cook it with all the parts of long pepper (pippalī) ground in portions of one akṣa each;
this perfected oil, composed by Ātreya, is beloved by kings. (214–215)
It destroys cataract, film, opaqueness, night-blindness, as well as tumors, other [eye diseases], white spots, loss of vision, blue spots, and freckles;
it also removes foul odor from the mouth and nose, premature graying of hair, and lockjaw.
It quickly destroys asthma, cough, consumption, hiccup, stiffness, as well as eye disorders,
facial numbness, hemiplegia, diseases of the arms, stiffness of the head,
and all diseases of the upper body. (217–218)
Pippalī, triphalā, lākṣā, iron powder, and rock salt, ground in the juice of bhṛṅgarāja, are intended as a pill-ointment (guṭikāñjana) for arman,
timira, kāca, itching, śukra, and likewise arjuna.
It destroys diseases of the eyes, including those of the goat-like [blind] eye, leaving none remaining.
(220) Sandalwood, rock salt, harītakī, and the blood of the palāśa tree—this powder, increased in quantity in successive order, scrapes away [the growths] such as *śukra* and *arma*. (221)

This is a *rasakriyā* (solid extract) made from equal parts of *puṣpākhyatārkṣya*, white ocean foam (*sitodadhiphena*), conch shell, *sindhūttha* (rock salt), red ochre (*gairika*), black stone (*śilā*), and black pepper (*marica*), all ground together with honey.
It destroys diseases of the eye such as arma, kāca, timira, and arjuna-vartma.
When ground and stirred with honey, it is placed within a bamboo thicket;
because it is prepared with juice and honey, it is called a *rasakriyā*.
One should then pacify śuktikā with the drinking of lukewarm ghee, and with purgatives, ointments, and affusions that are sweet and cool;
furthermore, with collyriums made of coral, pearl, lapis lazuli, conch-shell, crystal, and sandalwood.
Gold, silver, honey, and collyrium remove the film over the eye (*śuktikā*).
(225) In cases of *arjuna*, an eye-drop (*āścyotana*) consisting of sugar, whey, and honey is beneficial.
(226) Conch-shell combined with honey, or *kataka* nut with rock salt [is also used].
Or sea-foam with sugar, or separately,
*añjana* with *arjuna*; filling [the ear] with sugar, licorice, *kaṭvaṅga*, curd-whey, honey, sour [substance], and rock salt destroys redness, *raktarājī*, and *arjuna*.
One should perform the entire Pitta-remedial procedure for the pacification of Arjuna.
Equal parts of Vaidehī, white Marica, Nāgara, and Saindhava,
ground with the juice of Mātuluṅga, form an ointment that destroys Piṣṭaka.
Having incised the phlegm-born upanāha after applying pressure all around, one should scrape it with a maṇḍalāgra instrument;
then, one should prepare a wick (varti) using the pulp and seeds of harītakī, akṣa, and āmalaka in proportions of three, two, and one parts respectively.

One should apply this as an ointment for eyes filled with tears; it removes even severe inflammation. In cases of excessive lacrimation (srāva), one should administer a decoction of triphalā according to the specific humor involved, mixed with honey, ghee, and pippalī; likewise, one should perform venesection.

For a *krimigranthi* that has been incised, a medicinal paste (*rasakriyā*) made from *triphalā*, urine, *kāsīsa*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and *rasāñjana* should be used as a rubbing agent (*pratisāraṇa*). Having fomentated and incised an *añjananāmikā* that has burst open, one should squeeze out its contents.
One should rub [the area] with realgar, cardamom, natron, and rock salt mixed with honey. Alternatively, one skilled in surgical procedures should,
after incising it, rub it with *rasāñjana* and honey, or apply warm collyriums derived from the flame of a lamp.

One should apply fomentation with a rubbed finger and extract the blood using leeches. For a ruptured *lagaṇa*, each of the following is prescribed as a rubbing agent (*pratisāraṇa*): yellow pigment (*rocanā*), alkali (*kṣāra*), blue vitriol (*tuttha*), long pepper (*pippalī*), and honey. (236)
In a single blink of an eye, one should drink ghee through the nose, and with that, fill [the cavity].

Having fomented the lotus-root knot (bisagranthi) and having opened its openings without support, once it is cooked, one should incise it with a surgical instrument and dust it with rock salt (saindhava). || 237-238 ||
One suffering from *pilloroga* (pterygium) should repeatedly undergo scraping of the eyelid margin, bloodletting, and purgation.
A patient with *pillī* (pterygium) should first undergo oleation and then emesis; once the blood has been drained by venesection, [the treatment continues].

One should apply collyrium made from *śilārasa*, *añjana*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), and cow-bile to the eyes. Alternatively, *tagara* ground with *haritāla*, *vacā*, and *dāru*, or ground with the juice of *abhayā*, destroys *pillaka*.

A wise person should fumigate one afflicted by pillar-disease (pillara-roga) with Devadāru wood that has been soaked in goat's urine and mixed with oil, along with a single fruit of Kākamācī combined with ghee; worms will fall away before long. || 242-243 ||
Rasāñjana, sarjarasa, jasmine flowers, realgar, sea-foam, salt, red ochre, and black pepper— these,
taken in equal parts and ground with honey, [are used] for a moistened eyelid (praklinnavartman).
This collyrium alleviates moisture and itching and promotes the growth of eyelashes.

(245) The root of *guhā* combined with rock salt (*sindhūttha*) and black pepper, rubbed together with fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*) in a copper vessel, is a collyrium that destroys eye-pustules (*pilla*). (246)

Having ground yellow myrobalan, the three myrobalans, *lodhra*, *madhuka*, and red sandalwood in the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, one should rub them in an iron vessel, and likewise in copper, for seven days; then, having made a wick or a powder, [one should apply it]. 247.
Piccaṭī and Dhūmadarśī, when used daily at dawn and dusk by one whose vision is impaired by Timira (cataract), remove all eye diseases.
Mañjiṣṭhā, Madhuka, Utpala, the froth of the ocean, the bark of Udadhikapha, Sevyā, and Gorocanā— [248] ...
This collyrium, prepared from equal parts of māṃsī, candana, śaṅkha, patra, girimṛt, tālīsa, puṣpa, and añjana, is always recommended for the eyes;
it removes itching, moisture, impurities, lacrimation, blood disorders, pain, pilla, arma, and śukra. || 249 ||
One *pala* of *tutthaka* (copper sulfate) and twenty white peppercorns should be ground with thirty *palas* of fermented rice-water (*kāñjika*) and placed in a copper vessel;
it produces pills that cure cataracts, even those developed over many years.
Its application by sprinkling destroys ointment-residues, tears, itching, and swelling.

(251) Having finely crushed the seeds of *Karañja*, *Surasa*, and the buds of *Sumana*, one should prepare a decoction; when it has been strained, a medicinal extract (*rasakriyā*) is made from it. (252)
Collyrium made from medicinal pills promotes the growth of eyelashes.

Alternatively, a powder of *puṣpakāsīsa* (green vitriol) saturated with the juice of *surasā* for ten days, when applied as a collyrium to the copper [vessel], cures diseases of the eyelids and eyelashes.
The obstruction of the eyelashes (*pakṣmoparodha*) is treatable by the extraction of the hairs;
that which has accumulated on the eyelid (*vartman*) should be scraped away, and excited blood should be drained.
Hairs that have grown inward (*antarmukha*) should be removed slowly from a patient who is capable of enduring the procedure.
The wise physician should extract the visible hairs with forceps;
then, using a needle-point heated to the color of fire, he should cauterize the hair-follicles.
Cooling plasters, nasal therapy (nasya), and surgical procedures remove the obstruction of the eyelashes.
While protecting the eye, one might cauterize the eyelash with a heated gold probe; however, once the eyelashes have been thus treated, they will never grow back again.
A person should drink ghee prepared with triphalā, vyoṣa, and rock salt.
It is beneficial for the eyes, promotes digestion, is heart-pleasing, stimulates the digestive fire, and destroys phlegm.
(259) Chapter 62: In diseases of the head caused by Vāta, one should employ oleation, sudation, and nasal medications (nasya).
One should prepare drinks, food, and poultices that remove diseases caused by Vāta.
Kuṣṭha and the root of eraṇḍa, ground with kāñjika and applied as a paste, quickly destroy headache; or else, the flower of mucukunda [applied in the same way] achieves this.

One should administer milk boiled with the five roots as a nasal drop (nasya) for diseases of the head. Having stretched a piece of leather over the head so that it is sixteen finger-breadths high, one should wrap it around the head and smear the area below with a paste of black gram (māṣa).
While the patient is sitting motionless, one should fill [the head] with warm oils. One should retain it for a watch (yāma) or even half a watch to pacify the pain;
this head-enema (śirobasti) conquers diseases of the head caused by Vāta.
For one suffering from pain in the jaw, eyes, or ears, or afflicted by shaking of the head,
one should fill the head with oil; the patient suffering from head disease should remain for five hundred *mātrās* if there is phlegm, eight if bile, or ten if wind.
This same procedure should be performed for the filling of the ear-canal.
In cases of head disease caused by pitta, one should properly administer an unctuous purgative using the juices of grapes, triphalā, and sugarcane, as well as milk and ghee.
One should sprinkle the head with sugar, milk, and water;
it is beneficial to hold ghee that has been washed a hundred times over the head,
and immersion of the head in cool water is also recommended.
The cool sensations of white water-lilies, blue lotuses, and red lotuses, along with sandalwood waters and pleasant breezes, should be utilized for the alleviation of the pain of burning heat.
[One should also use] sandalwood, ushira, licorice, balā, vyāghranakha, and utpala.
An external application (pradeha) should be made with milk and flour, or a pouring of decoctions (pariṣecana) should be used;

likewise, one should apply a cooling, unctuous paste to the head consisting of lotus stalks, lotus roots, lotus tubers, sandalwood, blue lotuses, and filaments, or similarly with myrobalan and blue lotuses.
Ghee prepared with yaṣṭyāhvā, candana, anantā, and milk is beneficial;
it is used as nasal drops (nāvana), or alternatively, [ghee] with sugar, drākṣā, and madhuka is used for [diseases] born of pitta.
In those born of blood (rakta), everything—diet, ointments, and affusions—is the same as for pitta.
In the case of [fever] born of phlegm (kaphaja), there should be a reversal of cold and heat, bloodletting, fasting,
sudation with dry and hot substances that promote digestion,
sharp nasal drops (avapīḍa), medicated smokes (dhūma), and sharp gargles (kavala) are beneficial. || 14-15 ||
One should have him drink clear, aged ghee, and then apply sudation;
once his head has been fomented with the essence of *madhūka*, one should purge it.
[This is done] with *pathyā*, ginger, *madhuka*, *śatāhvā*, blue lotus, and *pākala*.
An application of these ground with water as a head-paste immediately relieves pain.
Devadāru, nata, kuṣṭha, nalada, and viśvabheṣaja,
ground with kāñjika and mixed with oil, form a paste that cures headache.
In a state of combined morbidity (*saṃnipāta*), a treatment that removes the three *doṣas* should be administered; indeed, they prescribe specifically the drinking of ghee, or rather, aged ghee.
[The recipe consists of] the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), lotus seeds (*puṣkarabīja*), *karañja*, *rāsnā*, *turaṅga*, and *gandhā*.
A decoction, when inhaled through the nose, wards off a multitude of headaches.
Milk mixed with the paste of *nāgara* (ginger), when applied as a nasal drop (*nasya*) to men,
destroys even the most intense headache arising from various disorders.

Oil boiled with *śatāhvā*, the root of *eraṇḍa*, *ugrā*, *vakra*, *vyāghrī*, and the fruits [of *vibhītaka*], used as a nasal drop (*nasya*), removes wind-disorders, phlegm, cataracts, and diseases of the upper body. [Likewise, oil prepared with] *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, *drākṣā*, sugar, the two types of *yaṣṭī*, and *utpala* [is beneficial].
Oil prepared with milk is used as a nasal medication (nasya) for diseases of the head caused by vāta and pitta.
[The ingredients are: jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, drākṣā, madhūka, madhuka, balā, nīlotpala, candana, vidārī, and sugar.
One should slowly cook one prastha of oil with these [drugs] in six times as much milk and with the broth of half a tula of wild animal meat;
this prepared oil is an effective nasal medication (nasya) for hemiplegia (ardhāvabhedaka).
It cures deafness, earache, blindness, and tonsillitis;
it subdues diseases of the head caused by wind (vāta) and bile (pitta), and it removes toothache, headache, and facial paralysis.
Castor root, tagara, śatāhvā, jīvantī, āsnā, and the best salt (saindhava),
bhṛṅga, viḍaṅga, madhuyaṣṭikā, and viśvauṣadha (ginger),
along with black sesame oil and goat’s milk mixed with oil— these should be cooked together with four times the amount of bhṛṅga juice. || 28 ||
Six drops [administered] through the nose quickly destroy all disorders of the head;
they make fallen hair grow back, stabilize loosened teeth, strengthen their roots, grant vision equal to that of Suparṇa, and bestow excessive strength upon the arms. (29–30)
In the case of [headache] born of depletion (*kṣayaja*), once depletion has been reached, a nourishing (*bṛṃhaṇa*) regimen should be applied;
ghee processed with Vata-alleviating and sweet substances should be used for drinking and as nasal drops (*nasya*).
In the case of that born of worms (*kṛmija*), nasal medication (*nāvana*) should be made with the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *nakta*, *ahva* (or *anka*), and the seeds of *śigru*.
Nasal medication (nasya) with goat’s urine is supreme for killing worms in cases of worm-borne disease;
likewise, ginger with jaggery, or long pepper with rock salt, is used as nasal drops (nāvana) in all diseases of the arms and other conditions affecting the upper parts of the body. || 33 ||
In the case of Sūryāvarta, medical treatments such as nasal therapy (nasya) should be administered;
