one should cause [the patient] to drink ghee mixed with jaggery and consume cakes fried in ghee.
In Sūryāvarta, venesection and nasal drops made from milk and ghee should be employed.
The habitual consumption of milk and ghee is beneficial, as is purgation with those two;
fomentation with sesame seeds ground in milk and with the *jīvanīya* drugs is recommended.
In cases arising from wind and blood, a nasal medication (*nasya*) consisting of saffron mixed with sugar and fried in ghee should be administered.
In cases of pain in the eyebrows, temples, ears, eyes, or the upper part of the head, and in diseases arising from an increase in the humors during the day,
one should administer an *avapīḍa* (nasal drop) made from the roots and fruits of the *śirīṣa* tree;
or an *avapīḍa* prepared with *vacā* and *pippalī* would be beneficial.
One should prepare a poultice using the meat of wild animals;
by this, his most dreadful disease, sūryāvarta, is pacified.
[Likewise,] a fresh juice made from mahauṣadha along with vacā and pippalī [is effective].
A pressed extract (avapīḍa) should be administered to destroy Sūryāvarta;
this entire procedure should also be performed for Ardhabhedaka.
Sārivā, utpala, kuṣṭha, and madhuka, ground with sour liquids, [should be used].
An ointment consisting of ghee and oil is for [the treatment of] *sūryāvarta* and *ardhabheda*.
This very same [ointment] should be applied in cases of head diseases caused by *kapha*.
One should drink milk with sugar, or water from a coconut.
Either very cold water or clarified butter should be administered through the nose (nasal drops) for these two conditions.
For Anantavāta, the therapeutic procedure beneficial for Sūryāvarta should be performed,
and bloodletting by venesection should also be carried out to pacify Anantavāta.

And a diet that destroys vāta and pitta should be prescribed, as well as the regimen consisting of *madhumastaka*, *saṃyāva*, and *havippūra*; whatever is beneficial for *sūryāvarta* is also beneficial for *śaṅkhaka*, with the exception of sudation (*sveda*).
They praise the use of milk and ghee for both nasal administration and internal drinking in cases of Śaṅkhaka.
One should properly apply a medicinal paste consisting of śatāvarī, black sesame, madhuka, blue lotus, dūrvā grass, and punarnavā.
Sprinkling with cold water and cool milk-baths, as well as an ointment of the pastes of milky trees and conch-shell;
[and the flesh] of the krauñca, kādamba, haṃsa, śarārī, and tortoise. || 48 ||

Then, once that conch-shell has been nourished with the tastes (rasas), the wise physician should indeed incise the three upward-tending vessels arising from its joints, but must not strike them [otherwise].
[This should be done with oil] prepared by boiling liquorice, balā, rāsnā, and the ten roots (daśamūla) in water.
Ghee prepared with sweet substances cures diseases above the clavicle.
A peacock— excluding its wings, bile, entrails, excrement, feet, and head— [should be cooked] together with the ten roots, balā, rāsnā, madhuka, and the three myrobalans.

Having cooked one *prastha* of ghee in water, one should cook it with an equal amount of milk and a paste (*kalka*) of one *karṣa* each of the sweet drugs; this removes diseases of the head caused by *ardita*,
and destroys diseases of the ears, nose, eyes, tongue, mouth, and throat.
This preparation beginning with peacock [meat] is renowned for curing diseases above the clavicle.
Oil prepared with *prapauṇḍarīka*, *madhuka*, *pippalī*, *candana*, and *utpala* in the juice of *dhātrī*, administered as nasal drops or by massage, [is likewise effective].
When practiced regularly, it destroys all upward-moving diseases as well as gray hair.
(55) [Adhikāra 63] Curd, sauvarcala salt, cumin, madhuka, and blue lotus—
A woman afflicted by Vāta-āsr̥gdara (menorrhagia due to Vāta) should drink [the juice] mixed with honey.
She should drink the blood of a deer combined with sugar and honey;
likewise, in cases of Pitta-type [āsr̥gdara], she should drink the fresh juice of vāsaka or the juice of guḍūcī.
In cases of anemia (pāṇḍu) and menorrhagia (asṛgdara), one should drink the paste of the root of *rohītaka* with water;
or the paste of the seeds of *āmalaka* with sugar and honey.
Alternatively, one may take one *akṣa* measure of *dhātakī* or *āmalaka* mixed with honey as a liquid.

One should drink either the root of *kākajaṅghā* or the root of *kārṣāsa*, with rice-water, for the purpose of pacifying *pāṇḍu* and *pradara*. Milk boiled with a decoction of *aśoka* bark and well-cooled [should also be taken].
One should drink this in the morning according to one's strength; it destroys severe menorrhagia.
A decoction made from *dārvī*, *rasāñjana*, *kirāta*, *vṛṣa*, *abdatikta*, *bhallātaka*, and *āragvadha*, mixed with honey, [is likewise effective].
When drunk, it overcomes excessively powerful menorrhagia accompanied by pain—
whether characterized by yellow, black, reddish-brown, crimson, blue, or white discharge.
*Rasāñjana* and the root of *taṇḍulaka*, mixed with honey and drunk with rice-water, [achieve this].
Bhārgī, together with ginger, destroys menorrhagia of every origin and also asthma.
(7) Having gathered the root of Kuśa grass, one should grind it with rice-water;
by drinking this for three days, a woman is completely freed from pradara. (8)
One should drink the juice of the fruit of the *udumbara* tree mixed with honey for the destruction of menorrhagia, while consuming rice and milk with sugar.
The root of *balā* drunk with milk and mixed with honey cures *pradara*.

The root of *kuśa*, *vāṭyālaka*, and *raktākhya* taken with rice-water pacifies the effects of drinking wine; likewise, both the substances known as *rakta-saṃjña* and *śuklākhya* do so. Similarly, the powder of *badarī* with jaggery, or *mocā* and goat's milk, [achieve the same].
Yellow lac mixed with ghee, taken separately, destroys [excessive] blood;
for a young woman who follows beneficial regimens, the physician should appropriately treat that condition with few complications according to the protocol for *raktapitta*.
Pāṭhā, jambu, āmra, madhyama, śilābheda, rasāñjana, ambaṣṭhakī, mocarasa, samaṅgā,
padmakesara, bāhlīka, ativiṣā, mustā, bilva, lodhra, and gairika— [these are the ingredients]. (14)
One should collect equal parts of kaṭphala, marica, śuṇṭhī, mṛdvīkā, raktacandana,
kaṭvaṅga, vatsaka, anantā, dhātakī, madhuka, and arjuna under the Puṣya asterism, and have them ground into a fine powder. || 15–16 ||
Having mixed these with honey, one should have them drunk with rice-water in cases of hemorrhoids and dysentery where blood is passed;
they also destroy those ailments of children caused by the bodily humors (doṣas) or external factors (āgantu).
One should forcibly eliminate the defects of the womb, the defects of the menses, and [discharges] that are white, blue, yellow,
or dark-red in women; this beneficial powder named Puṣyānuga is honored by Ātreya.
Ghee prepared with a decoction of mung and māṣa beans, along with rāsnā, citraka, ginger, pippalī, and viśva, is excellent for asṛgdara (menorrhagia).
One should crush a prastha of śatāvarī juice and squeeze it out.
The physician should provide one prastha of ghee combined with twice as much milk,
and then add these following paste ingredients in the quantity of a large udumbara fruit:
the eight drugs of the jīvanīya group, along with yaṣṭīmadhu, candana, and padmaka.
Śvadaṃṣṭrā, ātmaguptā, balā, and likewise nāgabalā;
śāliparṇī, pṛṣṭhaparṇī, vidārī, and the two types of sārivā; sugar should be added in equal measure, as well as the fruits of kāśmarya. || 23 ||
Having ascertained that it has been properly prepared,
one should administer that ghee in disorders of *rakta-pitta*, those caused by *vāta* and *pitta*,
as well as *vāta-rakta*, consumption, dyspnea, hiccups, and difficult-to-cure cough.
It pacifies burning sensations in the limbs and the head arising from blood and bile, menorrhagia, and all types of severe dysuria— just as the sun dispels darkness. (26)
Kumuda, padma, uśīra, wheat, and red śāli rice;
mudgaparṇī, payasyā, kāśmarī, and madhuyaṣṭikā; the roots of balā and atibalā, utpala, and the top of a palm tree. || 27–28 ||
Vidārī, śatapuṣpā, śāliparṇī, jīvaka, the fruit of trapusa, and fresh plantain fruit—
take half-pala portions of each of these, along with four times as much cow's milk. || 29 ||
Having added twice as much water, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee;
this is used for *pradara*, blood-clotting tumors (*raktagulma*), hemoptysis (*raktapitta*), chlorosis (*halīmaka*),
and that multi-formed bile disorder (*pitta*) which occurs in jaundice accompanied by blood.
In cases of loss of appetite, fever, chronic indigestion, jaundice, intoxication, and vertigo; for young women, those with scanty menses, and those who do not conceive—
this [remedy] increases their pleasure day after day.
The supreme elixir (rasāyana) known as Śītakalyāṇaka has been described;
furthermore, the Kuṭajāṣṭaka electuary is especially beneficial in this case.
(33–34) Chapter 64.
In cases of gynecological disorders (*yonivyādhi*), treatments that overcome *vāta* are most highly recommended:
enemas (*basti*), massage (*abhyaṅga*), affusion (*parīṣeka*), medicinal pastes (*pralepa*), and the application of medicated cotton swabs (*picudhāraṇa*).
[One should also use] *vacā*, *upakuñcikā*, *jīraka*, black pepper, *vṛṣaka*, and rock salt (*saindhava*).
Having ground ajamodā, yavakṣāra, and citraka together with sugar,
one should stir it with *prasannā* and eat it fried in ghee for the relief of pain in the vagina and flanks, heart disease, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and hemorrhoids.

Milk boiled with *rāsnā*, *aśvadaṃṣṭrā*, and *vṛṣaka* removes colic; likewise, sprinkling [the body] with decoctions of *guḍūcī*, *triphalā*, and *dantī*. [One should also use] *nata*, *vārtākinī*, *kuṣṭha*, *saindhava*, and *amaradāru*.
A tampon (picu) prepared with clarified butter should be inserted into the vagina to alleviate pain.

For those with pitta-type vaginal disorders, treatments such as irrigation, massage, and the application of tampons should be performed using substances that alleviate cold-pitta; furthermore, medicated ghees should be used for the purpose of oleation.
When the vagina is afflicted by *balāsa* (phlegmatic disorders), all dry and hot medicinal remedies should be employed.

A suppository made of long pepper (*pippalī*), black pepper (*marica*), black gram (*māṣa*), dill (*śatāhvā*), costus (*kuṣṭha*), and rock salt (*saindhava*), equal in size to the index finger, should be inserted; it purifies the vagina.
A woman who drinks the root of the *lakṣmaṇā* plant, uprooted during the Puṣya asterism and ground by a maiden, with ghee and milk at the end of her menstrual period, obtains a son.
Likewise, milk prepared with a decoction of *hayagandhā* and mixed with ghee [achieves the same].
A woman who has bathed after her menses, having drunk this, will conceive; of this there is no doubt.
Mañjiṣṭhā, madhuka, kuṣṭha, triphalā, sugar, balā, medā, payasyā, kākolī, and the root of aśvagandha—[these are the ingredients].
One *karṣa* each of *ajamodā*, the two types of *haridrā*, *hiṅgu*, *kaṭurohiṇī*,
*utpala*, *kumuda*, *drākṣā*, the two types of *kākolī*, and the two types of *candana*— with these parts, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee.
One should add the juice of śatāvarī and milk four times the amount of ghee. By drinking this ghee, a man always acts like a bull among women,
and a woman gives birth to sons who are endowed with intelligence and are pleasing to behold.
It is recommended for those who have unstable pregnancies, or who give birth to stillborn infants, or who give birth to short-lived children, or who give birth only to daughters;
it is also indicated for defects of the womb, defects of the menses, and miscarriages. || 15 ||
This is known by the name Phalaghṛta, proclaimed by the Aśvins; it increases progeny, promotes longevity, and wards off all malevolent grahas.
Physicians add the root of lakṣmaṇā here, even though it was not mentioned.
Kuṣṭha, musta, the two types of haridrā, pippalī, kaṭurohiṇī, kākolī, kṣīrakākolī, viśālā, triphalā, utpala, medā, rāsnā, viḍaṅga, devadāru, and asafoetida (hiṅgu). || 18 ||
The two types of sārivā, śatāhvā, vacā, yaṣṭī, priyaṅgu, ajamodā, mahāmedā, sandalwood, red sandalwood, jasmine flowers, tugākṣīrī, kaṭphala, and white sugar. || 19 ||
With these medicinal pastes equal in weight [to the ghee], the best of physicians should cook one prastha of ghee with four times as much milk over a fire of cow-dung,
using a sturdy copper vessel on an auspicious day joined with the Puṣya constellation.
Having drunk this clarified butter from a golden jar in which auspicious marriage-rites have been performed, a man always acts like a bull among women.
And whatever woman may be barren, or one who gives birth only to daughters—
Whether she be one whose fetus is unstable, or one who, having given birth, remains [unstable] again;

or whether she be one who gives birth to a short-lived child, or one who gives birth to a dead child—[by this rite] she shall give birth to such a son as one who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. || 23-24 ||
Endowed with beauty and grace, living for a hundred years, and free from fever—
this indeed is the "Fruit-Ghee" (Phalaghṛta) prepared by Bhāradvāja.
[It contains] white mustard, vacā, brāhmī, śaṅkhapuṣpī, and viṣāṇikā.
Payasyā, madhuka, kuṣṭha, as well as kaṭukarohiṇī,
sārivā, triphalā, coraka, sumanolatā, vṛṣapuṣpa, mañjiṣṭhā, devadāru, and mahauṣadha. || 26–27 ||
One should boil pippalī, bhṛṅgarāja, niśā, śyāmā, suvarcalā, daśamūla, apāmārga, aśvagandhā, and śatāvarī—
each in a portion of two palas— in one droṇa of water.
Having strained that decoction, one should cook half an āḍhaka of ghee in it.
This should be administered with skill and consecrated with the Gāyatrī mantra; a woman pregnant for two months should consume it, and she may continue its use until the eighth month.

By the application of this [mantra], one shall give birth to a son who is omniscient and free from all diseases; even while remaining in the womb, he speaks with clear speech. This applies also to women whose wombs are afflicted and men whose semen is impaired.
Even a barren woman obtains a son who is heroic and considers himself wise.
One who is dull-witted, stammering, or mute is cured by merely drinking it;
through its use for seven nights, it makes a man possess a beautiful voice.
By using it for three months, one makes a man a possessor of sacred learning (śrutidhara).
Fire does not burn his house, nor does lightning strike it;
and no child dies where that which is named Soma resides.

Ghee cooked with blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), ushira, madhuka, liquorice (*yaṣṭī*), grapes (*drākṣā*), vidārī, kuśa grass, the five roots (*pañcamūla*), and the life-promoting (*jīvanīya*) drugs, mixed with the juice of *śatāvarī* and milk,
and combined with a quarter-part of sugar, is highly recommended for menorrhagia caused by wind (*māruta*) and blood-bile (*raktapitta*).
When strength is exhausted, semen is lost, and there is difficulty or a Pitta-originated Gulma,
one should immediately cut the flesh of a rat into many small pieces and cook it in oil until it certainly melts thoroughly. || 36 ||
Constantly wearing a garment soaked in that oil on the region of the womb destroys the shameful consequences of the female organ; there should be no doubt in this matter. (65) Adhikāra 65.
Madhuka, śākabīja, payasyā, and suradāru;
aśmantaka, black sesame seeds, tāmravallī, and śatāvarī;
vṛkṣādanī, payasyā, and likewise utpalasārivā.
Anantā, sārivā, rāsnā, padmā, and madhuka;
the two types of bṛhatī, kāśmarya, the sprouts of milk-exuding trees, and their bark; ghee; pṛśniparṇī, balā, śigru, śvadaṃṣṭrā, and madhuyaṣṭikā. || 2-3 ||

Śṛṅgāṭaka, lotus stalk, grapes, kaseru, madhuka, and sugar—these seven formulations for the months [of pregnancy] consist of half-verses; they should be administered in sequence during the seven months in cases of miscarriage, combined with milk. || 4 ||
In the eighth month, the physician should administer the roots of *kapittha*, *bilva*, *bṛhatī*, *paṭolī*, sugarcane, and *nirguṇḍī*, boiled in milk.
In the ninth month, she should drink *madhuka*, *anantā*, *payasyā*, and *sārivā*.
In the tenth month, milk boiled with ginger and then cooled is recommended;
alternatively, ginger, madhuka, and devadāru taken with milk are beneficial.
In this way, the fetus is nourished and severe pain is alleviated.

The clay from a potter’s wheel, mixed with the milk of a goat whose offspring is a male, will certainly stabilize a displaced embryo through the application of this drink. [8] Also, [one may use] the roots of *kuśa*, *kāśa*, castor plant (*uruvūka*), and *gokṣuraka*.
Milk boiled with sugar is an excellent remedy for the colic of a pregnant woman.
Milk prepared with *kaseru*, *śṛṅgāṭaka*, the *jīvanīya* herbs, lotus, water-lily, castor root, and *śatāvarī*, mixed with sugar, will stabilize the fetus and alleviate severe uterine pain.

A woman suffering from colic and discharge during pregnancy should drink a mixture of *kaseru*, *śṛṅgāṭaka*, *padmaka*, *utpala*, *samudga*, and *yaṣṭīmadhuka* with sugar and milk; she should then eat her food with milk. [11] [One may also use] *pāṭhā*, *surasa*, *siṃhāsya*, *mayūra*, and *kuṭaja* individually.
By applying a paste to the navel, the bladder, and the vulva, a woman gives birth easily. Alternatively, an application made from the root-bark of *parūṣaka* or the root of *sthirā*,
applied to the navel, bladder, vulva, and other areas, draws out a dead fetus.
The roots of *mātuluṅga* together with *madhuka*, mixed with honey and drunk with ghee, cause a woman to give birth easily.
O beautiful lady, Indra, Amṛta, Soma, and Citrabhānu [are the deities of this remedy].
And let the horse Uccaiḥśravas dwell in your palace.
O woman, may this nectar extracted from the waters quickly release this embryo of yours;
and may Fire, Wind, Sun, and Indra, together with the salt oceans and the clouds, grant you peace.
The fetters are released, the unfettered are released; the rays are released by the Sun.
Released from all fear, O embryo, come, come! Do not delay! Svāhā!
(17) Water consecrated seven times with the *cyāvana* mantra.

Having drunk [the wine], a woman gives birth; and having seen both sets of thirty, [she does so] with the nadīs, ṛtus, vasus, and likewise with the pakṣas, directions, and eighteen, together with the suns, worlds, and oceans—this is the wonder of both sets of thirty. (18–19)
An incense made of bitter gourd, snake-skin, kṛtavedhana, and mustard seeds,
combined with pungent oil, causes another woman to fall [into submission].
When rubbed on the throat with a finger wrapped in hair, another woman falls [under one's influence] easily.
When the hands and feet have been smeared with the root of *lāṅgalikī*,
one should drink *upakuñcikā* and *pippalī* along with wine as it becomes available, combined with *sauvarcala* salt; this cures pain in the womb.
In the case of a Sūta woman suffering from pain in the heart, head, and bladder known as *makkalla*, she should drink *yavakṣāra* with ghee or warm water;
or she should drink a decoction of the *pippalyādi* group of drugs mixed with salt. (23–24)
Pigeon dung, when drunk with rice-water,
prevents the flow of blood that arises immediately after a miscarriage.
Water boiled with *amṛtā*, *nāgara*, *sahacara*, *bhadretkaṭa*, the five roots (*pañcamūla*), and *jalada* [is likewise effective].
Boiled and cooled, and mixed with honey, it wards off the afflictions of childbirth (sūtikātaṅka).
Water boiled with the roots of sahacara, puṣkara, and vetasa, along with an equal amount of vaikaṅkata wood and kulattha,
combined with salt, asafoetida, and mantha, immediately removes fever and the pains of childbirth.
The strained decoction of the ten roots (daśamūlī) immediately removes the pains of childbed;
or one should drink the decoction of the five roots (pañcamūla) combined with heated iron, or that beneficial liquor (surā) for the destruction of puerperal diseases.
Pippalī, pippalīmūla, cavya, śuṇṭhī, yavānikā, the two types of jīraka, the two types of haridrā, biḍa, and likewise sauvarcala—
having ground these very medicinal herbs, one should cook them with āranāla.
It removes *āmavāta*, is aphrodisiac, destroys *kapha*, and kindles the digestive fire. Known as Vajraka, this *kāñjika* increases the strength of women,
pacifies colic and indigestion, and greatly promotes the production of breast milk.

One should drink the root of *vanakarpāsa* or sugarcane with fermented rice-gruel (*sauvīraka*), or the tuber of *vidārī* with wine; this increases breast milk. Alternatively, one should drink the *haridrādi* or *vacādi* groups of drugs for the purification of breast milk.
In that case, if the breast milk is characterized by a predominance of wind (vāta), one should drink water boiled with the ten roots (daśamūlī).
If it is vitiated by bile (pitta), both the wet-nurse and the child should drink a decoction of amṛtā, abhīru, paṭolī, nimba, candana, and sārivā.
Observing a swelling that has arisen on the breast, the physician should apply the various treatments prescribed for an abscess (vidradhi),
whether it is in the unripened (āma) stage or has reached the state of suppuration (pāka).
One should indeed constantly suckle her breasts.
An ointment made from the root of *viśālā* destroys pain arising from the breasts.
(35–36) Adhikāra 66.

One should administer this linctus— consisting of kuṣṭha, vacā, abhayā, brāhmī, and kanaka, mixed with honey and ghee— to a child to produce a healthy complexion, longevity, and luster. In the absence of breast milk, one should drink goat's or cow's milk, which possesses similar qualities.

One should apply fomentation to a protruding navel using a lump of clay heated by fire, sprinkled with milk, and still warm; by this, the swelling subsides. For inflammation of the navel (nābhipāka), a decoction prepared with niśā, lodhra, priyaṅgu, and madhuka [should be used].
Oil is recommended for massage, or alternatively, [the child] may be dusted with these same powders.
A decoction prepared from the two types of *haridrā*, *yaṣṭyāhva*, *siṃhī*,
and *śakrayava* cures fever and diarrhea in an infant and overcomes defects of the breast milk.
The powder of *ghanakṛṣṇā*, *aruṇā*, and *śṛṅgī*, combined with honey,
cures fever and diarrhea in children, and removes cough, dyspnea, and vomiting.
[5] With *dhātakī*, *bilva*, *dhānyāka*, *lodhra*, *indrayava*, and *vālaka*...
This electuary with honey cures fever, diarrhea, and vomiting in children.
Long pepper, deodar, sarala resin, śreyasī, the two types of bṛhatī, pṛśniparṇī, and dill, when licked with honey and ghee, [produce the same effect].
It stimulates the digestive fire (*grahaṇī*), destroys the affliction of wind (*māruta*), along with jaundice (*sakāmalā*), fever, diarrhea, and anemia; it conquers all diseases of children.
[This is prepared] with *miśī*, black pepper (*kṛṣṇā*), collyrium (*añjana*), parched grain (*lāja*), *śṛṅgī*, black pepper (*marica*), and honey (*mākṣika*).
A linctus should be administered to the child to alleviate vomiting, cough, and fever.

Having powdered *kaṭphala* (śṛṅgī), *mustā*, and *ativiṣā*, one should prepare a linctus with honey for children afflicted by cough, fever, and vomiting; or one may give *ativiṣā* alone with honey. (9–10)
A linctus made of mango stone, parched rice flour, and rock salt, taken with honey, cures vomiting.
One who vomits every time they drink breast milk should be given the juice of two vārtākī fruits and pañcakola to lick with honey and ghee. 11–12.

In cases of fever caused by vāta, pitta, or kapha, clarified butter is unwholesome for one who drinks milk for one, two, or three days; otherwise, it is like [the treatment for] the middle part of the body.
Bilva, dhātakī flowers, water with lodhra, and gajapippalī— [Note: This is a partial translation of the provided fragment.]
Decoctions and electuaries mixed with honey should be administered to children suffering from diarrhea. Water boiled with samaṅgā, dhātakī, lodhra, and sārivā, combined with honey,
should be given even to an infant suffering from difficult-to-cure diarrhea.
One should have the child drink in the morning a decoction prepared with *nāgara*, *ativiṣā*, *mustā*, *vālaka*, and *indrayava*; it destroys all types of diarrhea.
[Also] *mocarasa*, *samaṅgā*, *dhātakī*, and *padmakesara*...
A gruel made from these ground together destroys bloody diarrhea. A paste of *priyaṅgu*, the pulp of *kola* stones, *musta*, and *rasāñjana*,
when licked with honey, removes vomiting, thirst, and diarrhea in a child.
A paste made from leadwort (leha), oil, sugar, honey, sesame,
and liquorice will certainly stop the flow of blood and dysentery in a child.
Likewise, parched grain (lāja) along with liquorice, sugar, and honey [is effective].
Combined with rice-water, it quickly cures dysentery.
In the case of anal inflammation (gudapāka) in children, one should administer treatments that pacify pitta;
rasanjana is especially beneficial when used for drinking and as an ointment.
A linctus prepared with kaṇā, uṣaṇa, sugar, honey, sūkṣmailā, and rock salt is an excellent remedy to be administered to children for the retention of urine.
By licking a powder of saindhava, viśva, elā, hiṅgu, and bhārgī with ghee, one [overcomes] [retention of urine].
Or a child may overcome wind-born constipation and colic with water.
Having drunk a paste of *harītakī*, *vacā*, and *kuṣṭha* mixed with honey along with breast milk, the boy is freed from the falling of the palate.

An ointment for an infant made from house-soot, long pepper, kuṣṭha, black mustard, and indrayava, mixed with buttermilk, quickly destroys sidhma, pāmā, and vicarcikā. Milk boiled with the decoction of the five roots (pañcamūlī) and combined with ghee [is likewise beneficial].
One afflicted by hiccups should drink ginger with jaggery when it is cold.
Powdered grapes, yava, harītakī, and pippalī, licked with honey and ghee, quickly destroys dyspnea as well as cough and tamaka-pāṇḍuroga.
A powder made from puṣkara, ativiṣā, śṛṅgī, māgadhī, and dhanvayāsaka, when licked with honey, conquers the five types of cough in children.
This is the same medicine previously prescribed for adults suffering from fevers and other ailments.
In children, the treatment for those [doshas] should be administered without burning and other such measures.
Those very same doshas and dūṣyas, as well as diseases such as fever and others, are the same; therefore, the medicine is the same, but its dosage should be smaller.
Chapter 67:
A bath with a decoction of *sahāmūṇḍitikā* and northern plants (*udīcyaka*) removes the influence of the planets;
likewise, anointing with *saptacchada*, *āmalaka*, *niśā*, and sandalwood [is beneficial]. 1.
Snake-skin, garlic, mūrvā, mustard seeds, the sprouts of ariṣṭa, cat’s hair, human excrement, goat’s hair, meṣaśṛṅgī, vacā, and honey—
this incense destroys the fever of a child and eliminates all grahas.
Rites of pacification through offerings (bali-śāntīṣṭi-karmāṇi) should be performed for the sake of pacifying the planetary influences (graha-śāntaye).
3. And this mantra, which is efficacious for all purposes (sārvakārmika), should be employed there at the beginning:
*kaṃ ṭaṃ yaṃ śaṃ* to Vainateya, obeisance! *oṃṃ hvāṃ hvīṃ kṣaḥ*. 4.
Taking a flower garland of the size of a child's body, a propitiatory offering (bali) consisting of fistfuls of cooked rice should be given from all sides with the mantra:
"Oṃkārī, golden-winged one, protect, protect the child, svāhā! (5)
Vacā, kuṣṭha, brāhmī, and likewise siddhārthaka;
or else sārivā, saindhava, and pippalī, with ghee as the eighth ingredient—
this prepared ghee, which promotes intelligence, should be drunk day after day.
The prince shall possess firm memory, swift intelligence, and become wise.
Neither Piśācas, nor Rākṣasas, nor Bhūtas, nor Mātṛs shall afflict those princes who drink the Aṣṭamaṅgala.
One should cook ghee with a paste of *aśvagandhā* and ten times its quantity of milk; this should be drunk by children to promote nourishment and increase strength.
(9) Oil prepared with an equal amount of lac juice and four times the quantity of *mastu* [whey] should be used.
With rāsnā, candana, kuṣṭha, abda, vājigandhā, the two types of niśā, śatāhvā, dāru, yaṣṭīmadhu, mūrvā, tiktā,
and hareṇu— this [oil], through massage, destroys fever and demons in children and bestows strength and a healthy complexion. || 10–11 ||
Having ground *karkaṭaka*, that oil should be prepared with milk;
when used as an oil massage for the feet, it prevents the sound of a child's teeth [grinding].
(68) Adhikāra 68.

For one who drinks the root of *pratyaṅgirā* ground with rice-water on a day of the auspicious *śuci-bhadra-yoga*, how can there be any fear of snakes? Even if a serpent, overcome by pride and delusion, should bite that root-drinker out of sheer arrogance— how could it harm him?
At that very moment, his mouth will certainly and swiftly go to the abode of Yama.
(1) If one eats peacock flesh with nimba leaves when the sun has entered Aries, there will be no fear for one afflicted by poison for one year; of this there is no doubt. (2)
The knower of mantras should immediately bind a tourniquet made of linen or similar material, four finger-breadths above the bite, using a cord and empowered mantras;
by such binding, the poison is checked, like water by the construction of a dam.
The veins reaching even his vital organs and joints do not flow [with poison],
and no surge of venom arises, just as a sprout does not grow from the destruction of its seed.
Having taken hold of one's courage, the serpent-enemy must be bitten at that very moment.
Whether it be something soft or any other cool drink, cow's ghee;
or whether I am called by the name Nīlakaṇṭha, or the form of Garuḍa is meditated upon—
that poison becomes void through the mere meditation on emptiness.

An application made with phlegm and earwax using the left ring finger destroys even terrible poison, as does sprinkling with human urine. By means of a nasal administration of the root of the *kulika* plant, even one bitten by Kāla (the God of Death) survives.
There is nothing surprising in this: if the root of *piṇḍītagara* is uprooted under the asterism Puṣya and applied to a bite, it causes even a man who has died from being bitten to move again.
Likewise, black pepper soaked for seven days in the fresh juice of *śirīṣa* leaves [achieves the same].
This prepared [mixture] is beneficial for those bitten by snakes when used as a drink, nasal drop, or collyrium. Naktamāla fruit, the three pungents (vyoṣa), bilva root, the two types of niśā,
saurasa, puṣpa, and mārkava, along with urine, constitute an awakening collyrium.
The root of *vandhyākarkoṭakī*, processed with goat’s urine and ground with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), used as a nasal drop (*nasya*) for one whose mind is afflicted by poison;
likewise, *trivṛt*, *viśalyā*, *madhuka*, the two types of *haridrā*, the *māñjiṣṭha* group, and all the salts.
One should place the three pungent substances (kaṭutrika) ground into powder, mixed with honey, inside a horn.
This medicine, when employed through the methods of drinking, collyrium, massage, or nasal drops, destroys the force of poison;
it possesses irresistible power, is known as Mahāgada, and is of great efficacy.
The barks of *kaṭabhī*, *arjuna*, *sairēya*, *śelu*, and milky trees (*kṣīridruma*),

used as decoctions, pastes, or powders, destroy wounds caused by insects and spiders (15). [Likewise, a preparation] with house-soot (*āgāradhūma*), *mañjiṣṭhā*, turmeric (*rajanī*), and the best salt (*lavaṇottama*)...
An ointment [of *kāsamarda*] overcomes the poison of rats and causes the falling out of the *karṇikā* [ear-wax].
That man who, having placed the root of *kāsamarda* in his mouth, blows into the ear, quickly overcomes the poison of scorpions. (16–17)

Ghee combined with *rajanī*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and honey is an excellent drink prescribed for one afflicted by root-poison (*mūlaviṣa*) or pierced by a poisoned weapon. Furthermore, regarding wounds caused by the claws or teeth of quadrupeds or bipeds: [the same treatment applies]. (18)
It swells, suppurates, exudes pus, and causes fever.
A plaster made of *somavalka*, *aśvakarṇa*, *gojihvā*, *haṃsapādī*, the two types of *rajanī*, and red ochre (*gairika*) removes poison from the nails and teeth. (19–20)

Having drunk this ten-ingredient antidote (daśāṅga-agada) prepared by Kāśyapa— consisting of vacā, hiṅgu, viḍaṅga, rock salt (saindhava), gajapippalī, pāṭhā, prativiṣā, and the three pungents (vyoṣa)— one shall conquer the poison of all insects.
All treatments for insect bites are the same as those for leeches.
One should wander by day and night carrying an umbrella and a jharjhara staff;
terrified by its shadow and sound, serpents flee from this place.
Trembling with agitation and covered in horripilation, he gazes repeatedly at her face; biting his sprout-like lower lip with his teeth, he moans with a whistling sound;
and being utterly consumed by passion, he falls into a state of feverish stupor—he who is thus bitten truly yearns for her.
One should not venture into the fierce cremation ground, which is filled with bones and tattered rags;
one should avoid incompatible foods, overeating, anger, hunger, fear, heat, and sexual intercourse, and especially avoid sleeping during the day, even if one is freed from poison. (24–25)
Chapter 69: That which destroys old age and disease is *rasāyana*;
one who has purified the body should practice it in the first or middle stage of life. (1)
The procedure for elixirs (rāsaāyana) is appropriate for one whose body is not yet purified;
it does not shine upon a soiled garment, like a dye applied to it.
[This purification is achieved] by means of rock salt, sugar, ginger, long pepper, honey, and jaggery, respectively.
During the rainy season and other such times, one who desires the qualities of a rejuvenative tonic (rasāyana) should consume abhayā.
One should coat a new iron vessel with the paste of triphalā;
this coating, having remained for a day and night, should then be drunk dissolved in honey and water.

When that food has been digested, one should consume a meal with abundant fat; by practicing this regularly, one becomes free from old age and disease, and may live for a hundred years. The fresh juice of *maṇḍūkaparṇī* should be used, as well as the powder of *yaṣṭīmadhuka* mixed with milk.
The juice of *guḍūcī* along with its roots and flowers, or indeed the paste of *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, should be employed.

These are rejuvenatives that bestow longevity, destroy diseases, and increase strength, digestive fire, complexion, and voice; they are also intellect-promoting, and among them, *śaṅkhapuṣpī* is especially so for promoting the intellect.
Those who drink the fresh juice produced from *bhṛṅgarāja* every day for one month, subsisting on milk alone, become endowed with strength and a fine complexion, and live for a hundred years.
He who eats the sprouts mixed with black sesame seeds [attains the same].
If one constantly drinks the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* here for a month,
that person becomes long-lived, freed from diseases,
possesses hair like that of a bee, and becomes a man who acts according to his will. 9.
Yellow *aśvagandhā* taken for half a month with milk, ghee, oil, or warm water,
bestows nourishment upon the body of one who is emaciated, just as rain brings growth to young crops.
(10) Other men should eat *dhātrī* and sesame seeds mixed with *bhṛṅgarāja* in the prescribed order.
They shall have black hair and pure senses, and remain free from disease until death.
Those who consume *vacā* for a month with milk, oil, or even clarified butter become invincible to *rakṣasas*, highly intelligent, and possess pure, polished speech.
One should have the roots of vṛddhadāruka made into a fine powder and soak it seven times with the juice of śatāvarī. Then,
one should administer that powder in a dose of one akṣa together with clarified butter.
By consuming it for only a month, a man becomes wise, intelligent, and possessed of memory, and is freed from wrinkles and grey hair.
Having risen in the morning, one should eat the dust from an elephant's ear with clarified butter.
Even if he consumes food according to his desire, that man shall live for a thousand years;
he shall be intelligent, powerful, and lustful, approaching hundreds of women.
By means of honey, moreover, he shall possess the speed of a horse, be exceedingly strong, and approach a thousand women.

This mantra should be employed by the physician during the consecration: Oṃ, homage to Vināyaka! Protect, protect my nectar; grant, grant me the attainment of the fruit, by the word of Rudra, svāhā! || 17 ||
One who drinks half a pala of fresh *punarnavā* ground with milk for half a month,
or for twice that duration, or for three times that, or for a year, shall become young again even when aged.
One *kaṃsa* of *dhātrī* powder saturated with its own juice, combined with equal parts of honey and clarified butter—

Having placed this [substance], together with eight handfuls of black and white [mustard seeds], upon a heap of ashes, one who consumes it at the end of the year becomes free from grey hair; endowed with beauty, complexion, and splendor, he is free from disease and possessed of intelligence, wisdom, memory, eloquence, strength, stability, and courage. (19)
Guḍūcī, apāmārga, viḍaṅga, śaṅkhinī, vacā, abhayā, śuṇṭhī, and śatāvarī,
taken in equal parts and licked with ghee for three days, makes a man capable of retaining a thousand verses.
Brāhmī, vacā, aśvagandhā, and pippalī, combined with honey, [achieve the same].
By the application of these for seven days, one is sung of even by the Kinnaras.
He whose body is afflicted with severe leprosy, if he should eat Somarājī according to the rule for a year, accompanied by black sesame seeds, will surpass Somarājī herself in beauty of form.
Having cut five bhallātaka fruits, one should prepare them according to the prescribed method in water.
One should drink the cooled decoction with the lips and palate smeared with ghee;
one should drink it in increments of five up to seventy, and thereafter decrease the dose.
When it has been digested, one should eat cold boiled rice combined with ghee and milk;
this is a rejuvenative (rasāyana) that promotes intelligence and destroys wrinkles and graying hair.
It cures skin diseases, hemorrhoids, and parasites, removes deranged humors, and purifies vitiated semen.
In some traditions, this mantra is recited when drinking the decoction of *bhallātaka*:
"O Varuṇa, you indeed provide the nectar of the gods; become the granter of boons for us, for the sake of attaining longevity and health. (26-27)
One should drink the oil of *bhallātaka* for a month according to one's strength;
freed from all complications, one shall live firmly for a hundred years,
[cured of] cough, asthma, diarrhea, fever, pustules, hip-eruptions, leprosy, and urinary disorders.
Milk drunk at the end of the night removes urinary obstruction, abdominal enlargement, hemorrhoids, swelling, and diseases of the throat, head, ears, temples, and eyes;
furthermore, whatever other diseases exist in a person caused by vāta, pitta, wounds, or kapha, it dispels them all through the practice of regular consumption. 29.
Indeed, the man who, having risen every morning at dawn when the thick night has passed, drinks water through the nostrils,
becomes full of wisdom and his vision becomes equal to that of Tārkṣya.
Free from wrinkles and grey hair, and liberated from all diseases,
a man who drinks eight handfuls of water before the sun has risen destroys disorders of wind and bile and shall live for a hundred years.

Nasal inhalation of water at the end of night removes deformities, wrinkles, and graying hair; it cures chronic rhinitis, hoarseness, cough, and wasting, acts as a rejuvenative (rasāyana), and promotes vision.
Similarly, triphalā water kept overnight removes wrinkles and graying hair, bestows sight, and is excellent.
Two handfuls should be drunk through the nose; more than that is not recommended.
He who duly practices this elixir (rasāyana) does not merely enjoy a long life here, but attains the auspicious state frequented by the celestial sages, as well as the imperishable Brahman.
Chapter 70:
When the mind of one desiring sexual pleasure is wounded by various unpleasant thoughts, the penis falls limp and impotence arises in men. || 1 ||
The depletion of the somatic elements (saumyadhātu) caused by the excessive consumption of sour, hot, and salty foods is observed; that other form is known as impotence (klaibya).
Or, one who is habitually addicted to excessive sexual intercourse but does not engage in aphrodisiac practices (vājīkriyā) [suffers from it].
He suffers the collapse of his virility caused by the depletion of semen.
Regarding the incurable congenital impotence and that which arises from the cutting of vital points (marmans),
the procedure for aphrodisiac therapy (vājīkara) should be applied to the remaining curable types.
He who eats the testicles of a goat, prepared with long pepper and salt in milk and clarified butter, may approach a hundred women.
One should repeatedly soak sesame seeds in milk in which goat's testicles have been cooked.
The man who eats it shall approach a hundred women as if they were new.
Having licked well-prepared powder of *vidārī* infused with its own juice,
combined with clarified butter and honey, a man may approach ten women.
In this manner, having licked the powder of *āmalaka* processed with its own juice and combined with sugar, honey, and ghee, one should drink milk;
by this, even a man of eighty years rejoices like a youth. (8–9)
A man who eats a powder of *vidārīkanda* equal in size to an *udumbara* fruit, along with boiled milk, becomes youthful even if he is old.
Likewise, the powder of the seeds of *svayaṃguptā* and *ikṣuraka*, mixed with sugar—
By drinking milk that remains warm after being drawn from the cow, a man shall not suffer depletion.
Likewise, the powder of *uccaṭā* is said to be excellent when taken with milk;
the powder of *śatāvarī* and *uccaṭā* should be drunk in this same manner with lukewarm water.
He who licks one karṣa of madhuka powder combined with ghee and honey, followed by a draught of milk as an after-drink, shall no longer suffer from constant seminal discharge.
Gokṣuraka, kṣuraka, śatamūlī, vānarī, nāgabalā, and atibalā—
This powder should be drunk with milk at night by one who has a hundred women in his house.

Four *prasthas* each of the powder of *trikaṇṭaka*, *vidārī*, husked sesame, and *bahuputrī*, two *prasthas* of *bhallātaka*, and seven less than that [two *prasthas*] of *guḍūcī*—[these should be prepared]. 14–15.

Thirty-five palas of honey, eight palas of trikaṭu, ten palas of citraka, double that amount (twenty) of vārāhī, and seven times the amount of citraka (seventy) of sugar; with half as much ghee as the honey— having rubbed these together, this [mixture] is placed in a greased vessel.
Day by day, it destroys the host of diseases such as consumption and cough (17),
as well as urinary stones, abdominal ailments, fistula-in-ano, leprosy, wrinkles, graying hair, and chronic rhinitis;
and one obtains the desired offspring, possessing prowess like that of the Man-Lion (Nṛsiṃha) (18).
Having used for a year the powder named Nārasiṃha, which is endowed with strength, complexion, voice, radiance, intelligence, enthusiasm, and courage, one becomes a person of purified body.
The bulb known as Vārāhī-kanda has a head like that of a boar.
In the absence of those physicians, it is considered a substitute for a leather-worker.
One should cook ghee containing śatāvarī in ten times its quantity of milk;
when combined with sugar, pippalī, and honey, it is called an aphrodisiac.
Having boiled one hundred palas of wheat in one āḍhaka of water until reduced to one-fourth and strained, one should add the following substances:
wheat, muñjāta fruit, black gram, grapes, and parūṣaka.
One should take equal parts of kākolī, kṣīrakākolī, jīvantī, śatāvarī, aśvagandhā, kharjūra, madhuka, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), sugar, bhallātaka, and svayaṃguptā. || 23–24 ||
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee in this manner, having added four times as much milk, using a gentle fire; then, once it is prepared, one should add these ingredients:
cinnamon, cardamom, long pepper, coriander, camphor, and *nāgakeśara*.
Having placed eight palas of sugar and honey therein according to what is available,
and having stirred it with a stalk of sugarcane, one should employ it according to the prescribed rite;
one may eat it with boiled śāli rice or drink it with meat broth.
One should drink one *pala* of this alone according to the prescribed measure;
for such a person, there shall be no flaccidity of the penis nor any loss of semen.
It is supremely strengthening, a subduer of Vāta, and a great generator of semen.
It is praised for alleviating dysuria even in the elderly.
One should consume two *palas* of it for ten nights without indolence;
having drunk it, one may enjoy a hundred women, and afterwards one should drink milk.
And this elixir (rasāyana) consisting of wheat and clarified butter was prepared by the two Aśvins.
[It is compounded] with camphor, agallochum, uśīra, bola, nalikā, lac, śaṭhī, dhātakī flowers, saptaparna leaves, elavāluka, sarala, śaileya, māṃsī, and puru.
With cardamom, saffron, gorocana, damanaka, śrīvāsa, nutmeg, kaṅkola, betel nut, jaṭāmāṃsī, madamurā, kāntālā, and cloves; with oil, uśīra, hareṇukā, sandalwood, sthauṇeya, caṇḍā, and nakha...

Having cooked one āḍhaka of oil with *rājī*, *kośa*, *kulīra*, *padmaka*, *nata*, *spṛkkā*, *pālikā*, lac, *yojanavallī*, and *lodhra* in water, one should anoint the body with it; even an old man will become most beloved by women. || 32 ||
One becomes rich in semen, radiant, and possessed of many sons; even a eunuch becomes eager for sexual pleasure;
a barren woman becomes pregnant, and likewise an old woman gives birth to a son;
it removes itching, perspiration, scabies, and disease, and destroys foul odors and leprosy.
This great, fragrant oil, possessing many virtues, has been proclaimed by the two Aśvins.
One hundred palas of well-steamed kūṣmāṇḍaka, with the seeds removed,
and one prastha each of ghee and oil should be added when that [oil] has been heated.
Cinnamon bark, cardamom, dried ginger, the three pungents (ginger, black pepper, and long pepper), cumin, the two types of elā, and citraka;
likewise, pippalīmūla, cavya, gajapippalī, śuṇṭhī, śṛṅgāṭaka, kaseru, pralamba, and the top of the palmyra palm. || 35 ||
One should cook one pala of this powder with one tula of jaggery.
When it has cooled, one should add eight palas of honey;
this [preparation] removes phlegm, bile, and wind, and stimulates the digestive fire of those with weak digestion.

It is the best nourishment for the emaciated and the most excellent aphrodisiac for those addicted to women and those whose semen is diminished; for those afflicted by wasting disease, this is the supreme remedy prescribed by physicians. (38)
It destroys cough, dyspnea, fever, hiccup, vomiting, and loss of appetite.
This preparation known as Guḍakūṣmāṇḍaka was proclaimed by the two Aśvins;
its vessel and the juice of the steamed pumpkin are prepared like those of Khaṇḍakūṣmāṇḍa.
Whatever is sweet, unctuous, nourishing, life-sustaining, heavy, and gladdening to the mind— all that is said to be aphrodisiac (vṛṣya).
A woman who is beautiful, in the prime of youth, and adorned with ornaments [is likewise].
A woman who is submissive and well-trained is considered the most conducive to virility.
A man desiring long life should not engage in sexual union with women before the age of sixteen, nor after the age of seventy. (42-43)
There were various foods and diverse drinks, words that were pleasing to the ear, and touches pleasant to the skin;
there were delightful fragrances, beautiful forms, and wonderful groves.
And the unimpeded flow of the mind makes a man vigorous.
Semen is diminished by old age, by anxiety, by diseases, by the exhaustion from labor, by fasting, and by excessive indulgence with women. (45–46)

Due to its depletion, its perishability, lack of trustworthiness, and the grief it causes; due to perceiving the faults of women, their lack of appreciation for aesthetic pleasure (rasa), and because of injury or non-consumption [of the substance];
[and] due to *bhallātaka* seeds, water-thorns (*jalaśūka*), and lotus petals— || 47 ||
The wise man, having burnt the interior with Sindhu salt,
should apply this as an ointment ground with the juice of *virūḍha* (germinating) *bṛhatī* fruits upon a body cleansed with buffalo dung. 48.
It makes the penis large, swift like a noble horse, and brings about the desired result; of this there is no doubt.
[This is achieved] by that which is cooked with kāsīsa, turagagandhā, sāvaragaja, and pippalī.
The breasts, ears, genitals, and limbs certainly undergo growth through oil.
(Adhikāra 71) [One should apply it] according to the *doṣa*, according to the disease, according to the time, and according to the strength.
The physician should administer medicated ghee, whether cooked or uncooked, for drinking.
In a condition of pure Pitta, ghee alone should be given; in Vata, it should be combined with salt; and in cases of excessive Kapha, it should be combined with the three pungents (vyoṣa) and alkali.

One who is accustomed to unctuous substances, capable of enduring hardship, and firm, should drink the unctuous substance while it is still clear during cool weather; indeed, drinking it while clear is excellent.
Furthermore, the drinking of warm water as an after-drink for unctuous substances is recommended.
Except for the oil of *bhallātaka*, water should be very cold in that case.
However, a person who has drunk the oil should drink warm water if thirst arises;
if the thirst is not thus relieved, one should remove the oil with warm water.
If, due to improper conduct or because of its excessive quantity, the unctuous substance (sneha) does not undergo digestion,
or if it digests with difficulty by becoming obstructed, one should induce vomiting with warm water. Then,
once the patient's digestive tract has become light, one should administer the unctuous substance again.
When there is doubt as to whether the food has been digested or not, a person should drink warm water; by that, the eructation becomes pure, appetite for food returns, and one feels well.
When the food is being digested, thirst, burning sensations, dizziness, exhaustion, loss of appetite, and fatigue may occur.
Then, after sprinkling the person whose oil has been digested with warm water,
one should have him drink warm gruel made with very few grains;
this should be done for three days, four days, five days, or six days.
After seven nights, the unctuous substance becomes habituated to the body.
For the sake of further purification, one should administer it again once the evening meal has been digested;
or, when feeling hungry at the time of eating, one may drink a pacifying (saṃśamanīya) oil.
One should cause those who hate fats, the emaciated, the elderly, the delicate, and even children, as well as those suffering from thirst during the hot season, to drink [this] along with their meal;
it is a ghee-enriched gruel made from roasted [grains] in meat broth with very few rice grains.
When consumed with honey, it is said to provide immediate unctuousness (snehana).
A person should drink lukewarm gruel containing plenty of sesame seeds, little rice, and clarified butter; by this, one is instantly freed from dryness (raukṣya).
One should likewise milk a cow into a pitcher mixed with sugar and ghee;
one should then drink this *akṣa* measure, for it is said to provide immediate oleation.
Long pepper, salt, the four types of fats, and curd-whey [are also used].
Indeed, this combination of ghee and oil is called "instant emollient therapy" (sadyaḥ-snehana).
One should avoid the drinking of unctuous substances (sneha) when suffering from indigestion, acute fever, weakness, anorexia, obesity, fainting, pain, or intoxication.

A person who has been treated with emesis, one who is thirsty, exhausted, or afflicted by the fatigue of travel; one who has received an enema, undergone purgation, or vomited; and a woman who has given birth prematurely—these should avoid the drinking of fats at an improper time.
The feces are dry and knotted; food is digested with difficulty.
The chest feels as if it is burning, and the wind moves upward from the abdomen.
The person becomes discolored, weak, and parched.

Lassitude, weakness of the limbs, and the appearance of oiliness in the lower part of the body are the signs of one who has been properly oleated; likewise, an aversion to oil, an aversion to food, painful discharge from the rectum, burning sensation in the anus, and dysentery [are signs of over-oleation]. (21)
Excessive discharge of feces is the characteristic of one who has been excessively lubricated.

For the dry person, there should be lubrication with unctuous substances; for the excessively lubricated, there should be drying with *śyāmāka*, *koradūṣa* grain, rice, buttermilk, oil-cake, and parched grain flour.
Out of affection for [the patient], the practitioner should have the person drink [the oil] after abstaining for three nights.

Indeed, a man who habitually uses unctuous substances becomes one whose internal fire is kindled, whose digestive tract is purified, whose tissues are fresh, and who possesses strength and complexion; he has firm senses, slow aging, and lives for a hundred years. (23–24)
One should know that unctuousness alone is supreme for kindling a weak digestive fire; even very heavy food is not sufficient to pacify a fire already kindled by unctuousness.
(25) Chapter 72.
Alternatively, sweating may be induced by means of heated sand, palms, bell-metal vessels, or cloths;
or by applying hot emollient pastes that alleviate Vata along with sour, salty, and oily substances;
likewise, by sprinkling with heated milk, water, air, or decoctions that pacify Vata, and so forth.

Fomentations (sveda) are performed sequentially using heated stones and other materials, characterized by the application of heat, poultices, liquids, and profuse steam. Among these, the last and the first are indicated for Kapha;
the second is prescribed for Vāyu; and the third is ordained when Vāyu is afflicted by Pitta.
Those embodied beings for whom nasal therapy (nasya) and enema (basti) are to be administered,
as well as those who require purification (śodhana), are considered to have been previously treated with sudation (sveda).
After the foreign body (śalya) has been removed, or in the case of a malpresented fetus (mūḍhagarbha) that is free from complications, sudation is to be performed afterwards.
One who has delivered properly at the right time should subsequently be treated with sudation by the physician.

Likewise, a patient suffering from fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, or urinary calculi should be treated with sudation both before and after [the surgical procedure]. The remaining cases will be discussed under the section on surgical instruments.
The humors (doṣas) residing in the tissues (dhātus),
those situated in their own locations, and those adhering within the channels (mārgas)—
when treated with proper sudation— attain a state of liquefaction.
Once they have reached the digestive tract (*koṣṭha*), they are eliminated entirely by purificatory therapies (*śodhana*).

When properly applied, sudation (*sveda*) produces a stimulation of the digestive fire (*agni*), softness of the skin, clarity of the complexion, a desire for food, and cleanliness of the channels (*srotas*); it also destroys drowsiness and sleep, and quickly restores stiffness in the joints.
One should administer all types of sudation in a windless place once the food has been digested;
for one whose body has been anointed with oil, having covered the eyes, heart, scrotum, and sight with cool cloths, one should apply sudation either gently or not at all.
When the cold and piercing pain have subsided, when stiffness, heaviness, and numbness have been overcome, and softness and perspiration have arisen, it is considered the time to cease the sudation.
The outflow of sweat, the alleviation of the disease, lightness, a desire for cold, and softness belong to the patient.
They say these are the signs of proper sweating; in the case of improper sweating, these very same signs occur in reverse.
[The symptoms of improper sweating include: the eruption of blisters, the provocation of blood and bile, intoxication, fainting, vertigo, burning sensations, and exhaustion.

If there is excessive sweating, pain in the joints, and thirst, one who knows the procedure should apply cooling treatments. Furthermore, for one who has sweated excessively, it is beneficial to comfort them and then administer a sprinkling with cold water.

One should bathe with warm water and lead the patient to a sheltered room; one should feed them food that does not cause internal secretions (anabhiṣyandi) and instruct them in all the proper conduct.
Sveda (sudation) should never be applied by those skilled in sudation to one who has not been anointed with oil or whose body is not lubricated.
In the world, it is observed that dry wood, when subjected to the application of heat and moisture, quickly undergoes splitting.
(15) Those suffering from *pāṇḍu* disease, urinary disorders (*meha*), hemorrhagic fever (*raktapitta*), thirst, chest wounds, emaciation, weakness, or indigestion;
those with abdominal dropsy, pregnant women, habitual drinkers, and any person suffering from diarrhea—these should not be subjected to sudation therapy (*sveda*). (16)

Through sudation and other such measures, their bodies undergo destruction, and their disorders cease to be curable. (Adhikāra 73) Emesis, purgation, nasal medication, non-unctuous enema, and unctuous enema— The provided text contains a fragment from a medical treatise (likely *Vāgbhaṭa’s Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā*).
