The object of knowledge is fivefold; its classification is now being described.

Sometimes the humors (doṣas) become aggravated when they have been merely suppressed by emesis and purgation, but those which have been eliminated by cleansing therapies (saṃśodhana) do not arise again.

Emesis is recommended for diseases born of *kapha*, purgation for those born of *pitta*, enemas (*basti*) should be administered for diseases born of *vāta*, and digestive treatments (*pācana*) and so forth for those born of undigested matter (*āma*).
[One should treat] a person who has been properly oleated and sudated while seated on a stool reaching up to the knees.
The physician should cause the patient to vomit by touching the throat with a castor seed stalk.
One should drink a decoction of liquorice mixed with honey and a paste of black indrayava, rock salt, and rāḍha; by this, one vomits thoroughly and effectively.
Having drunk kṛśarā prepared with rāḍha, or milk boiled with its seeds,
or the decoction of rāḍha combined with rock salt (sindhulavaṇa) and long pepper (kṛṣṇā), one should vomit. A man who drinks rice ground with water in the forenoon shall vomit.
The bark of the *phalinī* plant is hot in potency and removes artificial poison (*gara*) along with disorders of phlegm and bile.
Having boiled *āṭarūṣa*, *vacā*, *nimba*, *paṭola*, and the bark of *phalinī*,
one should drink that water together with *madana* to induce vomiting.
Having boiled one *kuḍava* of the medicinal substance in one *āḍhaka* of water until one-fourth remains, one should employ it for emetic purposes.
Likewise, *jīmūtaka*, *ikṣvāku*, *kuṭaja*, and *kṛtavedhana*.
Dhāmārgava should be administered separately for emesis, as described for Rāḍha. This emetic, combined with a decoction of nimba and [the addition of] phalinī, gada, madana, madhuka,
and rock salt, along with honey, is recommended when the stomach is filled with kapha.
Having diligently provoked the doshas with various phlegm-inducing foods,
emesis administered to one who has been lubricated and fomented proceeds properly. [It cures] excessive salivation of kapha, impurity of the heart, cold fever, flatulence, and indigestion.
Heaviness of the head, a sweet taste in the mouth, and itching that is difficult to suppress are said to be the signs of insufficient vomiting (durvāmita).

An empty head, intense and extreme trembling, a burning sensation in the sides and chest, excessive discharge of bile, loss of consciousness, and pain in the heart and throat occur when one has vomited excessively (ativānta).

When the pitta has moved easily following the kapha, when the heart, throat, and head have been cleansed, when the body feels light, and when the discharge of kapha has ceased, one should determine that the person has vomited well. Then, in the afternoon, his body thoroughly purified, he should have his limbs sprinkled with warm water.
One should feed him with soups or meat broths made from horse gram (kulattha), mung bean (mudga), āḍhakī, or the meat of wild animals.

Through emesis, the following afflictions never occur in a person: excessive salivation, hoarseness of voice, drowsiness, lethargy, foul breath, the onset of poison, heaviness, itching, and disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī).
Just as flowers, fruits, and sprouts on a tree perish suddenly when the tree is cut down,
so too, when phlegm is removed by emesis, the disorders born from it go to dissolution.
One should not administer emetics to one suffering from cataracts (timira) nor to one suffering from abdominal tumors (gulmin).

Nor should one treat those afflicted by jaundice or abdominal disease, nor those who are obese, wounded, emaciated, thin, or very old, nor those suffering from hemorrhoids, facial paralysis, or convulsions. || 19 ||

One should not induce emesis in a person suffering from dry (rūkṣa) prameha, during early pregnancy, when there is severe upward bleeding, or when the internal organs (koṣṭha) are corrupted by worms or when the feces are excessively increased. These [conditions] are also exceptions; however, those afflicted by indigestion (ajīrṇa) or those suffering from poisoning should indeed be made to vomit.
Furthermore, those whose phlegm (kapha) is excessively abundant should be treated with Madhuka-water.
If these individuals undergo emesis when they are unfit for it, their diseases become difficult to cure or even incurable; therefore, they are traditionally considered not to be fit for emesis.

The physician should treat one who has vomited excessively by immersing them in cold water after they have been anointed with ghee, and then administer linctuses mixed with sugar and honey. Furthermore, when vomiting is excessive, a heart-tonic purgative should be administered.
If purgation has proceeded excessively, the physician should administer emesis.
(Chapter 74) To one who has been oleated, sweated, and vomited, a purgative should be administered.
For if this [medicine] is administered otherwise, it is considered to cause diseases of the *grahaṇī*.

The digestive tract may be soft due to *pitta*, or harsh due to the predominance of *vāta* and *kapha*; when the *doṣas* are balanced, it is moderate. Therefore, the dosage should be applied according to these conditions.
Combined with sugar and honey, and sprinkled with the powder of *trivṛt*, this is a purgative for those of delicate constitution; it contains one part each of cinnamon bark, leaves, and black pepper.
Having split a stalk of sugarcane in two and smeared it with the paste derived from the three *bhaṇḍī* plants, wrap it with a cord.
Once properly cooked by the method of *puṭapāka*, one suffering from bile disorders should eat it when it has become well-cooled.
For diseases of phlegm, one should lick a purgative consisting of long pepper, ginger, alkali, black turpeth, and trivṛt, together with honey.
Harītakī, viḍaṅga, rock salt (saindhava), ginger (nāgara), trivṛt, and black pepper—
all these together with cow’s urine constitute a purgative.
Triphalā equal to three śāṇas of trivṛt, and [other ingredients] equal to that [triphala], [should be used].
One should lick the powder of kṣāra, kṛṣṇā, and viḍaṅga with honey and ghee; or, having made it into pills with jaggery,
one should administer it for gulmas caused by kapha and vāta, as well as for splenic enlargement, abdominal dropsy, and fistula-in-ano.
This purgative also destroys other [doshas] and is free from danger.
Abhayā, pippalīmūla, marica, viśvabheṣaja, tvak, patra, pippalī, musta, viḍaṅga, and āmalaka [are used]. 9.
These [other ingredients] should be taken in equal parts, while *dantī* should be three times that amount;
*trivṛt* should be given eight times the amount, and sugar six times the amount.
Having bound these into boluses (*modaka*) with honey, they should be the size of an *akṣa* in measure.
One should eat them one by one in the morning and drink cold water afterwards. The person continues to purge until they consume something hot;
furthermore, they must exercise restraint regarding their drinks, food, and activities.
It cures pallor, cough, intermittent fever, loss of digestive fire,
and pains in the calves, thighs, back, buttocks, abdomen, and sides;
as well as hemorrhoids, ear-wax-like growths, fistula-in-ano, swelling, and abdominal tumors.

This elixir, when administered by a physician, destroys abdominal distension, wandering of the bowels, burning sensations, dysuria, splenic disorders, eye diseases, wind-disorders, urinary stones, skin diseases, and urinary disorders.
Inexpensive, yielding great fruit, to be used constantly, life-prolonging, and a destroyer of graying hair— this was seen by Aśvin.
One should drink a paste of *pathyā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and long pepper (*kṛṣṇā*) with warm water.
This purgative, known as Nārāca, destroys all the humors (doṣas) and is the most excellent.

One pala each of the essence of viḍaṅga, āmalaka, and abhayā, along with three palas of trivṛt, should be combined with jaggery in portions of six and twelve [palas] respectively; thirty pills should be prepared over the course of a month. || 15–16 ||
It is said that this Māṇibhadra was created by the preeminent Yakṣa Nivāraṇa for the sake of the Śākya monk;
indeed, it is the destroyer of cough, consumption, leprosy, fistula-in-ano, splenic disorders, dropsy, and hemorrhoids.
[One should take] castor oil with a threefold decoction of Triphalā.
When properly administered, [the emetic] mixed with milk causes purging before long.
Impurity of the heart and abdomen, burning sensations, itching, and retention of feces and urine do not occur when there has been a wholesome purging.
Fainting, prolapse of the rectum, excessive discharge of phlegm, and the onset of colic are the signs of excessive purging.

When the doshas ending with kapha have been expelled, when lightness is felt at the navel, when there is satisfaction of the mind, and when the vāyu has returned to its natural downward course, one should determine that the person has been properly purged.
One should not administer gruel on that day to a patient who is weak in digestion, whose tissues are not diminished, or who has been inadequately purged.
One should cause a person who is emaciated, afflicted by thirst, and well-purged to drink thin, lukewarm, and light [gruel], which brings clarity of intellect, strength of the sense organs,
stability of the bodily constituents (dhātus), and a brightening of the digestive fire.
And after a long time, when properly administered, it brings about the ripening of one's age through purgation;
just as for aquatic creatures moving on land, destruction is certain once the dam has burst.
When pitta is destroyed, there is the certain destruction of those complications that are of the nature of pitta.
(23) One whose tissues are diminished, who is emaciated, dry, a child, or old; one who is dejected, suffering from wasting, or tormented by fear and grief;
one who is exhausted, afflicted by thirst, or has undigested food; a pregnant woman, or one whose blood flows downward—[these should not be treated with strong purgatives]. (24)
Those whose bodies are afflicted by acute coryza, those suffering from acute fever, those who have recently given birth,

those habitually addicted to astringent decoctions, and those who have not been prepared with oleation and other therapies, should not be subjected to purgation. Furthermore, those with weak digestion, those excessively oleated, children, the elderly, the obese, those suffering from chest wounds, the emaciated, and those tormented by fear [should likewise be avoided].

Those who are exhausted, afflicted by thirst, or whose food has not yet been digested; those who are pregnant, or whose blood flows downward; those suffering from acute coryza, alcoholism, or acute fever; those who have recently given birth;

those afflicted by a foreign body (śalya); and those who are unfit for purgation, as well as those who have not been prepared with oleation (sneha) and other preliminary treatments—these are not to be treated with purgatives.

One should administer purgatives very gently even to those whose bodies are excessively overwhelmed by pitta. Men who are unfit for purgation may meet their destruction if administered purgatives by the ignorant.
Furthermore, one should not give an oily purgative to a person whose body is already excessively oleated.
The humors (doṣas), having been displaced, settle once again in the eyelids;
therefore, after first applying dry oleation (virūkṣa-sneha) as appropriate, one should again apply oleation and then administer purgation (recana).
By this means, his humors, being bound by the oil, are destroyed.
If one should drink a purificatory medicine without first performing oleation and sudation,
his body will split apart from the navel upward like dry wood. [The doshas],
having been mobilized by oleation and sudation, are then driven upward by unctuous tastes.

The humors (doṣas) located within the digestive tract of a person can be easily removed by purgatives. Having administered an enema and oleation therapy, one should purge with strong [purgatives] those who have been insufficiently purged.

The commentary *Kusumāvalī* has not been digitized. One should employ *padmakośī*, *nāgāhvaya*, and *candana* through drinking, external application, and sprinkling in cases of excessive purgation. (34)

The paste of *sahakāra* (mango) ground with *sauvīra* (sour gruel), when applied as an ointment to the navel, cures diarrhea. Basti (enema therapy) is recommended for disorders of vāta, pitta, kapha, and rakta.
In cases of combined disorders (saṃsarga) and the three humors in equilibrium (saṃnipāta), the enema (basti) alone is always beneficial.
When seven nights have passed since the purgation (virecana), once strength has been restored and a meal has been taken, an oil enema (anuvāsana-basti) should be administered in the evening.
If the caustic Vaitaraṇa enema has not been administered, the patient should be given an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) after two or three days.
One should administer the unctuous enema while the patient is asleep on his left side and has consumed food.
The physician should apply the enema once the man has voided flatus, feces, and urine.
Otherwise, an enema administered incorrectly will not reach its destination within the body.
5. Holding the enema bag in the left hand, one should squeeze it with the right hand;
with a single, steady squeeze that is neither too fast nor too slow. 6.
With one leg extended and the other bent over it, one should apply a cup to that anus for the purification of the humors. Then,
once the unctuous substance has been introduced, the patient should remain supine for a hundred measures of speech.
When all the limbs are thus extended, the vital energy (vīrya) flows forth.
Then, one should slowly contract the thighs and arms three times each;
thereafter, one should gently strike him with the palms three times each.
In this same manner, he should then lift the buttocks and the hips three times from the bed.

When the penis has been thus positioned, even one who is not accustomed to exertion, being free from excessive speech and devoted to his customary practice, may lie at his pleasure upon the well-spread bed.
The maximum dose for an oil enema (anuvāsana) should be six palas, the medium three palas, and the minimum half a pala; thus there are three grades of dosage.
At the first administration, two palas should be given; at the second, the dose increases by half a pala; thereafter, it increases by one pala and then by one akṣa.
Two karṣas should be increased by eight māṣas for each subsequent bladder; this sequence has been declared.
That [urine] should be combined with powdered rock salt and śatāhvā, and being comfortably warm, it shall thus pass out easily and suddenly. 12–13.
One *māṣa* of powder [should be added] to one *pala* of oil, along with *sindhujanman* (rock salt) and *śatāhvā* (dill).
One *māṣa* of *sindhujanman* and *śatāhvā* [should be added] to one *pala* of oil.
For whomsoever an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) has been administered, it may recur immediately after a single application.

If the oil is excessively hot, or too sharp, or afflicted by wind (vāta), or if it is accompanied by wind, or if the dose is excessive, or if the medicine is too heavy, then another smaller dose should be administered; for [the previous one] does not become unctuous and does not remain in place. || 15-16 ||
If a person follows this regimen for three watches of the night, he shall become a man of purified body.
By consuming rice and ginger water at intervals of one day, his digestive fire is kindled and a desire for food arises.
In the morning, one should drink water boiled with coriander and dry ginger in a dose equal to half the quantity of the decoction;
then, in cases where pitta is predominant, one should drink lukewarm water in that same measure.
This [lukewarm water] pacifies the indigestion of unctuous substances and breaks up kapha.
One should ensure that the wind is favorable for men by using warm water.
An oil enema (snehabasti) should not be administered to a person whose body has not been purified; otherwise, the potency of the oil will not permeate throughout the body.
Even if impure, one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) at all times of day and night when afflicted by vāta alone.
When the pain is severe, one should administer an unctuous enema after having the patient eat food that has been fully digested.

For one who is dry and has an excess of Vāta, after administering two or three unctuous enemas (anuvāsana) and knowing that the body has become properly lubricated, one should subsequently administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha).
Alternatively, even for one who is not unctuous but is excessively afflicted by pure Vāta, [one should proceed as follows].
The wise physician should treat the patient with non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) enriched with abundant fats.
One should not practice either the unctuous enema (snehabasti) or the non-unctuous enema (nirūha) exclusively for a long time;
for from excessive unctuousness there arises the provocation of pitta and kapha, while from excessive non-unctuous enemas there is danger from vāta.
Having fed him a meal reduced by one-quarter from the prescribed amount, one should administer the enema.
The unctuous substance must never be administered to one who has not eaten; because of the emptiness of the digestive tract due to its lack of food, it would otherwise quickly rise back up.

In a disorder arising from kapha, one should administer one enema; in a pitta-type disorder, three; in a vāta-type disorder, five, seven, nine, or even eleven enemas; the skilled physician should thus apply an odd number of enemas.
If the oil enema (anuvāsana) is deficient in unctuousness, it results in the obstruction of flatus, feces, and urine.
Excessive oil enema causes burning, exhaustion, and distressful discharge.
However, he whose oil, along with wind and feces, returns quickly without the sensations of heat or parching, has been properly administered an oil enema.

Then, at the time of evening, when the food has been digested and the oil has returned [to its natural state], one should feed light food as desired, provided that person has a stimulated digestive fire. Even if the oil returns after a full day and night, it does not cause harm.
It should also produce the benefits of enema; however, when digested, it becomes of little benefit.
If an unexpelled oil enema causes no complications—whether it is entirely retained, partially retained, or obstructed by dryness—it should be disregarded by the wise physician.
If the oil does not return within a day and night, one should remove the oil along with the complications; when the oil has not returned from an unctuous enema, no other oil should be administered.
Furthermore, if the oil of an impure person returns mixed with feces, it should not be allowed to go back in.
Then, weakness of the limbs, flatulence, colic, and dyspnea arise, as well as heaviness of the colon;
in such a case, one should administer a strong non-unctuous enema (nirūhaṇa), or an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) prepared with sharp medicinal drugs. || 36-37 ||
In a person who has been purified but whose residual oiliness persists for a long time,
there is an appearance of oiliness on the face, a coating and exhaustion of all the sense organs, an oily odor in the mouth, as well as cough, dyspnea, and anorexia. || 38 ||
Having squeezed [the patient] by the neck there, one should quickly and diligently shake him; furthermore, a very sharp and pungent purgative should be administered.
A bed with a footstool is recommended, neither too high nor with feet that are too low.
Provided with a primary head-covering and a white cloth as an upper garment, with the head facing east,
having been scented, anointed, and sweated, one should administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) while the patient has not yet eaten; one should squeeze the bladder quickly and without delay.
Wrapping his right hand around the kneecap, he should remain there with great force, making hundreds of sounds as the eyelids are pulled back,
for a second, a third, or a fourth time, according to the purpose.
When the signs have been correctly established and the patient has arrived, one should administer the enema (basti).
For those suffering from diseases of Vāta, the quantities of honey, unctuous substance, paste, decoction, and additive should be three, six, two, ten, and three *palas* respectively.

In cases of pitta, there should be four, four, two, two, five, four, six, three, and two non-unctuous enemas (nirūhaṇa); or likewise in kapha. In vāta, one unctuous enema (sasneha) with meat is used; in pitta, two sweet and cold ones with milk.
Three non-unctuous enemas (nirūhas) containing urine, which are pungent, hot, and dry, should be administered for the alleviation of *kapha*.

One [such enema] draws the *vāyu* from its own path, the second draws the *pitta*, and the third draws the *kapha*. An enema that is deficient is characterized by very slight urges and a lack of feces and flatus.
Accompanied by fainting, colic, and an abundance of phlegm, it is characterized by great force and excessive noise.
When his urine, feces, phlegm, and wind pass in succession and he experiences lightness, that person is well-purged (sunirūḍha). || 9-10 ||
Then, once the patient has been well-prepared, bathed, and has eaten rice with flavorful broth, one should administer an unctuous enema (snehabasti) according to the prescribed procedure.
On that day, a powerful fear of vāta (wind-disorder) is expected for him.
On that day, rice with meat broth (rasaudana) is recommended, as well as an oil enema (anuvāsana). Once properly purged, the patient should be anointed with oil, sprinkled with warm water,
and then fed a small amount of fat followed by the broth of wild game.
One should administer an unctuous enema (snehabasti) at that very moment with a small dose.

The first, middle, and small doses are those which have been used by [patients] who, due to weak digestion, have undergone purgation (nirūha); for them, the oil enema (anuvāsana) should be half that amount.

Thereafter, having assessed the strength of the digestive fire and the activity of the wind (vāyu), an unctuous enema (snehabasti) is prescribed once the gastrointestinal tract has been supported by food.
Isolation, mental contentment, unctuousness, and the suppression of disease [are the signs of success].
When an unctuous enema (snehabasti) has been administered correctly, its signs [of success] appear.

However, if the non-unctuous enema (nirūha) does not return within a muhūrta, the wise physician should expel it with purificatory [non-unctuous] enemas combined with alkali, urine, and sour substances.

A non-unctuous enema (nirūhaṇa) that remains for a long time because it is obstructed by vitiated wind (viguṇānila) causes pain, restlessness, fever, flatulence, or even death. It is an established rule, however, that an āsthāpana enema should not be administered to one who has eaten. 18–19.

If it is administered while the food is still undigested (āma), it may cause vomiting, induce excessive nausea, or aggravate all the doṣas; therefore, it should be given when the patient has not yet eaten. Furthermore, considering the specific stage of the disease, the non-unctuous enema (nirūhaṇa) should be administered.
When [the enema] is withdrawn too early, there is no presence of excessive strength in the doshas. An enema that is excessively compressed may then enter the stomach and,
impelled by vata, emerge through the nostrils or the mouth.
It may cause vomiting, nausea, fainting, and other such symptoms, as well as burning sensations.
In that case, one should quickly apply pressure to the throat, perform shaking (avadhūnana), administer strong head and body purgatives, and apply cold affusions. || 22–23 ||
Having first given one *akṣa* of rock salt (*saindhava*) and two *prasṛta*s of honey, one should then stir it well and add two *prasṛta*s of oil.
Once the oil has become unified, one should then throw in one *prasṛta* of the medicinal paste (*kalka*).
When the mixture has been thoroughly blended, one should add a decoction (kaṣāya) measuring five prasṛtas;
likewise, at the end, one should add an addition (āvāpa) measuring two prasṛtas. Thus prepared, the enema (basti) shall consist of twelve prasṛtas.

A well-administered Nirūha enema does not cause the medicine to run out through the hand, nor does it remain after being applied, nor does it produce a parting of the hair (sīmanta). [The following are the ingredients:
sprouts of Badarī, Airāvatī, Śelu, Śālmalī, and Dhanvana.
Those prepared with milk should be very cold, containing blood, and designated as "viscid" (picchila).
In viscid enemas, fresh blood from a boar, buffalo, sheep, cat, antelope, cock, or goat should be administered.
One should grind *śatāhvā* and *akṣa* with a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūlī*).
To that, one should add an equal amount of rock salt (*saindhava*), four *palas* of honey and oil, and one fruit of *madana*, administering it according to the appropriate dosage. || 1 ||

After eating, the wise physician should administer an enema using the *āsthāpana* method; in this case, there is no requirement for oil massage (*abhyaṅga*), fomentation (*sveda*), or any restrictive regimen (*parihāra-vidhi*).
Indeed, according to the authority of Ātreya, this [method] is the destroyer of all diseases.
It destroys consumption, destroys worms, and especially destroys colic; it indeed generates semen, cures vāta-śoṇita (gout),
produces strength and complexion, acts as an aphrodisiac, and is known by the name Ardhamātrika.
Although there are hundreds of *nirūha* enemas described by Suśruta and Caraka,
physicians nevertheless practice with only this half-measure:
oil, jaggery, meat broth, milk, sour liquids, urine, honey, and rock salt.
One should cause these, even if not explicitly mentioned, to be administered in the preparation of *nirūha* enemas, as well as the fruit of the *madana* tree.
One should give one *karṣa* of salt and one *madana* fruit for vāta; in cases of pitta, jaggery and sugar; and in cases of kapha, *siddhārthaka* and other such ingredients.
Taking one akṣa of rock salt (saindhava) combined with one akṣa of śatāhvā,
along with eight palas of cow urine, two palas of amlikā,
and two palas of jaggery (guḍa), one should carefully mix everything together.

A wise physician should administer an enema that is strained through cloth and pleasantly warm. When used, it immediately destroys colic, constipation, flatulence, severe dysuria, worms, upward movement of gases (udāvarta), abdominal tumors (gulma), and other such ailments.

This enema, consisting of one *pala* each of *śukti*, *karṣa*, and *kuḍava* measures of sour gruel, jaggery, rock salt, and cow’s urine, combined with a small amount of oil, removes colic, abdominal distension, and *āmavāta*.
It is recommended for everyone after they have been fed in the evening.
If, however, a person is strong, he may at times consume it even without having eaten;
yet he should follow the inferior sequence and never the excessive one.
Especially for those who are delicate, the inferior sequence alone is beneficial.
Those suffering from fear, insanity, thirst, emaciation, indigestion, anorexia, or urinary disorders;
those afflicted by fainting, leprosy, abdominal enlargement, obesity, cough, asthma, or consumption;
and those with swelling, vertigo, intoxication, vomiting, intolerance of enemas, or weakness—[these should not undergo the procedure]. || 2 ||
Men should not be administered non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana) nor unctuous enemas (anuvāsana), except in cases of wind-diseases (vātaroga).

A person suffering from abdominal enlargement (udarī), urinary disorders (pramehī), skin diseases (kuṣṭhī), or obesity must necessarily be given non-unctuous enemas; they should by no means be given unctuous enemas.
By means of its potency (*vīrya*), the enema (*basti*) draws out the humors (*doṣas*) from the feet to the head;
situated in the receptacle of digested food (*pakvāśaya*), it is like the sun in its own domain drawing up water from the surface of the earth.
It likewise draws out the wind (*samīraṇa*) located in all parts of the body or even in a single limb.
The enema alone restrains [the disease], just as a mountain restrains the force of the wind.
No other treatment besides the enema can withstand the force of the wind,
just as the shore withstands the force of the ocean whose waters are tossed by the wind.
Just as trees, when their roots are watered, possess glossy foliage and tender shoots, so too does a man who receives enemas become endowed with beauty, strength, and other virtues.
He who practices eighteen sets of eighteen enemas [attains these benefits].
By means of the prescribed method and the sequence of avoidance as stated,

that man— possessing the strength of an elephant, equal to the speed of a horse, radiant like an immortal, free from sin, a retainer of sacred learning, and possessing a lifespan of a thousand years— shall become such.

"For whom venesection has been performed, and for whom purification has been carried out..."
He should avoid [these] for a month, or as long as he remains weak.
The patient should avoid each enema every third day;
however, during the third period of avoidance, he should act according to his specific requirements.

The bodily fire of a person who has drunk oleaginous substances, vomited, undergone purgation, had blood let, or received a non-unctuous enema (nirūha), becomes weak. That fire increases when nourished by small quantities of light foods.
Like a fire kindled by small and scanty pieces of wood. (14) [No verses of the *Siddhayoga* appear on this page.

When the fire is balanced, the embodied being lives long; when it has undergone a disorder, he becomes diseased; and when it is extinguished, he meets his death. Therefore, fire is the best [of elements]. (15) Adhikāra 77
There are five types of medicinal smoke: the habitual (*prāyogika*), the cough-relieving (*kāsa-hara*), the purgative (*virecana*), the oleaginous (*snaihika*), and the emetic (*vāmanīya*).

For the habitual type, one should smear linen with *elā* and other drugs excluding those used for leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), and prepare a wick (*varti*) the thickness of a finger and eight digits (*aṅgula*) in length; this is the recommended nozzle (*netra*), which should be six times that length. || 1 ||

The two types of *bṛhatī*, the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), *śṛṅgī*, the bark of *iṅguda*, and realgar (*manaḥśilā*)—this wick (*varti*) removes cough; its nozzle (*netra*) is sixteen finger-breadths long.
A wick for head-purgatives (*śirovirecana*) is considered to have a nozzle measuring one cubit (*hasta*).
With these unctuous substances— namely marrow, beeswax, oil, guggulu, and sarjaka—

one should prepare an unctuous wick for the eye-tube thirty-two finger-breadths in length. For the purpose of reducing [excessive secretions], however, one should use dried meat, sinews, bone, hoof-horn, and skin.
The wick is ten finger-breadths long and the pipe is fivefold; such is the smoke considered to be.
In circumference, it is thick in the middle and thin at the two ends; a sixth part of the pipe's measurement is praised as the proper size for the wick.
Through the use of medicinal smoke, a person’s senses, speech, and mind become clear;
his hair, teeth, and beard grow firm; and his face becomes fragrant and bright.
Those who know this practice desire to inhale the smoke deeply through the mouth.
When the *doṣas* are located in the chest and throat, a person should drink [the medicine] through the mouth alone.
When they arise in the head, ears, eyes, and nose, one should drink the pacifying remedy through the nose (*nastaḥ*).
One should expel [the medicine] through the mouth alone, and never by any means through the nose.
For smoke moving in reverse quickly causes a delusion of vision.

Pratimarśa, avapīḍa, nasya, pradhamana,
and śirovirecana— these are proclaimed as the five types of nasal therapy (nasya).

Now, for an oleaginous nasal medication (nasya), eight drops are to be administered to each nostril of men; this is the settled rule.

Lightness of the head during yoga, easy sleep and awakening, the subsiding of disorders, purity of the senses, and happiness of the mind;
lightness of the head, purity of the channels, and victory over disease.
Clarity of the mind and the sense organs, as well as cleanliness of the head, are the signs [of proper purification].
Itchiness, coating, heaviness, and the discharge of phlegm from the channels are proclaimed to be the signs when the head is under-purified.

If the head is excessively cleansed by strong purgation, there occurs the emergence of brain matter (*mastuluṅga*), vitiation of *vāta*, confusion of the sense organs, and a sense of emptiness in the head.
If the head is insufficiently cleansed, one should apply treatments that subdue *kapha* and *vāta*.
One should employ medicated ghee as a nasal drop (nasya) once the head has been properly purified.
When the oil, administered via the nose, reaches the mouth due to slight sniffing, one should know that by measure it is a pratimarśa. || 10–11 ||
One should not sip this [medicine] by snorting it up, nor should one spit it out once it has entered the mouth.
Diseases of the regions above the clavicle in men are pacified by nasal administration;
it also brings about clarity of the sense organs and makes the mouth fragrant.
It provides strength to the jaw, teeth, head, neck, thighs, arms, and chest,
and prevents the occurrence of wrinkles, graying hair, baldness, and freckles.
Oil is used when kapha is associated with vata, while muscle fat (vasā) is used for vata alone.
One should always administer ghee in cases of pitta, and marrow in cases of vata;

this is proclaimed as the procedure for the four types of unctuous substances (sneha). Because it does not conflict with the sites of kapha, oil is especially recommended for those [sites]. || 15-16 ||
In cases of fainting, delusion, or apatantraka caused by being overcome by poison;
in intoxication, epilepsy, grief, pain, anxiety, anger, fear, and the like;
and in mental diseases affecting those with deluded or agitated minds—|| 17 ||
One should cause a medicinal squeeze (avapīḍa) to be administered for the purpose of awakening consciousness.

Then, one should blow the powder— measured at three *mucuṭis* and containing pungent substances— into the nose with a tube six finger-breadths long and having two openings, in cases of fainting due to poison and similar causes.

One should administer sugar-cane juice, sugarcane juice, milk, ghee, and meat broth— each separately— into the nose (via *nastaḥ*) for those who are emaciated, as well as in cases of hemorrhagic diseases (*raktapitta*).

In Vata, it is unctuous and hot for oleation; in Pitta, sweet and cold for pacification;

That measure which can be moved with ease is considered appropriate for a mouthful (kavala);

Thus, [the instruments] are filled with oil, milk, honey, meat-broth, urine, and sour liquids.

Gargles with decoctions or warm water are beneficial according to the specific humor (doṣa). The signs of purity in gargling are the reduction of disease, satisfaction, clarity, lightness of the mouth, and serenity of the senses.
In the case of a deficient dose, there is no perception of taste due to dullness and the provocation of *kapha*.

From an excessive dose, there is burning of the mouth, along with dryness, thirst, loss of appetite, and exhaustion; these specifically constitute the symptoms of those requiring purification (*śodhanīya*).
Sesame seeds, blue lotus, clarified butter, sugar, and milk, along with honey,
used as a gargle for one whose mouth feels as if it were burnt, destroy the burning sensation. Thus,
this procedure for gargling has been proclaimed in brief.
Having analyzed the medicine with the intellect, one should prepare a fourfold *pratisāraṇa*: a paste (*kalka*), a medicinal extract (*rasakriyā*), honey (*kṣaudra*), and powder (*cūrṇa*).
That which is rubbed with the finger is called *pratisāraṇa*.

For those with diseases of the mouth, one should apply [medicines] as prescribed for each case using the tips of the fingers. In that regard, one should discern between the proper application and the improper application of the gargle (kavala) as previously described; furthermore, one should feed the patient food that is non-obstructive and highly effective in subduing the humors (doṣas).
A gargle pacifies those very same diseases that it eliminates.

There is no death that does not have its precursor in ill omens (ariṣṭa).
Indeed, death following such an omen is certain; however, it may be averted by stainless Brahmins who are devoted to elixirs, austerities, and the recitation of mantras.

therefore, a skilled physician should diligently examine the signs of impending death (ariṣṭa).
[Those who are] impotent, women, many [in number], those who do not share a common purpose, and those who are envious—[these are not to be treated].

their clothes are damp, tattered, worn over the right shoulder, soiled, and disheveled.

Those who speak harsh and cruel words, those who utter inauspicious names, those who cut grass or wood, those who touch the nose, the breast, the hem of a garment,
a finger, the hair, the nails, or the fringes of a cloth— [these are ill-omened].
Those who carry skulls, stones, ashes, bones, husks, and charcoal; who scratch the earth slightly, break clods of earth, and release them;

Holding ripe fruit that is pithless, or another similar object,
or [scratching] one nail with another, or likewise [touching] the feet with the hand;
or carrying shoes or leather in their hands— such persons are deformed and afflicted by disease.

Or, having pulled the hand of the physician, one should place it upon one's head and chest;

Or he whose three fingers do not fit into his own mouth, or whose teeth become parched;

Health is the supreme root of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation; diseases are the destroyers of that [health], as well as of prosperity and life itself. 1.

Therefore, a wise person who possesses self-control should always practice diet, conduct, and medicine so that health may be maintained. One whose humors (doṣas) are balanced, whose digestive fire (agni) is balanced, and whose bodily constituents (dhātus), wastes (malas), and functions (kriyās) are balanced, [attains health].
One whose self, senses, and mind are serene is called "established in one's own nature" (*svastha*).

The equilibrium of the humors (*doṣas*) is health; their imbalance is called disease.

The increase of all [doshas] occurs through similar factors, while their pacification occurs through the opposite factors. Obstruction of the channels, loss of strength, heaviness, confusion of the wind (vāyu), laziness, indigestion, vomiting, retention of waste products, loss of appetite, and exhaustion [arise from the increase of the doshas].
The signs of the *mala*s (waste products) when accompanied by *āma* are as described; the opposite indicates they are free from *āma*.

Due to the diminished strength of the digestive heat (*ūṣman*), the bodily tissues (*dhātu*) are impaired and remain undigested; the vitiated *rasa* located in the stomach (*āmāśaya*) is termed *āma*.
When the *doṣas* and *dūṣyas* are vitiated by being combined with that *āma*,
they are designated as *sāma*, as are the diseases arising therefrom.
Vāyu associated with *āma* is characterized by constipation, loss of digestive fire, stiffness, and rumbling in the intestines.
Afflicting the limbs sequentially with pain, swelling, and piercing sensations,
or even seizing them all at once when provoked, it increases greatly through the application of unctuous substances and the like during the rising of the sun or clouds, and at night. (8–9)
The pitta that is dry, clear, rough, unobstructed,
and associated with little pain finds relief especially through substances possessing opposite qualities— namely, those that are unctuous (snigdha).
Pitta that is foul-smelling, greenish, dark-brown, sour, stable, and heavy [is characterized by its own specific qualities].
One should designate that which causes acidity, burning in the throat and heart, as *sāma* (undigested).
That which is coppery-yellow, excessively hot, pungent in taste, unstable, odorless, and digested (*pakva*) should be known as providing appetite, digestion, and strength. (11–12)
The turbid, thickened *tantula* phlegm remains in the region of the throat;
it is undigested (*sāma*), foul-smelling, and causes loss of appetite and suppression of belching.
It is frothy, clumped together, pale, insubstantial, and odorless. (13)
That very [substance] is to be known as ripe when it possesses the quality of being cuttable and effects the cleansing of the mouth.
Of these [sixteen types], three each are respectively characterized by being sharp, bitter, pungent, sour, sweet, astringent, and astringent. 14–15.

When the *āma* (undigested matter) is being digested, and when the *vāta* and other doshas have been digested, digestive (*pācana*) and pacifying (*śamana*) treatments are applied respectively, as is the alleviation of the fever itself.
[The qualities of vāta are: dry, cold, light, subtle, mobile, clear, and rough.
The wind (vāta) is pacified by substances possessing qualities opposite to its own.
Pitta is quickly pacified by substances that are unctuous, hot, sharp, liquid, sour, laxative, and pungent— possessing qualities opposite to its own.
The qualities of phlegm— heaviness, coldness, softness, unctuousness, sweetness, stability, and sliminess— are pacified by qualities that are their opposites.
(19) Hunger arises when the rasa, the doṣas, and the waste products have been digested.

Whether it be the proper time for food or not, that time is praised. Even if one eats at midnight, being truly hungry and having abandoned medical treatment, such a person with an appetite is not overcome by diseases.

Since all diseases arise from contact with unwholesome food, that which is unwholesome must be abandoned; it is right to follow a wholesome diet. (22) *Kalamas*, *śālis*, red rice, *nīvāra*, *ṣaṣṭika*, and *aṅgukas*—(23)
Śyāmāka, kodrava, uddāla, satīna, barley, mung beans, lentils, āḍhakī, wheat, the hariṇa, eṇa, and kuraṅga deer;
the partridge, krakara, quail, vartīra, and vartikā—these are the best. || 24 ||
Suniṣaṇṇaka, vāstūka, cillī, maṇḍūkaparṇikā,
taṇḍulīyaka, jīvantī, pomegranate, āmalaka, honey, rock salt, and cow’s clarified butter— this is the excellent group of wholesome foods. || 25-26 ||

Physical exercise, sleeping at night, sheltered and warm water, food that promotes longevity when digested, not suppressing natural urges, celibacy, non-violence, and the avoidance of rash acts [are conducive to long life]. (27)
Flour is eight times more effective than food; milk is eight times more effective than flour;
meat is eight times more effective than milk; ghee is eight times more effective than meat;
and oil is eight times more effective than ghee for massage, but not for eating.
Milk is incompatible with the fruits of the *vallī* creeper, sour *kulattha* pulse, leafy vegetables, fish, liquor, meat, sesame seeds, sprouts of the *karīra*,

oil-cakes, *jambū* fruit, salts, and curd— whether used individually or all together. The *kapiñjala* partridge, *lāvaka* quail, *tittiri* partridge, monitor lizard, and peacock are [incompatible] with *rubu* oil and wood.
Likewise, *siddha* and *viruddha* pigeons, even when fried in oils and sprinkled with mustard, [are not harmful]; however,
honey undergoes a transformation when combined with hot divine water, pork, iguana meat, or radish.
Ghee that is warm, ghee mixed with buttermilk, ghee kept for ten days in a bronze vessel,
as well as ghee, parched grain, buttermilk, curd, liquor, and cocks [are forbidden].
The crane is not beneficial when consumed with intoxicants, nor with surā, kṛśara, or milk-rice; likewise, fish, upodakā, preparations of sugarcane,
sauvīra, sesame cakes, and kākamācī are incompatible with jaggery.
A self-controlled man should avoid what is excessively unctuous, excessively dry, and so forth.
A man lacking self-control, by consuming foods of conflicting tastes and potencies, encounters disease, weakness of the senses, and even death.

Whatever food, having provoked a disorder, is consumed but not eliminated from the body, or which remains in the rasa and other tissues according to its nature, tends toward the production of morbid transformations. Purgation overcomes diseases born of incompatible foods.

Emesis and pacification, or even wholesome food taken beforehand, may prove ineffective when administered to one who has a kindled digestive fire, to a young person, or to those who are unctuous, habituated to exercise, and strong; likewise, contrary food becomes futile [under these conditions]. Dried meat, old women, the morning sun, fresh curd,
sexual intercourse at dawn, and sleep [after a meal]— these six are immediately life-taking.
Fresh meat, new food, a young woman, and a diet of milk [are beneficial].
Ghee and warm water—these six are the immediate restorers of life-force.

In the winter, the digestive fire of strong individuals becomes even stronger when restrained by the touch of cold winds; it then becomes capable of digesting food that is heavy both in quantity and substance.

having smeared one's limbs with sandalwood and agallochum, one should eat a diet of barley and wheat.

A man of windy temperament (vātaprakṛti) is emaciated, dry, has sparse hair, is fickle-minded and unstable, speaks much, and in dreams travels through the sky. (51–52)
A man of a pitta constitution has prematurely grey hair, is fair-complexioned, perspires easily, is irascible, wise, and in dreams beholds radiant objects.
He is steady-minded, possesses well-knit limbs, has excellent offspring, and has glossy hair on his head. (63)
A man who observes reservoirs of water in his dreams is of a phlegmatic (ślaiṣmika) constitution;
those who possess a mixture of these characteristics are to be known as having a combination of two or three humors (doṣas).
An Anūpa person lives by much water and resides near mountains; such a person is prone to diseases of phlegm and wind (vāta).
A *jāṅgala* region has sparse water and vegetation and is dominated by diseases of wind (*vāta*) and bile (*pitta*).
A region endowed with the combined characteristics of these is known as *sādhāraṇa* (temperate).
In a *sādhāraṇa* region, cold, rain, heat, and wind are balanced, which is why it is so called.
Because it neutralizes all defects equally, it is therefore the most excellent common remedy.
One should employ a tooth-stick twelve finger-breadths long, made from substances that are milky, bitter, or astringent, which destroys diseases of the mouth. (67–68)
O Bhārata, one suffering from acute fever, dryness of the mouth, or dental disease should not use a tooth-stick on the first day of the lunar fortnight, the new moon, the sixth, or the ninth day;
for contact with a wooden stick destroys one's family up to the seventh generation.
There, the cleaning of the teeth should be done with the leaves of the *bakula* and other such trees;
for by scraping the tongue, diseases located therein are indeed eliminated.
Diseases caused by bile and blood, such as facial blemishes (*vyaṅga*) and the like, will not occur in the mouth.
By washing with a decoction of *bhilloṭaka*,
a decoction of *dhātrī*, or a decoction of *āmalaka*; or by rinsing both eyes with cold water,
[one achieves] the clearing of vision, the beauty of the face, and the pacification of the three *doṣas*.
The Sage has prescribed sauvīrāñjana as a collyrium for the eyes;
for the sake of beauty, one may apply black collyrium with applicator-sticks as desired,
so that the eyes become long-lashed, clear, lovely, and possess a stainless, radiant orb.
Through the application of collyrium, the eye becomes clear and its pupil pure. However,
collyrium is not recommended when one is exhausted, weeping, intoxicated by liquor, suffering from a recent fever, staying in a hot room, or experiencing a burning sensation.
Through the application of collyrium, the eye becomes free from discharge and pure;
thereafter, an emetic should be administered to remove diseases of the supraclavicular region.
Furthermore, purification of the mouth should be performed with betel nuts and the like, camphor, flowers, and fruits.
Adorned with oil-massages, body rubs, bathing, perfumes, garlands, and the like, he may move about at his pleasure with sandals, an umbrella, and a staff;
furthermore, he should constantly apply oil to his ears, nose, head, and feet, and inhale medicinal smoke. (79–80)
One should serve the sun from behind, the fire with one’s belly,
the master with one’s whole being, and the next world without deceit.
O King, eat the *harītakī* fruit and drink buttermilk with salt.
"Eat with vāstuka greens; by that, may your [ailments] perish.
One should not forcibly suppress the urges of sleep, wind, feces, urine, semen, yawning, tears, sneezing, belching, breath, thirst, vomiting, or hunger.
When these are maintained, diseases arising from staying on that path do not occur.
One should restrain the undesirable impulses of the mind, speech, and body; one should neither afflict the senses nor indulge them excessively.
One should follow the middle way in all phenomena at every step; the self-controlled person should enjoy sense objects at the proper time, having abandoned excessive attachment.
One should avoid excessive wakefulness and sleep, and cultivate the desire for the welfare of all beings.

One should always honor the gods, cows, Brahmins, teachers, elders, and preceptors. One who bows at crossroads, who is generous, who speaks kindly, who pacifies those who are angry, and who is free from malice toward the distressed— [such a person attains these fruits].
He is a source of consolation for the frightened and a kinsman to all embodied beings;
devoted to the Dharma, he is the destroyer of the causes of passion and hatred. Always practicing wholesome food and conduct, acting with circumspection, he is unattached to sense objects.
One who is a giver, impartial, devoted to truth, patient, and a servant of the wise becomes free from disease;

he who always honors his head and his feet, and does not covet the wife or the fortune of another; he whose mind is not fickle and who does not let the [right] time pass by—[he attains success]. 90–91.
One should not speak words of affection nor of malice; non-violence must be practiced constantly, and the stability of the mind must be maintained.

The physician, the patient afflicted by disease, the medicine, and the attendant—
these are the four pillars that serve as the means for accomplishing medical treatment.
One who has mastered the meaning of the scriptures, has observed clinical practice, and is personally skillful [is the physician].
One who is dexterous-handed, pure, brave, equipped with ready instruments and medicines, possessed of presence of mind, wise, industrious, confident,
and devoted to truth and righteousness— he is called a physician of the highest rank.

A patient who possesses longevity, strength, wealth, and self-control; who follows the physician’s instructions and is full of faith—such a person is said to be curable. [The medicine] produced in an auspicious place and extracted on an auspicious day, || 4 ||

Medicine that is used in small doses, possesses great potency, is endowed with excellent fragrance, color, and taste, which destroys the *doṣas*, does not cause exhaustion, and is free from adverse effects when administered at the proper time after due consideration— this is called the "quarter" (*pāda*).

One who is affectionate, free from disgust, strong, intent on protecting the patient, obedient to the physician’s word, and tireless is known as a *paricara* (attendant). Faults that have been accumulated in one's own country may, upon reaching another place, become provoked.
Likewise, aquatic creatures brought to dry land would not remain strong;
for one who abides in what is appropriate, there is no danger arising from the location,
provided that the qualities of that place— such as food, sleep, and activity— are favorable.

When the disorder is slight, the treatment should be great; when the disease is minor, the procedure should be light. These two constitute lack of skill; skill consists in the appropriate application of action.
Furthermore, if the desired result is not obtained from the current treatment, one should employ another course of action.
In the eastern [quarter] called Śāntavegā, no confusion of ritual actions is recognized.
Even when the desired quality is not attained, the action should be performed again after an interval of rest; otherwise, there is danger of confusion, as before.
Some sages maintain that the transformation of the *rasa* generally occurs after six days and nights, while others hold it to be seven;
through this very transformation of the *rasa*, the activity is considered to have its momentum stilled. (13–14)

One who is fierce, reckless, timid, ungrateful, or agitated; one who hates a good physician or the king, or is hated by them; one afflicted by grief, acting impulsively, or desiring death; and one who is deficient in his sensory faculties. (15)
One who is hostile, clever at deceiving physicians, devoid of faith, highly suspicious, and disobedient to physicians— such a person should not be treated by the best of physicians.
If a physician should treat these individuals, he may incur many faults.

Other than these, there are men who, having approached with all possible medical treatments, do not redeem their treated body; that evil-minded person enjoys all the merit he performs, while the physician receives it. (17-18)

One should never, out of greed, engage in the sale of medical treatments as merchandise; rather, one may seek wealth from wealthy lords for the sake of one's livelihood. Seven *guñjās* make one *māṣa*, and four *māṣas* make one *śāṇa*.
Two *śāṇas* make one *vaṭaka*, which is a *kola*; two of those make one *karṣa*, known as an *udumbara*.
An *akṣa*, a *pāṇitala*, a *suvarṇa*, and a *kavalagraha* are synonyms.
A *picu*, a *biḍālapadaka*, and a *śukti* consist of two *pāṇitalas*.
Two *pala*s are called a *muṣṭi*, a *prakuñca*, and a *bilva*.
One should know that two *pala*s are a *prasṛta*; two of those are a *kuḍava* and an *añjali*.
Eight *pala*s are a *mānikā*, and two of those are a *prastha*; four times that [is a *āḍhaka*].
An *āḍhaka* is contained in a bronze vessel (*kaṃsapātra*), and four of these are said to be a *droṇa*. Its synonyms are *ghaṭa*, *unmāna*, *nalvaṇa*, *armaṇa*, and *sūrpaka*.
A *tulā* consists of one hundred *palas*; twenty of those are said to be a *bhāra*.

This measurement applies to dry substances; however, for liquids and moist substances, it should be known that the measure is double from the *kuḍava* upwards, according to the scriptural rules for the *prastha* and other measures.
Those who know measurement understand that this doubling does not apply to measurements by weight (*tulā*).

The *goṇī*, *droṇa*, *āḍhaka*, *prastha*, *kuḍava*, *pala*, *picu*, *śāṇaka*, and *māṣaka* are each four times the size of the preceding one. (27) [No verses from the *Siddhayoga* appear on this page.]
